A 27-second long video has gone viral on social media over the past week. The clip shows a mob, predominantly comprising men, kicking and attacking a woman in the middle of a busy street, while police personnel in the vicinity do little to nothing to prevent the attack.
The X user, Vikas Pokhariyal (@vikasindiafirst), posted the clip on August 31, claiming that a female Hindu teacher had been attacked by Islamists in Bangladesh. At the time of this article being written, the post had been reshared over 3000 times. (Archive)

Another X user, Deepak Sharma (@SonOfBharat7), posted the same clip, with a seperate claim that in Bangladesh, a Dalit teacher had allegedly offered water to an upper-caste Muslim child, following which she was chased down in the streets and thrashed. (Archive)

— Yati Sharma (@yati_Official1) August 31, 2026
Fact Check
To verify the authenticity of the claims surrounding the viral clip, Alt News broke it down into keyframes. A reverse image search on one keyframe led us to a news report published by the Bangladeshi news portal BD News 24 on August 30.
According to the report, the incident took place at Bangladesh’s Rajbari clothes market, on August 29. The victim in the video is reportedly a female shop owner, who managed her own clothing shop in the market for 12 years. She had allegedly found that one of her female employees had started working in a different shop on August 22. In response, she dismissed the worker from her role at the shop and asked her collect payment in the following month.
Further, another news report published by The Dhaka Tribune on August 30, identifies the female shop owner as one Zakia Sultana, and the ex-employee as Shahana Parveen Bristy. In another report by the outlet Ajker Patrika, Sultana accused Bristy of turning up at her shop with 15-20 men on August 23 and intimidating and verbally abusing her.
This prompted Sultana to launch a protest at the clothes market on August 29 afternoon, along with her female employees. Enraged by this, several shop-owners from the Rajbari clothes market then attacked her, in the presence of police officers who had turned up at the spot to offer her protection, the report states. However, in the video it is visible the that men continue to kick and attack Sultana despite police presence.
We also found a video report from BBC News Bangla, uploaded on August 31, which shows recorded evidence of the attack.
News reports from Bangla TV, Views Bangladesh, and Jago News 24, dated September 1, also reveal that three people have been arrested in relation to the violent attacks on Sultana, as recorded in the viral video.
In conclusion, the viral clip which shows a woman being violently attack is indeed from Bangladesh, but the woman seen in the clip is Muslim, thereby refuting any allegation of a communal angle at play.
Further, the reason for the attack arises from a business dispute as reported by several credible news outlets, thus the aforementioned claims, including that Sultana is a Dalit teacher who was beaten up for offering water to a Muslim child or that she complained about the other shop under the Consumer Rights Protection Law, are false and misleading.

The iPhone Duo is Apple’s first folding smartphone. The company announced the device at its annual September event at Apple Park in Cupertino, California, alongside new iPhone 18 Pro models.
Apple is a late entrant to the foldable phone market, which has been around since Samsung debuted the first Galaxy Fold in 2019. Since then, phone makers like Honor, Google, Motorola, and Oppo have all made folding phones. In recent years, devices have rapidly gotten slimmer, lighter, and more durable.
The iPhone Duo has a book-like shape and is similar in size to Samsung’s recent Galaxy Z Fold8, reminiscent of Google’s original Pixel Fold. This “passport-style” fold—which stands shorter and unfolds wider than many of the first wave of foldable designs—is better suited for media consumption since it eliminates the severe letterboxing that places thick black bars around the TV show or movie you’re watching.
Apple is expected to help grow a category that has been declining for five straight quarters by 13 percent year over year—potentially capturing up to 30 percent of the foldable market share by the end of 2026, according to IDC’s Nabila Popal, a senior research director. But the folding phone market is still niche, “around 2 percent by the end of this year of the global smartphone market.”
Popal says a recent IDC survey asked consumers whether they were interested in buying a foldable smartphone when it was time to upgrade, and 60 percent said they are not likely to buy one. However, when asked if Apple released a folding smartphone, almost 33 percent said they “absolutely” would.
“Apple has such a strong market pull,” Popal tells WIRED. “The average consumer didn’t know about [memory price increases] until Apple made an announcement that they’re going to increase prices. “Coming into foldables, it's going to create overall excitement for the category. And it's good for the consumer too. It's always good to have more competition and more choice.”
One area of concern is the device’s durability and repairability, as folding phones are notoriously more prone to damage and are tough to fix. Elizabeth Chamberlain, director of Sustainability at iFixit, tells WIRED her team has never taken apart a foldable they’d call truly repairable.
“Manufacturers have come a long way since the Galaxy Fold first dropped,” she says. “But the gains in durability haven’t come with gains in repairability.”

Can a love-thy-neighbor, stop-the-division campaign win over masses of rural voters? Rob Sand, the Democratic candidate for governor in Iowa, has his hopes pinned on it.
Why Iowa is a state to watch in the midterms
Meet Rob Sand, the Democrat who’s favored to become Iowa’s next governor.
Key to Sand’s campaign is a promise to end the red-blue warfare in politics. He’s made embracing independents and disgruntled Republicans a core part of his campaign, in addition to ending government corruption, holding big agriculture and big chemical companies responsible for the state’s high cancer rates, and addressing cost-of-living concerns. And his pragmatic approach seems to be working.
Polls have reliably shown Sand, who currently serves as Iowa state auditor, ahead of his Republican opponent, Zach Lahn — despite the GOP’s significant voter registration advantage. Democrats haven’t won the governor’s mansion in Iowa since 2006.
On top of the gubernatorial race, Iowa also has competitive Senate and House races, which could be key to Democrats’ hopes of gaining control of Congress during this November’s midterm election.
To break down what’s happening in Iowa, Today, Explained co-host Noel King spoke with Laura Belin, publisher and reporter for the Iowa political website Bleeding Heartland.
Noel and Belin discussed Sand’s unique candidacy, whether it could have lessons for other Democrats looking to succeed in Midwestern states that have grown redder, and how President Donald Trump’s policies could be laying the groundwork for a rural backlash in this year’s midterm elections.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
This midterm season, all eyes seem to be on Iowa. Why is Iowa so crucial?
What has happened in Iowa, where we used to be a swing state and we’ve moved into the red column, is not unique to Iowa. Every part of the country that looks like Iowa has seen the same trend of voters moving away from Democrats. It’s happened especially in these working-class communities where the electorate is predominantly white people without a college degree.
Iowa as a whole voted for Barack Obama twice and then voted for Donald Trump three times. So if Democrats can figure out how to start winning again, or at least losing by less, in that kind of area, it could have implications not only for the future of Iowa, but for other states like Ohio, Michigan, Wisconsin, and Pennsylvania.
What are the main issues that people there are voting on and campaigns are campaigning on?
The high cost of everything is definitely the top issue. Democrats have really been hammering on the tariffs and the war in Iran, driving up the cost of everything.
Also, healthcare costs have skyrocketed.
We’ve seen healthcare access be an issue, because we’ve already seen some clinics close, and the companies that control those hospitals or clinics have talked about how it’s partly a reaction to the big Medicaid cuts that were passed in the [GOP’s 2025] budget reconciliation bill.
According to many polls that I’ve seen, Trump is underwater in Iowa. His policies are not popular; the tariffs are not popular in Iowa. They’re widely understood to be hurting the Iowa economy. Anyone can see that the cost of everything has gone up.
So Trump is less popular this year. What are the Democrats doing to campaign on that? Are they running on Trump?
Most of the Democrats are not running directly against Trump. Rob Sand, the candidate for governor, hardly talks about Donald Trump at all. He really focuses on statewide issues.
Josh Turek, the candidate for Senate, is running [on] the idea that [Republican Senate nominee] Rep. Ashley Hinson has just been a rubber stamp for policies that have hurt Iowa, whether that be the war in Iran [or] tariffs. It’s more running against the Republicans who have been a puppet [for Trump] rather than running against Donald Trump himself.
Let’s talk about that governor’s race and Rob Sand. This guy has gotten a fair bit of national interest. What do you know about him?
I’ve followed his career for a long time, since he was running for state auditor the first time in 2018. He’s been very visible. He’s gone out every year, done a hundred town halls a year, done them in every county.
He is reaching out to independents because Iowa Republicans have a pretty large voter registration advantage. So he’s talked a lot about trying to empower independents more in our political spaces. He’s talked about getting Iowa back to divided government. He’s talked about how, with the large Republican majorities we have in the legislature, he would be a check on what they’ve done with 10 years of one-party rule.
He used to be a model.
A long time ago, when he was in college. It’s funny, Republicans post these old modeling photos of Rob Sand from the ’90s and even [Sen.] Chuck Grassley’s campaign account posted some of those over the weekend.
And I always wonder — I mean, Republicans seem to think that they’re going to get traction out of that, but I don’t really see that as something that Iowans care about at all. I think a more common criticism that I hear is that Rob Sand has a very strong social media presence and has for years. In addition to making videos talking about political issues and what needs to be done in state government, he does a lot of things like reviewing pizza and donuts.
They try to portray him as someone who’s not serious about his job. But I think that that’s just more [that] he has this goofy online persona. And I don’t really think it’s a detriment to his campaign.
Tell me more about the town halls. We’ve seen a certain type of Democrat emerge in the last few years and become very visible this campaign cycle: angry at the Democratic Party, angry at the direction of the country.
Rob Sand — from what I’ve seen of him, it does not seem like anger is what he wants to tap into. Tell me what you’ve seen when he’s out in public.
No, he does not strike an angry note. And he’s not really part of this whole debate between progressives and moderates or centrists in the party. He’s really tried to chart, I would say, a completely different course of saying that he wants to get back to common-sense government, focusing on the issues that people can agree on.
He’s talked about how if he’s governor and the legislature sends him culture war bills, we’re gonna have veto ceremonies instead of bill signing ceremonies. He doesn’t want to do any of this culture war thing. And one thing that he does at the beginning of every town hall is he asks people to raise their hands if they’re a registered Republican or a registered independent, and then he asks everybody to applaud for those people.
He has everybody in the room sing the first verse of “America the Beautiful” together.
And he talks about how our politics has become so divisive. The way he frames it is that two private clubs, as he frames the major parties, he says, ‘They’re trying to make us hate people we used to love. And I’m sick of it. I’m sick of the division.’
Sometimes he asks for a show of hands: How many of you have had a family relationship or a longtime friendship disrupted over the last 10 years because of politics? There are always a lot of hands that go up. And he says, ‘I’m just sick of this.’ So he is running on trying to bring people together, but it’s not really in a kumbaya way, like we’re all going to agree on everything.
When he’s criticizing his Republican opponent, Zach Lahn — and one of his main talking points is that Zach Lahn doesn’t live full-time in Iowa, that he’s a part-time Iowan and spends a lot of time in Kansas — but before he even gets to that, he leads into it by saying, “There’s one thing that I want you to remember about my opponent that’s the most important thing. He’s a human being.”
The Democrats need a type of candidate who can win in red states. Rob Sand is interesting because it seems people have identified him as possibly that template. What do you think?
I don’t know how easy it would be to replicate Rob Sand. He grew up in a small town; he grew up hunting and fishing. He talks about his faith. I don’t know that everybody would be able to pull that off so naturally.
But sometimes when people ask me, well, what happened to Iowa? It’s not anything specific to Iowa. It’s every part of the country that looks like Iowa has seen the same trend of Democrats losing ground. It’s the same reason Trump was able to win the states that used to be called the Blue Wall: Michigan, Wisconsin, and Pennsylvania. It’s the same reason Ohio has moved into the red state category.
I think people are watching Iowa, especially Rob Sand and Josh Turek, the candidate for Senate, because if Democrats can find a way to turn things around in those types of areas — working-class communities that are predominantly white — there could be lessons that apply to other states.

Jammu, Sep 09: A 32-year-old man died after he allegedly fell unconscious at a border police post in R S Pura sector near here early Wednesday, official sources said.
The deceased, Uttam Chand, a resident of Rakh village, was called to the Chakroi police post following a complaint filed by a woman neighbour over a property dispute, the sources said quoting the preliminary information.
They said the individual fell unconscious and was subsequently taken to the Sub-district Hospital R S Pura at around 4 am.
Chand was referred to Government Medical College Jammu but died on way to the hospital, the sources said, adding the body was shifted to a mortuary for postmortem.
Following the death, the family members and relatives of the deceased staged a protest, demanding clarity over the circumstances leading to the man's death and seeking appropriate action.
Senior police officers have rushed to the spot, while additional personnel have been deployed both at Chakroi and at the hospital mortuary to maintain law and order, the sources said.

A Chinese rescue team has reached the all-but-obliterated Gyirong border crossing complex for the first time and found “nothing but ruins” as Nepal and China continue their arduous rescue operations in the flood-hit Himalayas.
Surveillance camera footage from the worst-hit Gyirong border crossing complex showed huge torrents of water and debris on Wednesday engulfing buildings and people trying to flee. Only on Friday were rescuers able to reach that area.
State media reported that the Chinese team of 21 rescuers and a search-and-rescue dog crossed mountains and valleys and used ropes to navigate forests and cliffs after roads to the complex, hemmed in by steep Himalayan slopes, were destroyed.
“There was no road … it was all virgin forest and sheer cliffs,” rescue worker Zou Mingqi said. At the complex, “as far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins.”
The glacier collapse which unleashed a deadly torrent through Himalayan mountain river systems has killed at least 579 people in Nepal and seven in China’s Tibet. The number of missing in Nepal has nearly doubled to 1,924, officials said on Friday. At least 558 were missing in Tibet’s Gyirong County, Chinese state media said. Among the missing are at least 540 foreigners, many of them Hindu pilgrims from India.
More than 90,000 people have been affected by the disaster, the Red Cross estimated.
Amid the deepening crisis, Nepal has now said it needs foreign help in specialised and technical areas in which it does not have expertise, but not in search and rescue.
Earlier on Friday, Nepal’s foreign ministry had said that Kathmandu could manage the rescue efforts on its own for now and declined foreign involvement.
The areas Nepal is seeking help include opening transport and communication services in places where bridges have been destroyed, identification of dead bodies, DNA testing and storing bodies for longer durations, foreign minister Shisir Khanal said late on Friday.
Asked about that stance of his government, Khanal said there was no need for assistance in general search and rescue which was being done by Nepali rescuers. “We think there is no need for repetition in this,” he said.
India and China, between whom Nepal is wedged, have been requested to supply bailey bridges to reopen transport and communication in an area where about two dozen bridges had been destroyed.
Nepal is continuing to monitor two barrier lakes upstream of the flood zone, with an official warning that flood risks will persist until both lakes fully drain.
Satellite imagery showed the second lake growing larger with no visible outlet, raising concerns that water pressure could still be building.
China’s state-run Xinhua news agency said that the first barrier lake was reducing in size, citing analysis by the water resources ministry. A Chinese government geo-hazards expert warned, however, that the lake may be unstable and that over 100 glacial lakes scattered throughout the area could pose a threat.
In Beijing, a politburo meeting chaired by President Xi Jinping called for stronger monitoring of glacier lakes and landslide risks, and for closer international disaster cooperation, Xinhua reported.
China’s Premier Li Qiang, the country’s No. 2 official, arrived in the area of Gyirong on Thursday afternoon, Xinhua said. The visit suggested Beijing was treating the disaster as a matter of the highest national priority.
In China, strict controls on the flow of information from one of its most sensitive regions are hampering the public’s understanding of events.
The BBC and NY Times have reported videos of the catastrophic floods, widely shared globally, have not appeared on Chinese social media sites.
Chinese state media has carried several broadcasts about the floods and dispatched their own journalists to the area, but reports have focused on the rescue efforts rather than the scale of the devastation. In one broadcast from a relief centre in Tibet, the journalist did not speak to any of the people sitting behind him.
Tibet, brought under Chinese control in the 1950s, is the most sensitive and tightly controlled region in the country.
The Gyirong border port plays a key role in China’s Belt and Road network linking the country to South Asia, with logistics zones and parking lots built there in the past decade.

The claim emerged in response to criticism of U.S. President Donald Trump's executive orders changing the names of the geographic features known as the Gulf of Mexico, Denali and Lake Ontario. It's based on a false equivalence, however. In 2021, Biden's Interior Secretary Deb Haaland signed an order renaming the roughly 650 geographic features because their existing names contained a racial slur demeaning Native American women.
U.S. President Donald Trump has, as of this writing, issued two executive orders during his second term mandating that the Interior Department, in coordination with the country's Board on Geographic Names, rename these familiar landmarks:
- the Gulf of Mexico, to the Gulf of America
- Denali, to Mount McKinley, restoring the government's official name for the tallest mountain in North America from 1917 to 2015
- Lake Ontario, to Lake America
Trump's orders were criticized around the world, including by many Americans.
But according to posts on social media, former U.S. President Joe Biden's administration engaged in its own renaming spree, changing the official names of approximately 650 different geographic features. This, the posts said, is evidence that the public holds a double standard against Trump.
Snopes readers searched the site looking to see whether the government had actually renamed 650 different locations during Joe Biden's presidency. We found the claim was true, though comparing the two actions was a reach.
The Biden-era efforts, led by then-Interior Secretary Deb Haaland, had one goal: renaming locations throughout the U.S. whose names included a racial slur demeaning Native American women. Trump's executive orders, by contrast, targeted some of the country's most prominent landmarks, including two bodies of water only partially controlled by the U.S.
"Derogatory names have previously been identified by the Secretary of the Interior or the Board on Geographic Names and have been comprehensively replaced," read the Interior Department's November 2021 news release announcing the order. As precedent, it cited a 1962 order eliminating the use of the N-word and a 1974 order eliminating the use of a slur for Japanese people.
In September 2022, the Interior Department published a news release announcing that the Board on Geographic Names had approved new names for each of the affected locations, alongside a list of all the changes and a map of the renamed locations. There were indeed approximately 650 new names.
It's worth noting, though, that beyond the renamed Olympic Valley, California, which hosted the 1960 Winter Olympic Games, none of the locations that underwent a name change under Biden could be considered nationally prominent in the same way as Lake Ontario, the Gulf of Mexico or Denali.
For further reading, we've also covered a rumor suggesting that Trump signed an executive order renaming the state of New Mexico to "New America."

AI is all set to take centre stage at the Global Fintech Fest (GFF) in Mumbai this week, with product launches, live demos and industry conversations on how this emerging tech is reshaping financial services. But beyond the buzz, the bigger story is how deeply AI-powered systems are entering the Indian fintech stack, from customer onboarding and credit decisions to fraud detection, servicing and payments. To understand where the industry stands and where it is headed, Inc42 spoke with senior executives from Zeta, HyperVerge, TruCommerce and RevRag AI, who are participating in the seventh edition of GFF. The experts believe Indian fintechs have moved beyond the proof-of-concept phase: voice agents are handling customer interactions, AI is accelerating KYC and verification, fraud systems are becoming more sophisticated, and in-app assistants are beginning to execute tasks rather than simply answer questions. The next challenge is figuring out where these applications can deliver measurable value, and how far fintechs can take them without compromising trust, compliance and accountability. So, where is AI delivering the most immediate value for fintechs today? Let's unravel in this edition of The AI Shift… Fintech’s First AI Moves Are Now Operational Fintech companies are using AI to make existing processes faster and more efficient rather than letting it make financial decisions on its own. Kedar Parikh, the CPO of HyperVerge, an AI-powered identity verification and KYC platform, divides the sector’s adoption of AI into three broad phases. Digital onboarding: This includes KYC, face matching and liveness checks. Customers across banking, financial services, insurance and telecom can now be onboarded in minutes instead of days Fraud prevention: Faster onboarding also creates more opportunities for fake documents, synthetic identities and deepfakes to enter the financial system. This is pushing regulated entities to adopt AI for document forgery detection, biometric checks and deepfake prevention, although adoption remains a work in progress. AI-assisted decision-making: This phase is still at an early stage. AI can collect data, spot patterns and present useful inferences, but lending, insurance and other high-value decisions continue to require human judgement. This pattern is visible in customer service as well. According to Sivaram Kowta, the president of digital banking at Zeta India, a digital banking and card-issuing technology company, customer support, fraud management and underwriting are among the most active areas for AI adoption. Zeta’s AI agent resolves around 80% of customer-service calls for US-based subprime credit-card fintech Sparrow, Kowta said. Ashutosh Prakash Singh, the cofounder and CEO of RevRag AI, an AI voice and chat agent startup focused on banking and financial services, said fintechs have moved from testing voice AI and in-app agents to scaling them and measuring their return on investment. Singh said the next wave of deployment will go beyond contact centres, with fintechs, banks and non-banks such as PhonePe and Bajaj Financial Services exploring AI across in-app journeys, back-end workflows, branches, kiosks and other customer touchpoints. He expects these use cases to move from early deployments to broader scale across the BFSI sector by the end of this year and into next year. AI As A Paper Pusher The closer AI gets to a financial decision, the more difficult deployment becomes. In lending, for example, an AI system can collect customers’ financial history, classify information and apply existing rules but cannot become the final authority to approve a loan. Kowta said the RBI has made it clear that regulated entities cannot shift responsibility for credit decisions to an AI model. A bank must understand the decision and remain accountable for it. As a result, banks and NBFCs are using AI in underwriting while retaining a human at the final decision point. “AI is not doing something fundamentally new. It is a paper pusher, just an extremely capable or efficient paper pusher,” Kowta said. If every other step in the lending process is automated but the final credit review remains manual, the overall process may become faster, but it does not become fully autonomous. The compliance challenge is more complex. These constraints are not stopping adoption, but shaping the ecosystem. Currently, the main regulatory and compliance issues faced by Indian fintechs include: The DPDP compliance: AI systems must account for consent, data use and the right to erase personal information under the Digital Personal Data Protection framework. Data localisation: Banks and fintechs need clarity on whether financial information sent to overseas AI models remains in India. User-level authentication: Agents need permissions linked to the authenticated customer, not broad access to an institution’s systems. Payment authorisation: Agent-initiated payments in India require additional safeguards, including OTP-based authentication in several use cases. Human accountability: Regulated entities remain responsible for lending, underwriting and other critical decisions, even when AI performs the supporting work. According to Viren Inaniyan, cofounder and CEO of TruCommerce, a commerce infrastructure platform for AI agents, basic building blocks for agent-led commerce are already falling into place. These include AI platforms, commerce protocols, payment networks, gateways, merchant catalogues and checkout systems. India’s payment ecosystem also has safeguards in place to make transactions more secure. For instance, card details need to be encrypted and cannot be exposed to or stored by an AI agent. However, the bigger challenge is that very few people are using AI agents to make payments today. Agentic commerce accounts for an estimated 100 Mn transactions, or just 0.04% of UPI’s total transaction volume. This dataset is still too small for payment companies and merchants to understand how consumers behave when an AI agent is making purchases on their behalf. The Shift From Features To Foundations The conversations ahead of GFF point to a fintech ecosystem that is increasingly focused on scale, but not yet equally prepared for the cost of scaling. Kowta said less than 10% of bank budgets currently go towards AI, with spending often taking place project by project. However, he expects the approach to change over the next one year. Smaller banks may slow down their AI plans, while larger banks could commit significantly bigger budgets, potentially investing ₹500 Cr to ₹1,000 Cr at one time to build shared infrastructure, governance and AI capabilities rather than funding disconnected projects. For now, much of the industry is still in an AI computerisation phase. It is using the tech to perform existing tasks faster. The bigger change will come when banks redesign workflows around AI instead of adding an AI assistant to an old process. The message from the ecosystem is not that AI adoption is slow. It is moving quickly in customer service, onboarding and fraud prevention. But the next jump, allowing AI to influence decisions involving money, will depend on whether Indian fintechs can build the compliance and accountability layers that make those systems trustworthy. Top Stories From India & Around The World KRAFTON To Invest $250 Mn In Indian Startups: The South Korean gaming giant is committing an additional $250 Mn (₹3,300 Cr) to Indian startups across AI, robotics and deeptech over the next three to four years, taking its total planned India investment to over $1 Bn. Chairman Byung Gyu Chang announced the plan after a meeting with PM Narendra Modi. Navana.ai Raises ₹40 Cr: The Mumbai-based voice AI startup has raised ₹40 Cr ($4.2 Mn) in a Series A round led by existing investor and upGrad cofounder Ronnie Screwvala, with Antler India, Neysa.ai founder Sharad Sanghi and WestBridge's Sandeep Singhal also participating. The company will deploy the capital to deepen its Indic-language speech models and AI contact centre. OpenAI Launches GPT-6 Astra: OpenAI has released GPT-6 Astra, with a 1 Mn-token context and a headline API price of $10-$50 per Mn tokens. Because it is the first OpenAI model rated critical on cybersecurity, the cyber-sensitive capabilities are gated behind a trusted-access programme, and it is rolling out to enterprise customers first before wider ChatGPT availability. Nvidia’s PAIR Turns Idle PCs Into Personal AI Data Centres: Announced at IFA 2026, Nvidia's free, open-source Personal AI Router (PAIR) pools idle laptops, desktops and Macs on a home network to run local AI models for agentic workloads, using existing Ollama or LM Studio installs. The tool routes agent subtask requests to whichever machine is free, letting developers run multi-agent setups locally without cloud fees or privacy trade-offs. The Weekly Buzz: An Alien Mind OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki published a striking essay titled “An Alien Mind,” warning that increasingly capable systems may develop goals misaligned with human values. He argues that no lab has solved alignment and monitoring well enough to continue scaling at maximum speed for much longer. Pachocki calls for voluntary slowdowns, stronger third-party auditing, and international coordination, describing advanced AI as something that has ‘grown more than designed’. The essay has intensified debate inside and outside the lab. Supporters see it as a rare moment of candour from a frontier institution; critics note the tension between the warning and OpenAI’s continued rapid deployment. The contrast with Jensen Huang’s simultaneous “AGI has arrived” statement has only sharpened the discussion. Coming amid a week of cascading model releases, the essay reframes the central question of 2026: not only how capable the systems are becoming, but whether the institutions building them are prepared for the consequences of their own progress. Startup In The Spotlight: Antimattr Founded in 2025 by Sridipto Ghosh and Sirsho Chakraborty, Bengaluru-based Antimattr is building a voice-first computing system designed around memory and productivity. AI assistants are growing increasingly capable, but using them in the real world still means pulling out a phone or sitting in front of a screen. The problem surfaced while the founders were building voice agents: the AI worked, but noisy environments such as cafés, airports and open offices made voice interactions unreliable. Instead of putting a screen between the user and the machine, Antimattr pitches voice as the primary interface to AI. Its Project Mnemosyne combines a smart ring with a pair of voice-isolation earphones: the ring captures thoughts, records and summarises conversations and controls AI agents, while the earphones use six microphones and proprietary voice-isolation technology to enable clearer conversations and dictation even in noise. The startup counts Y Combinator, Nikhil Kamath's WTFund and gener8tor among its backers, with YC investing $500K. Antimattr operates in India's AI wearable market, projected to reach $19.1 Bn by 2033. As the company bets on a screenless AI future, its longer-term roadmap extends beyond Mnemosyne to a privacy-focused AI computer and, eventually, an AI-native vehicle. Prompt Of The Week What prompts and hacks are CTOs, CEOs and cofounders using these days to streamline their work? Here’s the prompt Ram Khizamboor, COO at Indium, uses to run a pre-mortem on a client engagement, essentially forcing the AI to imagine failure: "Assume it's twelve months from now and this client engagement has failed. The contract wasn't renewed, the relationship soured, and leadership is asking hard questions about what went wrong. Write the post-mortem for it, answering these three questions in detail: What were the three most likely causes of the failure Which early signals did we ignore in the first 90 days of the engagement What would the client's CIO say, in hindsight, we should have seen coming Be specific and unsparing. Don't hedge or soften the findings just because this is a hypothetical exercise. Treat it the way a real post-mortem would be treated internally, with names, timelines, and decisions called out where relevant." Seoul – North Korea has built a new uranium enrichment facility at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex that could house up to 28 centrifuge cascades, and started operating an expanded annex at its Kangson enrichment site, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said.
The Vienna-based nuclear watchdog said in a report the findings pointed to a steady expansion of North Korea’s nuclear infrastructure at multiple locations.
In the report, dated Aug. 28, the IAEA said it relied on satellite imagery and open-source material, including photographs published by North Korean state media, to track Pyongyang’s nuclear activities. The agency has had no inspectors in North Korea since 2009.
It identified a new two-story building at Yongbyon as the site’s second uranium enrichment facility by comparing state media photographs of a June visit by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un with satellite images taken during the building’s construction.
Photographs from the visit indicate gas centrifuge cascades are installed on both the upper and lower floors of the main building, the report said, adding the building could accommodate up to 28 of the cascades shown in the photographs.
The report also said there were indications that operations began in January at a uranium enrichment facility in Kangson, near the capital Pyongyang, within an annex that had been constructed in 2024.
The IAEA said the developments in North Korea’s nuclear program violated U.N. Security Council resolutions.
“The ongoing operation of enrichment facilities at Kangson and Yongbyon and the reported further expansion of the DPRK’s production of weapons-grade nuclear material is a cause for serious concern,” IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said in a statement to the board of governors on Monday, referring to the North’s official name, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.
The report accompanied Grossi’s statement.
Pyongyang has repeatedly rejected the agency’s authority. North Korea’s mission to the United Nations in Vienna said last September that North Korea’s status as a nuclear weapons state had become irreversible and the IAEA had “no legal right … to interfere in the internal affairs of a nuclear weapons state which exists outside the NPT“, referring to the Non-Proliferation Treaty.

Police widen criminal probe into Reform UK over foreign funding claims
The party has denied wrongdoing and says it will ‘fully cooperate’ with the police investigation
British police said on Wednesday a criminal investigation into the populist Reform UK party would be widened to include allegations made in a documentary that officials planned to break electoral law on foreign funding.
Reform, led by veteran Brexit campaigner Nigel Farage, denied any wrongdoing and a spokesman for the party said it would “fully cooperate” with the investigation.
Farage, under investigation by a parliamentary watchdog about earlier donations, was forced to sack two of his closest aides last week, after the undercover investigation was aired.
It showed two senior officials in Reform – then head of policy James Orr and Farage’s former right-hand man, Dan Jukes – speaking about funding with a supposed US businessman and his British-based son, including conversations about a payment for three opinion polls commissioned by the party.
On Friday, Reform launched an internal investigation and denied the allegations, saying the party had been the victim of a hoax. Farage described some of the comments as little more than “loose pub talk”.
London’s Metropolitan Police said in a statement its detectives had assessed a number of “reports relating to donations and polling involving a political party” and had decided “there are potential offences requiring investigation”.

Experts say there is no universal clock time that works for everyone. What matters more is when dinner falls in relation to the body’s biological clock and bedtime. An earlier dinner may be beneficial, but there is no fixed 7 p.m. or 8 p.m. cut-off. The gap between dinner and sleep, the quality and composition of the meal, physical activity and individual health needs all play a role.
Insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance generally decrease as the day progresses, so the body may not handle a heavy meal as well later in the day. However, dinner timing is only one part of the picture. The amount and quality of food, physical activity, sleep and health conditions such as diabetes and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) also affect how the body responds to a meal.
The gap before sleep
“There is no evidence-based ideal dinner time,” said Aafrin Shabbir, medical director, senior consultant and diabetologist, Tambaram Medical Centre and CODE Clinic. The body’s metabolic efficiency is generally better during the daytime, she said, making a smaller and lighter dinner preferable.
She also cautioned against assuming that eating at 10 p.m. is unhealthy for everyone. Someone who sleeps at 1 a.m. has a different biological rhythm from someone who sleeps at 10 p.m. “One rule doesn’t fit all,” she said.
Saravana Bharathy S. P., internal medicine, Dr Mehta’s Hospitals, recommends leaving about two to three hours between dinner and bedtime. This is particularly relevant for people with reflux or digestive discomfort, as lying down soon after a meal can worsen symptoms.
Swathi Padmanaban, consultant, paediatric & adolescent endocrinologist and diabetologist, Rainbow Children’s Hospital, Chennai, said eating dinner earlier is generally better for metabolic health when practical. She advised against making dinner the largest meal of the day, particularly when it is eaten close to bedtime.
Meal timing is linked to the body’s circadian rhythm. The liver, pancreas and gastrointestinal tract have their own biological clocks that work with the brain’s central body clock. As the biological day progresses, insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance tend to fall, meaning the same meal may cause a greater rise in blood glucose when eaten later.
Late eating
Studies have found that eating dinner at 10 p.m., compared with 6 p.m., led to higher overnight blood glucose and changes in fat metabolism, despite the meals having the same calories and nutrients.
“Late eating may have greater metabolic implications for people living with diabetes, prediabetes and obesity. A carbohydrate-rich meal late at night can cause a larger rise in blood glucose, particularly when physical activity is low,” Dr. Swathi said.
Late, heavy meals can also cause bloating, indigestion and acid reflux and may affect sleep. However, an occasional late dinner is unlikely to carry the same significance as a regular pattern of late-night eating.
Eating after a particular hour does not, by itself, cause obesity or heart disease. Overall calorie intake, food quality, physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep also play major roles. “People who regularly eat late may also snack more, sleep less or have irregular work schedules. This makes it difficult to separate the effect of dinner timing from other lifestyle factors,” Dr. Bharathy said.
Healthier dinner timing
For children and adolescents, the focus should be on regular meals, adequate nutrition, appropriate portions, physical activity and good sleep rather than restrictive eating windows.
If a late dinner is unavoidable, a moderate and balanced meal is preferable. Vegetables, protein and fibre can be included, while sugary drinks, sweets and fried or fatty foods should be limited. It is also better to avoid coming home extremely hungry and eating a large, carbohydrate-heavy meal just before bed. If possible, part of the meal can be eaten earlier and the later meal kept smaller. A short walk after dinner may also help with post-meal blood glucose control.
For people living with diabetes, meal timing should be planned around their medication, insulin requirements, blood glucose levels and HbA1c rather than a fixed cut-off.
The practical approach is to eat earlier when possible, leave about two to three hours between dinner and bedtime, keep late meals light and balanced, and maintain regular eating and sleep schedules.

India, China military commanders hold rare border talks in Arunachal sector
The first session of the flag meeting between the senior military commanders was held on the Indian side on Sunday and the second session on the Chinese side.
Top Indian and Chinese military commanders met for the first time in the Arunachal Pradesh sector during two sessions held on both sides of the border this week as a follow-up to recent meetings of the Special Representatives and a border mechanism, the external affairs ministry said on Tuesday.
The first session of the flag meeting between the senior military commanders was held on the Indian side on Sunday and the second session on the Chinese side on Monday, external affairs ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal told a regular media briefing. He did not go into the details of the discussions between the military officials.
The military talks focused on issues along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in the eastern sector, including maintaining peace and tranquillity along the frontier, people familiar with the matter said. Lt Gen Girish Kalia, who heads the Dimapur-based 3 Corps, led the Indian side. The Indian army has not commented on the talks.
The 24th round of talks between the Special Representatives – India’s National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi – in New Delhi on August 19 had resulted in 10 points of consensus, including creating mechanisms for talks between military commanders in the eastern and middle sectors of the LAC.
“Pursuant to the understandings reached between the Special Representatives of India and China in August 2025 and August 2026 and subsequent discussions at the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination (WMCC), meetings of which were held in Beijing and New Delhi in May and August 2026 respectively, the first senior highest military commander-level flag meeting was held at Wacha on the Indian side in Arunachal Pradesh on September 6 and in Damai on the Chinese side on September 7,” Jaiswal said at the media briefing.
He noted that a similar mechanism for talks between military commanders already exists in the western sector, which includes Ladakh.
A military face-off between India and China in the western sector, which began in April-May 2020 and dragged on for more than four years, had taken bilateral ties to their lowest point in six decades. Since the two sides reached an understanding in October 2024 on ending the standoff, they have taken a number of steps to normalise the relationship and put in place confidence-building measures along the LAC.
Also Read: India, China must first settle smaller disputes
It is not usual for Indian and Chinese military commanders to hold talks on both sides of the border, and discussions in the western sector are usually held alternatively on either side of the LAC. People familiar with the matter said the talks in the Arunachal Pradesh sector were held over two days as there were several issues to be discussed.
This week’s meeting was the first since tensions erupted between the Indian Army and the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) at Taksing, a remote area of Arunachal Pradesh’s Upper Subansiri district, in July and August. The Indian side at the time that the two sides had agreed to use diplomatic and military mechanisms to “avoid misunderstanding and miscalculation” along the border.
New Delhi has also maintained that the state of the border will determine the overall course of the relationship.

The U.S. Postal Service said on its website that it handles prepaid and stamped mail-in ballots as first-class mail unless voters pay for priority or priority express services.
In September 2026, a claim (archived) circulated online that adding postage to a prepaid mail-in ballot would "force" the U.S. Postal Service to treat it as first-class mail, a service that allows postcards and small envelopes to be delivered in one to five days.
The claim circulated as states began sending out mail-in ballots for the 2026 midterm elections, despite the Trump administration's ongoing court battles to enforce an executive order that would restrict voting by mail.
One Threads user who shared the claim wrote:
By adding a 1st Class Postage Stamp to your postage prepaid ballot, it will then force USPS to handle it as 1st Class Mail, instead of Bulk Mail! SHARE EVERYWHERE!
The claim also circulated on Facebook (archived) and X (archived). Snopes readers contacted us to verify whether it was true.
The claim was false. According to the USPS, the service always handles mail-in ballots as first-class mail unless voters pay for priority or priority express services. In other words, adding additional postage will not expedite the delivery of a standard mail-in ballot.
The USPS included the following message on its webpage about "Election Mail" (emphasis ours):
Mailpieces containing a completed ballot are handled as First-Class Mail® service, regardless of whether they are prepaid by election officials or mailed with a stamp affixed by the voter. The only situation where a completed ballot is not handled as First-Class Mail is when the voter opts to pay for a premium service like Priority Mail® service or Priority Mail Express® service.
Who pays postage on a mail-in ballot varies by state. According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, a bipartisan, nonprofit organization that represents lawmakers in the 50 U.S. states, 19 states and Washington, D.C. require local election officials to pay postage while voters in other states must pay.
In a June 2026 FAQ, the USPS said its policy directs employees to deliver ballots with insufficient postage and attempt to recoup the payment from the local election board.
Mail-in ballot return deadlines vary by state. The USPS advises that voters mail their ballots "before Election Day, and at least one week prior to the deadline by which your completed ballot must be received by your election office."
Voters can check deadlines for returning mail-in ballots with their local election office. Some states also allow voters to deliver completed ballots to drop boxes that are emptied by election officials, which eliminates the need to use the postal service to vote.
At the time of this writing, the Trump administration sought to implement new federal regulations on mail-in ballots that could require states to submit lists of eligible voters to an online portal and follow a uniform envelope style. In an August 24, 2026, opinion, the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to proceed with implementing the proposed regulations but did not rule on whether they were legal.
The Associated Press reported that "legal wrangling" continued over Trump's executive order in lower courts. Therefore, it was unclear at the time of this writing if, or how, the proposed changes to mail voting would affect the 2026 midterm elections.
Despite having previously voted by mail himself, U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly criticized mail voting, including after he lost the 2020 presidential election.
Snopes' archives contributed to this report.

US military interests control or have access to more than 100 defence facilities on Australian soil, in what some analysts describe as a “saturation” – even a “colonisation” – of the Australian continent.
New data compiled by the Nautilus Institute and published by Guardian Australia maps the extent of US militarisation. The US military controls 17 facilities on mainland Australia and has access to 75 more Australian-run military installations. US defence corporations have access to an additional 18.
In total, the US military and US defence corporations have control of or access to 110 facilities on Australian territory, well over half of all the military installations in Australia.
“We have been thinking about American influence on Australian defence policy as a matter of penetration,” the database’s author, Prof Richard Tanter, tells the Guardian, “and we’re aware of the closeness of the alliance, the integration of the armed forces …
“But what this database shows is it’s not a matter of penetration, it’s a matter of saturation. Over half of the defence facilities that we have looked at have some level of American access: that means American personnel, it means American corporations, some of the biggest armaments companies in the world.”
| US access to Australian defence facilities |  | 
|---|---|
| Access level | Facilities | 
|---|---|
| United States-controlled facilities with Australian access | 17 | 
| Australian facilities with US military and US corporate access | 24 | 
| Australian facilities with US military access | 51 | 
| Australian facilities with US corporate access | 18 | 
| Australian facilities with no significant US access | 41 | 
| Australian facilities with US access unresolved | 17 | 
‘Aligning ourselves completely’
The US military controls or has access to 92 defence facilities on Australian soil for:
- 
  Gathering intelligence, accessing satellite data for targeting information and communications intercepts.
- 
  Training, including for 2,500 marines on dry-season rotation in the Northern Territory.
- 
  Pre-positioning warfighting assets such as Osprey aircraft.
- 
  Logistics hubs holding weapons, munitions and fuel, stored in case of a war in the Pacific.
Some bases, including Pine Gap, play critical roles in identifying targets for US strikes overseas and are well known by Australians, even if their operations are highly classified.
Others are massive – the Bradshaw field training area in the Northern Territory is the size of Cyprus – but barely known.
Announced in June, Bandiana base in Wodonga will be the site of tens of millions of dollars worth of pre-positioned US weapons, munitions, fuel and vehicles, stationed for rapid deployment in the event of conflict in the Pacific.
Beyond the military’s presence, at least 42 Australian military facilities are accessed by US defence contractors – some of the biggest weapons manufacturers in the world – which use Australian sites for manufacturing, testing and training of weapons systems deployed by militaries across the globe.
Lockheed Martin assembles guided missiles in Port Wakefield, South Australia. Northrop Grumman signed a multimillion-dollar contract this year to build rocket motors for guided weapons at Mulwala in New South Wales. Collaboration with US manufacturers will “promote allied interoperability and provide a second source of supply for critical munitions”, the Australian defence force says.
Of the military bases that operate under US control, with Australian access, Pine Gap is the best known. But its precise role in US warfighting is hidden from public view.
Like several large military bases across Australia, Pine Gap hosts multiple defence facilities, each with distinct functions: a ground-control station for signals intelligence satellites; a relay ground station for early-warning missile launch systems; and a site for intercepting foreign satellite communications.
The Nautilus Institute database counts defence facilities, rather than bases, so Pine Gap consists of three distinct, co-located facilities.
Critical to US operations around the world, including conflicts in the Middle East, it is formally a “joint defence facility” but it is always commanded by an American.
The Force Posture agreement – “with full respect for Australian sovereignty” – gives US forces and contractors “unimpeded access to and use of” agreed Australian facilities, including for deploying forces and materiel, bunkering vessels and refuelling aircraft.
The US military presence will continue to expand. From next year up to 1,200 uniformed military personnel will operate from the HMAS Stirling submarine base just off Fremantle. The government insists that technically this will not be a US base – rather a “rotation” – but there is little contestation of its actual implication.
Arguing in favour of the Aukus nuclear submarine agreement, the former defence minister Christopher Pyne told a public inquiry the multibillion-dollar deal was “a lot more than the submarine procurement”.
“From a strategic point of view, it’s not something that’s ever really discussed in the public, but it’s one of the most important aspects of it: Aukus is also a new United States submarine base in the Indian Ocean.
“For the Americans, being able to have a submarine base in the Indian Ocean is a massive strategic advantage.”
Tanter, a senior research associate at the independent public policy thinktank the Nautilus Institute for Security and Sustainability and an honorary professorial fellow at the University of Melbourne, says the US military’s expanding presence is not in service of its junior alliance partner but rather US interests alone.
“Over more than a decade, the United States has been preparing the capacity for high-tempo warfighting operations with China, springboarding from Australia,” he says. “And that means we are aligning ourselves completely with American strategic planning.
“From a Chinese perspective, Australia is not so much hosting US bases on its territory, it’s a US base in its own right … Australia is a serious piece of real estate in the US warfighting machine.”
There exists no comprehensive public record of foreign military access to bases on Australian territory. This database has been compiled from open-source information, responses provided to parliament, and government and commercial reporting.
Tanter argues that the acceptance of the US military presence has become so ingrained within the government and defence that unwinding Australia’s enmeshment within the world’s most powerful military is increasingly difficult.
“This is a massive institutional failure in Australia, a kind of learned incapacity at a political, parliamentary and bureaucratic level,” he says. “We’ve learned how not to ask those questions.”
‘Waltzing its way into a war’
At a press conference in June, the defence minister, Richard Marles, demonstrated the breadth of the US military presence in Australia.
Speaking in Rockingham, Western Australia – across a narrow bay from HMAS Stirling – Marles was announcing the establishment of a $30m US logistics base in Wodonga, Victoria.
“We are seeing a growing US footprint in Australia that is important in terms of building our own military capability but also it’s very important for Australia’s national security,” Marles said.
Marles said the “hugely significant American presence” in the region was a balance to China’s “very significant military buildup”.
Earlier, the minister told the Defending Australia Summit that US military presence in Australia was indispensable to deter conflict in the region.
“We will see an increasing American military footprint on our continent over the course of the next few years.”
Just last week Marles met the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, at the Pentagon, where both leaders “agreed to accelerate force posture initiatives at Australian bases, bolster cooperation in combined logistics, and build greater interoperability through joint exercises”.
The Guardian put a series of questions to Marles’s office about the implications of an “increasing American military footprint” across Australia. A spokesperson for the defence department said Australia held a fundamental principle of “having no foreign bases on Australian sovereign territory”, and that the Australian government retains sole control over deployment of the ADF and over the use of Australian territory.
But, the spokesperson said, Australia’s 2026 national defence strategy reiterated “Australia’s alliance with the United States remains fundamental to our national security and the Australian Defence Force’s (ADF) capacity to generate, sustain and project credible military capability”.
The alliance with the US allowed Australia to “pursue our national security interests far beyond what we could achieve alone”, they said.
Australians’ fragile faith
Government ministers are fond of the reassuring line that the Australia-US relationship is broader, deeper and more enduring than the tenures of prime ministers and presidents.
But Australians’ faith in the US is fragile and fracturing.
A Lowy Institute poll showed Australians’ “trust in the United States to act responsibly in the world” has fallen to 31%, the lowest level in its polling history.
Just 21% of Australians have confidence in “Donald Trump to do the right thing in world affairs”, the lowest level of confidence in a US president yet.
Just more than half of Australians (55%) said they were either “strongly” or “somewhat” in favour of allowing the US to base military forces in Australia, down eight points from 2022 (63%).
Australians feel the alliance with the US remains important: 73% rate it as either “very important” or “fairly important” to the nation’s security.
Other findings are more damning: a poll for the Australia Institute found more than half (52%) of Australian voters believed Trump was a greater threat to global security than Vladimir Putin (17%) or Xi Jinping (16%).
More than twice as many Australians (59%) now believe Australia’s interests are best served by a more independent foreign policy rather than a closer alliance with the US (23%). Just 13% of Australians believe the US is a “very reliable” security ally.
This represents, Dr Emma Shortis says, a “seismic shift” in Australia’s perception of its once-great and powerful friend.
“After following the US into nearly every war since World War II, Australians have had enough. They see tangible risks in being so close to President Trump’s bleak and violent version of America.”
Shortis, the director of international and security affairs at the Australia Institute, argues that the Trump administration has repeatedly demonstrated that the US is willing to jettison security commitments made to allies. US bases across the Middle East have been repeatedly attacked by Iran.
“Trump has demonstrated that it’s all contingent, it’s all insecure,” she says. “And what he has also highlighted – particularly with his illegal war in Iran – is the way those US bases themselves become targets.
“It doesn’t matter what you do, it doesn’t matter how much you give him, you can literally give him a plane, and it’s not enough, he will not defend those bases.”
Shortis says Australia’s increasing integration with the US military has resulted in “an accelerating erosion of Australia’s independent, sovereign, decision-making power”.
“Instead of having the option of saying ‘no’ to involvement in United States wars, involvement becomes the default position.”
She cites the March attack by a US nuclear-powered submarine on an Iranian frigate, sinking it and killing more than 100 people. Three Australian naval personnel were onboard, part of the submarine’s crew: the US did not forewarn Australia of the attack.
“Australia might maintain the pretence of sovereign decision-making power, but that’s not the reality.”
Dr Albert Palazzo, an adjunct professor at the University of New South Wales Canberra and formerly the director of war studies for the Australian army, tells the Guardian the US military’s accelerating buildup carries danger for Australian security.
“The Australian government seems to be waltzing its way into a war between the United States and China, by allowing this country to become an outpost or bastion of the US military, and as a platform from which they will launch military force against China,” he says.
Dr Vince Scappatura, the author of The US Lobby and Australian Defence Policy, described US base access across Australia as a kind of “second wave of colonisation”.
“Today we are shaping up to be the ‘tip of the spear’ for US power projection into the region – that’s what the sprawling US base access represents,” he says.
“Each one of those dots on the map represents a point of leverage Washington has over Canberra when it comes to matters of defence and foreign policy. Not that they really need to use it.”
Scappatura says the phrase “empire by invitation” was originally coined to describe US hegemony over western Europe “but it is applicable equally here. I sometimes describe it as ‘voluntary subordination’.”
- 
  The Australian bases & US involvement database is coordinated by Prof Richard Tanter at the Nautilus Institute

New Delhi, Sep 09: Lower levels of serotransferrin, the blood protein that transports iron through the body, are an early indicator of coronary artery disease (CAD) and can help identify heart conditions earlier than routine clinical diagnoses, say scientists.
Iron deficiency is prevalent in patients of CAD, a common cardiovascular condition characterised by a narrowing of the coronary arteries due to atherosclerosis, primarily resulting from an accumulation of plaque or fatty deposits. An analysis of blood serum proteins by Delhi’s Centre for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR)-Institute of Genomics and Integrative Biology (IGIB) has revealed the critical role of serotransferrin in identifying cardiac disease.
"Serotransferrin may have value as an early diagnostic marker, meaning it could potentially help identify CAD earlier than routine clinical diagnosis," Sagarika Biswas, corresponding author on the study, told PTI.
A deeper understanding of how CAD develops is crucial for developing effective diagnostics and therapeutics, the IGIB researchers said. Serotransferrin, found in previous studies to contribute to CAD, presents a potential avenue for investigation, they said.
Exploring molecular and cellular processes related to serotransferrin may help shed light on how CAD develops and identify new targets for treatment, the team said.
"Of the total 197 differentially expressed proteins, serotransferrin (TF), an iron transporter, showed downregulation in samples from CAD patients compared to healthy," the authors wrote in the study published in the journal Acta Cardiologica. Downregulation means lower than normal levels
The study, involving 50 CAD patients and 40 healthy people, also showed an increased level of the cardiac marker 'troponin I' among those affected by the heart disorder, demonstrating an inverse relationship with serotransferrin levels.
Troponin I is a specialised protein present in heart muscle cells, a damage or injury to which causes the protein to leak and enter the bloodstream.
"TF (serotransferrin) protein was significantly associated with CAD progression and inversely correlated with cTnI (troponin I), suggesting it (serotransferrin) could be a potential therapeutic target pending further molecular and clinical investigation," the authors said.
Longitudinal studies would be required to estimate the duration in years before which serotransferrin could help identify CAD, explained Biswas, former distinguished chief scientist and professor at CSIR-IGIB's department of integrative and functional biology.
The study linked reduced levels of serotransferrin with the inflammatory environment created due to damage in the inner lining of arteries, which leads to an immune response against the accumulated fatty deposits.
According to Biswas, worsening ischaemia -- local anaemia due to a reduced blood flow caused by narrowed or blocked vessels -- and tissue injury can increase troponin I, whereas inflammatory and metabolic stress may suppress serotransferrin expression or availability in CAD.
Further, levels of serotransferrin can reflect iron status in an individual.
"In standard iron studies, transferrin saturation below 20 per cent is commonly taken as evidence of iron deficiency, meaning less than 20 per cent of transferrin's binding sites are occupied by iron," Biswas said.
Transferrin refers to the family of iron-binding proteins, while serotransferrin is a subtype found in blood serum and plasma. A region on a protein's surface to which another molecule attaches itself is a binding site.
"Serotransferrin is an iron-transport protein, so a lower level suggests (a) reduced iron-binding and transport capacity. The protein may contribute to the functional iron deficiency component of CAD by limiting plasma iron transport, but the study did not quantify its contribution as a percentage," Biswas said in response to a question.

In Summary
- The Live 780NC are the latest headphones in JBL’s premium mid-segment Live series of wireless ANC headphones.
- Featuring a different design from their predecessors as well as some flashy colors, the JBL Live 780NC boast good mainstream sound as well as a number of smart features.
- Priced officially at Rs 15,999 (but available at lower prices), the JBL Live 780NC are one of the best pairs of headphones one can get for about Rs 15,000 in the Indian market.
They let you not only pump up the bass or turn up the treble of the audio playing on them but can also add bass and treble to your voice and the person you are talking to during phone calls. They come with good ANC that adjusts itself to your surroundings and come with very good battery life. Get them in orange, and you can be assured of being the center of attention in every room. All this at a price of USD 199/Rs 15,999. But can these features (and many others) and that price tag help the JBL Live 780NC become the perfect headphones for those who want a lot of sound and smarts, without parting with a truly premium price?
Table of Contents
JBL Live 780NC Looks: Comfortable and delightfully colorful
The JBL Live 780NC can look smart or spectacular depending on the shade you choose. We got the very elegant Black ones, which are at home everywhere, from cafes to campuses to corporate offices, but the Purple, Green, or Orange will definitely turn heads, thanks to their unusually bright shades. They follow the classic over-ear headphone design, with a band connecting two earcups, but look different from their predecessors, the Live 770NC.
The headband of the Live 770NC was of the same thickness throughout, whereas the band of the Live 780NC becomes thinner as it nears the earcups, giving it a sleeker and more contemporary look. There is plenty of cushioning on the earpads as well as the headband. There’s plenty of JBL branding too, which appears on the earcups and headband, but as the lettering is in the same color as the headphones, it does not get overwhelming. The earcups have left and right printed inside them, which is always better than having tiny letters on the frame.
The right earcup has the sliding on/off and connectivity button, as well as a button for switching between ANC and Ambient Aware mode, as well as a Type-C port. The volume controls are on the left earcup. The outer part of the right earcup is also a touch panel. There is no 3.5 mm audio jack, but a Type-C to 3.5 mm cable in the box lets one use the headphones with a device with a 3.5 mm audio jack.
The headphones are mostly made of plastic but have metal hinges, and best of all, fold all the way inwards, making them very easy to bunch up and carry. There is a rather basic cloth bag in the box, which is not as good as a case but should suffice for most of us. At 260 grams, the JBL Live 780NC are not exactly super light (the Sony WH-CH 720N are the bosses there at 192 grams), but not uncomfortably heavy either. We have worn them for 3-4 hours without ever feeling too burdened. All the padding in the ear cushions and headband makes them very comfortable to wear, and the clamping force is just right – tight enough to let us move our head without making the headphones wobble, and loose enough to never make us feel squeezed in the head.
The JBL 780NC have a very solid and substantial feel to them. But they come with no dust or water resistance, so we would advise due caution while using them in the gym or using them for running sessions.
JBL Live 780NC Specs and Features: An impressive feature list
The JBL Live 780NC come with a very good spec and feature lineup. Sound is handled by 40 mm drivers, which deliver the famous mainstream JBL Signature Sound. Also on board are support for high-quality LDAC, adaptive ANC, six microphones (most headphones in this price have four), spatial audio, and a number of smart features, such as ear detection (audio pauses when you remove the headphones) and an AI-trained algorithm for clearer calls.
On the connectivity front, they come with Bluetooth 6.0, multi-point connectivity, and support for Auracast (so one can listen to public broadcasts and announcements wirelessly). They also boast a battery life of 80 hours (without ANC) and support fast charging. There is no charging cable in the box, though one does get a Type-C to 3.5 mm cable and a basic cloth carry bag. On the software side, the headphones work with the JBL Headphones companion app, which gives one access to a number of features as well as detailed equalizers and regular software updates. For their price, the JBL Live 780NC are pretty well stacked in the spec and feature department.
JBL Live 780NC Controls and Interface: Buttons for some, touch for others
Connecting the JBL 780NC is as simple as putting them in pairing mode (just slide the on/off button towards the Bluetooth icon) and selecting them on the other device’s Bluetooth device list. To experience all their features, however, one should also connect them via the JBL Headphones app, which is available for both iOS and Android. While connecting the headphones is simple, the app takes some time to recognize them every time it connects to them, which can be a little irritating.
The JBL Live 780NC controls are a blend of physical buttons and touch, although the touch works only on the right earcup. A single tap on the earcup pauses audio and also resumes playing it; a double tap takes one to the next track; a triple tap takes one to the previous track, while tapping and holding accesses the voice assistant. A double tap can also enable one to take or end a call, while tapping and holding rejects an incoming call. One can customize the touch controls to an extent, and add options to access equalizer settings and spatial audio, although there is no way to access ANC or volumes through touch – those are accessed through buttons on the earcups.
The combination of touch and buttons controls works well enough, once one gets the hang of them – we kept forgetting that touch worked only on the right earcup, and ended up tapping the left one initially, out of habit.
JBL Live 780NC Performance: Super audio, decent ANC and great smart touches
Most users will love the warm and detailed sound that the JBL Live 780NC deliver. While there is an emphasis on bass, it does not overwhelm the vocals. Those who want a sharper sound can tweak the equalizer in the app (move it to ‘Jazz,’ we suggest) to enhance treble, but most users will love the sound of these headphones right out of the box. Enabling spatial audio makes the sound a little more airy, although the absence of head tracking gives one much more of a “sitting in a room with the music” feels. There are three kinds of spatial audio – Movie, Music and Game – and although there is not much difference between Movie and Game, Music is rather different and seems to add slightly more detail to the sound. One can also use the Person-fi feature to let the app personalize a sound signature for it, although we were not too convinced by it.
The app allows one to tweak the sound significantly. LE Audio makes a huge difference to audio quality whenever supported (although turning it on and off requires restarting the app), adding greater detail and depth to sound. One can also choose from six equalizer settings – a relatively plain Studio, a thump-friendly Bass, a rumbling Club, a boosted bass Extreme Bass, a mids-stressing Vocal, and a treble-oriented Jazz. There is also the option to completely come up with one’s own EQ setting under the My EQ option. Most mainstream users will prefer the Bass setting, while purists will like either Studio or Jazz. One can also adjust the balance of sound between the right and left earcups, although we found no reason to do so.
The JBL Live 780NC are perfect for mainstream audio, whether one wants to listen to pop, trance or rock, or watch a film, play games or just lend an ear to podcasts. At their price, they are perhaps the best-sounding wireless ANC headphones out there.
JBL Live 780NC ANC and calls: Super sound over calls, decent sounds of silence
The JBL Live 780NC come with adaptive ANC. You can either specify the level of ANC you want using a slider, or enable Adaptive ANC and let the headphones decide the level. We suggest simply keeping it at maximum. Noise canceling on the headphones is good for their price. Of course, one does not get the kind of ANC that comes on Sony and Bose flagships; the Live 780NC do enough to dull a lot of the traffic sound, kill the hum of the Metro, and can even make a noisy cafe a little quieter.
Call quality is where the Live 780NC shine. Not only do they handle calls very well, with very good levels of clarity, but the app even lets you adjust the tone of the person you are speaking to and your own voice as well. You can actually add more bass or treble to both sides of the conversation on the JBL Live 780NC. The headphones are also able to keep out a fair bit of the ambient noise – we have used them on auto rickshaw rides, with the person we are speaking to not even realizing that we are in the midst of noisy traffic. That AI algorithm for clear calls definitely helps.
JBL Live 780NC Battery life: Charge them once a week only!
JBL claims that the headphones come with 80 hours of battery life without ANC and 50 hours with ANC. We mostly used them with ANC – it does not affect audio quality, apart from making it a little more bass-y – and got a comfortable 40-45 hours of battery life (we admit to hearing them at slightly higher volumes). In practical terms, charging them once easily got us through close to a week of hectic use, where we used them for everything from making calls to listening to music to watching videos, shorts, and reels to playing games. That makes them great daily drivers.
The headphones charge off their USB Type-C port and take about two hours to charge from empty to full. They also come with a fast-charging function that gave us about four hours of audio listening after being charged for five minutes. One can tweak the power settings for the headphones to switch off automatically after 30 minutes, an hour, or two hours, to further conserve power. There is no charging cable in the box, but any Type-C charging cable should work just fine with it.
JBL Live 780NC Review Verdict: In a zone of their own in the Rs 15,000 segment
The headphones are priced at Rs 15,999, but are often available at lower prices (they are available on Amazon India at Rs 14,999 even as this is being written). Their closest competitors are the Sony ULT Wear, which are now available at close to Rs 15,000 but have a very bass-centric sound. The ULT Wear have better ANC than the Live 780NC, but the Live 780NC beat them easily in terms of call handling. offer almost double the battery life and also have a more elegant and foldable design.
Audio purists might like the sound of the Sennheiser Accentum Plus, which are available for Rs 13,999, but they lose out to the Live 780NC in ANC, call quality, and battery life. Those looking for head-turning headphones might also be tempted by the Nothing Headphone (1), which come with a transparent-ish appearance and very good audio quality (if one is ready to spend time adjusting the equalizer), but are more expensive at Rs 17,999, and again, do not match the Live 780NC in ANC and battery life.
We would say that they are comfortably the best all-round mainstream ANC headphones you can get for around Rs 15,000. They deliver decent ANC, very good audio, and excel in calls and battery life. Get them in orange, purple, or green, and they are a sight for sore eyes too!
