ఫాక్ట్ (నిజం): ఇండోనేషియాలోని అనాక్ క్రాకటోవా దీవిలో అగ్నిపర్వత విస్ఫోటనం జరిగినప్పటికీ, వైరల్ అవుతున్న ఈ దృశ్యాలు ఏఐ ద్వారా రూపొందించబడినవి. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్టులో చేసిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టిస్తుంది.
వైరల్ వీడియో గురించి తెలుసుకోవడానికి వీడియో యొక్క కీ ఫ్రేములను ఉపయోగిస్తూ ఇంటర్నెట్లో వెతికితే, ఈ వీడియోకు సంబంధించి ఎటువంటి ఆధారాలు మాకు లభించలేదు. కానీ ఈ వీడియోను జాగ్రత్తగా పరిశీలిస్తే కొన్ని అసమానతలు కనిపించాయి. ముఖ్యంగా పరుగెత్తుతున్న వ్యక్తుల కదలికలు, వారి రూపాల్లో కొన్ని అసమానతలు కనిపించాయి.
తదుపరి, మేము ఆ వీడియోను Hive Moderation టూల్లో పరీక్షించగా, ఆ వైరల్ క్లిప్ AI-జనరేటెడ్ అని నిర్ధారించబడింది.
అనాక్ క్రాకటోవా అగ్నిపర్వతం విస్ఫోటనం చెందిన అసలు వీడియోను ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ చూడవచ్చు.
చివరిగా, అనాక్ క్రాకటోవా విస్ఫోటనం అంటూ వైరల్ అవుతున్న వీడియో ఏఐ వాడి తయారు చేసింది.

Deadly Russian strikes on Kyiv fail to cancel Ukrainian soldier’s wedding
The couple dug their wedding clothes out of the rubble and got ready for their big day
Liudmyla Ryzhak spent the eve of her wedding ironing her delicately embroidered dress, laying out a full white tulle skirt beside her husband’s traditionally patterned shirt, before hanging them on the bedroom door.
Following repeated delays caused by the war with Russia, she was only hours away from marrying her partner, a Ukrainian soldier, in a ceremony in the capital scheduled for Tuesday morning.
However, as the pair slept, a Russian strike struck a warehouse across the street from their building. The resulting blast wave ripped through the apartment, threatening to stop the wedding.
The couple were soon digging their wedding clothes out of the rubble, with Ryzhak pulling her skirt from beneath the debris and shaking off pieces of broken glass.
Strike followed visit by US envoys
The strike came soon after US envoys visited Ukraine on Sunday, a trip that brought a lull in Russian attacks. The assaults then resumed with drones and missiles.
Explosions were heard in Kyiv for almost five hours overnight. Strikes continued during the day Tuesday.
Like many others in Kyiv, the couple decided the attacks would not derail their lives and forged ahead with the ceremony. It had taken a long time for her fiancé, Leonid Ryzhak, to make it back from the front lines in eastern Ukraine.
“If God gave me a continuation of life, then why should I put it off?” the bride said. “For someone, it ended. And who can guarantee this won’t happen again tomorrow? That tomorrow won’t come for us? At least for now, I have the right to be happy. Both him and me.”
Liudmyla and Leonid awoke from the blast, which blew out the apartment's windows and scattered its furniture. A burned curtain hung in shreds.
Their ears deafened by the explosion, the couple's only immediate thought was the risk of a second strike. They fled to a shelter with Liudmyla’s 6-year-old daughter and two guinea pigs but without the cat, which had hidden in fright and could not be found.
They were lucky: By the time the second strike hit, they were already safe. The apartment was rendered uninhabitable until repairs are made.
A friendship deepened into love
The two met three years ago through mutual friends, coming together as adults who weren’t looking for anything serious. Both had children from previous marriages.
But the friendship deepened. She supported him through his deployments to the front, and slowly the relationship grew into love. Leonid Ryzhak, who serves as part of a team that deploys bomber drones in the Pokrovsk area, arrived in Kyiv for a long-awaited vacation a week and a half earlier, just as near-constant air raid alerts and daytime attacks began disrupting life in the capital.
For six days straight, the couple went to the registry office but could not submit their documents because of constant air raid sirens.
When they finally succeeded, they were assigned 8 September. Nobody could have predicted that their apartment would be badly damaged on the same day.
It wasn’t the first time for Liudmyla. She had already lived through one attack, on 20 August, when a strike cut the gas lines and shattered windows in her home. She was badly frightened and for a time was afraid to go back.
Eventually, ordinary life pulled her back in: The wedding was coming, and the children had to go to school.
More attacks hit as they wait at registry office
Eventually, the two put on their wedding clothes and headed to the registry office.
Leonid tried to keep their spirits up. What mattered most to him, he said, was for his bride to be smiling.
“It’s fine. We’ll get through it,” he said.
When they stepped outside their apartment, the courtyard looked almost apocalyptic, with a column of black smoke rising behind a brightly colored children’s playground. Neighbors clearing debris stopped to congratulate the couple.
“We should all be celebrated, that we survived,” Liudmyla replied.
The couple arrived at the registry office on time, at 10:40am.
Leonid wore an embroidered vyshyvanka, a traditional Ukrainian shirt, with a pattern that matched the one on Liudmyla’s dress.
In place of black dress pants, he wore army trousers — he couldn’t dig his own out of the rubble — and black sneakers with fluorescent yellow soles and laces, for the same reason. Liudmyla’s white tulle overlay had tiny, barely visible holes that were torn as she pulled it out from the rubble and broken glass.
Shortly after they arrived, a siren sounded: Another attack had begun, and the registry office closed for safety. The couple waited in the courtyard, unsure how long it would last.
Explosions echoed nearby as strikes hit surrounding districts and fires broke out. Almost three hours passed before the alert finally ended, and the couple hurried back inside.
Against all odds, they became husband and wife
Just before entering the hall for the ceremony, they paused, trading nervous jokes.
“I didn’t even get to finish the repairs at home,” Leonid joked about their now-wrecked apartment.
“I’ve never had such a spectacular day,” his bride replied.
The ceremony went ahead as the officiant told them, “Love is when two people become a team.”
Moments later, the two were officially married.
“We’re gaining a new life, because we survived,” Liudmyla said. “You could probably call (it) a new life because it could have ended today, and none of this would happen.”
In a different scenario, “I wouldn’t be wearing this dress. Someone would be picking out something else for me instead, something darker.”

Volunteer firefighter dies in Turkey while tackling wildfire, 8 people injured
A volunteer firefighter has died while battling a large wildfire in Turkey’s Antalya province
ANKARA, Turkey -- A volunteer firefighter died on Wednesday in Turkey after helping local emergency services tackle a large wildfire in the Mediterranean coastal province of Antalya, an official said.
The fire broke out on Monday in Antalya’s Aksu district and, fanned by strong winds, quickly spread into the neighboring Kepez district, forcing hundreds of residents from their homes. The cause of the wildfire is not known.
Hasan Kahya, an Aksu resident who was helping firefighters tackle the blaze, suffered a heart attack after being affected by the smoke and later died in hospital, the district’s mayor, Isa Yildirim, said.
Two people were hospitalized with burns to their legs on Tuesday, while six others were treated for smoke inhalation. More than 100 dogs were evacuated from an animal shelter in Aksu.
Turkey’s forestry directorate said efforts to bring the blaze under control were continuing on Wednesday, adding that the fire’s intensity had been “reduced.” At least three firefighting planes, nine helicopters, 169 fire extinguishing trucks and more than 1,000 firefighters were deployed, the state-run Anadolu Agency reported.
Separately, firefighters were also tackling a wildfire in the district of Kozan, in the southern Adana province, where hundreds of residents have been evacuated, the forestry directorate said.

Australians will be able to switch off social media algorithms under planned legislation
- Published
Australians would be able to switch off social media algorithms under draft legislation to be proposed this week.
Communications Minister Anika Wells, who last year helmed the government's world-first social media ban for under-16s, said the digital duty of care laws would ensure "some basic safety protections on an industry that hasn't had to observe it".
If tech firms such as Meta, Google and TikTok did not give the option to turn off algorithms, they should face "substantial" penalties, she said.
Some members of the opposition have criticised the proposal, with Liberal Party leader Angus Taylor saying he was "highly sceptical" and arguing the move could amount to censorship.
The government will be taking "expert advice" on whether users would have to opt in or out of the algorithms feeding them content online, Wells said.
This means that, as with its social media ban, the government is looking to bring in legislation before fully hammering out the specifics of how it would work.
"We want to give Australians more choice over what they see on their social media feeds," Wells told the ABC on Monday.
"We know that a lot of Australians appreciate the algorithm both for the enjoyment they get out of it or the utility that they get out of it, seeing local businesses in their suburb.
"A lot of Australians will want to choose the algorithm. But we think that big tech should offer them the choice in the first place and they should respect that choice.
"Big tech is not a protected species and they should offer their customers basic safety standards."
But she admitted that so far no tech firm had been fined for not enforcing the social media ban, despite research consistently showing that the vast majority of under 16s who were on platforms before the ban was introduced last December, still use them.
Some members of the opposition have said they support the idea in principle, but others argue it is an attempt to curtail freedom of speech.
Taylor told News24 he feared this was "an attempt by the government to censor social media" and that Labor should first try to plug holes in the social media ban.
Speaking to Channel Nine's Today show, Wells said: "This isn't about censorship. This is about identifying risks or making big tech identify the risks on their own platform and making big tech mitigate against those risks on their platform."
Last week, high-profile consent advocate Chanel Contos gave a speech at Australia's National Press Club calling on the government to seek an opt-in for algorithmic social media feeds, making it harder for tech firms to find a way round any reforms.
She argued algorithms were fuelling the prevalence of sexual violence in Australia and exposing young people to misogynistic "manosphere" material.
The draft legislation is expected to be introduced in the coming days. As well as addressing algorithms, it is also expected to put an onus on platforms to stop harmful content, such as illegal pornography and videos promoting disordered eating, from being shared.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

Delhi HC asks WFI’s stand on Vinesh Phogat’s participation in World Championship trials
A bench of justice Swarana Kanta Sharma directed WFI’s counsel to seek instructions on the issue and listed the matter for Thursday
The Delhi high court on Wednesday asked the Wrestling Federation of India (WFI) whether it was willing to permit wrestler Vinesh Phogat to participate in the selection trials for the 2026 Senior World Wrestling Championship scheduled for Monday and to defer passing a final order in the disciplinary proceedings initiated against her.
A bench of justice Swarana Kanta Sharma directed WFI’s counsel to seek instructions on the issue and listed the matter for Thursday.
“Take instructions on both the matters. I will hear them tomorrow,” the judge said to WFI’s lawyer.
The court issued the direction while hearing two applications filed by Phogat through advocates Ashita Khanna and Ritwik Prakash.
In one, she sought an early hearing of her petition challenging the disciplinary proceedings which stemmed from the show-cause notices issued to Phogat alleging indiscipline, violations of anti-doping regulations and misconduct during the 2026 Asian Games selection trials.

In the second application, Phogat challenged WFI’s September 7 circular prescribing the eligibility criteria for the selection trials for the 2026 Senior World Wrestling Championship, to be held in Astana, Kazakhstan, from October 24 to November 1. The selection trials are scheduled for September 14 at the Indira Gandhi Stadium.
Under the circular, eligibility is limited to specified medal winners from the 2025 Senior National Wrestling Championship, the 2026 Senior Open Ranking Tournament at Gonda, the 2026 U23 National Wrestling Championship, the 2026 Federation Cup, wrestlers currently attending the National Coaching Camp, and those selected for the 2026 U20 World Wrestling Championship.
Phogat in her application contended that she did not fall under any of these categories and has consequently been excluded from participating in the selection trials.
During the hearing, Phogat’s counsel Rajshekhar Rao submitted that although the court fixed September 29 as the next date of hearing in the petition concerning the disciplinary proceedings, the WFI subsequently issued a notice scheduling the disciplinary proceedings for September 9 and saying that the same was a last and final opportunity. He said Phogat was ready to participate in the proceedings but urged the court to direct the committee not to pass any final order.

Rao further submitted that the WFI issued another circular on September 7, effectively barring Phogat from participating in the selection trials scheduled for Monday. “My maternity cannot come in the way of my eligibility to participate. I’m not asking for a free pass,” Rao submitted.

Are we on the precipice of a white Christian nationalist takeover?
How Christians can fight back against Christian nationalism
A new book argues the future of democracy depends on a segment of American Christians. What should they do?
The author and religion scholar Robert P. Jones sure feels like we’re close. “This is our 1933,” he writes in his new book, referencing the year that Weimar Germany fell to a Nazi takeover.
Panicked allusions to Nazi Germany have been a common occurrence in the Trump years. But Jones, who has studied religion for decades and grew up Southern Baptist, has a very specific perspective on why those references are warranted now, particularly because of the role Christians played then — and it all worries him.
It was in 1933, Jones writes, that the German Lutheran pastor Martin Niemöller began resisting Nazi rule. He was arrested four years later and imprisoned at the Dachau concentration camp until 1945. Revisiting Dachau after World War II, Niemöller remembered 1933 as not just the year the camp opened, nor a reminder of a time when he was still a free man, but also a marker of how much time he had wasted in the preceding years supporting the Nazis. From their rise in the 1920s until that moment, he’d been supportive of much of the Nazis’ movement, voting for them in three different elections. After his release, every day of that time felt like a missed opportunity to do something to avert a tragedy.
Jones doesn’t make this historical parallel lightly. In his new book, Backslide: Reclaiming a Faith and a Nation After the Christian Turn Against Democracy, he spends a significant amount of time building the case that the actions of the second Trump administration, combined with rock-solid support from white Christian evangelicals, are resulting in escalating religious authoritarianism, pointing to evangelical support for mass deportations earlier this year and Christian nationalist rhetoric by members of the administration, such as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. “We are now living in a democratically back-slidden nation, abetted by an apostate white Christianity,” he writes.
But his book isn’t just a panicked observation; it’s a call to action. Like Niemöller, he argues, religious people who’ve sat out or passively supported MAGA can still effect change. And churches are just as important to stopping a slide into religiously backed authoritarianism as many were in abetting its rise.
So what should Christians who don’t buy into this vision of their faith do to resist it?
Jones is the president and founder of the Public Religion Research Institute, the leading research and polling think tank on politics and religion, and a scholar of religion — spending his career analyzing and writing books on the relationship between race, white supremacy, and faith in America. I decided to chat with him to figure out what the road map for Christian resistance to Christian nationalism might look like. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
Why are you taking on this project now?
If you look back at the three previous books I’ve written in the last decade, they have been responding in various ways to the rise of Christian nationalism that we’ve seen in the country and the threat that that poses. This book is motivated by a sense of urgency.
I’m also trying to turn the corner in this book by saying, For those of us who care about the integrity of Christianity and the future of democracy, the real question is what are we going to do in this moment?
Throughout the book, you argue that there is very little daylight between what the administration is doing and what white Christian evangelicals will support. I think immigration policy comes to mind: that it’s hard to propose draconian enforcement policies that these Christians won’t tolerate. Do you really expect people to change?
So the line you’re thinking about — because I remember writing this line — it was, “In the Trump era, white evangelical attitudes about undocumented immigrants are so extreme that it seems virtually impossible to construct a policy that is too brutal for them to support.”
I go through the options [offered in PRRI polling]: Do you support putting things like razor wire and barricades in a river that might make people drown? Yep, we’re good with that. Do you put people in internment camps? Yep, we’re good with that. And so I do think it should be shocking to hear those kinds of responses, again, from people who say they follow a Bible that talks more about caring for the widow or the orphan and has a lot to say about immigrants and the stranger who resides among you and being kind to them, not oppressing them.
I even say at the beginning of the book, I’m not writing for the people who have completely given themselves over to this MAGA worldview. And the evidence shows that it is the vast majority of white evangelicals that have done that. But among white Catholics, among white mainline Protestants, it’s less of a complete acquiescence to that seductive political worldview. That’s who I’m writing to.
“The biggest challenge has been apathy among many white Christians who have watched this extremism take hold, have watched it grow, and have really been uncomfortable speaking out.”
I’m a pragmatist on this point. At the end of the book, I talk about the need for division, and that we have to realize that there are going to be some people who are so wedded to this kind of power and violence that they’re beyond persuasion. The only solution is to out-organize and resist that movement and to stand up something else in its wake.
We’re starting to see some of that as well. White evangelicals only make up 13 percent of the country. And even though almost 85 percent of them are all in on the MAGA movement, that’s nowhere near a majority of the country.
And even if you take everyone who supports a Christian nationalist worldview, it’s only about three in 10 Americans. Now that’s a lot, and it’s a majority of Republicans and it’s two-thirds of white evangelicals in that camp. But it does mean that the country as a whole rejects that worldview by a margin of 2-to-1.
The biggest challenge has been apathy among many white Christians who have watched this extremism take hold, have watched it grow, and have really been uncomfortable speaking out and saying, Wait, wait, wait, that’s not how I understand Christianity. That’s not how I understand the Bible or the teachings of Jesus. And so I think this book is in some ways aimed at that group and saying, Yeah, it’s kind of now or never. If you want a different version of Christianity to exist in this country, it’s time to stand one up and make it a very publicly visible thing.
So where does that leave us in terms of resisting and out-organizing? What is the playbook for beating back this takeover?
I’m pretty convinced that if we’re talking about persuading the folks that have been all in for Trump for a decade now, for three consecutive elections, that’s a fool’s errand.
But I do think there’s a bunch of folks in the middle that aren’t that group. The white mainline Protestant world is much more divided. The white Catholic world is much more divided. The Latino evangelical world is much more divided than the white evangelical world. And so there are other groups of Christians that I think are still debating this out. And I think those are the places where I think there’s fertile ground for a conversation to be had. And I also think there is a great mass of Christians that have been very deeply but quietly disturbed at the way that Christianity has been portrayed and hijacked, but haven’t really found their voice or their feet in putting out a different version.
One thing to say here too is that we have long had Christian voices and, to talk Democratic politics for a minute, in the Democratic Party, they’ve just mostly not been white: the late Rep. John Lewis, Democratic Rep. Jim Clyburn from South Carolina, Sen. Raphael Warnock, who have been very eloquent about talking about their own faith. Warnock is himself a pastor at Martin Luther King’s old church, so very prominent.
But I think what we’ve had less of is people who come out of the white Christian denominations who have been willing to speak from their faith perspective in that way. And I think it’s why Texas Senate candidate James Talarico’s gotten so much attention because he doesn’t fit the mold in many ways. But we are seeing half a dozen other folks running up and down and from a lot of Midwestern states, which is interesting.
And partially that’s because in those Midwestern states, the white evangelical group is typically smaller than the white mainline — in Iowa, in Michigan, and those kinds of upper Midwest states. And so I think we’re seeing more people coming out of that mainline Protestant, Presbyterian, Lutheran world that are representing that. And in Minneapolis, we saw that as well [the active organizing of Lutheran and other mainline Protestant communities to protest ICE, aid immigrant communities, and monitor ICE agent movements].
I’m also thinking in Texas, there was just a story about a Catholic bishop and parishes in a community outside of El Paso that looks like they’ve successfully stopped ICE from building a very large detention center. And Pope Leo has been speaking out about this as well. So I think there are these signs that this other voice of Christianity is emerging, particularly out of alternative white Christian spaces. And I think that’s super, super important.
What does that mean for the average person reading this? What should they be doing?
In the last three years, I’ve probably been invited to well over a hundred mostly predominantly white Christian churches who are asking the question: What can we do? And how do we resist this in our communities? How do we stand up and be a witness to a different kind of Christianity that centers love rather than fear and inclusion rather than exclusion?
And there’s now either five or six major denominations that have either already adopted or are in the process of adopting official statements against Christian nationalism, in their denominations, which are ways of signaling to all the local pastors and all the local churches in their denomination that we see this as a danger and trying to help them draw some bright lines that are helpful at the local level.
So there is movement. And I do think that many of the people that have left Christianity are realizing that there are some alternatives out there.
One thing we political journalists wrestle with is making sure we’re not talking down to voters or readers, or asserting feelings or attitudes about people to them. Did you wrestle with that, in making the case that a segment of white evangelical Americans are racist or bigoted?
Of course, and this is where I have standing as an author. I bring an insider and outsider perspective to this topic, having been raised inside the Southern Baptist world in the Deep South. I have my undergraduate degrees from a Baptist college. I have a master’s degree from a Baptist seminary. So these are waters that I have drunk fairly deeply from the inside. And since I have the sociological data, I have an external perspective on it as well. What the book does is work as a back-and-forth between these two lenses.
And it actually gives me some empathy because, if for no other reason, these are my people. These are my friends, these are my relatives, these are my family. So I’m not looking down my nose or a foreigner wagging their finger in disgust. That’s not who I am.
I’m not afraid to make some moral judgments in the book. I mean, that’s a deeply distorted and destructive story that we’ve inherited in the country that the US was intended to be of, by, and for Christians of European descent. So I’m partially trying to show how it’s destructive and how, for example, these kinds of beliefs connect to things like racism against African Americans and anti-immigrant attitudes, antisemitic attitudes, a whole denial of systemic racism and history in the country. I think if we’re going to have a healthy country and frankly a healthy faith, we really are going to have to reckon with these things.
So should we be promoting a return to these churches and denominations as an effort to revive Christianity and fight back against the encroachment of Christian nationalism?
I should be clear that this book is really not defending Christianity. I fully understand why people have left the church in such large numbers over the last two decades. All I can do is nod my head when people narrate the reasons why they’ve left. I think what I can say for myself is that I’ve found that sometimes, even despite myself, I still care very deeply about the faith of Christianity in this country.
This book is speaking into that. It’s not a proselytizing book. I’m not arguing that anybody who’s left should come back.
But the point is to say that we have this threat of the faith being hijacked for this Christian nationalist purpose. And for those of us who do still feel connected to this faith, it is really a critical time to reclaim it and to put forward a version of it that I would say is more consistent with a religion that emphasizes love and care for the vulnerable, and that is fully compatible with a pluralistic democracy. It’s a really critical time in our country’s history for that faith to emerge as it can.
That faith is actually quite compatible and would find a common cause even with the people who have left for all those reasons. So I think that’s the thing. It’s not a faith that sets itself against those who’ve left, or, if anything, is fairly sympathetic to the reasons those people have left.

“The offer was good; I’m not going to lie. They knew it would have to be a good offer for me to entertain it, with contracting and what would come up,” Santner told the New Zealand Herald.
“I did entertain the thought of it, but coming back to what we’ve got coming up, even if I’m not going to play every game of Test cricket, I still feel like there’s a role for me,” he added.
The Kiwis have home white-ball and Test series against India and a Test tour of Australia coming up this year, and Santner noted that his decision was also based on how playing in Australia’s domestic Twenty20 competition would have impacted his role as skipper.

Walmart-backed fintech major PhonePe has partnered with global card network Visa to launch three cardless payment solutions for consumers and merchants in India. The partnership will introduce Tap to Pay for domestic in-store transactions, Cross Border Scan to Pay for payments overseas, and Smart Accept, which will enable small merchants to accept contactless card payments directly on their smartphones. With Tap to Pay, Android users will be able to tokenise their Visa credit or debit cards on the PhonePe app and make contactless payments by tapping their smartphones at compatible point-of-sale (PoS) terminals. The feature is being rolled out in phases starting today (September 9). PhonePe said the feature would also work in low-connectivity environments. Notably, PhonePe launched a similar Tap & Pay feature for Mastercard cardholders last year. Cross Border Scan to Pay will allow users to scan Visa-supported QR codes and pay through their tokenised cards while travelling abroad. The service will be rolled out across 14 international markets, including Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, Indonesia, Sri Lanka, Japan, China, and South Korea. PhonePe said the feature would be launched soon but did not disclose a specific timeline. It claimed that it would become the first Indian app to offer Visa’s cross-border QR payment functionality. The announcement comes a day after Prime Minister Narendra Modi called for connecting UPI with the payment systems of more countries, particularly those with large Indian diasporas and strong trade ties with India. While PhonePe and Visa’s cross-border offering will run on Visa’s card network rather than UPI, it similarly seeks to make overseas payments easier for Indian users. UPI is currently operational across 11 countries. The partnership also includes Smart Accept, which will allow small merchants to accept card payments by letting customers tap physical cards or tokenised mobile wallets against the merchant’s smartphone. This would remove the need for merchants to purchase a separate PoS machine. Transactions made through Smart Accept will be integrated with PhonePe’s existing merchant QR dashboard for daily reconciliation and dispute resolution. However, PhonePe did not disclose when the service would become available to merchants. The latest offerings build on PhonePe’s device-tokenisation solution launched in February 2025. The solution allows users to store tokenised credit and debit cards on their devices and use them for bill payments, recharges, travel bookings, and transactions at merchants integrated with PhonePe’s payment gateway. Once a Visa card is saved on PhonePe, users will be able to use the tokenised card for online checkout, tap-to-pay transactions at physical stores, and QR-based payments in supported overseas markets. The partnership was unveiled at the Global Fintech Fest (GFF) 2026 in Mumbai. PhonePe cofounder and CPTO Rahul Chari said the tie-up would bring online tokenisation, tap-to-pay, and cross-border QR payments together on the platform. It is pertinent to mention that PhonePe is also preparing to go public. The company filed its UDRHP with SEBI in January for an OFS-only IPO, under which Walmart, Tiger Global, Microsoft, and General Atlantic plan to pare their stakes. However, it paused its IPO plans in March amid geopolitical tensions in West Asia and volatility in global equity markets. On the financial front, PhonePe’s operating revenue rose 11.5% to ₹7,920.5 Cr in FY26 from ₹7,105 Cr in the previous fiscal year. However, its net loss widened 62% to ₹2,792 Cr from ₹1,727.4 Cr in FY25.

TOI correspondent from Washington
: A researcher at the Artificial Intelligence firm Anthropic quit his job on Tuesday with a grim warning over the rapid progress in the field which he fears could kill humanity as soon as 2030.
“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt.” Coxon, who is himself among those building AI, wrote on X while announcing his resignation, igniting a firestorm of alarming -- and some frivolous -- responses.
A researcher who has spent the past three years working on AI pretraining at OpenAI and Anthropic, he accused both firms of “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” arguing that increasingly capable systems could hack computer systems, conduct scientific research, acquire resources and eventually become sufficiently autonomous that humans lose control.
Coxon’s prognosis could have been dismissed as the bitter farewell note of a departing employee -- except his colleague, Evan Hubinger, Anthropic's Alignment Science lead, essentially endorsed his views.
“Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Hubinger wrote. More unsettlingly, he acknowledged that Anthropic does not yet have a plan to solve “alignment” for superintelligence and is not clearly on track to do so.
Samuel Marks, another Anthropic researcher specializing in scalable oversight, added an even more uncomfortable observation: AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction “in the next few years,” and, he said, the more senior the employee, the more concerned they tend to be.
“Why do AI developers continue despite the risk? Due to a mixture of commercial incentives and a belief that they are in a race with other, less responsible AI developers that will abuse the technology or develop it less safely,” Marks explained.
“Unlike traditional software, we can’t “program” AIs to behave how we’d like. AIs frequently severely misbehave. For instance, AIs from multiple developers recently hacked their way out of secure evaluation environments and into real-world companies, even though no one asked them to do this,” he noted.
The technical concern among AI gearheads is recursive self-improvement (RSI): AI systems increasingly helping humans build better AI systems, eventually reaching the point where an AI can substantially design and develop its own successor.
Anthropic says that threshold has not been reached and is not inevitable. But its researchers say the trend is moving faster than expected. More than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic's codebase was reportedly authored by Claude by May 2026, while the company says its engineers were merging roughly eight times as much code per day in the second quarter of 2026 as they did in 2024.
This matters because if AI becomes much better at designing algorithms, running experiments, writing code and conducting research, the pace of improvement could accelerate dramatically. Today's AI helps humans build tomorrow's AI; tomorrow's AI might help build the AI after that. And if the improvement loop becomes fast enough, researchers worry that safety mechanisms developed at human speed could be hopelessly outpaced.
The race is already getting uncomfortable. OpenAI has just released GPT-6 Astra, which it describes as its most capable model yet, reaching the company's “Critical” level for cybersecurity capability -- meaning it can perform sophisticated cyber tasks that raise substantially greater misuse concerns. Anthropic, meanwhile, has released Claude Fable 5.1 and the more restricted Mythos 5.1 aimed at high-end cybersecurity and biological research and remains available only to vetted organizations.
Incidentally, Anthropic's brand was built partly around being the AI company that would be more cautious than OpenAI. Now Anthropic's own researchers are warning that Anthropic itself is caught in the race. Coxon says the problem is a classic prisoner's dilemma: each company may believe it would be safer to slow down, but fears that its rival will continue regardless.
Not everyone shares his alarm. On X, one commentator effectively prescribed the standard emergency procedure to address the issue: “Jacob, go back inside and unplug all the computers.” Another observer announced airily that, having learned Anthropic's alignment chief thinks AI has a greater-than-10% chance of killing everyone, he was going to “go play with my kids.”
AI’s math leap and humanity’s dilemma
Amid all this came a mathematics bombshell, with OpenAI announcing on Tuesday that an internal AI system produced what it says is a solution to the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of mathematics' seven Millennium Prize Problems. The problem concerns equations describing fluid motion — mathematics underpinning everything from airflow and aircraft to weather and blood flow.
OpenAI deployed roughly 10,000 AI agents working in parallel, which generated about 2.7 million messages and 130 billion output tokens on the Navier-Stokes effort, reaching their proposed solution in about 88 hours. If it survives scrutiny of mathematicians, the implications could be enormous.
Mathematics sits underneath physics, chemistry, engineering, computer science and much of modern medicine. AI that can generate genuinely novel mathematical insights could potentially accelerate scientific discovery across all of those fields.
Which brings human civilisation to the central paradox: The machines may be capable of helping us cure diseases, invent materials, solve physics problems and accelerate science — while some of the people building them simultaneously worry that the machines might eventually become too powerful to control. But precisely how a future system would go from brilliant software engineer to exterminator of Homo sapiens is still in the realms of speculation.
All this leaves humankind with a modest assignment for the rest of the decade: Build machines vastly smarter than ourselves; teach them human values; make sure they don't deceive us; make sure they don't escape our control; make sure they don't develop their own goals. And, ideally, do all this before they become clever enough to notice that we have assigned them the job.

In September 2026, a rumor spread that a U.S. airman's widow was denied death benefits because he died in the context of the war in Iran, which Congress hadn't officially declared. 
The rumor appeared on Facebook, Reddit and X. 
The meme included two images: one of a young man smiling as he posed in front of a U.S. flag and another of a couple posing on a tarmac, in which the man wore Army fatigues and a woman with long blonde hair smiled in his arms. The meme read:
This is Major Alex Klinner, a U.S. Air Force airman from Alabama. He was killed in Iran on March 12 during Trump's ILLEGAL "Operation Epic Fury" war.
On Sunday, his widow exposed that Trump is REFUSING to give her death benefits, as Trump never actually formally declared war.
Let that sink in. Trump and Republicans are too weak to actually declare war as the Constitution demands, and they're leaving dead soldiers' families holding the bag.
BEYOND DEPLORABLE!
Several Snopes readers shared the meme via email, asking us to verify its claims.
The rumor stems from an Instagram post by a woman named Libby Klinner, whose bio says she is the "surviving spouse of Maj. Klinner," a former teacher and a mother to a toddler and twins. On Aug. 29, 2026, she posted a video of herself rocking a baby, with on-screen text that read "The Air Force recently told me that because we haven't officially declared war, my kids and I aren't eligible for some benefits."
A review of Klinner's Instagram feed indicated she lost her husband Alex Klinner, who had been deployed to the Middle East, on March 12, 2026. According to a March 14 announcement from the U.S. Department of Defense, Maj. John A. Klinner died two days earlier in a plane crash in Iraq, 12 days after the U.S. and Israel launched attacks on Iran. (A separate post by Klinner said her husband went by his middle name, Alex, though his first name was John.)
On Sept. 1, 2026, Under Secretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness Anthony Tata said on X that someone had reached out to Klinner and her family "to confirm they have received all of the entitlements they are owed," though he did not specify if these included the alleged missing benefits Klinner referred to in her post.
Snopes found no reason to doubt Klinner's assertions. However, we were unable to independently verify details about the benefits in question without access to documentation or correspondence between Klinner and the Air Force. As a result, we also could not confirm whether Klinner was denied benefits because Congress hadn't declared war on Iran. For these reasons, we've left the claim unrated.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Air Force told Snopes via email that they had spoken with Klinner to ensure she is receiving the benefits she's entitled to and to answer her questions. We reached out to Klinner for further confirmation and await a response.
Klinner's claims about missing benefits
Klinner regularly posted on Instagram until March 11, talking about the difficulties of a loved one's deployment and sharing teaching tips. On March 14, she shared several photos of her husband, saying he had died. Her next post was dated May 9, asking her followers to support the families of other service members who died in the March 12 plane crash. The text in her images discussed grief and her husband's death.
On Aug. 29, Klinner posted on Instagram a video of her rocking a baby with the caption "Six months of a war we can't call a war..." (archived).
"The Air Force recently told me that because we haven't officially declared war, my kids and I aren't eligible for some benefits," the video's on-screen text read. "So not only was my husband killed in a war he never wanted to participate in, but now the benefits we're left with are being dictated by semantics and public perception."
"The missing benefits are combat pay-related and were missing from his final paycheck," the caption said.
On Aug. 31, Klinner posted again, saying the director of Air Force Mortuary Affairs Operations told her the agency was launching an audit into her benefits to ensure that she receives everything to which she is entitled, but provided no further details (archived).
We reached out to Air Force Mortuary Affairs Operations but did not receive a response by the time of publication.
Officials' response
In an email to Snopes on Sept. 2, the Air Force spokesperson said officials had talked to Klinner on Aug. 31:
We understand this matter has been difficult for Mrs. Klinner and her family, and we are committed to addressing her concerns with care and respect. Department of the Air Force officials spoke with Mrs. Klinner on Monday [Aug. 31] to ensure she is receiving all eligible benefits she and her family are entitled to, as well as ensure all her questions are fully addressed. We remain committed to providing clear information and continued support to Mrs. Klinner, as well as all the families of the Airmen who died in the KC-135 crash.
In his Sept. 1 post on X, Tata underscored the Department of Defense's commitment "to providing Major Klinner's wife and children with seamless, long-term support," but he did not reveal any details about possible missing benefits or whether Klinner may have received them (archived):

It’s a brand new era for Apple. The company is turning over leadership for the first time in 15 years, with former CEO Tim Cook handing off the reins last week to the new CEO, former Apple VP of hardware John Ternus.
At the first Apple product soiree hosted by Ternus, the company made an even bigger change: it announced its first ever folding device, the iPhone Duo.
The company also announced its new line of iPhone 18 Pro phones, some updates to its Apple Watch line, new AirPods, and new software capabilities powered by Siri AI.
As expected, there were no base-model iPhone 18 announcements; those are likely coming early next year. There was also no mention of Vision Pro, iPads, or Macs. Apple touted new desktop Macs in August.
Here’s everything Apple showed off today.
Apple iPhone Duo
Apple’s first ever folding device is the Duo, a “passport sized” foldable iPhone. It starts at $1,999 for a model with 256 GB of storage.
It’s a product category that Apple has been working toward for a decade. Now, it hopes to do that very Apple thing where it may not be the first company to the new tech party, but it definitely aims to be the snazziest.
The Duo is a landscape style foldable, meaning it has a vertical magnetic hinge that lets you open the device like a book. Closed, it has a 5.3-inch screen on the outside. Open it up, and the landscape display is 7.7 inches. The Duo is also heavy, weighing in at 254 grams, which might be a little too hefty for some users.
The Duo is made with a titanium frame and what Apple calls a “custom polymer” screen for increased durability. It runs on Apple’s proprietary A20 Pro chip (the same chip in the new Pro-model iPhones 18) and the company’s custom C2 modem. The horizontal format also means it's capable of running iPad-like apps, albeit ones that can adjust on the fly when folding the screen or setting the phone up at an angle. The Duo will also be able to work with the Apple Pencil Pro stylus.
On the back of the Duo are two 48-megapixel cameras, one standard, one for ultrawide shots. There are two 12-megapixel selfie cameras, one on the main screen and one on the inside when the screen is opened. The cameras can also capture 4K video.
Untypical of Apple, the Duo does not have Face ID. Instead, it uses a TouchID sensor in the power button. This is likely due to Apple’s desire to minimize the device’s bulk and allow for more components inside the device.
Like, for example, the massive battery. Apple says the iPhone Duo gets 31 hours of battery life, and up to 44 hours just using the smaller front screen. Storage options start at 256 GB for the base model, with options up to 2 terabytes of space. That top configuration puts the Duo at $3,199.
Expensive, yes, and very in line with Apple's upward adjustment to its prices due to the memory shortage. But Apple is also keen on enticing users to rent the most premium devices with Apple Upgrade, the leasing program the company introduced in July.
For more details about the Duo, check out WIRED’s deeper look at the company's very first foldable.
iPhone 18 Pro
As predictions suspected, Apple is not releasing its base model iPhone this year. Instead, the company focused on highlighting its new iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.
These look almost identical to the iPhone 17 Pro models, albeit slightly smaller. The iPhone 18 Pro is 6.3 inches and the iPhone 18 Pro Max is 6.9 inches. They come in black, silver, glacier, and burgundy color options.
They come with Apple’s new A20 Pro chips, which have been repackaged into a silicone casing that can connect directly to the new redesigned vapor chamber, a design flourish that aids in keeping the components from overheating and helps the phone last longer. Wireless charging is even faster, able to juice the phone up to 50 percent battery life in 15 minutes.
The iPhone 18 Pro battery is capable of up to 36 hours of video playback per charge. The 18 Pro Max gets around 45 hours of video playback.
The 18 Pro phones are also getting juiced up with a new and improved Siri AI. There is an all new Siri AI app on the iPhone. Siri AI is rolling out as a beta in English now, and will be available in French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish in October.
Adjustable Aperture
The iPhone 18 models also get a number of big improvements to their cameras. The biggest: a variable aperture on the iPhone 18 Pro's 48-megapixel main camera. Users can dial in their preferred aperture, which adjusts mechanically in the lens. This opens up new possibilities for shooting in different light environments, as well as adjusting the depth of field for adding real—not digital—bokeh effects to photos.
Apple is also touting improved photography and video capture controls, called Pro Controls, that let you change settings like white balance, aperture, and shutter speed. So if you’re a camera nerd, you have new software and hardware tools to play with.
Apple is also introducing Apple Reference Image, a watermarking tech that maintains an image the way it was originally shot. Apple refers to it as something close to “a digital photo negative” that you can reference if you need to prove a photo’s provenance.
The iPhone 18 Pro is $1,199, and the iPhone 18 Pro Max is $1,299. You can preorder the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max this Saturday, September 12. Apple says they’ll officially start selling September 18.
Apple Watch
Apple announced some revamps to its Apple Watch. There is a reengineered Apple Watch 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4.
Both watches get new sensor arrays. Apple’s new Health Sensing System includes LEDs that measure high-frequency heart rate data as often as every five seconds. This gives wearers a constant stream of health data all day long.
The Apple Health app gets some revisions that better track sleep and show personalized guidance about your daily readiness. This is something Google’s Pixel watches have had for a while, though Apple’s reports will benefit from its new sensor array.
Also on the watch are some features that make use of Apple’s ambient listening tech to record and log the things around you. That means the watch can transcribe the things people say and show the text right on your smartwatch’s screen. In a demonstration video today, Apple showed a server at a restaurant reciting menu specials, and the person sitting at the table was able to scroll back through a transcript of the last 15 seconds on their Apple Watch’s screen to read what the server said.
These features are opt-in—at least for the person wearing the watch—and the features that record audio will emit a chime when somebody uses them. You can learn more about how the Apple Watch listens in Lily Hay Newman’s report for WIRED.
The listening feature can also send alerts to your wrist when it detects important sounds like sirens, doorbells, and babies crying. Apple says the audio is not stored, the raw audio is inaccessible even by Apple, and that the transcriptions do not identify the people talking.
There are new ceramic cases and color options for the Series 12 Watch, including gray, black, light gold, and bronze. The Apple Watch Series 12 is $399. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is $799.
For more about the Apple Watch updates, read Boutayna Chokrane’s WIRED story about all the details.
AirPods 5
Apple’s new, cheaper AirPods 5 come with some of the features that the AirPods 4 had. The AirPods 5 come with noise canceling and adaptive sound controls. You can also use Siri AI directly on the AirPods and communicate via chat. They also have live language translation, though it’s not clear how well that will function out in the real world—of course, it works great in Apple’s demo videos.
The base model costs $129. There’s also a version with touch volume controls on the stems, a little more battery, and a wireless case-charging puck that also can charge your Apple Watch. Those nicer options cost $149.
Some rumors had predicted that Apple would show off a new pair of AirPods with cameras in the earbuds. Those are possibly still coming eventually, but Apple didn't say anything about them this time. We’re expecting at least one more Apple event before the end of the year, and they may show up then.

Ontario man found guilty of participating in terrorist group activities
Kristoffer Nippak was charged with contributing to activity of AWD, a designated terrorist group in Canada
An Ontario man was found guilty of participating in the activities of a terrorist group by an Ontario Superior Court judge Wednesday.
Kristoffer Nippak, 33, was arrested and charged in December 2023 with knowingly participating in or contributing to an activity of a terrorist group following an 18-month investigation by the RCMP in central Quebec, eastern and northern Ontario and the Niagara Region. He was arrested alongside another co-accused, Matthew Althorpe, of Niagara Region.
Althorpe was sentenced to 20 years in prison in March for three terrorism-related charges, according to a news release from the Public Prosecution Service of Canada.

Nippak's charge was tied to activity related to the Atomwaffen Division (AWD), a designated terrorist group in Canada. AWD is a "militant accelerationist" neo-Nazi terror group that was founded in the United States in 2015, according to the Canadian government's website.
The group, also known as the National Socialist Order, has carried out "training camps" where members receive hand-to-hand combat and weapons training, and it has also carried out violent acts at public rallies, the website said.
An AWD recruitment video was "central" to Superior Court Justice Maureen D. Forestell's decision in finding Nippak guilty, according to the court document.
The video shows armed men wearing skull masks and AWD patches "marching through a forest, firing guns, clearing a building and burning the flags of the United States, Israel, and the European Union," her decision outlined.
Forestell's decision said the Crown had proven "beyond a reasonable doubt" that Nippak knew AWD was a terrorist organization when he participated in the filming of the recruitment video.

Yes, peak TV is over — but we challenge you even to begin watching all the great shows that will premiere in the coming weeks, or even catch up with the new good ones that came out this summer. Are you all caught up on “Furious” on Hulu and “Sterling Point” on Prime Video and HBO’s “Lanterns” and Netflix’s “My Brilliant Career”? We didn’t think so! (Whispers: Neither are we.)
Just since September started a mere nine days ago, Season 2 of “The Gentlemen” and FX’s “The Drop: A Snowfall Saga” both premiered. What we’re saying is, peak TV or not, there continues to be an embarrassment of riches across television, and that will continue this fall, as you will see below. (Shout out to the actual show “Below,” where Josh Hartnett plays a small-town fisherman battling a sea monster! We’ve been too scared to watch the screeners, but will soon.)
This list doesn’t include everything, of course. There are shows that haven’t been dated, like Netflix’s highly anticipated “Pride & Prejudice” remake, starring Emma Corrin as Lizzy Bennet. And several network shows that typically come out in the fall, such as CBS’ “Matlock” and ABC’s “High Potential,” will be premiering midseason. As for network staples we know you’ll find on your own, there’s Fox’s “Best Medicine” and “Doc” double feature, premiering on Sept. 22; CBS’ “Marshals” and “Tracker” on Oct. 4; “Abbott Elementary” has its Season 6 (six! where does the time go?) premiere on Oct. 7; the One Chicago shows premiere on Oct. 7; “Law & Order: SVU” and “Law & Order” on Oct. 8; ABC’s “9-1-1,” “9-1-1: Nashville” and “Grey’s Anatomy” premiere on Oct. 15; and NBC brings back “St. Denis Medical” for Season 3 and “The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins” for Season 2 on Nov. 2.
“South America” — the artist formerly known as “South Park” — has already entered the zeitgeist before its Sept. 16 premiere on Comedy Central, with its Emmys win and Trump-mocking name change; the docuseries “Jay-Z in 8” premieres on Sept. 18 (but missed our cutoff for inclusion); Netflix’s Omar Sy-starring series “Lupin: Part 4” returns for the first time since 2023 on Oct. 23, and Season 2 of the streamer’s delightful spy thriller “Black Doves,” starring Keira Knightley, will drop on Nov. 5; Season 4 of “Tulsa King” premieres on Paramount+ on Oct. 16 — and, last but not least, Season 3 of “Percy Jackson and the Olympians” returns to Disney+ on Nov. 20.
One last disclosure: Obviously, Christmas will bring the series premiere of HBO’s “Harry Potter,” and that is decidedly … in the winter. This is an inarguable fact! But given that the show is going to be one of the biggest pop culture events of the year, and will also fuel the discourse machine because of J.K. Rowling, we just had to include it. Please don’t place us under one of the unforgivable curses; we only mean to serve.
Enough of these ramblings! Let’s get to the list.

The annual Global Fintech Festival 2026 kicked off on a glitzy note yesterday. As usual, the first day saw Indian fintech startups, from BharatPe to PhonePe, unveil a plethora of new launches and products for consumers and merchants. Moving beyond payments, the day saw a wave of fresh product launches by startups and NPCI around AI, credit, fraud prevention and embedded financial services. Here are the prominent announcements that caught our attention… BharatPe Rolls Out An Agentic AI Tool For Merchants As AI continues to disrupt the status quo, BharatPe announced the launch of an agentic AI platform, specifically catering to merchants and businesses. Built on Google Cloud’s Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, the new offering brings an AI assistant directly into BharatPe’s business app. The tool can understand the merchant's business, products and interaction history, allowing them to communicate in their preferred language and take action across more than 60 live systems in real time. Additionally, it also unveiled Credit Coach, which leverages AI to increase credit awareness amongst users. The platform generates personalised videos, featuring a digital avatar of former Indian cricketer Rohit Sharma. Jio Payment Solutions Unveils Cross-Border Payment Service Financial services giant Jio Financial Services’ (JFS) subsidiary has partnered with US-based Citi to launch a cross-border payments service. Under this, it will enable domestic businesses to accept international payments from customers worldwide. In a post on LinkedIn, JFS said that the service is designed to make international payments more seamless, efficient and cost-effective, with ambitions to reduce turnaround time and offer greater convenience for Indians across borders. Pine Labs Launches Agentic Commerce Stack The listed fintech major has partnered with L&T Finance to introduce an agentic commerce feature on the latter’s PLANET app. The agentic commerce feature allows AI agents to carry out transactions on behalf of users within predefined controls. The integration uses Pine Labs Payments Protocol (P3P) and the Grantex protocol to enable communication between AI agents and facilitate controlled transaction execution. The offering will initially focus on flight ticket bookings. Under the proposed setup, an AI agent can act on a user's stated intent and complete the booking process within the app, subject to user-defined parameters or "guardrails". Amazon Pay’s New Credit Card For Small Merchants Amazon Pay has joined hands with Kotak Mahindra Bank to launch co-branded credit cards for small business owners. The credit cards will be limited to merchants on Amazon Business, the company’s dedicated B2B ecommerce marketplace. The ecommerce giant said that the credit card will combine cashback on business expenses with an interest-free credit period, giving small businesses flexibility to manage their purchase payments. The card will also provide offers on AWS credits, covering services such as cloud computing, data storage and AI. Yubi Debuts New Lending Platform For Retail Borrowers Fintech giant Yubi has launched Pye, a new lending platform built for retail borrowers. The service will enable retail borrowers to connect with lending institutions through a single integration. Pye is designed to cater to everyday credit needs, such as weddings, home and education expenses, and medical emergencies. Rather than routing a borrower's application to a single lender, the platform connects it with a network of lending partners and matches the borrower with the creditor best suited to their profile, loan requirement and timeline. Besides this, it also unveiled a consumer credit-health app called TopScore, where users can access their credit score and view the information in simplified language across 10 languages.

What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong
- Published
The UN has just called for the predominant world map to be replaced with one that more accurately reflects the true size of continents like Africa.
The "Correct the Map" resolution adopted by the General Assembly aims to fix the discrepancy on the Mercator map, in which the African continent is shown as being of similar size to Greenland - even though it is in reality about 14 times larger.
It adopted a new map, the Equal Earth projection, which better represents the true sizes of landmasses - but comes with problems of its own.
There have been many prominent attempts over the years to solve the problem of accurately representing the surface of a sphere on a flat rectangle, each with its own benefits and drawbacks.
Mercator map
The now widely used Mercator map was created in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator.
Its main purpose was to help European sailors navigate the oceans, as cartography Professor James Cheshire at University London College explained.
"He wanted a straight line to be drawn on a map to look like a straight line in reality if you followed a compass bearing," he told the BBC. "That was what it was intended to do, and that's what it does brilliantly well."
To keep those angles correct on a flat map, Mercator had to stretch the grid lines wider as they moved away from the equator toward the poles.
His map accommodates for the curvature of the Earth by making countries near the equator seem much smaller than they are, with countries nearer the poles appearing stretched.
The distortion is a result of it being impossible to accurately represent the surface of a globe on a two-dimensional chart.
More than 450 years on, Mercator's creation is still the basis for many of the maps we see in classrooms, on TV and online, including Google Maps.
But critics of the Mercator map say there is a psychological effect to viewing some places as smaller than they actually are and others as larger, as we instinctively view bigger things as more important.
For Kenyan geographer Kioko Muendo, this has implicitly downplayed Africa's vast resources, population and investment opportunities.
"Maps are more than just guides for travellers - they shape how regions are perceived politically and economically," he told the BBC.
Equal Earth map
The Equal Earth map aims to address this problem with the Mercator projection.
It was developed by a team of cartographers in 2018 to present the size and shape of landmasses more accurately.
As a result, the Equal Earth map was initially adopted by 54 members of the African Union, before being adopted by the UN.
But to do this, it sacrifices the straight lines that made the Mercator projection perfect for navigating with - and it cannot be used for measuring the true distance between different places.
"You can preserve area, or you can preserve shape, or you can preserve distance and direction, but not everything at once perfectly, because otherwise you'd be back to a sphere," Cheshire said.
Peters map
The Peters world map was designed by German historian Arno Peters in the early 1970s. The rectangular map is based on the projection first described by Scottish cartographer James Gall in 1855.
The projection sacrifices accuracy of shape in favour of accuracy of scale. So, polar regions are squished, while the bits near the equator are stretched.
This fixes the Greenland-Africa size issue, allowing those who use it to get a sense of the comparative size of different landmasses, all while preserving straight lines of longitude and latitude.
However, the map severely distorts the shapes of Earth's landmasses, making them all look slightly off.
The straight lines on the Peters map do not represent true constant compass bearings and so are useless for navigation.

This past June, a Virginia mother named Karyann Parkinson took a bike ride with her 5-year-old son and stopped by a pond inside their gated community to collect goose feathers from the grass. The two of them rode back home, whereupon Parkinson’s son asked his mother if he could walk back to the pond by himself to fetch a few more feathers. Parkinson, who was eight months pregnant with her fifth child, studying for the bar exam, and—perhaps most pressing—making lunch, agreed. The walk was relatively short, along a sidewalk 10 feet from the road and across two intersections with crosswalks, which Parkinson knew her son could navigate successfully (he had done so six times that morning). But on his way, the boy was spotted by a concerned passerby, who notified a community security guard, who in turn notified the police. Before long, several police officers were at Parkinson’s door, followed by Child Protective Services agents. Officials in the case decided to press charges against Parkinson, and last week she was convicted of contributing to the delinquency of a minor and placed on Virginia’s child-abuse-and-neglect registry, where she will remain for seven years.
Parkinson told me that her son—who competently walked the security guard back to their house after politely explaining that he wasn’t allowed to get into cars with strangers—had become distraught upon learning that he had apparently done something very bad. And although the police treated Parkinson as though she were negligent, her husband, who works as a marriage and family therapist and sees a lot of anxious young adults, tried to explain to the officers that they had made a deliberate choice to let their children encounter appropriate levels of challenge and risk. But the officials remained unmoved. Two weeks later, two police officers showed up at Parkinson’s door with a warrant for her arrest. “It just kept escalating,” she told me. “No one was taking a step back and going, Oh, this is fine. This is a fine situation.” She gave birth to her baby a week later.
Last week’s guilty verdict, Parkinson said, has been disorienting. Having spent 15 years taking some pride in her mindful choices as a parent, she has lately been doubting herself—“and thinking, Am I really crazy?” Her lawyers have appealed the decision, and Parkinson will receive a new trial.
People are having fewer children around the world for a variety of reasons, but some observers suggest that the steep expectations placed on parents—and mothers in particular—may be at least partly to blame for the fertility cliff in the United States. In response to a pervasive atmosphere of parental stress, a number of social-media influencers and public intellectuals have recommended that parents just do less—no more assiduously planned birthday extravaganzas, no more enrichment programs scheduled from breakfast to bedtime, no more hawkish monitoring to rescue children from any hint of danger or discomfort.
But even though working parents may long for the days when children were more independent—a wish reinforced by countless editorials declaring the wisdom of letting children roam freely, away from their screens—society seems to have irrevocably changed. Most families now include two parents working full-time, and although many of these adults enjoyed the unchaperoned pleasures of a latchkey existence, the sight of children left to their own devices now horrifies not only the neighbors but also cops and prosecutors. In other words, parents are caught in a vise made up of financial demands and socially inflated expectations around parenting.
Parkinson’s story is not unique. In 2008, Lenore Skenazy made national news when she published a column about letting her 9-year-old son ride the subway home after a trip to Bloomingdale’s in Midtown Manhattan, a decision that many people likewise characterized as a form of child abuse or neglect. Skenazy, who has since founded what she calls the Free-Range Kids movement, occasionally publishes stories about mothers who are arrested or locked up for letting their children enjoy what used to be considered ordinary childhood pleasures. In 2020, a Georgia mother of five was jailed for allowing her 14-year-old daughter to babysit her younger siblings during the pandemic, when schools and day-care facilities were closed but parents still had to work. In 2024, a mother of four in Georgia was handcuffed when her 10-year-old son was found walking into town, less than a mile from their home, while she was taking one of her other children to a doctor’s appointment. Parkinson’s story has become a national phenomenon in large part because Skenazy first called attention to it in Reason magazine.
Raising children comes with enough trade-offs without enforcing unforgiving standards for parental attention, entertainment, and supervision. Notably, none of the cases in which police arrested mothers for their presumed negligence involved children who had been actually harmed. One hesitates to admit to such a taboo practice in print, but my own 10-year-old daughter has ventured out unaccompanied to hang out with her friends or pick up a few things from the store, and although I have fretted over getting pinched by the police, she treasures those opportunities to establish some independence even more than I appreciate time away from monitoring and enabling her various whims and desires. Mixing in activities that don’t require constant parental oversight is unfortunately a daring practice these days, but it seems crucial to balancing work and other adult responsibilities with the demands of raising children.
This is not to say that allowing kids some independence comes without risks: Cars pose a threat, as does every child’s latent desire to engage in mischief. Unknown adults assailing children with ill intentions, though a terrifying prospect, is exceedingly rare; stranger abductions account for less than 1 percent of missing-child cases nationwide. But these risks may nevertheless be overstated in our social imagination because ours is a low-trust society; in other countries, young people are granted much more freedom because parents presume that the adults they encounter will be helpful and supportive.
What Parkinson, Skenazy, and many other parents understand is that independence is good for children, who stand to build confidence and competence by doing things on their own. And fostering that independence is, in the end, the primary goal of parenting. The job is hard and bittersweet by design: Every step they take in the world is a step away from you. This, of course, is where their journeys are destined to lead.

The liver is a large, forgiving organ, but tumours can grow deep within it, spread across both its halves, or take root in a liver already scarred by disease. Up until recently, cutting out the cancer was often impossible without leaving too little healthy liver behind to keep a person alive. Today, however, a growing field known as transplant oncology is changing that.
What happens
Instead of trying to cut the cancer out of the liver, doctors remove the entire diseased liver and replace it with a healthy one. The most common type of liver cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), is frequently multifocal, meaning it appears in several places at once. A transplant solves both problems in a single operation: it removes every tumour, eliminates the scarred field that keeps producing them, and restores completely normal liver function.
The central challenge of transplant oncology has always been selection. Donor livers are precious and scarce, and a transplant only makes sense if the cancer is unlikely to return. What increasingly matters is a tumour’s biology: how aggressive it is, how it behaves, and how it responds to treatment. This shift is the heart of modern transplant oncology. Teams now weigh blood markers such as AFP (alpha-fetoprotein) and PIVKA-II, patterns seen on PET scans, and the tumour’s grade under the microscope.
One of the most powerful tools in this field is downstaging, which means deliberately shrinking tumours until a patient who was previously ineligible becomes a candidate for transplant. A cancer that shrinks and stays quiet is showing favourable biology. One that keeps growing despite treatment reveals itself as too aggressive for a transplant to help. Roughly half of appropriately selected patients can be successfully downstaged, and those who are then transplanted after a mandatory observation window do strikingly well.
Expanding limits
While HCC remains the main indication, transplant oncology is expanding into cancers that were, until recently, considered off-limits. Bile duct cancers (cholangiocarcinoma) are a prime example. For certain patients with tumours at the junction of the bile ducts that cannot be removed surgically, a rigorous protocol combining chemotherapy, radiation, and careful staging before transplant has produced survival rates far beyond what surgery alone could achieve.
Beyond HCC and bile duct cancers, this treatment modality is also relevant to several other complex liver tumours, including intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and cancers that metastasise to the liver, such as colorectal liver metastases and neuroendocrine liver metastases. In children, it also plays an important role in the treatment of paediatric liver cancers, including hepatoblastoma, HCC, and hepatic epithelioid hemangioendothelioma.
Two lives, one principle
A 54-year-old man with chronic liver disease arrived with two hepatocellular carcinomas involving the right lobe of the liver. Owing to the underlying chronic liver disease, he was not a suitable candidate for bridging therapy. As his tumour markers were within normal limits, and a PET-CT showed no evidence of extrahepatic disease, his 45-year-old wife came forward as a living donor and donated her right lobe. He then underwent a successful living donor liver transplant, made an uneventful recovery, and is now five months post-transplant with excellent graft function and no evidence of disease recurrence. This case highlights another important indication for liver transplantation, where it offers a curative treatment for patients with both decompensated chronic liver disease and underlying liver cancer.
Another patient, a man in his fifties, had liver cancer that had grown into a major blood vessel. Rather than turning him away, his team treated the tumour with targeted local therapies and precision radiation, watched his tumour markers fall steadily to normal, and confirmed the cancer had responded before proceeding. Nearly two years after his transplant, he remains cancer-free.
Transplant oncology has therefore shifted the question from “can this tumour be removed?” to “does its biology make a new liver worth giving?” As selection grows more precise, more patients who were once told nothing could be done, are finding a real path to cure.
(Dr. Jayanth Reddy is lead consultant - HPB & liver and pancreatic transplants at Manipal Hospital, Old Airport Road, Bengaluru. jayanth.reddy@manipalhospitals.com)
