Prescriptions for GLP-1 weight-loss drugs among children under 12 in the U.S. have risen more than 300-fold since 2019 as doctors seek new, effective treatments for younger patients with obesity, according to a study published on Friday.
The study, which included more than 3.5 million children aged between eight and 11 years with obesity but not diabetes, found that prescriptions for GLP-1 weight-loss drugs rose from 0.03% in 2019 to 9.3% as of June.
Although the drugs are not approved for use in children under 12 years, clinical guidelines allow the medications to be used for obesity in children as young as eight years old in certain cases.
94% of the children prescribed GLP-1s had severe obesity, and about 65% had at least one related condition, such as high cholesterol, high blood pressure, and sleep apnea.
Overall, 20,282 children received GLP-1 drugs during the study period - most often, Novo Nordisk's Wegovy. Doctors also prescribed Novo's Saxenda and Eli Lilly's Zepbound.
While the absolute numbers of children under 12 receiving GLP-1 treatment is still low, the study shows that GLP-1 use is accelerating rapidly, said lead investigator and obesity medicine specialist Dr. Babak Orandi of NYU Langone Health.
Orandi added that long-term safety monitoring is needed to ensure the drugs remain safe and effective.
Children living in higher-income communities were 55% more likely to be prescribed the medicines, suggesting emerging disparities in access, according to the study published in the journal Pediatrics.
"Physicians and health policymakers alike have a responsibility to ensure ... these valuable and sometimes costly treatments become available to more than those who have access to health insurance and can afford to visit pediatric clinics," said Allan Massie, co-author of the study and associate professor of surgery at NYU Grossman School of Medicine.
Researchers used Epic Cosmos, a national electronic health records database encompassing more than 300 million U.S. patients. Epic had no role in the study.

WHO and Netherlands Strategic Dialogue in The Hague, Netherlands 10 April 2024. Credit: Michel Mees Photography
The WHO and the Netherlands convened in The Hague on 10 April 2024, to discuss joint priorities and alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and WHO’s key strategic goals, marking a new milestone in their longstanding partnership.
Rooted in the Netherlands' unwavering commitment to global health, human rights, and universal access to comprehensive health services, the collaboration between the WHO and the Netherlands is instrumental in addressing global health challenges and fostering health and well-being, worldwide and in the country.
Against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts, disasters, and the escalating impact of climate change, and the interconnectedness of the Dutch public health landscape in the Netherlands with global health challenges, this year’s Strategic Dialogue emerged as a critical platform for reflecting on this partnership’s long-term vision.
“In this Strategic Dialogue, throughout all sessions, WHO and the Netherlands showed a commitment to cooperation and to deepening their partnership based on the strong alignment between their respective priorities and objectives”, said Ms Marjolijn Sonnema, Director General for Public Health at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport.
A key outcome of the Strategic Dialogue was the recognition of the alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and the WHO's forthcoming 14th General Programme of Work, paving the way for synergies in areas such as health system strengthening, pandemic preparedness, climate change and health, anti-microbial resistance (AMR) and mental health support.
"At a time when inequity in health and in access to essential health services and financial protection is increasing, disproportionately impacting the poor and most vulnerable, the Netherlands stands as a global health leader and trusted WHO partner. With shared priorities and commitment to sexual and reproductive rights, gender equity, health systems, security, climate resilience, and mental health, we look forward to strengthening our partnership to enhance the health and well-being of all, globally and in the Netherlands", said Dr Bruce Aylward, WHO Assistant Director-General, Universal Health Coverage, Life Course.
WHO acknowledged the Netherlands' global leadership as a flexible donor, with an agreement around the imperative to ensure WHO's financing is more sustainable, through the inaugural WHO Investment Round. This WHO initiative aims to mobilize predictable, sustainable and flexible resources essential for the WHO to respond swiftly and effectively to global health challenges and improve health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable populations.
Addressing contemporary challenges such as geopolitical tensions while seizing opportunities for advancing global health objectives were also on the table during the dialogue. Both parties stressed the importance of sustained collaboration to address pressing health issues comprehensively.
Taking stock of the joint achievements since the previous strategic dialogue in 2022
In 2022, the Strategic Dialogue between the Netherlands and WHO called on both partners to enhance synergies between WHO priorities and the new Dutch Global Health Strategy. Implementing this approach, the Netherlands and WHO:
- Expanded their cooperation to new areas of joint interest, e.g., climate change and health;
- Renewed their longstanding cooperation on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in health emergencies and humanitarian settings;
- Improved the flexibility and predictability of the Netherlands’ financial support through renewed General Arrangements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2022-2025) and the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (2024–2028) demonstrating the Netherlands’ commitment to WHO’s sustainable financing;
- Hosted together the 2nd World Local Production Forum in the Netherlands;
- Continued and deepened their technical cooperation through secondments, Junior Professional Officers and the Collaborative Centres.
The outcomes of the 2024 dialogue will inform future collaboration between the Netherlands and the WHO, so that efforts are aligned, and the optimal use of resources is helps achieve improved health outcomes worldwide. The enduring partnership between the Netherlands and the WHO stands as a cornerstone in the global health landscape, reflecting a shared commitment to advancing health and well-being globally.
-----------------
The Netherlands is a key supporter and strategic partner of the WHO.
In 2022- 2023, the Netherlands was one of the top five flexible WHO contributors with nearly US$ 19 million in core voluntary contributions. Overall, the Netherlands contributed more than US$ 106 million to the WHO in 2022 - 2023, of which US$ 93 million, nearly 90%, was voluntary funding.
The Netherlands also supports the WHO's technical expertise through secondments of staff and helps boost young people's careers in public health via the WHO's Junior Professional Officer Programme.
This demonstrates the Netherlands' commitment through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to the WHO’s central role in the global health architecture.
Through this support, the Netherlands contributes to crucial activities in the areas of sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.

Shelton beats Alcaraz in late-night epic to reach semis
- Published
Carlos Alcaraz's US Open title defence came to an end in a dramatic five-set quarter-final loss to Ben Shelton that ended at 03:34 local time - the latest finish in the tournament's history.
A large crowd remained captivated deep into the night as a modern classic unfolded over an unpredictable four hours and 28 minutes on Arthur Ashe Stadium.
The match did not begin until about 11pm in New York, after the start of the night session was delayed by Tuesday's earlier matches.
At its conclusion, eighth seed Shelton basked in a standing ovation from a delirious audience after completing a 6-7 (5-7) 6-1 6-3 1-6 7-6 (10-7) victory that will live long in the memory of all those still present.
It was the biggest - and certainly most significant - win of the 23-year-old's career.
Shelton had not beaten a top-three player in 17 attempts, and had lost each of his three previous matches against Spain's Alcaraz.
It also boosted home hopes of a first American men's singles champion in New York for 23 years.
Shelton was not born when Andy Roddick won the US Open in 2003 - but an American finalist is guaranteed when he and Frances Tiafoe meet in Friday's semi-finals.
Alcaraz was competing at his first tournament since a lengthy injury lay-off - but that is to take nothing away from Shelton, who produced a phenomenal performance.
Seven-time major winner Alcaraz had exceeded expectations on his return after more than four months out with a wrist injury, including sweeping past 20th seed Tommy Paul in straight sets to reach the last eight.
But the 23-year-old's lack of match fitness appeared to finally catch up with him in a high-octane encounter filled with breathless exchanges and astounding displays of athleticism.
Even when it appeared Alcaraz had emptied the tank, the two-time winner would not only forced a deciding set but go the distance as the players engaged in a tense 10-point match tie-break that provided a fitting conclusion to the contest.

Gay should open for England in South Africa - Cook
- Published
England opener Emilio Gay should retain his spot for their winter tour of South Africa, according to former captain Sir Alastair Cook.
Gay made a Test-best 60 from 114 balls to blunt Pakistan's attack which helped England seize control on day one at Edgbaston.
The 26-year-old left-hander's tally of 261 runs, at an average of 26.1, might not look particularly eye-catching.
But in an English summer where ball has dominated bat - Ben Duckett is England's only centurion in six home Tests so far - the Durham left-hander has shown a willingness to grind it out.
Cook, who made almost 12,000 runs as an opener for England, has been impressed with the character the Durham left-hander has shown to make tough runs at the top of the order.
"I think Emilio Gay's played really nicely. I would say he's confident and intense," Cook told Test Match Special.
"He is definitely a run-getter when he gets in. He seems to have that real stubborn and strong will to make it count if he can.
"He has done enough for me to take him to South Africa to continue the progress of a player where the pitches will be slightly easier to bat on and he should open the batting."
According to CricViz, Gay has left or defended 61% of the pace deliveries he's faced since his debut against New Zealand in June.
Dom Sibley in 2020 (68% left or defended) was the last English opener to register a higher percentage in a home summer.
During his innings on Wednesday, Gay left or defended 65 deliveries and Cook "likes how late he defends the ball" with a patient approach to more attacking strokeplay.
Gay scored the first 12 runs of his half-century off 43 balls before his next 38 came off 52 balls.
He hit nine fours and has scored 68% of his Test runs in boundaries - the joint-highest of any England batter with at least 250 runs in the red-ball format.
"If you take Gay's innings, and what I've seen of him, he's not hunting that drive too often. He waits for it to come into there," added Cook.
"He scores off the back foot through the off side as well. He scored through the leg side and timed them through mid-wicket so he does have an all-round game. He's not limited to the off side."
'Desperate for that first century'
Given Pakistan's flimsy batting - bowled out for 133 in their first innings here - it could end up being Gay's final Test innings of the summer.
With Jacob Bethell set to return for the tour of South Africa following injury, the selection of a top-order batter for the winter is likely to be a scrap between Jordan Cox, Dan Lawrence and Gay for two places.
Only Harry Brook (six occasions) has passed 30 more times than Gay (five) during a challenging summer for batters.
Although Gay has struggled to play back of a length bowling with seven dismissals in the 7-9 metre length range which has highlighted a potential weakness.
Former England captain Michael Vaughan said Gay "played nicely" but might reflect on an missed opportunity to reach three figures for the first time after he dragged on a delivery from Razaullah Khan.
"Emilio Gay found his balance early. He had it hard at the start and then he found his flow," Vaughan said.
"He'll be really disappointed to get out for 60. He'll be desperate to get his first Test match century and I thought it was on today.
"That extra little bit of pace from Razaullah and a little lack of concentration at the end of the day has cost him."
England seamer Josh Tongue said Gay's rigorous preparation has helped him develop the necessary powers of concentration for Test cricket.
"The one thing I've seen in Emilio is he trains really hard in the nets. He'll bat for ages, putting a lot of hard work in, and it's shown on the pitch," added Tongue.
"Even last week at Lord's, he had two quite horrible dismissals, but I felt today he batted unbelievable on a tricky pitch.
"He was obviously really disappointed with how he got out. It's not a nice feeling, chopping on, but he's put the team in a really good position for tomorrow."

- In August 2026, a claim spread that McDonald's lost a lawsuit against the TV chef Jamie Oliver, who — according to posts — proved that the fast food chain's food was "unfit for human consumption" because it was "highly toxic." The claim is unproven.
- Snopes previously investigated a variation of this claim in 2018 and 2026. We found then and now that Oliver said in a 2011 TV program that beef trimmings used for a product he called "pink slime" were "not fit for human consumption." We found no evidence that he specifically called McDonald's food "unfit for human consumption" or "toxic," as the posts suggested.
- The American Meat Institute, a trade association that represents processors of meat and poultry, said in 2012 that beef trimmings used to make "pink slime," which it calls Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings, were edible.

However, because we could not access a full version of the "Jamie Oliver's Food Revolution" episode where Oliver discussed "pink slime" to see if he specifically mentioned McDonald's, we leave this claim unrated.
- Snopes will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces. We contacted Oliver and McDonald's to ask whether Oliver has ever called the fast food chain's food "unfit for human consumption" or "toxic" or whether McDonald's ever lost a lawsuit involving Oliver and are waiting for responses.
A claim (archived) circulated on Facebook in August 2026 that fast food chain McDonald's lost a lawsuit against the TV chef Jamie Oliver after Oliver proved its food was "unfit for human consumption" because it was "highly toxic."
For example, one Facebook user wrote:
McDonald's loses lawsuit against chef Jamie Oliver, who proved that the food they sell is unfit for human consumption because it is highly toxic.
Chef Jamie Oliver won a lawsuit against the world's largest fast-food chain. Oliver demonstrates how hamburgers are made.
According to Oliver, fatty cuts of meat are "washed" with ammonium hydroxide and then used to fill the hamburger patties. Even before this process, the TV presenter says, this meat was unfit for human consumption.
Oliver, a radical activist chef taking on the food industry, says: "We are talking about meat that is sold as dog food and then served to humans. Aside from the quality of the meat, ammonium hydroxide is harmful to health." Oliver calls it "the pink slime process." What sane person would put a piece of meat soaked in ammonium hydroxide into a child's mouth?
Similar claims circulated elsewhere on Facebook (archived, archived, archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim, which we previously reported on in July 2026 and January 2018.
The claim contained three parts: that McDonald's sued Oliver, that Oliver made the comments about "pink slime" and that Oliver's alleged comments were specifically about McDonald's.
We found no evidence in online searches (archived, archived, archived) that McDonald's ever lost a lawsuit involving Oliver. AFP Fact Check reported in December 2021 that Oliver had never taken legal action against McDonald's.
According to an excerpt of a 2011 episode of his program "Jamie Oliver's Food Revolution," Oliver said that the meat used to produce a specific type of beef product that the celebrity chef called "pink slime" was "not fit for human consumption."
McDonalds reportedly ceased using "pink slime," which is also known as Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings, in their food in 2011, as we noted in 2018 when we fact-checked a previous version of this claim. Oliver did not mention McDonald's specifically in excerpts of the 2011 episode of "Jamie Oliver's Food Revolution" that Snopes reviewed.
However, because we could not access a full version of the "Jamie Oliver's Food Revolution" episode in question to see if it mentioned McDonald's, we leave this claim unrated.
Snopes contacted Oliver and McDonald's to ask whether McDonald's ever lost a lawsuit involving Oliver, whether Oliver had ever proved McDonald's food was "unfit for human consumption" or "toxic" and to ask whether McDonald's used Select Lean Beef Trimmings in 2026. We await replies to our queries.
Oliver's allegations
In the first episode of the second season of his program "Jamie Oliver's Food Revolution," in which Oliver attempted to reform school lunches and fight obesity in the U.S., the celebrity chef held a demonstration where he showed children and adults where on a cow different cuts of meat came from.
According to a segment of the episode (archived) that an internet user uploaded to YouTube in 2016, after spray-painting prices on a live cow to show where various cuts were found, Oliver then addressed what happened to the remainder of the animal.
He said (time code 00:01), "The public loved seeing that, that, equalling a steak. They never for a minute thought I would clear all the meat and cuts away and introduce them to a new world of food. It's called pink slime."
Oliver added (time code 00:12), "When you've broken down a whole beast, you're left with trimmings. You know, in my industry, we call those trimmings [BLEEP]."
Speaking to a crowd of people, Oliver described the trimmings used for "pink slime" as (time code 00:36) "not fit for human consumption."
Oliver went on to say that processing plants took trimmings that were "not fit for human consumption," separated the meat from the fat, killed harmful bacteria using ammonium hydroxide and sold the end product, which he called "pink slime," as human-grade food. Ammonium hydroxide is a watery solution that can be used to regulate acidity in food or in hair dye or cosmetics.
In an excerpt from the program included in a 2012 CBS report, Oliver said (time code 00:32), "We're taking a product that would be sold at the cheapest form for dogs, and after this process we can give it to humans."
(Snopes could not locate a complete video of the "Jamie Oliver's Food Revolution" episode in question. The clips we have found online appeared genuine and did not indicate any signs of possible manipulation.)
FDA says ammonium hydroxide 'generally safe'
Around 11 months after Oliver's episode discussing "pink slime" aired, the American Meat Institute President J. Patrick Boyle issued a statement to say that Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings was "a safe, wholesome and nutritious form of beef" that helped prevent food waste by utilizing trimmings that would otherwise go to waste.
The institute is a trade association that represents processors of meat and poultry.
Boyle's statement said, similarly to Oliver's demonstration, that processing Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings involved first separating the meat from the fat and using "food grade ammonium hydroxide gas" to destroy bacteria before blending the product into foods like ground beef.
However, he denied claims that the trimmings used to create Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings were not edible. The statement said:
Some recent media reports created a troubling and inaccurate picture, particularly in their use of the colloquial term 'pink slime.' The fact is, BLBT is beef. The beef trimmings that are used to make BLBT are absolutely edible. In fact, no process can somehow make an inedible meat edible; it's impossible. In reality, the BLBT production process simply removes fat and makes the remaining beef more lean and suited to a variety of beef products that satisfy consumers' desire for leaner foods.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration, which regulates ammonium hydroxide use in food, says the ingredient is "generally recognized as safe." This was also the case when we last reported on these claims in 2018.
In sum ...
While Oliver did call the cuts of meat used for Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings "not fit for human consumption" and claimed (time code 00:59) the product was "admitted to being in at least 70% of ground beef products" in a 2011 program, the episode excerpts Snopes reviewed did not show him specifically accusing McDonald's of using the product or calling the fast food chain's products toxic.
McDonald's said in a 2013 statement it had not used Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings in its products since 2011.
We found no evidence that McDonald's had lost a lawsuit involving Oliver since then. Given the prominence of McDonald's and Oliver, such a lawsuit would have been widely reported by reputable sources. That was not the case.
While the FDA generally recognizes ammonium hydroxide, which is used to process Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings, as safe, reporting by the publication Food Safety News claimed that fast food giants like McDonalds, Taco Bell and Burger King had all stopped using the product by January 2012.
Both ABC, which broadcast Oliver's program, and Oliver himself have faced lawsuits over their coverage of the product.
ABC settled out of court in 2017 in a $1.9 billion defamation lawsuit brought by Beef Products Inc., a producer of Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings, over Oliver's program and other stories the network had reported about the product in March and April 2012.
A man who Beef Products Inc. laid off after negative press heavily affected the company's sales sued Oliver, ABC and other defendants in 2012. He dropped the case in 2013.
Snopes' archives contributed to this report.

The arrival of fall means pulling out the pumpkins, moody autumnal colors, and cozy throw pillows.
However, while some fall decorations can make your home feel warm, elevated, and inviting, others can border on tacky.
Seasonal decor can also be expensive, so investing in a few timeless pieces that will last from year to year can ultimately save you money in the long run.
"A lot of times, I feel like the holiday decor is disjointed from what the aesthetic is of the actual home that you live in. It should be cohesive, in my opinion," Ashley Childers, an interior designer and home furnishings and accessories designer based in Arkansas, told Business Insider.
"On the opposite end of the spectrum, I see a lot of people who have very curated style who feel like they can't decorate for the holidays because they don't want it to be tacky or cheesy," she said. "If you want to decorate for the holidays, you can do it in a beautiful way."
Here are five tasteful fall decorations to add to your home, and three tacky ones to skip.
Let nature guide the colors you incorporate into your fall home decor.
Rather than leaning into trends or grabbing the first items she sees in the Halloween section at Target or Walmart, Childers said she looks to the colors she sees in nature each autumn for inspiration.
"I love to really let nature kind of guide seasonal decor," Childers, who's worked in the design industry for more than 15 years and in interior design for a decade, told Business Insider. "So, we always lean into beautiful wheats and burnt oranges, burgundies, sage greens, even into deep forest green, camel."
"All those warm, rich colors that you think about when you think of fall are what I love seeing brought in to fall decor," she continued. "I just think if you let nature guide you, you're never going to make a mistake."
Switching up your fall decor with a wool throw blanket can add texture to your space.
"A really beautiful wool throw blanket is iconic for fall, in my opinion," Childers said. "It can really be a capsule piece for your home regardless of the season."
In her own home, Childers said she frequently changes her throw blankets from season to season based on texture.
"I love fall and winter the most because the textures get so nubby and cozy. So my recommendation and tip would be to always choose natural fibers if at all possible," she said.
"With throws and blankets, we usually opt for beautiful linens, wools, something that's made out of organic cotton. Anything like that is going to stand the test of time and be a really good investment piece for your home."
For an elevated look, use more natural, organic-looking florals inside the home.
Childers said that for fall centerpieces or wreaths in her home-decor designs, she frequently uses dried plants to create a more organic feel.
"I think they're so obviously organic and beautiful, and there's just nothing like a real plant or a real dried plant or flower or something like that," she said.
To add a more natural feel to a room, she frequently uses grapevine wreaths and more architectural wreaths that are made out of sticks, branches, wheat, and other materials naturally found outside.
Textured pillows in organic materials are another tasteful addition to fall home decor.
Rather than opting for printed pillows or polyester options, Childers said she chooses natural fibers, "whether it's bouclé or a beautiful linen or gorgeous Dupioni silk."
"Anything like that just adds a textural layer. And then, if you add in that warm fall color, you're going to just layer in so much coziness into your home," she said.
Using real pumpkins and gourds can also elevate your outdoor and indoor fall decor.
Childers said that while less long-lasting than faux decor pieces, real pumpkins or plants inside your home or on your home's exterior can bring energy to a space.
"I just think keeping it natural and beautiful inside the home or outside is perfect for the fall season," she said.
In fact, the biggest mistake people make when decorating their home is going overboard with pumpkins, leaves, and plants, Childers said.
"Faux pumpkins, faux plants, faux everything, in my opinion, drains the energy out of a space," she said.
Childers added that living in Arkansas, she understands many people want to start decorating early — even when it's still hot outside — so real pumpkins, flowers, and other living decorations might not be practical.
"I would say maybe opt for dried branches and dried leaves and dried berries, those types of things that you can still get early in the season," Childers said.
Busy patterns and bright colors can also feel tacky.
Childers said the classic autumn shades sold at many home and craft stores can feel harsh, making it harder to create a calm, soothing space.
"They're not as naturally occurring," Childers said, recommending that sticking to more natural colors like dark auburn, sage green, and forest green can be more soothing than bright orange and black.
Choosing more neutral tones can also extend your home's decor beyond just the Halloween season, when black and orange tend to be more on-trend.
Colorful ribbon is another slightly dated trend.
Using brightly colored ribbon is another fall decorating choice that can make a space feel dated rather than seasonal.
For example, when decorating your home or front door with ribbon, neutral tones like brown, maroon, or sage green can look more elevated than black, orange, or yellow.
"If that's your style, go for it," Childers said. "I would say maybe that's not going to give you an elevated look. We usually don't go for a plaid, orange, yellow, and black ribbon."
Still, Childers encouraged people to experiment with what brings them joy.
"If you bring something in and it's not jiving, then maybe it doesn't work," Childers said. "You have to try things out. It's OK if something doesn't work. It's your home. It's your laboratory. You get to try to see what you like."
Childers also said that from year to year, she likes to change up her seasonal decor and try new decor pieces and trends with lower-cost items.
"It's easy to add pieces like throw blankets and pillows that give you an opportunity to inject a new feeling into your space, without having to invest in new furniture or lamps or something like that," she said.
Editor's note: This story was first published in September 2023 and was updated in September 2026.

A man has been shot dead in the car park of a Sydney community centre in the city’s south-west.
Emergency services were called to the community centre on Rossmore Avenue in Punchbowl on Wednesday evening after reports of a shooting.
A vehicle was seen driving away from the location after the fatal shooting, NSW police said in a statement.
Paramedics treated the man but he died at the scene. He is yet to be identified, police said.
The fatal shooting comes two days after the New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, announced measures to curb gangland violence in Sydney.
New laws being introduced in the state include new aggravated offences for conspiracy to commit gang-related murder. The maximum penalty will be increased to life imprisonment.
The government has repeatedly denied criminal gangs are “out of control” in the city after the mistaken identity shootings of electrician Joshua Macdonald and Marco Tapia, a 23-year-old biomedical engineering student last week.
Police said neither man had any link to organised crime.
The new laws being introduced in NSW aim to tackle organised crime by giving police more power, including using new interim serious crime prevention orders to restrict people suspected of serious and organised crime. Those would be applied while the state’s supreme court considers the full order.
Children’s indictable offences would include activities linked to organised crime, and public shootings and firebombings would be added to the scheme.
In a statement on Monday, Minns said people who conspire to arrange a gangland murder should face the prospect of “spending the rest of your life behind bars”.
“We want to hit these criminal networks at every point – the people who organise the violence, the people who facilitate it online and the people who ultimately carry it out,” he said.
Police are urging anyone with information about the Punchbowl incident to contact Campsie police station or Crime Stoppers.

CNA Explains: What goes into an MP’s allowance and what is it used for?
The monthly allowance for MPs will rise to S$18,500 from Oct 15. Here's a breakdown of who gets what and why.
SINGAPORE: Changes to the allowances of all Members of Parliament (MPs) accompanied revisions to political office holders' salaries announced on Tuesday (Sep 8).
Like ministerial salaries, this is the first change in MP allowance since 2011. The changes follow recommendations from an independent committee reviewing political salaries and MP allowances.
Prime Minister Lawrence Wong told parliament that the allowance is not a token sum, but a substantial amount that lets them carry out their responsibilities in parliament and in their constituencies.
Coordinating Minister for Public Services Chan Chun Sing said the increase to MP allowances will cost the government about S$6.6 million (US$5.2 million) more a year.
The independent review committee also noted that considerations for community-related roles, including MPs, may differ from those for full-time political appointment holders. It recommended that the government study delinking MP allowances from political salary benchmarks.
What goes into an MP's allowance?
An MP’s monthly allowance is currently S$13,750, and will increase to S$18,500 on Oct 15.
The allowance is subject to Central Provident Fund contributions and tax deductions. MPs also contribute a portion of their allowance to their political party.
MPs do not receive pensions. Their medical benefits fall under the Medisave-cum-Subsidised Outpatient scheme, aligned with the public service.
Who receives the allowance?
Elected MPs who entered parliament by winning a General Election receive the full allowance.
MPs who hold ministerial or other political office receive the allowance too, on top of their full-time roles running the day-to-day affairs of the state.
What about NCMPs and NMPs?
Allowances for Non-Constituency MPs (NCMPs) will rise from 15 per cent of an MP’s annual allowance to 30 per cent, or S$5,550 a month.
Mr Chan said this reflects the conferment of full voting rights to NCMPs since 2017, and brings their allowance into better alignment with their parliamentary responsibilities.
Nominated MPs will keep their existing peg of 15 per cent of an MP's allowance.
The Leader of the Opposition, currently a vacant position, will continue to receive double an MP's allowance, raising the role's annual allowance from S$385,000 to S$518,000.
What is the allowance used for?
The allowance helps MPs perform community-based and legislative functions, including looking after the needs of their constituents and raising their concerns in parliament.
“Fulfilling these duties well requires strong commitment and hard work from an MP,” the independent review committee said in its report.
The allowance typically goes towards expenses incurred in discharging MP duties. This includes transport costs for grassroots events, attending parliamentary committee sessions and official briefings.
It also covers less visible costs such as buying food and refreshments for volunteers or giving “bai jin” – condolence money – at wakes within the constituency. MPs with smaller networks of grassroots supporters may rely on the allowance more heavily to fund such activities.
MPs are paid an allowance for the time and expenses incurred in carrying out these roles. Most serve on a part-time basis, letting them bring experience from other fields into parliamentary debate.
Why is an allowance increase necessary?
Mr Chan, who delivered a ministerial statement in parliament after Mr Wong on Tuesday, said the increase was to account for inflation.
Mr Wong said providing a proper allowance has enabled both the People’s Action Party and the Workers’ Party to recruit and field strong candidates.
“We can see the result in this House. We have MPs with a wide range of backgrounds and experience, who bring different perspectives to our debates,” he said.
“We may disagree strongly across the aisle, but the quality of debate is high, and Singapore is better for it.”

Germany's Merz attacks AfD in stormy debate after far-right election win
- Published
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has clashed with AfD leader Alice Weidel in parliament, calling her party a "destructive force" with a migration policy that amounts to "ethnic cleansing" for skilled workers.
Merz was addressing the Bundestag in the aftermath of the anti-immigration party's sweeping victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt where it won almost 44% of the vote, while the chancellor's conservatives saw their vote halved.
Weidel told MPs that voters had shown that Merz's coalition with the centre left was a total failure and his time was up.
Merz hit back saying the AfD had harmed German interests by backing Russia, and its "remigration" policy would affect millions.
It is not yet clear whether the party will be able to form a government or not in Saxony-Anhalt, having fallen three seats short of an outright majority. No far-right party has won power in any of Germany's 16 states since World War Two, and Merz has admitted the "seismic" result has changed Germany.
The AfD's success has been praised by US President Donald Trump, who said "the Populist Party in Germany just had a really big night", linking the victory to "absolutely horrible immigration rules and regulations".
The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been labelled as "right-wing extremist" by German domestic intelligence and the party has promised a "deportation and remigration" offensive targeting irregular migrants.
Repeatedly heckled by AfD MPs, the chancellor told Weidel that one in six skilled workers had a migration background, and if her party had its way then its policy would amount to "nothing other than an ethnic cleansing in the skilled trades based on skin colour and origin".
While the government understood some deportations were needed, he said it make a careful distinction between those who contributed to German prosperity and those without permanent residency.
Disruption by AfD MPs became so loud that at one point Bundestag President Julia Klöckner threatened to start expelling people from the chamber: "We are not on a football pitch."
Weidel said mass migration had left Germans with daily knife violence and attacks on trains and in stations, but Merz warned that the AfD's plans would mean that no single care home, hospital or restaurant could function.
As leader of the main opposition party in the Bundestag, Weidel opened the session by telling Merz his Christian Democrats had been "pulverised" in Saxony-Anhalt, after winning 17.2% of the vote, and she accused his government with the Social Democrats of driving Germany towards bankruptcy.
Merz said her party had not won an outright majority in Saxony-Anhalt and it would not achieve one in Germany.
"You are and will remain a destructive force," he said, accusing the party of cheating the voters by saying before the election that their candidate for premier, Ulrich Siegmund, would only rule if he won a majority, but hours after the vote deciding to go and find one.
The AfD has opened the door to working with another party, perhaps the left-wing populist BSW, as long as it backs Siegmund to be state premier.
Siegmund's number two in Saxony-Anhalt, has even suggested that Merz's CDU could work with his party, if it abandons the so-called firewall (Brandmauer), under which no mainstream party will work with the far right.

The Delhi Police has arrested Sudhanshu, one of the operators of the 'Hostel Daze' paying guest (PG) facility being run from the five-storey building that collapsed in Delhi's Satya Niketan area on September 6, killing seven people, including five students.
The five-floor building was being operated by two business partners who had taken the property on lease in August 2025. One of the operators is still on the run.
Delhi Police is, meanwhile, investigating into the circumstances that led to the collapse and the roles of those associated with the building's ownership, maintenance, repair work and PG operations.
Quick answers to key questions
Sudhanshu was arrested by Delhi Police as one of the operators of the 'Hostel Daze' PG facility operating from the building that collapsed, resulting in seven fatalities.
The demolition of the adjacent building was ordered by Delhi CM Rekha Gupta due to its dilapidated condition, ensuring public safety after the collapse incident.
The building stood five floors tall before it collapsed, housing a PG facility operated under the name 'Hostel Daze.'
Students may need to reassess their use of PG accommodations, considering the concerns raised about safety and structural integrity of such buildings in the wake of the collapse.
The Delhi government is conducting inspections of all PG accommodations to ensure compliance with building regulations and to enhance safety measures following the Satya Niketan tragedy.
Delhi Police arrested Sudhanshu, one of the two business partners operating the PG facility from the building. The two operators, the other being Shubham Tyagi, had taken the property on lease in August 2025. Shubham remains on the run.
Police had earlier arrested property owners Hariram Bansal (81) and his wife Urmila Gupta (75) along with their 52-year-old son Mahesh Gupta. The couple was sent to 14-day judicial custody, while Mahesh was remanded to two-day police custody.
Mahesh's police custody ends on Wednesday and he is being taken from South Campus police station to be produced before a court. A building contractor and a mason are also being taken to court, according to an ANI report.
Police earlier apprehended labour contractor Sanoj from Uttar Pradesh's Kasganj. He was allegedly supervising repair work in the basement of the building.
Delhi CM Rekha Gupta has ordered the MCD to demolish the adjoining building as it is in dilapidated condition.
In a post on X, Delhi CMO wrote, "On the instructions of Chief Minister Rekha Gupta, MCD has been directed to demolish the dilapidated building adjoining the accident site in the interest of public safety. The belongings of students inside the building are being safely removed by Delhi Fire Service personnel in a systematic manner. All students and local residents are requested to cooperate with the authorities."
According to Deputy Commissioner of Police (South West) Amit Goel, repair work was underway in the basement for eight to 10 days because waste had accumulated during the rainy season. The ground floor was also being repaired and extended for commercial purposes.
Police found seven rooms spread across four floors -- two each on the first, second and third floors, and one on the fourth floor. The fourth-floor room had been partially converted into a single-room accommodation for three students. The ground floor had two shops and a basement.
The PG was being operated under the name 'Hostel Daze'. An officer said at least three other PG facilities operating under the same name were functioning in the neighbourhood before the collapse.
The Supreme Court has indicated that it will examine the issue of the Satya Niketan PG building collapse on a pan-India basis, ANI reported further. A bench of Justices Ahsanuddin Amanullah and R Mahadevan has listed the matter for hearing on Thursday.
It came after a mention of the tragedy by senior advocate Ajit Sinha, a court-appointed amicus curiae in an earlier matter concerning regulatory compliance with the apex court's directions on illegal buildings and structures across the country.
Seven people, including five students, died after the five-storey building came crashing down on Sunday afternoon. Several others were injured.

A former Nicaraguan paramilitary faces deportation or statelessness after ICE detention
A former Nicaraguan paramilitary faces possible deportation from the U.S. after being detained by immigration authorities
MEXICO CITY -- A former Nicaraguan paramilitary detained by U.S. immigration authorities could soon be deported to the country where he said he was imprisoned and tortured — or sent to another country where he would be rendered stateless.
Marlon Gerardo Sáenz Cruz, 65, who defected from the ruling Sandinista party, was among 222 prisoners stripped of their Nicaraguan citizenship and brought to D.C. through a U.S. State Department initiative in February 2023. Now, after being detained during his check-in with immigration authorities in Los Angeles on Aug. 17, he must make his case before an immigration judge to remain in the U.S.
His immigration court date on Sept. 8 comes as asylum denial rates have spiked under the Trump administration and as people granted lesser protections from deportation are increasingly being sent to third countries in Latin America and Africa where they have no ties.
“Even if he manages to get protection from a U.S. immigration judge, it’s not ensured safety,” said Savi Arvey, director of policy, refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First.
Sáenz's detention followed a letter sent to the U.S. State Department last year by a group of Nicaraguan exiles, mainly in Miami. They allege that he and dozens of other former government officials maintain their ties to the government of Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega and his wife and co-President Rosario Murillo.
The exiles also accused Sáenz of harassing other government opponents while in the U.S. A legal representative for Sáenz said he was simply responding to attacks against him.
“We are asking the State Department to investigate all these people because it’s unacceptable that they are washing the blood off their hands and covering up the actions of a criminal who shouldn’t be in the United States and who is a threat to national security,” said Aida Carrion-Vanegas, president of the advocacy organization Nicaraguan Americans United for the Republic.
In October 2025, U.S. Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau responded to Carrion-Vanegas on X, saying he would look into the allegations. She has not heard from him since. The U.S. State Department did not respond to a request for comment.
Sáenz’s potential deportation to Nicaragua would send a message that “discourages future defections and reinforces the regime’s narrative that there is no safe exit,” said accredited court representative Muriel Sáenz, who has been assisting with his asylum application and is not related to him.
Sáenz, known in Nicaragua as El Chino Enoc, became a guerrilla fighter as a teenager in the 1970s and remained close to high-level Sandinista figures for decades. He later spoke to Nicaraguan press about his involvement in a government-aligned paramilitary group that repressed protesters following mass anti-government marches demanding Ortega’s resignation in 2018. Hundreds were killed.
Ortega has claimed the 2018 protests were a U.S.-backed coup to overthrow him and that those imprisoned were involved in the plot.
Sáenz's accredited representative denied that he had killed anyone or committed any crime in Nicaragua.
Sáenz broke with the government in 2019, and began using his popular YouTube channel to denounce corruption within the Ortega-Murillo government, which has maintained its grip on power for nearly two decades while stifling dissent through the imprisonment and torture of opponents.
He was imprisoned in Nicaragua in May 2022 on drug and weapons trafficking charges that he has called politically motivated.
He now has a leg ulcer, glaucoma and other health issues, some stemming from being tortured and held in solitary confinement, according to Muriel Sáenz, who said she fears for his health. She said complications from having polio as a child have worsened in ICE detention and he now uses a wheelchair.
ICE did not respond to a request for comment, but its online locator shows Sáenz is being held at Central Louisiana ICE Processing Center.
Sáenz’s immigration case presents a legal dilemma because an immigration judge will have to weigh his alleged involvement in human rights abuses against the principle of not sending someone to danger, explained Heather Hogan, a lawyer and policy and practice counsel for the American Immigration Lawyer Association.
Sáenz and the other Nicaraguan prisoners entered the U.S. on humanitarian parole, a temporary status granted in emergencies that does not guarantee a pathway to citizenship. He then opened an asylum case within a year of entering the country as required.
Under U.S. immigration law, perpetrators of human rights abuses, including torture, enforced disappearances or extrajudicial killings, are barred from receiving asylum, and a judge would have to determine if Sáenz's past involvement with the Sandinista government makes him ineligible.
But a judge could also grant Sáenz deportation deferral under the Convention Against Torture, CAT, an international human rights treaty that the U.S. is party to, if he is found likely to face torture in Nicaragua.
That protection would prevent Sáenz from being deported to Nicaragua, but would not grant him permanent immigration status or prevent the U.S. from sending him to a third country, as has become common under the Trump administration.
“In some cases like this, people do get granted deferral,” said Hogan, who previously decided cases of people implicated in possible human rights abuses as an asylum officer for the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.
“Because our analysis is more about following our laws and international obligations … not carrying out a trial and imposing a punishment for their past actions.”
But the Trump administration has broken with the precedent of allowing people with CAT protections to remain in the U.S., instead sending them to third countries, said Arvey of Human Rights First.
“It’s a bleak situation because never before has this population been targeted in this way,” she said.
Nicaraguan exiles are split on how Saénz's case should be handled.
Miguel Mora, a former prisoner who arrived in the U.S. in the same group as Sáenz and also has a pending asylum case, said Sáenz’s involvement in the 2018 repression made the case “complicated,” but he said “it corresponds exclusively to U.S. authorities to determine, based on the law and the evidence in the case, if he does or does not have the right to asylum.”
Danny Ramírez-Ayérdiz, a Nicaraguan lawyer and founder of the Interamerican Center for Legal Assistance in Human Rights that investigates abuses of the Ortega-Murillo government, said that Sáenz should be held accountable for his alleged crimes — but only after a political transition in Nicaragua, when he could be extradited there to face justice.
“But if they send him to Nicaragua now, he’s at a risk of dying,” Ramírez-Ayérdiz said. “Just like other former Sandinistas, the government would be particularly cruel with him.”
Manuel Prado, vice president of the Miskitu American Organization, which advocates for the rights of Nicaraguan Indigenous groups, said the outcome of Sáenz’s case will send a message about how Nicaragua will move forward “to heal the nation.”

STMicro's 2027 AI revenue to be four-fifths optics, CFO says
Sept 9 : About 80 per cent of the more than $2 billion in AI data-centre revenue STMicroelectronics is targeting for 2027 will come from chips used in fibre-optic data links, its finance chief said on Wednesday, providing the first breakdown of a target the company raised in July.
The remaining 20 per cent will come from chips used for cooling systems and power conversion inside servers, Chief Financial Officer Lorenzo Grandi told Citi's Global TMT Conference in New York.
"Short term will be mainly driven by the connectivity portion," Grandi said.
He added that ST's presence in server power is currently limited and that the company does not expect meaningful revenue from the business before 2028.
The comments show that, for now, the AI business of one of Europe's largest chipmakers is concentrated in connectivity chips, with the larger opportunity in server power expected to emerge only after 2028.

- The claim that serial killer Jeffrey Dahmer, who cannibalized parts of his victims' bodies, said he didn't eat people with tattoos because "tattoos taste terrible" is unproven.
- The rumor stems from numerous posts on Instagram and Facebook affiliated with tattoo artists or tattoo parlors of a meme facetiously encouraging people to get tattoos.
- We looked through numerous recorded interviews and FBI reports about Dahmer and found no evidence he ever mentioned tattoos in connection with his crimes.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces.
In August 2026, an online quote spread online claiming serial killer Jeffrey Dahmer, who ate the flesh of some of his victims, said he didn't cannibalize people with tattoos because the ink tasted bad. The rumor spread on Instagram, Reddit and Facebook.
Snopes readers have been sending us this particular Dahmer anecdote for years. Some asked us to confirm whether Dahmer actually said, "I ate someone with a tattoo once. Made the meat taste like s***." A post on Instagram stated Dahmer said that "tattoos taste terrible" and used it facetiously to encourage people to get tattoos and save themselves from cannibals.
(Instagram user @dark_grey_tattoo)
Snopes looked closely at interviews, FBI reports and documentaries detailing Dahmer's crimes and found no evidence he ever made such a comment. We did find, however, that the claim is often posted by tattoo artists and studios as an advertisement encouraging people to get tattoos. Until we learn more, we will leave this claim as unproven.
Dahmer killed 17 young men and boys over the course of 13 years. In 1992, he was convicted of murder and handed 15 consecutive life sentences in prison. Two years later, another inmate beat him to death.
In interviews with the news media and FBI agents, Dahmer spoke of eating his victim's hearts, livers and thigh meat, and one time ate a bicep as a way of keeping them "a part of me." FBI agent Robert Ressler interviewed Dahmer, who described his actions as a "perverse sexual practice."
In 1993, Inside Edition conducted an interview with Dahmer while he was in prison. He didn't say anything about tattoos.
The Netflix documentary series "Conversations with a Killer: The Jeffrey Dahmer Tapes" shed more light on his inclinations. Interviews with law enforcement showed he liked certain body types and offered to take his victims' photographs. In one instance he cut off and preserved a victim's head and genitals. He also took photos of body parts of victims he liked. Dahmer described having sex with the insides of a person in his interview recordings with investigators.
We were unable to find evidence that Dahmer confessed a preference for eating untattooed skin in any of those sources.
Snopes has covered numerous claims about Dahmer, including the true story of how Milwaukee police returned a victim, Konerak Sinthasomphone, to Dahmer after accepting the serial killer's explanation that the injured 14-year-old boy was his lover.

The Last Thing Teenagers Will Let You Teach Them
An interesting shift happens when a kid is learning to drive, and you’re both inside a box with your fear, moving 40 miles an hour.
A strange thing happened to me in a deserted parking lot on a recent Sunday morning: My 16-year-old daughter actually asked me a question.
I was telling her everything I know about reversing a car without the help of a backup camera. “First turn your whole body, shoulders rotated, right hand on the back of the passenger seat, until you’re looking out the rear window at the world behind you.” Her hands were on the wheel. Her phone was face down in the cup holder. She turned her body the way I’d suggested and nudged the wheel to the left, and the car floated backward in a woozy arc that wasn’t quite what she’d intended. “Wait,” she said. “Do I turn with both hands? Did I do that wrong?”
I want to stop here, because I don’t think I can convey just how unusual such an exchange is these days—her listening to me and asking for help. Sometime in the past year, she stopped wanting anything from me other than my credit card and maybe my nicest suede boots. She definitely stopped wanting my instruction, my opinion, my take on anything, having concluded that she already understands pretty much everything.
The talking is what I have missed. For 14 or 15 years, my daughter narrated in a fire hose of chatter—to me, to her father, to whoever. So much talking: about why the sun sets, the kid she was mad at, the plot of a show she was three episodes into, how she wanted to decorate her room. Around the start of high school, the talking thinned out, siphoned almost exclusively to her friends. Nothing announced the change. It went the way a baby tooth goes, loose for a while and then simply absent.
When she got a learner’s permit, some measure of talking reappeared. It wasn’t fully restored, exactly, but confined within one small, sealed space that moves. Inside the car, she knows she doesn’t know: In no version of parallel parking can she wing it without asking for tips from someone who has done it 10,000 times. Learning to drive is something she cannot fake her way through.
This wobbly uncertainty, this return to a kind of innocence, is the rarest condition in a 16-year-old, and it lasts about as long as a learner’s permit does. So my daughter asks, and listens, and we manage to simply talk in some of the ways we haven’t in a long time: about what her friends did over the summer, which kid at the pool where she lifeguards asked her if she could babysit them. For an hour at a stretch I get a version of my daughter that I had filed away as gone for good.
But this is also, in some ways, the worst hour of my week, because the terms of a driving lesson are the exact inverse of the many other kinds of lessons that came before it. Everything else I ever taught my daughter, I did with one hand on the thing: I steadied the tail end of the bike, I held the knife and moved her fingers back from the blade, I grasped her hand crossing Seventh Avenue for so many years that my palm still expects to find hers at intersections. In the car, though, she has the wheel, and I have the fear. My only instrument is my voice, which is not connected to anything that stops the car.
Parents say they’re letting go or loosening the reins or handing over the keys, as if adolescence were a series of small, deliberate releases, each one manageable. Then you hand over the actual keys, and the metaphor becomes a physical arrangement staged on a public road at 40 miles an hour, at which point it breaks. First there is supervised driving, and soon there is nothing. In between, the passenger seat is one of the few places on Earth where a parent gets to occupy two conditions at once: maximum proximity plus zero control.
I have thought about this a lot from that seat, just 18 inches from my daughter, slowly understanding that being nearby was never the same as keeping her safe. Ever since she was born, I had assumed that being close to her was a form of protecting her. I could catch her if she slipped. In the car, that assumption comes apart, and all I can do is sit there with my fear.
What surprised me is that the fear runs both ways.
For the first time in years, my daughter is frightened of something in front of both of us rather than scared of something I might do to embarrass her—that is, afraid of me. That distinction turns out to be enormous. Since she hit adolescence, her anxiety, in my presence, has generally been about whether I would say something wacky (yes!), make a dumb joke (also yes!), or exist too loudly in a space containing her peers (duh). I have been the weather she is bracing against. But in the car, we are braced against the same thing, and it is outside the windshield. A massive truck backs out without looking; a cyclist suddenly appears. We both suck in air at the same instant, and her hand and my hand tighten—hers on the wheel, mine on nothing.
Coming to a stop at a red light, she sees me sending a text from the passenger seat. “I can’t understand how anyone texts and drives,” she says, almost bewildered, the way a fifth grader might talk about someone doing calculus in their head. At that moment, she is using every part of her brain to keep a two-ton object between two painted lines, and the idea that a person could do this and tap out a message strikes her as physically impossible. I agree with her, but what I don’t say is that practicing will help her rethink this. Competence makes the risk available. One day she will be good enough at driving to consider being more careless about it.
As she improves and gains confidence, the driving, for her, slowly grows less frightening and more thrilling. She presses the accelerator, her foot more sure, and we both know that she is on the edge of a huge new expanse of freedom and change—that driving lessons are not about a test to pass but a way to get farther than she has ever gotten on her own. The shared fear is temporary, and I can already feel the expiration date on it.
Some Sunday soon, we’ll have our last lesson. And what I’ll miss isn’t the driving; it’s the asking—the tacit admission that she doesn’t know everything—and how she lets her guard down while she’s admitting it. When the questions end, she’ll be very much on her way, and I’ll be the boots and the credit card again, which, I remind myself, is part of the assignment too.

Family of killed teen call for death penalty in D4vd trial
- Published
The family of 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez has lobbied for the death penalty if D4vd is found guilty murdering their daughter.
D4vd, who was born David Anthony Burke, is charged with killing the teenager, whose dismembered body was found in the trunk of a Tesla car registered to his address on 8 September 2025. Burke has pleaded not guilty to the charges.
The death penalty is under a temporary ban in California, where Burke is due to stand trial, but in a statement Hernandez' family said execution "would be perfect" if the singer was convicted of murder.
In a related development, Hernandez's parents filed a civil lawsuit against Burke on Friday, seeking monetary damages including burial and funeral expenses.
The lawsuit, lodged at Los Angeles Superior Court and reported by multiple, external US media outlets, external, makes similar claims to those raised by prosecutors in the criminal case against the singer.
Mercedes Martinez and Jesus Rivas allege that Burke caused the wrongful death, false imprisonment and childhood sexual assault of their daughter.
In the court documents, they say Burke and Hernandez first met in November 2023, when she was 13 years old.
Over the next 16 months, they claim, the pair would exchange almost 10,000 texts and have sex several times.
"At all relevant times Burke was an adult who occupied a position of authority over decedent, a minor, and was able to and did exercise undue influence and control over her," the parents say, in papers filed last Friday.
They go on to claim that Burke killed the teenager at his Hollywood Hills home, when she threatened to reveal their relationship, after allegedly sending a message that read: "I will end ur career and ur life".
In addition to Burke, the lawsuit names several of Burke's companies and managers, his mother and a live-in security guard.
Hernandez's parents allege that these people "enabled Burke to isolate" Rivas Hernandez and facilitated his travel, housing and security.
Burke's management company Mogul Vision and finance manager have previously denied knowing about Burke and Rivas Hernandez, the Los Angeles Times, external reported.
In July, a judge found enough probable cause for Burke to stand trial on the murder charge in the criminal case. At the time, the district attorney said he was weighing whether to seek the death penalty.
In a statement on Monday, which would have been Hernandez's 16th birthday, her family demanded that Burke be subjected to execution.
"If the death penalty were activated, it would be perfect for this kind of human being, devoid of feelings and emptiness inside, and without conscience, who only caused pain to our daughter, our family, and the world that supports our precious daughter," read the statement, released via the family's attorney.
Burke again pleaded not guilty to the charges last week and has since parted ways with his celebrity defence attorney. He is now being represented by a public defender and is due back in court on 19 October. His trial has been moved to next year.
Deputy public defender Walid Kandeel has said that Burke was "entitled to a defence that takes his circumstances seriously and carefully examines the evidence".
"We are committed to providing him with that defence," he said.
His office did not immediately provide comment on the civil lawsuit.

Tamil Nadu recorded nearly 45,000 fewer births in 2025 than the previous year, with the number of births falling by 5.3% from 8.47 lakh in 2024 to 8.02 lakh, pointing to a continuing decline in births in the State.
The decline comes against the backdrop of a long-term fall in fertility in the State. In 2026, five lakh-odd births were recorded so far, according to Civil Registration System data.”
While the decline in births reflects a broader demographic transition, with implications for the workforce and ageing population, experts say greater attention must be paid to education, childcare, social security, elderly care and standard of living.
T. Sundararaman, former executive director, National Health Systems Resource Centre, said the total fertility rate among women of reproductive age fell below the replacement level of 2.1 in Tamil Nadu nearly 20 years ago. “We continued to have a positive population growth rate because of population momentum. We have now moved beyond this phenomenon and a decline in the population is likely to occur,” he said.
S. Irudaya Rajan, chairperson, International Institute for Migration and Development, Thiruvananthapuram, pointed out that Tamil Nadu is better placed compared with Kerala, which has recorded around three lakh births.
“There will be no short-term impact. The State government can focus on creating a productive, healthy population of eight lakh-plus by investing in quality education over the next 20 to 25 years. The focus should be on quality rather than quantity,” he said.
“First of all, there is no need to worry about the low fertility rate or the decline in births,” Padmavathi Srinivasan, independent research consultant in demography, said, adding: “This opens up opportunities to increase and improve the standard of living and enable people to better access the State’s resources. The State government should seize this opportunity and capitalise on low fertility.”
Observing that politicians would worry about what would happen to the State’s labour force, she said, “but this is the time to focus on education and employment opportunities. Tamil Nadu is a prosperous State, but this prosperity needs to translate to better living standards.”
“It would be an injustice if the State focussed on increasing fertility and channelled government funds towards it. Rather, it should focus on the existing population, especially the youth. The State should pay attention to the foundations, such as quality education and the nutritional status of children. There are still pockets of people living in poverty, those who have no access to opportunities and have not benefitted from the State’s economic growth.”
Financial incentives to reverse low fertility rates have never worked, as evidenced in many developed countries, she said, asking: “So, why go down that route, when there are much more pressing issues we need to tackle.”
Professor Rajan said the State government’s “Thaimaman Thanga Mothiram Thittam”, under which one-gram gold rings will be gifted to babies born in government hospitals, is unlikely to help increase births. Increasing maternity leave to women government employees for a third child cannot be considered a meaningful incentive, he believed.
Policies alone will not help much. At best, they may add another 5,000-odd births, he said. “Children are assets, but when you ask couples today, many consider them liabilities. This mindset should change. Increasing the fertility rate is not simple, given factors such as delayed marriages. To motivate young couples to have children, we need out-of-the-box, innovative ideas.”
Priority areas
Professor Sundararaman said increasing longevity means that there will be more people aged 65 or 70 and above. “At the same time, we will have less working age population and a larger elderly population that needs to be cared for. This has already happened in most developed countries that have stronger social security systems and better elderly care,” he said.
“I am less worried about productivity and more concerned about social security and elderly care. We need policies that anticipate these changes,” he added.
Efforts simply to increase childbearing are unlikely to work. What can make a difference is providing child care support for the first two children, he said. “We need to have innovative thinking and creative community-based efforts for elderly care. Our priorities should include elderly care, social security, child care support, good quality primary education and measures that make it easier for working women for childcare. Funds should be better utilised to establish facilities, such as creches for working women,” he added.

ARPA-H, the government agency that funds cutting-edge health research, plans to commit $62.7 million to develop artificial intelligence bots that direct treatment of heart failure. Among the goals of the program, called ADVOCATE, is to produce partially autonomous AI devices authorized by the Food and Drug Administration to help treat patients, including assessing symptom severity, prescribing drugs, and ordering lab tests.
ARPA-H on Wednesday announced the first batch of awards to health tech companies Atman Health, UpDoc, Tempus AI, and teams from Stanford University, Duke University, and the Kaiser Permanente health system. ARPA-H may still fund additional teams. The amount committed for the first year is $33.7 million, and the remainder may be renegotiated up or down.
Many of the 6.7 million Americans with heart failure don’t get optimal treatment because of difficulty accessing specialists, and the hope is that AI agents developed with ARPA-H funding can help address the gap, especially in rural and other underserved settings.

What may be the earliest known evidence for human drug taking has been traced to ancient Indonesian foragers who sucked on mind-altering nuts as long as 25,000 years ago.
Analysis of two exceptionally rare skeletons from the Indonesian island of Sulawesi revealed dramatic tooth wear and traces of a psychoactive substance in the individuals’ remaining teeth, suggesting they routinely sucked on hard, abrasive betel nuts.
Although little known in western societies, betel nuts are the world’s fourth most widely used psychoactive substance after alcohol, caffeine and nicotine, with an estimated tenth of the global population chewing the seeds.
“We’ve found evidence for how this very common drug use habit, which is found throughout a lot of the Asia-Pacific region today, might have evolved,” said Prof Adam Brumm at Griffith University’s Australian Research Centre for Human Evolution in Brisbane.
The work began when the team examined skeletal remains of two pre-agricultural foragers unearthed at two different sites on the island. One was dated to about 7,000 years old, the other more ancient at 16,000 to 25,000 to years old.
Writing in Science Advances, the researchers describe how both adults had deep, rounded grooves in their teeth. Some went so deep they would have exposed the dental pulp. “I was thinking, what the hell were these people doing? It’s like someone had a drill head shaped like a gobstopper and wore away the inner part of the tooth,” said Brumm.
Betel nuts are actually the seeds of the Areca catechu palm, but are misnamed because they are often wrapped in betel vine leaves for chewing. Today, the nuts are typically chewed after being mixed with slaked lime made by grinding burnt shells to form a “quid”.
Brumm suspected the bizarre tooth wear was caused by the foragers holding hard, round and abrasive objects in their mouth, but what sort of object? “Imagine you kept a stone in your mouth and you moved it from one part of your mouth to another, and if you did that day after day, hour after hour. Eventually it would wear down your extremely hard dental tissue to form these grooves,” he said.
The team wondered whether the grooves were the result of foragers sucking on betel nuts before people realised that mixing the nuts with slaked lime helped release more of the psychoactive drug and intensify the “high”.
To test the hunch, the scientists soaked betel nuts in artificial saliva and found that it soon contained enough of the psychoactive compound arecoline to induce a high, albeit a milder one than when the nut is chewed. Analysis of the foragers’ teeth found traces of arecoline in the tissues.
“I’ve sucked on a nut as an experiment and it’s a really bitter, astringent taste. It makes your mouth go numb and I think that’s what they were interested in,” Brumm said.
“This might have been a traditional remedy for toothache, but if they did it for too long, sucking on the nut wore down their teeth so badly that it actually created much worse dental pain in the long term. These individuals were seemingly caught in a self-perpetuating cycle where they were continually sucking on the nuts to treat the tooth pain caused by this nut-sucking habit.”
While humans probably began using mind-altering plants as soon as they encountered them, the oldest traditions of psychoactive drug use are thought to have arisen about 13,000 years ago with fermented drinks such as barley beer.
Dr Elisa Guerra-Doce, an associate professor in European prehistory at the University of Valladolid in Spain, said the study provided “direct evidence of the antiquity of human drug use”.
“These findings not only represent the earliest known evidence to date of the use of psychoactive plants anywhere in the world, but also demonstrate that the consumption of Areca nuts is a millennia-old tradition dating back to prehistoric times,” she added.

Asian Games venues and athletes unharmed by extensive flooding in Nagoya, Japan
The mayor of Nagoya says athletes who’ve arrived early for the Asian Games were unharmed by extensive flooding that hit the central Japanese city
NAGOYA, Japan -- Athletes who've arrived early for the Asian Games were unharmed by extensive flooding that hit the central Japanese city of Nagoya, Mayor Ichiro Hirosawa said Wednesday.
“We are not worried about the conditions of the venues and we believe there is no problem holding the Asian Games as planned,” Hirosawa told reporters.
The Asian Games, an event with more athletes than the Summer Olympics, open Sept. 19 in Nagoya and surrounding areas and run through Oct. 4.
More than 11,000 athletes are signed up from 45 countries and regions in Asia. By comparison, about 10,700 athletes participated in the Summer Olympics in 2024 in Paris.
The previous edition of the Asian Games was held three years ago in Hangzhou, China.
Hirosawa said about 400 athletes and staff who are staying in converted shipping containers — remodeled to serve as temporary housing units for the Asian Games — were briefly evacuated to higher ground during the heavy rain.
He said there were a number of leaking roofs but nothing more serious around the dozens of Games venues.
Record rain fell in parts of the city on Tuesday, flooding dozens of roads and homes, and stranding pedestrians and vehicles. City bus and subway operations were temporarily suspended, the mayor said.
Reports said about 3,500 people took shelter at emergency evacuation centers.
