Trump’s Midterm Strategy Is All About Him
Traditionally, candidates laboring under the burden of an unpopular president seek to detach themselves from the national brand.
Is Donald Trump trying to help Republicans win the midterm elections? The obvious answer to this question is yes, of course, simply because all political leaders benefit from their party winning elections. Yet several of Trump’s actions throw this normally perfunctory question into at least some doubt.
Traditionally, candidates laboring under the burden of an unpopular president seek to detach themselves from the national brand. Trump is making this impossible. He has launched a national ad campaign focused on himself, and thrown a high-profile “midterm convention” designed to further reinforce the synonymity of the party and its leader. Trump has also made several remarks that convey an emotional detachment from the election’s outcome—comments such as “I’m not affected by the election” or “I don’t care about the midterms.”
Perhaps he is merely feigning indifference. Maybe he truly does not care. More likely, Trump cares about the outcome, but not enough to permit Republicans to acknowledge his lack of popularity. His approach, at any rate, nicely illustrates the drawbacks of handing total control of a political party to an egomaniac.
Midterm elections have historically disfavored the president’s party. Candidates for office who are running in neutral or hostile territory accordingly tend to emphasize their differences with the president—think of Joe Manchin running an ad in West Virginia in 2010 showing him firing an actual bullet at Barack Obama’s cap-and-trade bill, or the Republican Will Hurd in 2018 criticizing Trump’s racism and affinity for Russia.
Trump’s public standing is unusually dire. He is currently polling far worse than either he did at this point in 2018 or Joe Biden did four years ago. In theory, this ought to give Republicans an especially strong incentive to edge away from Trump and emphasize local themes in their elections.
Trump has decided to block this escape route. He is commandeering earned media with his “Trumpapalooza” show, drawing attention to the person endangered Republicans desperately need their constituents to forget. He has hoarded the party’s ad budget, warning Republicans, “This is my money that I control,” and that he would spend it on “Republicans that I think are good,” which is to say, slavishly loyal. He has promised to barnstorm the country, telling reporters, “I’ll be making a lot of stops,” including in Alaska, where the Republican Dan Sullivan is trailing.
There is an old Simpsons episode in which the elderly oligarch Montgomery Burns informs the obsequious Smithers that, upon his own death, his loyal aide will be buried alive at his boss’s feet. Trump appears to be thinking along similar lines.
This self-defeating behavior makes a degree of sense if you accept that Trump’s interest in politics is purely egocentric. He has difficulty caring about anything that does not directly involve himself, and the prospect of Republicans holding seats by repudiating his record is likely unpalatable.
The benefits of same-party control of Congress are also smaller for Trump than other presidents, because he governs mainly through executive action. To the extent that a Democratic majority in either chamber might threaten him with oversight, he will surely disregard it, as he did during his first term. Although he finds Republican majorities preferable, the size of those majorities matters to him far less than their composition—a fully loyal minority may seem preferable to a fractious majority.
What makes less sense is the willingness of many Republicans to cooperate with a strategy that consigns many of them to defeat.
Consider, for instance, Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate candidate in Michigan. Rogers came up through politics long before Trump entered it, and is trying to win office in a state where the president’s approval rating is 25 points underwater. A recent poll of the state found Trump’s endorsement made voters less likely, by a 55 percent to 27 percent margin, to support a candidate. Yet Rogers has opened no daylight whatsoever with the unpopular president, even echoing his false claims of having the 2020 election stolen from him. When Trump launched a trade war with Canada, a move that poses an especially dire threat to Rogers’s own state, he declined to take the opportunity to display independence. Instead, he issued a statement mumbling his approval. (“President Trump is right to put America First—and tariffs are necessary, but are not a one-size-fits-all solution.”) The same dynamic is occurring in other races, where Trump is throwing himself behind incumbents who are in danger mainly because voters don’t like him.
To be sure, some Republicans subscribe to the theory that the Trump era has suspended normal midterm election dynamics. According to this account, a decisive sliver of voters are loyal to Trump, and not his party. Republicans can win only by enticing them to vote, which means making the election about their hero. “We’ve seen that a lot of Trump voters—they will crawl over glass to vote for the president,” one Republican strategist explained to Politico.
Yet Trump has tried before to insert himself into non-presidential elections. And his efforts have mostly failed—not only in the 2018 midterms, when he refused to lie low, but also in multiple off-schedule elections (the most famous case being Georgia’s 2021 Senate runoff, which he made into a referendum on his effort to overturn the 2020 election). In the Trump era, his party has fared well only when it has been able to focus on the shortcomings of unpopular Democratic opponents, such as Hillary Clinton in 2016 and Biden and Kamala Harris in 2024. Making elections about Trump—which also occurred when he ran for reelection in 2020—has been a losing gambit.
The political tip sheets in recent days have been filled with the lamentations of fatalistic Republican operatives. “We have no choice. We’re stuck on the boat with him whether we like it or not,” a top Republican campaign official confessed to Axios. They cannot stop Trump from staging Trumpapalooza, so they are reduced to praying for low ratings. “My only hope is that no one watches it since it’s competing versus NFL opening games,” a person close to the White House told Politico. “Hopefully nobody notices the embarrassing show.” Republicans are cooperating in a strategy that sacrifices their best chance of political survival, because the past decade has trained them to believe that resistance to Trump is futile.
Trump did far less damage to the country during his first term, both because institutions and norm-following officials restrained him, and because his pathological instincts frequently undermined his support. The former limitation has broken down in the second term, but the latter one remains. Trump’s support has collapsed in large part because of his own poor choices.

Editor’s note: This article contains descriptions of imagery depicting child sexual abuse. Reader discretion is strongly advised.
Early last month, Meta deleted around 50 ads posted on Facebook, Instagram, and Threads that directly included child sexual abuse material (CSAM), following reporting by WIRED. At the time, the company said that most of the abusive ads had been published prior to it rolling out new AI tools designed to “better detect and block” harmful ads being uploaded. That AI system, however, doesn’t appear to have been entirely effective.
Instead of spotting a decline in the abusive ads in recent weeks, researchers say they have now discovered hundreds more of the disturbing ads containing graphic sexual scenes involving children—including some that were identical to those Meta recently removed. More than 250 additional ads containing CSAM have run across Meta’s social media platforms since the start of August, according to researchers at the nonprofit Tech Transparency Project who shared its findings with WIRED. Unlike the 53 ads TTP researchers initially discovered, they were able to identify images of real children in the new ads.
These included sexual content depicting a minor belonging to a European royal family, transforming an officially released photograph into a video of a “graphic sex act.” The researchers are not naming the royal to protect the victim and say they contacted officials in the country. WIRED confirmed the source image came from the official website of a royal family.
“What we’re talking about here is not simply AI-generated child sex abuse material,” says Katie Paul, the director of the TTP. The researcher says it appears some images have been taken from the web before being used in the ads. “There’s a lot of harm that can come from this all while Meta is raking in money in the process.”
Overall, the researchers discovered that Meta has published more than 350 of the abusive video ads since the end of last year, with many of them linking to harmful harmful “nudification” apps linked to Chinese developers. In each instance, the researchers immediately reported the ads to US child safety authorities and through Meta’s reporting tools when ads were live and being shown to users at the time of their discovery. The researchers shared detailed findings with WIRED, which independently identified hundreds of other related “nudification” ads containing explicit content of adults on Meta’s platforms.
While the child abuse ads have now been removed for violating Meta’s policies on child exploitation, adult exploitation, and nudity, all of the ads were originally published despite the company’s policies saying it reviews all ads that run on its platforms. In some instances, the TTP researchers say, it took Meta a week to review live ads they had reported for containing CSAM with Meta’s tools. During that time, the ads racked up hundreds more views, according to screenshots seen by WIRED.
When some ads containing child sexual abuse were removed, TTP says, they did not initially include disclosures indicating that they violated Meta’s child sexual abuse policies; those details only appeared to be added after WIRED asked Meta about the discrepancy.
The cache of video ads published across Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, Threads, and Meta’s broader advertising network since the end of last year follow similar patterns. Many include an innocuous picture of a preteen or teenage girl—only one contained a boy, according to the researchers—and overlaid text saying it is “not just a photo” and “there are no restriction” [sic] on what can be done with the image. When the seconds-long video ads start playing, the children’s faces are morphed into graphic sexual videos, often showing them performing sex acts. When clicked, the ads directed people to download AI-face swapping or video apps from Apple and Google’s app stores. “This is the AI that men actually use,” many of the ads say.
Paul says the researchers were able to find the real-world identities of four minors whose images were used in the ads, three of which are from the US. “There were several photos from the same teen who has a social media influencer account on one of Meta’s platforms,” Paul says. The second instance involved another teen influencer who had a public account, the researcher says. “One was a stock photo model that was a real person,” Paul says of the third instance. “It was actually labeled as pre-teen on the stock photo websites.” The final instance was the European royal family member.
The researchers reported all of the ads they found to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children’s (NCMEC) CyberTipline, which allows people to report online child sexual abuse material, and say they are consulting on how to appropriately disclose their discoveries to the those impacted.
The ads were collectively shown to more than 29,000 accounts in countries across the European Union, plus around 7,000 accounts in the United Kingdom, according to data in Meta’s ad library, which shows live and archived ads, including the harmful ads that were no longer being shown to people. The ads were likely seen by thousands more people than Meta’s ad library indicates, with more than 250 of them appearing in the United States, 120 in Australia, and 80 in India, where Meta does not publish granular ad performance data.
“We don’t tolerate nudify apps or any kind of child exploitation, whether real or AI-generated,” says Meta spokesperson Tracy Clayton. The company has previously removed hundreds of thousands of ads for violating its policies on nudification. The statement claims that “many” of the ads found by the researchers had already been removed and most had fewer than 200 impressions, with the company receiving “under $5,000” in ad payments.
In an email to WIRED, Meta says it reports child exploitation content to NCMEC and is reporting the ads to the organization. Meta minimized the findings by saying that the AI-generated videos featured adults and the clips of the minors were brief or blurred, which made detection of the content more difficult. “The criminals behind this activity know we’ve built strong defenses, including systems that block violating ads as well as ongoing monitoring in case we initially miss something,” Clayton says.
The TTP researchers’ discovery of hundreds of ads containing child abuse material comes amid Meta paying up to $16.7 billion to settle lawsuits over its social networks allegedly harming children. Meta is also appealing a New Mexico court decision that, if enacted, would require it to improve its CSAM reporting processes and include human reviews in the state.
Multiple lawmakers and regulators now say they are investigating or looking into the ads following WIRED’s reporting. “It is disappointing that Meta continues to run ads featuring child sexual abuse material and nonconsensual intimate images after it was brought to their attention,” says Virginia senator Mark Warner, who sent Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg a letter following WIRED’s initial reporting. The letter has not been replied to yet, according to Warner’s office. “Meta needs to follow their own advertising standards, heed the call, and put an end to these illegal and inappropriate ads,” he says. (Meta tells WIRED it will reply to the letter).
A spokesperson for Michigan’s attorney general says their office “is aware of reports concerning AI‑generated child sexual abuse material appearing in advertising on Meta. This is extremely troubling, and we are actively looking into the matter.” Similarly, Florida attorney general James Uthmeier posted on X that his office is “investigating.”
Meanwhile, a spokesperson for Australia’s eSafety internet regulator says it is “highly concerned” by the reports and that it is assessing Meta’s compliance with its rules. It says it has requested “information on this matter from the company at a senior level.”
Lacking Protections
Over the last six years, dozens of AI nudification or “undress” apps and websites have flourished online, with them being used to harm countless women and girls. As this dangerous nonconsensual intimate imagery (NCII) ecosystem has continued to grow, with those behind it estimated to be earning millions each year, child protection organizations have warned the technology is “increasingly” used to create CSAM.
“AI apps are making it far too easy to create realistic criminal imagery of child sexual abuse, creating the new risk of everyday photos of children being taken and transformed into sexual content,” says Emma Hardy, director of communications at the Internet Watch Foundation, a UK-based nonprofit which removes child abuse content from the web. “Platforms and companies must make sure there is nowhere these apps can be advertised and spread.”
As WIRED previously reported, some of the ads discovered by TTP researchers were posted by Chinese companies that act as ad “resellers” in the country, where Meta’s platforms are banned. Many of the apps the ads linked to also appear to have Chinese connections, according to TTP. (Meta has previously launched legal action against a Hong Kong-based company linked to one set of nudifier platforms).
The ads pointed people towards almost 50 apps combined across Google’s Play Store and Apple’s App Store. Of the 350 ads, the researchers say that around 300 of them directed people to AI image or video generator ads, with most of these apps being linked to China-based developers. Some apps had already been removed by the time WIRED started reporting this story.
Among those that would generate explicit imagery of adults were eight identical apps listed on Apple’s App Store, multiple of which were linked to Chinese developer names. When the apps opened, they would show explicit AI-generated content, including a menu of sexual scenarios, including one called “threatening knife” where a knife is held to a woman’s throat. WIRED identified another seven identical apps that shared the same design, explicit content, and listed the same developer contact details.
“The App Store was designed to be a safe and trusted place for users, and we have zero tolerance for developers who deliberately attempt to evade our review process,” says Apple spokesperson Adam Dema. “The developers mentioned in this report initially submitted apps that are compliant with the App Review Guidelines, only to later surface nudify capabilities, which are against our rules.” The company says that 17 of the 20 apps included in the research had already been removed from its store and it has taken action against the remaining three, as well as removing the seven apps WIRED found.
Google spokesperson Dan Jackson says the company does not allow apps that contain sexual content or the ability to nudify. “We continually take proactive steps to detect and remove apps with harmful content,” they say, adding that it removed all the apps included in the report. “When violations are reported to us, we investigate and take swift action, which in the case of these apps has included suspending hundreds of violating apps and restricting related search terms like ‘nudify’ on our store.”
“The share of Chinese developers creating nudify apps has grown year over year,” says David Pham, a former Meta employee who investigated nonconsensual imagery and abuse on its platforms. Pham says that while at Meta he observed similar ads to those discovered by the researchers and those uploading the content would constantly try to get around safety systems.
“Every time the platform or investigators would build a new detection model or a new way to have some type of enforcement, they quickly—within a day, maybe five days—built a new way to avoid detection,” Pham says. Those uploading the ads would change domains they used, obscure who posted them, and include measures such as blurring imagery or subtly changing images to avoid detection. However, Pham, who left Meta last year, says it has the funding and resources to be able to tackle the uploads. “I would like to live in a world where we’re not getting CSAM or NCII material sent directly to our phones,” he says.
Meta’s current protections against ads containing CSAM and NCII appear to need work. More than 11,000 undress ads have appeared on Meta’s platforms since February this year, according to a recent Indicator Media report, with many of these being reportedly posted by “repeat offenders.” Analysis by WIRED also found hundreds of ads including explicit content that contain similar language to those ads found by the TTP researchers. (Meta says malicious advertisers use adversarial tactics to continually try to avoid its detection systems and it has “incorporated” the language in the ads highlighted by WIRED into its moderation systems.)
One ad containing one of the teenagers that the researchers found the real-world identity of was reported to Meta when it had reached four accounts in Europe, according to the TTPs research. However, when it was removed days later, it had been seen by more than 330 users. “This is not something that it should take a small nonprofit doing research to stumble across and then have to investigate and report,” Paul from TTP says. “We’re talking about one of the most well-resourced— technologically and financially—companies on the planet.”

A plane carrying Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy narrowly avoided a collision with an unidentified drone while taking off from Moldova en route to Oslo for the funeral of King Harald V.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store confirmed the incident in an interview with public broadcaster NRK on Wednesday, highlighting the security risks surrounding the Ukrainian leader's movements.
“His plane was almost hit by a drone as it was taking off from Moldova. That is the reality he is facing,” PM told NRK.
The incident has not yet been confirmed by Ukrainian authorities.
Zelenskyy safely arrived in Oslo on Tuesday evening after departing Moldova to attend the royal funeral service alongside world leaders and international dignitaries. He had earlier met Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre.
Providing further details, State Secretary Bhanuja Rasiah at the Prime Minister's Office told NRK that the airspace threat affected the Ukrainian president's flight schedule.
"There was a drone threat in the airspace over Moldova yesterday, which delayed Zelenskyy's flight on its way to Oslo. These are threats he lives with every day. It is uncertain how close the drones were to his plane." 
NRK cited him as saying.
Norwegian finance minister Jens Stoltenberg also confirmed that Zelenskyy personally recounted the incident shortly after arriving in the Norwegian capital.
"He told us about it last night when we had a meeting with him. I don't dare go into the details about it, but he was delayed, and there were some threats against the plane. But I don't know enough about the details to explain anything more," Stoltenberg said.
"There were some problems getting out, but it's never easy to get out of Ukraine. But the most important thing was that he took the time, the effort it took for him to come to the funeral," he added.
Despite the security risks during the journey, Stoltenberg said Zelenskyy's presence at the funeral was significant. He noted that it was impressive to see the Ukrainian president walking alongside other world leaders during King Harald's funeral on Wednesday, NRK reported.
Following his attendance at the funeral, Zelenskyy paid tribute to the late monarch in a post on X.
"We paid our respects to King Harald V. Ukraine will always be grateful to Norway for all its assistance. This support comes not only from the government, but also from the Royal Family and all the people of Norway. I recall with gratitude our warm meeting with His Majesty and the special attention he paid to Ukraine. He was a monarch who, for over 35 years, embodied Norway – its openness, dignity, and respect for people. Over that time, our bond with Norway has grown especially strong."
Zelenskyy also expressed gratitude for Norway's continued support for Ukraine amid the ongoing conflict.
"We are grateful that Norway has stood with Ukraine all these years. Thank you for the decisions that are helping us protect people and stand firm today."
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy said Ukrainian defence forces had carried out successful long-range strikes against a major Russian naval base, as Russian drone and missile attacks killed and wounded civilians across several Ukrainian cities.
In another post on X, Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces had struck key targets deep inside Russian territory, including the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk in the Krasnodar region.
The strikes against Russian infrastructure came as emergency crews were deployed across Ukraine following another wave of deadly Russian drone attacks targeting civilian infrastructure.
Zelenskyy said Russian strikes in Sumy, Kyiv and Mykolaiv had killed several people and left others seriously injured.
Calling on international partners to increase their support to help end the escalation, he wrote, “Right now, it is important for all partners to focus as much as possible and work on the relevant steps toward de-escalation and an end to the killing,”
Zelenskyy said he had discussed the situation with representatives of US President Donald Trump's team as well as European leaders.
His remarks came after talks in Kyiv with US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.
Zelenskyy said three rounds of discussions with the US delegation had taken place and described them as substantive, expressing hope that the talks would help revive negotiations and lead to a lasting peace agreement.
Earlier, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Russia welcomed US President Donald Trump's efforts to bring peace to the region.
With Russia continuing its strikes and diplomatic efforts yet to yield a breakthrough, a lasting peace agreement remains elusive.

Google Workspace is that ubiquitous modern business tool that almost feels invisible. We use it every day here at WIRED, whether that's for writing first drafts of articles in Docs, analyzing data in Sheets, or sharing files in Drive. And recently, I've been using the Gemini AI implementation that's built right into these tools, which is handy in all sorts of ways.
Google Workspace grants access to all kinds of productivity features that can help streamline processes and increase communication within a team or organization. It's not free, but here's the good news: If you're looking at a Workspace account for yourself (or for your team), Google is offering discounts until the end of 2026 using one of the Google Workspace coupon codes below. You can save up to 14 percent on plans for the first three months, whether you're signing up as an individual or as a business. Either way, the Google Workspace promo code down below is what you want to use.
Save up to 14% Off These Google Workspace Promo Codes 2026
There are some notable differences between each Workspace plan – I’ll dig into them in the next section – but all three plans come with access to the full slate of Workspace apps. You get Gmail, Drive, Calendar, and Meet, of course, but even the cheapest Starter plan includes basic access to Google’s other apps, such as NotebookLM and Gemini inside the Workspace suite. If you want to save, make sure to click one of the promo codes at the top of this page to secure your discount.
What Is the Best Google Workspace Plan?
Google offers four different Workspace plans, though only three are relevant for most people. There’s Starter, Standard, and Plus, as well as Enterprise, which is only available if you contact Google’s sales team. There isn’t a minimum number of users on any of the plans, but the bottom three options (Starter, Standard, and Plus) support up to 300 users. If you need more than that, you’ll need an Enterprise plan.
Although you have access to all the apps regardless of the plan you choose, there are some important differences, particularly between the Starter and Standard plans. Both include secure storage through Google Drive, but Starter comes with 30GB per user while Standard comes with a massive 2TB per user. Plus bumps that up to 5TB per user. Across all plans, storage is in a shared pool, so each additional user adds to the total pool of storage your organization can use.
Gemini is also a big difference between Starter and Standard. Although both have access to the Gemini app, Starter only has Gemini in Gmail and Vids. Standard (and Plus) includes Gemini across the full suite, including in Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, Meet, and Chat.
Starter is a great option for anyone just getting started, regardless of if you’re a freelancer or a small business with a handful of employees. In addition to 30GB per user and limited access to Gemini, Starter comes with a few other limitations. It doesn’t support e-signatures in Docs, nor advanced features of Meet, such as noise cancellation. The bread and butter of Workspace is all here, though. You get a custom domain in Gmail, up to 100 participants in Meet, and the full Google suite of productivity apps.
Standard, as the name suggests, is Workspace proper, and it’s built for teams that need room to grow. That shows up most clearly in storage space, jumping from 30GB to 2TB per user. Standard basically cuts all the red tape on Starter. There aren’t any limitations on Gemini (it’s available across the full suite), Meet features like noise cancellation are available, and you can host up to 150 participants in a Meet call. Standard even comes with expanded access to NotebookLM, Google’s AI-driven note and research tool, with different chat modes and up to 20 generative audio overviews per day.
At the top of the range is Plus, which is focused on larger businesses. You don’t get any extra apps with this plan, but you do get 5TB of storage per user, along with up to 500 participants in Meet calls. The real reason to upgrade to Plus is security and admin controls, however. It includes Vault for data retention, along with LDAP access – basically a server for centralized account management, if you aren’t familiar.
Most people should use the Standard plan, not only for the large amount of storage space over Starter, but also due to the extra Gemini functionality. If you need to upgrade to Plus down the line, you can. And, more than likely, you’ll have a member of your IT team begging you to do so.
Why Teams Love Using Google Workspace Flows with Google Workspace
Google has updated Workspace a lot over the past several months, building in new functionalities via Gemini throughout the suite. But earlier this year, Google announced that it’s bringing all of those functionalities together through Workspace Flows. It’s a no-code automation tool that lets you build automatic workflows; i.e. update a Sheet when there’s a new email in Gmail from a particular address. The interesting thing about Flows, however, is that Gemini is built into it.
You can set up basic automations, which is great given how interconnected Google’s Workspace apps already are, but Flows become powerful when you throw Gems into the mix. Gems are AI agents built with Gemini, and you can create them with specific parameters.
Let me give you an example. Say you need a marketing plan, and an employee sends you a draft. You can have a workflow set up with a Gem that’s been trained on the budget, requirements, and tone of the campaign to quickly know if it can be approved or not. Or, you can create a Gem to scan your email, trained on your organization chart and role responsibilities, to notify you whenever you receive an email that has action items for you.
Flows give you a way to add a bit of context and reasoning to the often rigid constraints of simple automation systems, and it can save you a lot of time in the process. You may be able to gather customer feedback and put it into Sheets easily, for example, but Gemini can automatically sort, summarize, and categorize that feedback so you know what you should tackle first. Flows are centralized to Workspace, as well; you don’t need to install add-ons or configure anything outside of setting up your Workspace account.
Google Workspace Flows is a new tool integrated with Google Workspace. It is powered by Google’s Gemini AI and helps you get tasks done with Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Calendar and Chat. It can fix up emails, make plans, correct sheets, or write a follow up message. No apps or links are needed.

Can AI fix health care?
It depends who you ask! But in the current chaos of emergency rooms, the technology has not yet changed the status quo, STAT’s Brittany Trang reports. In CDC restructuring, Covid now part of flu division
The CDC’s National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases is undergoing a reorganization, with Covid-19 and other respiratory diseases operations being consolidated under the influenza division. The change, which went into effect on Sept. 4, was revealed Tuesday in the Federal Register.
Though anything related to Covid is politically charged with the current administration, former CDC staffers — including Demetre Daskalakis, a former director of the NCIRD — say this change had been in the planning since the Biden administration and makes organizational sense. Funding for Covid has dropped as the disease burden from the virus has declined; putting its operations into the flu division will leverage resources both use. Daskalakis and others, though, warned that the consolidation itself could be rocky; NCIRD has had a series of acting directors since Daskalakis quit in August 2025. Telemedicine company offers GLP-1s for addiction
A new company, Quel, announced yesterday that it is launching as the first telemedicine venture built around GLP-1s for addiction. The services, available in 41 states, are an extension of a treatment program first tested at Caron Treatment Centers in Pennsylvania. STAT’s Lev Facher wrote last summer about the elite center’s use of semaglutide for addiction, describing it as a journey into uncharted territory. Only a handful of clinical trials existed at the time to test the ability of GLP-1s to reduce substance use. Dozens more such studies exist now, many of which focus on alcohol use disorder.
The FDA has not approved GLP-1s for substance use, so the medications will be prescribed off-label. “We’re using something off-label under the umbrella of addiction, whether that be food, sex, alcohol, or opioids,” physician Steven Klein told Lev last year. Klein is a co-founder and chief medical officer at Quel. Reread Lev’s great story.

WHO leader will not run for director-general
Jeremy Farrar, a global health leader who was long rumored as a potential candidate to become the next director-general of the World Health Organization, is definitely not entering the race. PATH, a leading global health NGO, announced Wednesday that Farrar is joining its staff on Oct. 1 to serve as chief of the Asia, Middle East, and Europe regional division, based in Geneva.
Farrar has a long history in global health work. He headed Oxford University’s Clinical Research Unit in Vietnam for 18 years — including during the 2003 SARS outbreak — before being named director of the Wellcome Trust, the London-based charity that funds biomedical research. 'Embarrassing' Pakistan break record in innings to forget
- Published
The only thing gloomier than the leaden skies at lunch on day one of the third Test at Edgbaston will have been the mood in the Pakistan dressing room as things went from bad to worse.
Downcast might be understating it.
A raft of controversial changes made by the Pakistan Cricket Board were supposed to act as a defibrillator to this team.
Despite the shock treatment there was little sense the tourists will be sparked back to life to finish this series with a flourish as they slumped to 133 all out.
There may have only been 33.5 overs in the game but already their cause in Birmingham looks a forlorn one. If you have tickets, even for day three, it might be worth considering making other plans.
Former Pakistan captain Ramiz Raja said Pakistan's "technique and mindset" were "pretty ordinary".
"There's mental fatigue and turmoil in the dugout, I can understand that," he told Test Match Special.
"They have not been proactive at all. They have to have a plan. This is a flat pitch, it's not a demon-like pitch, like the third day at Lord's."
In mitigation, CricViz's bounce inconsistency rating had this pitch at 5.7 which is higher than at Edgbaston in 2025 (2.6 vs India), 2024 (3.2 vs West Indies) and 2023 (3.3 vs Australia).
England, of course, bowled well. Their four-pronged seam attack hitting their straps after Joe Root had won the toss in Autumnal conditions.
Former England captain Michael Vaughan said that Pakistan were "clearly shot for confidence" after such a disastrous morning.
"I feel for Pakistan because this is embarrassing with everything they've had to cope with in the last week," he said.
Pakistan's top five were all gone with the score on the Thwaite Memorial scoreboard showing just 48.
It meant unwanted history for the tourists.
It was the 12th time a team's top five have all been out for single figures in a Test match - but the first time it has happened in the first innings.
They are closing in on a second record too.
A team has never started an innings worse than Pakistan during a series in England.
Their second wicket in this series has fallen with the score of 6 and 13 at Leeds, 16 and 7 at Lord's and 14 when the second wicket fell on Wednesday.
That is a total of 56 runs for the first two wickets - an average partnership of 5.6 and 11.2 runs for the fall of the second wicket this series.
They are set to break a record set by Australia in 1888, who averaged just 16 for the fall of their second wicket in that series.
It's hard not to feel some sympathy.
For example opener Saim Ayub, one of those called up for this Test, is playing in a first-class match for the first time since October 2025.
Facing Ollie Robinson in these conditions meant that his dismissal felt like a fait accompli from the moment the opener marked his guard.
Yet there was an end-of-term feel to some of the strokeplay from the Pakistan batters, too. At odds with the discipline they needed to show.
Four wickets down and Saud Shakeel and Babar Azam were extravagantly flashing their blades outside off stump. Two players into their thirties with plenty of experience, who should know better.
Pakistan's false-shot percentage in the morning session was 40%, the second highest in the opening session of a Test since 2006.
Saud survived until lunch but Babar perished 40 minutes before the interval - bowled by Tongue - gesticulating at the pitch.
"He [Babar] disintegrated. It's tough for him," added Ramiz.
"He's got to explain all this mayhem and then he has to look after himself and then he's got to work with the lot that are more T20 in nature than Test cricket."
There has only been two teams in a three-match series that have been bowled out six times for under 200 and they were both in the 19th century - the 1888 Australians and South Africa in 1895-96.
Pakistan need to find some resolve when they bat again to avoid joining them.
How a chaotic innings unfolded
- 11:13 BST - Ollie Robinson traps Saim lbw for a duck, the ball nipping back into the left-handed opener and clipping the front pad. 8-1.
- 11:30 - Jofra Archer has Azan Awais caught by Josh Tongue at mid-wicket for nine after he makes a mess of trying to work the ball into the leg side. 14-2.
- 11:44 - Robinson draws an edge from the bat of Abdullah Shafique and Dan Lawrence takes a sharp catch at gully. 24-3.
- 11:51 - Archer has Shan Masood caught by substitute Theo Wylie at mid-on after he mistimes it and the ball spoons up. 26-4.
- 12:20 - Tongue bowls Babar Azam for seven with the ball staying a fraction low and skidding into off stump. 48-5.
- 12:33 - Ghazi Ghori perishes lbw for four in his first Test innings, with a delivery from Tongue jagging back and hitting the top of middle. 64-6
- 12:53 - Mohammad Imran's off stump is broken after he is beaten all ends up by a superb yorker from Tongue. 84-7
- 13:48 - Three balls after lunch and Razaullah Khan, on debut, wafts at one outside off stump from Robinson and edges to Ben Duckett at first slip. 101-8
- 14:01 - Saud Shakeel's off stump is uprooted after a nip-backer from Tongue bowls him through the gate. 107-9
- 14:37 - Archer provides the coup de grace to Pakistan's first innings when Muhammad Abbas edges to Harry Brook in the cordon. 133 all out
'External influences make it hard'
Former Pakistan coach Jason Gillespie told TMS it was "heartbreaking" to see the team's struggles at Edgbaston but it should not come as a surprise.
Gillespie, who played 71 Test for Australia, had a stint in charge of Pakistan in 2024 but resigned after just over seven months into a two-year contract after he claimed he was kept in the dark over key decisions.
The 51-year-old said some of the challenges he faced in the job left him "scarred" and went some way to explaining how difficult it is to get Pakistan's players performing to the best of their ability on a consistent basis.
"There always seemed to be a lot of things going on behind the scenes and a lot of messaging from different sources," he said.
"To say Pakistan was unique is an understatement. It was very different to anything I have experienced.
"Once outside influences come in and start to take over it compromises how you work with the players. External influences make it hard.
"I questioned whether I wanted to be involved in coaching any more because parts of that experience were absolutely fantastic, exhilarating, but dealing with the other stuff, the external people, I found that incredibly challenging and incredibly deflating."

The father of two Australian surfers killed in Mexico two years ago testified in court on Tuesday that his life had been turned into hell, as the high-profile trial continued into its second day.
Three men are charged in the killing of Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, respectively, and their 30-year-old American friend Jack Carter Rhoad, who were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast in April 2024.
Authorities say the three were killed in an attempted robbery, and their bodies were found dumped in a cliff-top shaft with gunshot wounds to their heads.
“It’s hell,” the victims’ father Martin Robinson told the court. “It’s hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons.”
“It’s not just the loss, but also the potential they had the dreams that lay ahead of them, the places they travelled, and the love they had for others,” he said.
Robinson described the ordeal of having to identify his sons’ bodies: Callum by a tattoo on his forearm, while identifying Jake was more difficult and required photographs.
Rhoad’s mother Page compared the crime to an execution.
“I miss my son every day, and I don’t know if I will ever be able to regain my balance,” she testified. “Carter loved Mexico. He spoke fluent Spanish and loved dancing, Mexican food and its people.”
Authorities say the men were killed during an attempt to steal their pickup truck, which was later found burned near their bodies.
A protected witness testified Monday that they accompanied one of the defendants to the crime scene and fled after hearing gunshots, and were later threatened into silence.
The surfers’ disappearances and deaths sparked widespread outrage and grief in Australia and the United States, prompting a major social media search for their bodies.
“We hold no resentment toward the people who did this, but we cannot understand how they could have taken the lives of two beautiful people,” Martin Robinson told the court.
The trial is expected to run until the end of September.
Rhoad’s widow, Natalie, is scheduled to testify on Wednesday.

A Louisiana case could upend telehealth abortion. What exactly is it?
TUCSON, Ariz. — Dr. William Richardson says his patients are pretty floored that telehealth is now an option for abortion.
"I think people are shell shocked," says Richardson, a board-certified OB-GYN in Tucson, Ariz. "'What do you mean? I can just get on my cell phone and get abortion pills? What? You know, that can't be possible.' People just don't get after all this time that that's possible."
It's actually been possible in much of the country for several years. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the Food and Drug Administration began allowing the abortion pill mifepristone to be prescribed through telehealth and sent to patients in the mail. The agency then made that rules-change official in 2023.
In Arizona, although abortion is legal, mifepristone hasn't been available through telehealth because of state-level restrictions. That changed in February of this year, after a judge ruled in favor of Richardson in a lawsuit filed by the Center for Reproductive Rights clearing the way for telehealth access.
After 25 years of providing abortion in person in his Tucson clinic, Choices Women's Center, he launched telehealth services in May, and it's taken off. "I would say 95% of our patients want to use telemedicine in some form," he says. "Patients are loving it."
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
He's very aware, though, that telehealth access could go away again. This week, the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals in New Orleans hears oral arguments in Louisiana v. FDA, which aims to end telehealth access to the abortion pill mifepristone for the whole country.
"Our victory has the potential to be short-lived," he says. "We're just going to have to brace and see what happens."
Richardson's telehealth set-up
Choices Women's Center is a brown stucco building in a medical center. He shows off the room he calls the "telehealth suite." It has colorful portraits of famous women on the wall like Rosa Parks, Princess Diana and Angela Merkel, plus a few comfy chairs.
Medication abortion is approved by the FDA for use before 11 weeks of pregnancy. When patients aren't sure of the date of their last period, they can come into the office for an ultrasound, and then sit in the telehealth suite for a consult with the doctor.
To demonstrate, Richardson goes down the hall to his office, and soon his face appears on an enormous screen.
He says whether he's seeing a patient in person or virtually, he begins by talking with a patient about their medical history, and then gives them information about the two medications used for abortion: mifepristone, known by the brand name Mifeprex, and misoprostol.
"Mifeprex stops the pregnancy from developing by blocking the action of one of the critical hormones," he says, as if he's explaining the process to a patient. "24 hours to 48 hours later, we'll have you take your four misoprostol tablets all at once by placing two on either side between the cheek and the gum for 30 minutes and swallow. Expect cramping and bleeding within 4 to 6 hours of swallowing."
If that's too much information or too fast for the patient, the instructions are all written out along with a 24/7 number for the clinic that patients can call if they have questions or concerns.
"That pretty much is what the appointment looks like," he says. "I would say that most of the time it's less than 30 minutes."
Patients in the office can receive the medications right away from a small stockroom down the hall. If they're doing the telehealth appointment on their phone or laptop, the medication comes to their house from a mail-order pharmacy in a few days.
"Sometimes I have to catch myself, like – I can't believe that that was that easy," Richardson says.
He's seeing a patient virtually later in the day who lives 100 miles from the clinic. Because of this option, he explains, she won't have to drive the whole way and back, or take time off her hourly job, or find childcare for her two children. When you're facing those kinds of obstacles to get to the clinic, he says, telehealth access is "the difference between receiving care and not receiving care."
A legal challenge to stop telehealth access
The problem, as far as anti-abortion rights activists and politicians see it, is that when patients can have a telehealth appointment on their phone and receive abortion medications through the mail to their house, state level abortion bans really can't stop people from ending their pregnancies.
A patient in Louisiana, which has a strict abortion ban, can consult over telehealth with a doctor in a state with a shield law, like Colorado, and have abortion medications shipped in the mail right to their door.
That's why anti-abortion rights groups have filed several lawsuits to stop telehealth abortion access nationally.
Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill told a Senate committee in January why she thinks the FDA telehealth rules must be changed. "Until then, Louisiana's efforts to protect mothers and their unborn children and to hold out-of-state abortion pill traffickers accountable for the harm they inflict will be all but futile," she said.
In Louisiana v. FDA, the state questions FDA's decision-making process for allowing telehealth access, argues that the rules violate states' rights, and alleges that it's less safe for patients not to see a doctor in person. If the lawsuit succeeds, telehealth abortion access could be restricted across the country.
The case has already been considered by the Supreme Court earlier this year and is likely to end up there again.
Contingency plans
Dr. William Richardson says that his connection with patients and the information he shares is the same, whether he sees a patient in person or through telehealth. The medications that patients take are the same, too.
"My sense, as well as the sense of every other legitimate medical organization, is that medication abortion has been proven to be safe, effective and well-tolerated by patients worldwide," he says.
Beyond the federal court cases, Arizona could restrict telemedicine abortion again at the state level, through new laws or through an appeal of Richardson's lawsuit. He says, at age 66, instead of fretting, he's made contingency plans to be completely remote, completely in person or anything in between.
"We are ready to do all of those things if we have to, based on what happens here locally or what happens at the federal level," he says. "We try to be ready for all of that."

Colombo, Sep 9: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said on Wednesday that secure sea lanes, freedom of navigation, respect for international law and unhindered maritime trade should remain pivotal priorities as they are crucial for the growth and prosperity of South Asia.
Singh made the remarks at a public event after he held an "extremely productive" meeting with Sri Lankan President Anura Kumara Dissanayake during which they reaffirmed that as civilisational twins, close neighbours and maritime partners, India and Sri Lanka would continue to work jointly to ensure the safety, security, peace and prosperity of the region.
Speaking on 'India-Sri Lanka Maritime Cooperation in the Indian Ocean Region-Civilisational Partners with intertwined destinies’ in Colombo, Singh also said that Indian and Sri Lankan ports can become engines of shared economic growth, while their maritime industries can become the drivers for the future prosperity of the region.
"Together, India and Sri Lanka are well positioned to serve as the closest partners in safeguarding peace, security and stability across the Indian Ocean Region," he said.
Singh, who arrived in Colombo on Tuesday for a three-day visit, becoming the first Indian defence minister to visit Sri Lanka in 38 years, said that freedom of navigation and ensuring open trade routes are crucial for the growth and prosperity of the region.
"Therefore, secure sea lanes, freedom of navigation, respect for international law, unhindered maritime trade and commerce should remain our pivotal priorities," he said.
"It is essential that we work together towards shaping a favourable, secure maritime environment, remaining ready to address emerging maritime challenges in the first instance, before they become a serious threat to our developmental interests and the bright future of our region," he said.
Singh said that Sri Lanka occupies a salient strategic location in the Indian Ocean Region, overlooking a vast ocean characterised by crisscrossing busy trade routes. "These routes are not only the arteries for global trade, but also determine the trajectory of our growth and development as well as the safety and security of our region," he said.
Today, the Indian Ocean is not merely a waterway, but the stage on which the economic and strategic future of our region will be written, he said.
"For India and Sri Lanka, both maritime nations bound by this shared ocean, this is not a matter of abstract theory but of lived, everyday reality — one that shapes our trade, our security and our destinies alike," he said.
Sri Lanka, like India, is undoubtedly central to any strategic discourse on maritime security in the Indian Ocean Region, the minister said.
"In Sri Lanka, India sees a friendly neighbour, a longstanding friend and a reliable partner. India-Sri Lanka Maritime Cooperation is thus not only mutually beneficial but quintessential to our collective safety and security," Singh said.
"In a rapidly changing geopolitical landscape, the Indian Ocean has come to occupy a place of immense contemporary relevance. As emerging economies and fellow democracies, we have a shared future," he said.
Singh said India would be delighted to share its experience and work closely with Sri Lanka for the continued growth and prosperity of the region. "Our development projects in Sri Lanka are always focused on the requirements of the people of Sri Lanka and the priorities set by the Sri Lankan Government."
As the Indian Ocean is entering into a period of profound strategic and economic transformation, India and Sri Lanka must synergise their efforts and build upon our collective competencies to tackle the emerging challenges, the minister said.
"Our ports can become engines of shared economic growth, while our maritime industries can become the drivers for the future prosperity not only of our own people but our region as well. The future of India–Sri Lanka relations should therefore be based on a simple premise that proximity creates interdependence, which in turn creates immense opportunities for a shared evolution," he said, terming Sri Lanka a trusted global friend.
On the fishermen issue, Singh said the two countries need to work together to address fisheries disputes in a mutually beneficial manner, keeping in view the relevant laws and geographic jurisdictions.
"We need to work together to strengthen our systems to avoid fisheries disputes, handle them with due care and concern as this is a livelihood issue, while at the same time ensure maritime law enforcement," he said.
"I foresee a future where our two countries move forward as joint stakeholders in developing a mutually beneficial and integrated maritime domain awareness system to provide comprehensive maritime information on a real-time basis. This would entail systematic cooperation and interaction amongst concerned agencies, navies and Coast Guards of the two countries with a view to addressing the challenges of illegal fishing, suspicious vessel tracking, narcotics trafficking, smuggling, terrorism and other security threats," he said.
India is always willing to join hands with Sri Lanka in areas like capacity building and exercises, Singh said, adding that India is also committed to assisting Sri Lanka in whichever way possible to further enhance such cooperation.
He said that going beyond the traditional template, the two countries need to build upon the existing complementarities and develop new paradigms for a closer and stronger maritime partnership. "This is the basis of MAHASAGAR, Prime Minister Modi’s vision for the Indian Ocean Region. ‘Mutual’ and ‘Holistic’ are key words in this concept, underscoring the importance of synergy, cooperation and collaboration," he said.
"Our two countries can establish a joint maritime HADR system by involving all concerned agencies, disaster management and scientific organisations to cooperate and provide rapid response in cases of natural calamities and man-made disasters," he said.
Singh said maritime cooperation should include, in addition to the security framework, an institutionalised structure for deepening and strengthening an economic framework in areas including fisheries and aquaculture, marine biotechnology, ocean science, maritime environment protection and preservation and maritime tourism.

When rescue dog Chloe is not tumbling across the grass on a farm outside India's tech capital Bengaluru, she is learning to sniff human breath for cancer with a little help from AI.
Fitted with a 3D-printed helmet and harness packed with sensors, Chloe is part of experimental efforts to use dogs' extraordinary sense of smell to develop a non-invasive test for the disease.
A growing body of global research suggests dogs can be trained to detect cancer and other human illnesses, from Parkinson's to Covid-19.
The Bengaluru-based startup Dognosis is using AI to analyse dogs' brain activity, respiration and body language, turning their reaction to scent into data.
"In an hour, they can do thousands of sniffs," co-founder Akash Kulgod, 26, told AFP. "Each sniff can evaluate a sample."
Dognosis hopes to launch commercially next year, which it says would make it the third company of its kind, after firms from Germany and Israel.
Early detection can make a crucial difference to cancer survival rates, but in India many patients are diagnosed only after the disease has advanced.
Dog sniffs could provide an easy and affordable first layer of screening to be deployed at scale, finding potential cases for further testing.
As it chases commercial approval, Dognosis, backed by venture-capital firms including Accel India, is collaborating with government medical institutions for its research.
Chloe, a Labrador mix, is one of 15 dogs being coached by the startup, clad in customised data-gathering helmets.
"It's like a doggy 'Iron Man' suit," said Kulgod, who comes from a family of doctors and studied cognitive science at the University of California, Berkeley.
Research suggests diseases can alter the chemicals released by the body, creating distinctive odours.
Dogs have around 300 million scent receptors, compared to about five million in humans.
The testing method is simple: a patient breathes into a cotton mask for about 10 minutes, and the mask is then sealed in a bag and taken to the lab. Patients do not meet the dogs.
A recent Dognosis study of more than 1,500 participants, involving six hospitals in Karnataka state, was published in the Journal of Clinical Oncology.
The company said it achieved an accuracy rate of more than 90 percent across seven major types of cancer, and now plans to test in real-world programmes.
Cancer specialists in Bengaluru independent of the project voiced cautious optimism.
"The study is promising, as an early signal," said Santhosh Kumar Devadas, head of oncology at Ramaiah Memorial Hospital.
"But they need to do the study with a much larger group before we make any definitive conclusions."
Neelesh Reddy, a senior consultant oncologist at Manipal Hospitals, told AFP that "only time will tell how this technology will be useful to the actual patients".
Dognosis says it aims to improve "proactive and preventative medicine" while boosting "human-canine communication".
Most of the dogs are beagles, along with some Malinois and Shepherd mixes, brought on board through adoption or legal breeders.
But only the best are selected, said Kulgod. The dog team individually lists each animal on the company website as an official "sniffer", alongside their photographs.
All have a great "work-life balance", with work time limited to around 30-45 minutes a day, he added.
At a centre called "Sniffspace", dogs test human samples on platforms equipped with automatic feeders dispensing dog treats.
Kulgod's co-founder Itamar Bitan, 28, who spent four years in an Israeli special-forces canine unit, said the dogs were trained using "positive reinforcement" to detect a "specific funky smell" for a reward.
"Some of the dogs run directly to the feeder expecting rewards, some dogs freeze, some dogs will scratch the sample with excitement," Bitan said.
"But, as long as the machine that learns how the dogs react to the sample is very consistent... we don't really mind."

AI cancer cures slowed by chip shortage, says UK's biggest tech boss
- Published
The boss of the biggest UK-headquartered tech firm has said that artifical intelligence will find a cure for cancer that humans cannot in our lifetimes.
Rene Haas, chief executive of Cambridge-based chip designer Arm Holdings, said while modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer was currently "too complex" a problem, computers are "going to solve it" in the future.
Haas also told the BBC that AI would lead to widespread humanoid robots in the next five years, but that its current rapid growth was being held up by a shortage of chips needed to build data centres.
However, he was sceptical about the idea chips could be manufactured in the UK in the future.
Arm designs the brains or CPUs of microchips already used in hundreds of billions of phones, cars, smartwatches and gadgets across the globe.
Earlier this summer, the company's peak share price amid the AI boom made it, in cash terms, the most valuable UK-based company in history.
Haas, who stepped down from the board of British pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca in April, told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast: "AI is going to... find a cure for cancer that today you and I, other humans [could] not in our lifetimes. I believe in our lifetime, AI will help cure cancer.
"Modelling a cell, modelling a human, modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer - it's too complex a problem, not only for humans today, but the computers that run AI.
"However, going forward, as we feed more and more of the models into these computers, and the computers get more sophisticated to run the models, they're going to solve it," said Haas, who also holds a key role in Arm's main owner, the Japan-based Softbank, which has a range of investments in tech including in OpenAI.
Prof Chris Bakal, from the Institute of Cancer Research, London, and CEO of Sentinal4D, said the real question was no longer whether we use AI, it's what we feed it.
He said in labs like his, they are training AI on data generated themselves from patient samples.
"It is not scraped from the internet. It does not need a giant data centre to run. The future of medical AI will not belong to whoever builds the biggest computer. It will belong to whoever has the right measurements.
"That kind of prediction could cut years from the time it takes to develop new treatments. This is where AI delivers real benefit to patients."
Job losses 'overstated'
In a wide-ranging interview, Haas said the chips Arm designs would fuel self-learning AI robots "in a very large way" in manufacturing, cleaning, security, building bridges, and doing repairs within a decade.
"With artificial intelligence, these robots can see, learn, and essentially be reprogrammed for new tasks. So, in the service industry, the robot that was programmed to make a bed can also learn how to arrange the towels in a room, or clean the dustbins, or whatever you want to go off and do."
Addressing concerns that AI would lead to mass job losses, Haas said while there would be some change for workers, "the estimates of jobs going away and being completely replaced by machines is a bit overstated" and outweighed by new opportunities.
He also said fears over a correction in the remarkable rise in the stock market value of AI companies were overstated, because of the long-term demand for AI.
Arm's power-efficient technology was now being used in half of AI data centres worldwide, he said.
This has led to a significant evolution in its business in recent months, selling its own microchips. Facebook-owner Meta asked Arm to develop the Arm AGI chip and "demand has been off the charts", according to Haas, with more than $2bn worth of demand since it was launched in March.
Big Boss Interview: Arm Holdings Rene Haas
The CEO of chip design company Arm tells the BBC AI will help cure cancer, lead to widespread humanoid robots in the next five years, but says its rapid growth is being held up by a shortage of chips needed in data centres.
There have, however, been challenges in the supply of many types of chips, which Haas believes is holding back the roll-out of AI and data centres.
He pointed to plans for massive "multi-gigawatt" data centres in France and the US as well as plans to put them in space.
"We are absolutely in a supply-constrained environment. Can you get enough chips? We need more fabs [chip factories] before we can put a data centre in space."
But he does not believe that manufacturing, currently centralised around Taiwanese giant TSMC, could eventually occur in the UK, despite the government holding talks with the industry about the possibility of bringing parts of the physical chip supply chain over here.
"I don't think it's necessary for the UK to [build] fabs. Fabs are very expensive. They take a lot of specialised workers. They take a lot of natural resources, and there's a pretty broad ecosystem for those."
As the great hope of UK tech for decades, some government ministers have lamented Arm's sale to Japanese investors in 2016 and subsequent partial flotation on New York's Nasdaq rather than in London.
But Haas maintained that half of Arm's employees remain in the UK and said the company was "by far and away the largest employer in Cambridge".

Russia and North Korea have opened the first road bridge across their shared border, in the latest sign of the rapidly deepening ties between the two countries since the start of the war in Ukraine.
The one-kilometre bridge spans the Tumen River between Khasan in Russia’s far east and Tumangang in North Korea, along a remote and sparsely populated stretch of the countries’ shared border just a few miles from the coast.
Speaking by video link during the bridge’s opening ceremony on Monday, Russia’s prime minister, Mikhail Mishustin, said the new crossing would spur development in a range of areas, including tourism, while creating new jobs
“I am convinced that the expansion of cross-border transport infrastructure will provide a powerful impetus for the further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation,” Mishustin said.
The road bridge is named after the Soviet officer Yakov Novichenko, who is credited with saving North Korea’s founding leader, Kim Il-sung, from an assassination attempt by a pro-South Korean group.
After the opening ceremony, convoys of vehicles crossed the bridge from both sides.
Russia and the secretive North Korea regime are already connected by a railway bridge across the Tumen, as well as regular flights between Vladivostok and Pyongyang.
Ukrainian human rights groups have warned that the bridge may be intended to provide a discreet military logistics corridor between the two countries.
Truth Hounds, a Ukrainian human rights organisation, has described it as a likely future corridor for moving North Korean troops, construction brigades and military officials into Russia, while allowing Russian technology and resources to travel in the opposite direction with less risk of detection.
Ties between Moscow and Pyongyang have strengthened dramatically since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. North Korea has sent thousands of troops to Russia’s Kursk region to help Moscow repel a Ukrainian incursion launched there in 2024.
In return, Russia is believed to have provided North Korea with air-defence missiles, electronic warfare equipment, drones and spy-satellite technology, according to South Korean intelligence.
Russian and North Korean officials have also touted North Korea as a new holiday destination since the country reopened to Russian tourists in 2024, with thousands of Russians visiting its newly opened beach resorts and ski slopes since then.
Russia’s increasingly close embrace of totalitarian North Korea has raised eyebrows even in Moscow.
During an interview with the Russian broadcaster RBC last month, a reporter asked Sergei Lavrov, Russia’s longtime foreign minister, how the country had “ended up” with just “two allies – North Korea and Iran”.
Lavrov pushed back against the premise, saying there was “nothing wrong” with such company.
At the same time, some of Russia’s traditional partners have shown growing frustration with Moscow’s continuing war in Ukraine and the fallout it has caused across the region.
During a meeting in July, Kazakhstan’s president, Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, a longtime ally of Moscow, told the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, that he was hearing from leaders of many countries who questioned why Russia was still waging the war.
“The nature of the conflict isn’t entirely clear for many, including us,” Tokayev told Putin.

Russia and Ukraine exchange strikes as two killed at Moldova border
- Published
Two people have been killed after Russian drones struck a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
The Starokozache crossing, around 500km (310 miles) south of Kyiv, was closed after the overnight attack. Images from the scene showed several cars left completely scorched, with wreckage and debris strewn across the border post.
Meanwhile, four people, including a child, were killed in the southern Russian city of Novorossiysk in a Ukrainian drone attack, the regional governor said.
Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up long-range strikes in recent months, despite renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war.
Zelensky renewed calls for international support in the wake of the Starokozache crossing attack, saying "the aggression must be stopped here and now before it spreads any further".
The border link between Ukraine and Moldova was shut after the attack killed two people and injured three others, Odesa regional governor Oleg Kiper said.
A Moldovan driver was also injured, according to the country's foreign ministry.
Moldova has increasingly found itself caught up in the conflict, with Prime Minister Vasile Tofan confirming that 17 drones had struck Moldovan territory in August alone - more than during the whole of last year.
"Those who ignore or downplay these threats - and refuse to name the aggressor - are denying reality," he wrote on social media.
"Russia started this war. Russia alone bears responsibility."
Russia's defence ministry said its forces had shot down 596 Ukrainian drones overnight.
Novorossiysk – in the south of the country on the Black Sea coast - was hit hardest in what governor Veniamin Kondratiev described as a "massive overnight enemy drone attack".
As well as the four deaths, 29 people were injured, and damage was reported to residential buildings, a church and a preschool.
The strikes came a day after Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke to US President Donald Trump by phone about efforts to end the conflict.
The Trump administration has been pressing for direct talks between Russia and Ukraine, with Kyiv saying they could take place this month. The Kremlin, however, has said it is too early to discuss a date or venue.
The call followed talks between US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff and Putin in Moscow, before the pair travelled to Kyiv for meetings with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Ezekiel J. Emanuel and Abe Butler-Baker have been debating the proper place for AI in medicine with American Medical Association CEO John Whyte. Now, they are taking their discussion to STAT’s First Opinion. Read Emanuel and Butler’s essay below and read Whyte’s essay here.
In 1867, Joseph Lister published his research on carbolic acid and antiseptic surgical technique. In September 1871, he was summoned to Queen Victoria, who had a rapidly growing abscess in her left armpit. Using his antiseptic surgical technique, Joseph Lister successfully drained the pus. Queen Victoria recovered without fever or other complications. The antiseptic technique quickly gained approval in the U.K. and Europe, but not among American physicians.
In fall 1876, Lister arrived in the U.S. for an international medical meeting and traveled to Philadelphia, New York, and Boston where he demonstrated his antiseptic technique to leading American physicians. In fall 1881, 14 years after Lister’s publication and five years after his American demonstrations, President Garfield was shot. The nation’s leading surgeons of the day attended him. Skeptical of Lister’s innovation despite the strong data supporting it, these haughty surgeons repeatedly stuck their unwashed hands and unsterilized instruments into Garfield’s wound to try to locate the bullet. With good intentions but ignoring science, they infected President Garfield and killed him.
In August, we co-authored an article in JAMA with Vinod Khosla and Neal Khosla arguing that autonomous artificial intelligence will likely soon exceed both unaided physicians and physicians aided by AI at five core cognitive medical tasks: patient information gathering, differential diagnosis, selecting cost-efficient tests, prescribing guideline-concordant treatment, and managing chronic illnesses.
We reached this conclusion by evaluating all studies comparing autonomous AI to physicians with or without AI published since January 2024. Based on the data, we project autonomous AI will be superior to AI-aided physicians at, and ready for real-world implementation, on some, maybe all, of these five tasks by 2030.
The preponderance of studies shows autonomous AI beating unaided physicians at the five cognitive medical tasks. Data from medicine and other fields including chess suggest that once autonomous AI beats unaided humans, autonomous AI shortly thereafter consistently beats human-AI hybrids.
While regulatory barriers and physician resistance have limited real-world trials of autonomous AI, the data we do have is remarkable. A few examples: Google’s AMIE is statistically significantly better than physicians at eliciting all portions of patient history. ChatGPT beats physicians at differential diagnosis by 18 percentage points (92% vs. 74%). Microsoft’s AI Diagnostic Orchestrator produced correct final diagnoses 4.02 times more frequently than physicians (80.4% vs. 20%) at an average testing cost ($2,397) which was 19.1% lower. MIRA, an autonomous AI, prescribed guideline-concordant treatment 35 percentage points more frequently than doctors. And a study at Stanford showed autonomous AI trounced physicians at managing diabetes, achieving a stable insulin dose in 15 days while doctors still could not after eight weeks.
And, nine of 13 studies since January 2024 comparing autonomous AI to AI-aided physicians show autonomous AI is superior. For instance, autonomous AI beats physicians with AI at diagnosis by 21.3 percentage points. It sounds counterintuitive — why would having the doctor involved be worse? However, data show that when AI is highly capable, doctors add more errors and false corrections than beneficial insights. AI is rapidly improving, which will intensify this phenomenon.
American Medical Association CEO John Whyte, who is a friend, and others have criticized our conclusion that autonomous AI will beat AI-aided physicians. They have three main arguments.
First, Whyte and others argue that AI should not practice autonomously because we do not have adequate licensure and liability structures for autonomous AI. We agree. Current licensure and liability structures for autonomous AI are inadequate, but the answer is to create adequate structures, not to reject autonomous AI. Indeed, we proposed such a licensing structure in JAMA and currently have a paper under review proposing a feasible, comprehensive liability structure for autonomous AI.
Second, Whyte and colleagues argue doctors will still be needed for the “art of medicine”: trust, emotional awareness, compassion, patient relationships, and communicating difficult decisions. As a result, they say, doctors will still need to be “on-the-loop.”
Studies indicate that AI can handle difficult conversations and demonstrate empathy better than doctors. In 2025, Alastair Howcroft and colleagues found that 13 out of 15 studies comparing empathy in medicine showed statistically significantly higher empathy ratings for AI than human health care professionals. Patient actors felt more at ease (97% vs. 65%, p < 0.001) and listened to (95% vs. 72%, p < 0.001) by Google’s AMIE than by primary care physicians. Humans may be needed for tasks that only humans can perform, like holding patients’ hands, but doctors may not be best for compassion and empathy.
Third, Whyte and others dismiss our conclusion because many of the studies examining AI in medicine are simulations. They argue that AI would fail to perform in a real-world clinical environment.
While they correctly observe that much of the medical AI literature is simulated, their conclusion is inaccurate. The lack of real-world autonomous AI testing is attributable not to poor capability but rather to doctors, regulators, and laws that restrict such tests.
Indeed, the real-world data we do have show autonomous AI beating physicians using AI. In the Annals of Internal Medicine, a team led by Dan Zeltzer studied 461 real patient visits. AI had a structured online chat with the patient and then generated treatment recommendations. Physicians then saw the patient and had access to the AI treatment recommendations, and they generated their own recommendations. Physicians’ treatment recommendations were worse than AI’s, even though physicians had access to the AI’s recommendations. These were real patient cases with information gathered directly from patients by AI. The answer to the “simulated cases” objection is to test autonomous AI in the real world, not to dismiss autonomous AI’s capability.
AI will not take over all roles from doctors. After all, AI cannot independently perform surgeries, deliver babies, or conduct physical procedures since it lacks physical capability.
But data indicate that autonomous AI will be better than physicians working with AI at core cognitive medical tasks. We need to test autonomous AI at real-world deployment. If we do not, we may harm our patients by denying them what science shows is likely the best medical care, just as American surgeons did to President Garfield in 1881.
Ezekiel J. Emanuel is vice provost for global initiatives and co-director of the Healthcare Transformation Institute at the Perelman School of Medicine and the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania. Abe Baker-Butler is a research fellow in the Department of Medical Ethics and Health Policy at the University of Pennsylvania.
