As the author of a newsletter about artificial intelligence, I consider it my duty to experience the bleeding edge of this technology firsthand. This week, that meant embracing some agentic mayhem.
You’re probably aware that frontier AI models have attained advanced cybersecurity capabilities in recent months. They can find zero-day bugs in large codebases and scan computers for vulnerabilities at lightning speed. To make things even more exciting, cybersecurity agents sometimes go rogue, colluding with one another and hacking into outside systems to gain an edge.
To get a closer look, I decided to unleash one in my own home network. Over the course of a few days, I watched as my own rogue agent found vulnerabilities in various household devices, hacked into a PC, and showed me that several vibe-coded projects were—unsurprisingly—riddled with bugs. (My wife knew what I was up to, and rolled her eyes each time I proudly announced the discovery of a new vulnerability.)
But Will, you might be thinking, giving an impish, all-powerful cybersecurity agent access to your home network is batshit. And you would be correct! Nevertheless, I believe that a good way to understand the cybersecurity hellscape in front of us is to pay it a visit.
In the end, my experiment was revealing, but oddly reassuring, too. My little network gremlin showed me how vulnerable my home life would be to AI hacking, but it also told me how to make everything a lot more secure. In the end, I discovered that the best way to deal with AI hacking may well be having your own AI hacker.
Maverick Model
I got the idea for the experiment after discovering Abliteration AI, a startup that offers access to powerful AI models with the usual guardrails removed.
Most mainstream AI models will refuse to respond to certain queries, and they will certainly refuse to find and exploit vulnerabilities in computer systems. But it’s possible to remove these restrictions by finding and modifying certain patterns within an open-weight model’s internal parameters. You can tweak the patterns that lead to refusals through a process known as abliteration.
Removing AI’s guardrails might seem risky, but it’s not uncommon. Academic researchers use these de-aligned models to better understand how AI actually works, while cybersecurity firms use them to probe software and systems for vulnerabilities. Technically speaking, Anthropic’s Mythos and OpenAI’s Astra work similarly: They’re basically conventional models that lack the usual cyber controls, with access limited to trusted customers for the time being. (The companies also offer wider access to models with a medium number of guardrails so that companies can vet their code and systems for problems.)
Abliteration AI offers several fully de-aligned models, the most powerful of which is a version of Z.ai’s latest agentic coding model, GLM 5.3. This puts similar cyber capabilities to Mythos and Astra right in your hands for as little as the cost of a pizza.
Devon, Abliteration AI’s CEO, believes that making de-aligned models widely available is smart defense: It will help good guys counter bad guys by probing systems for vulnerabilities and by mimicking the behavior of hackers, scammers, and, yes, rogue AI agents. (Devon asked that I use his first name only because his day job doesn’t know about his side project.)
“You have all these critical infrastructure companies, from airlines to banks, that are rolling out agents like crazy,” Devon says. “How do you make sure that a nefarious actor can't use some of these agents in a bad way?”
To start, I created an Abliteration AI account and installed a software harness called CyberStrike, which helps guide a large language model through different cybersecurity tasks.
Using CyberStrike, I asked the abliterated version of GLM-5.3 to take a look at my local network. A few moments later, it found around a dozen hardware systems on the same network—and catalogued several vulnerabilities.
My unruly helper told me, for instance, that my printer was misconfigured, which meant that anyone on the network could log into it. That could be a problem if there were sensitive documents—tax returns, bank statements, medical records—in the print queue.
The agent also noted that my Wiim stereo was leaking a lot of information. (It knew that the last song played was Rein Me In by Sam Fender and Olivia Dean, if you must know.) Anyone on the network could play what they wanted or adjust the volume. The model also found a bunch of internet-of-things (IoT) devices on the network with firmware that needed updating.
An ungovernable agent could be very useful to a hacker. But mine offered a number of helpful tips for keeping my network secure. Besides updating outdated firmware and securing the printer, it recommended putting IoT devices like smart speakers on a guest network; if one were compromised, it wouldn’t be able to see any of my PCs. Not bad for a model with no morals.
I also asked the agent to take a look at a directory containing a bunch of vibe-coded projects, including some that I turned into simple websites. It found dozens of problems, including unprotected API credentials and a misconfiguration that might let an attacker send out emails. Hardly surprising for a bunch of casually vibe-coded stuff, but still chastening. The sheer number of bugs makes me think I won’t be deploying a line of code without doing some AI vetting first.
Fear Factor
Running an abliterated model is, to put it plainly, a bit scary.
I asked my agent to probe a Linux machine on my network for vulnerabilities. After running a bunch of scans, it reported that the machine seemed relatively secure. I then asked if it could figure out how to log in. It cleverly figured out a working username based on the name of other systems on the network. It tried a bunch of obvious passwords, which didn’t work. It also offered to write a script to try “brute forcing” the password, but I told it to stand down.
To my amazement, the agent then found a cryptographic key on my machine, used it to log in without a password, and started hunting for the password in order to gain root access. I felt a moment of pure panic as I saw it rummaging around the directories. It made me wonder how far the agent might go in order to achieve its goal. Might it have hacked into something else, like a machine outside of my network, in search of the key? Probably not, but who knows with these agents.
Some behavior could prove even more precarious. When I connected to my Wi-Fi network a few hours later and asked the model to see if it could find any new machines, it not only found the router, but decided to try logging in by trying several common “admin/passwords” combinations. If it had decided to do this on an outside network, I could have been in big trouble.
Shaanan Cohney, a computer scientist at Tufts University who specializes in cybersecurity and the law, says that a cyber-reckoning does seem to be coming.
“Attackers are often early adopters,” Cohney says. “There’s also an asymmetry, in that to secure a castle, you need to make sure that there are no holes anywhere or no loose bricks in your wall. To invade a castle, all you need to do is to find that one loose brick.”
Over the long term, Cohney says, the proliferation of cyber-capable models may make software more secure in general. The challenge is that many companies aren’t thinking about shoring up their defenses. “Most organizations have other things to worry about,” he says.
After all that, I shut down the model and went back to using a regular, fully aligned version. Claude Code or Codex will only do certain things related to cybersecurity, like help you configure your laptop’s firewall. But at least they won’t hack your system before you know it. Hopefully.
AI Hacking for All
Unless open-weight models are banned outright, advanced AI hacking capabilities will soon be very widely available. My experiment made me think that this might be just what we need. Assuming that bad guys will have access to AI, shouldn’t we all use it to defend ourselves?
“We need to help people use these capabilities,” says Aleksander Mądry, an MIT professor who studies AI safety and who is currently on leave while he works for OpenAI. “I do think there will be room for open source and independent tools. If only because, ultimately, these kinds of approaches have the real staying power in the world of security.”
Mądry notes, however, that a key issue may be ensuring that those who manage critical infrastructure like power plants or financial markets have access to more powerful AI than the average script kiddie (or AI writer).
Using AI that lacks regular guardrails is both thrilling and alarming. But if a cyber-reckoning is coming, then it’s probably time to tool up.

"I have made the decision to resign from my position as Deputy Assistant Secretary/Acting Assistant Secretary for OSERS to return home to Florida, effective September 11, 2026," Rogers wrote on Wednesday morning to staff. "While I am stepping away, I remain confident in the team's ability to continue moving forward with strengthened outcomes for individuals with disabilities through the HHS partnership."
Education Department Press Secretary Savannah Newhouse confirmed Rogers' forthcoming departure to NPR and said Rogers is moving home to "take on a great opportunity and be closer to her family."
Disability rights advocates have widely condemned shifting special education staff to a different agency.

PM Modi says UPI now live in 11 countries, pushes for further global reach
Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday said UPI is not only a tech story but also a civilisational one.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday exhorted the fintech ecosystem to further expand the global reach of India's unified payments interface (UPI), connect it with other countries' local systems and help the diaspora save on remittance costs.
In his address after inaugurating the 7th edition of the Global Fintech Fest, Modi said the Indian economy's 7.8 per cent real GDP expansion gave confidence to the world at large because the performance came in a challenging quarter when the impact of the West Asia conflict was the highest.
Urging the fintech (financial technology) ecosystem to not rest on the laurels of the past decade that saw real-time payments using UPI rise to 24.51 billion transactions, as of August this year, the PM said the next aim should be to expand UPI's global reach.
He said the focus should be on countries that are home to a large Indian diaspora, have high trade volumes with India or are willing to partner with New Delhi in connecting their systems.
"This is essential because Indians work in large numbers in foreign countries. They are the largest remitters of money. A part of the remittances goes away as transaction costs; UPI can help in saving on these costs and the money can also reach families faster," he said.
Modi said the UPI platform is now live in 11 countries and has been connected with the local system in Singapore, which has brought transactions between the two countries on a par with payments done between two local neighbourhoods.
He said global card payments currently run on systems designed in other countries, but underlined that India now has the alternative.
"We can set our own rules and standards and connect them with the world," he said.
Reiterating French President Emmanuel Macron's words, Modi said UPI is not only a tech story but also a civilisational one.
Modi said after the high number of successes on the payments front over the past several years, the next chapter for the Indian fintech industry should be non-payment transactions such as enabling access to saving products, pensions, insurance and other financial services.
He said the PM-SVANidhi initiative of supporting street vendors with working capital credit was made possible by UPI, which helped increase the average annual income of the beneficiaries by 20 per cent.
Technology makes it possible to have curated models targeted keeping in mind a particular person's needs, the PM said, adding that the fintech sector should address the same by making non-payment transactions as easy as undertaking a payment transaction by scanning a QR code.
Modi said upcoming technology sector developments such as agentic artificial intelligence, tokenisation, quantum tech, etc open doors of new possibilities and urged the fintech sector to focus on them by setting specific goals.
"As we go about doing that, the fintech community should ensure that cyber security is top notch in India, the industry has its own ethical data protection standards and also a fintech consumer protection index to rate every company transparently," Modi said.
India also needs to create a strong fintech-regulator-industry-innovation ecosystem, the PM said.
On the geopolitical front, Modi said the world is going through conflicts and uncertainties, energy and commodities supply chains are under pressure, and there are challenges regarding oil. He underlined that India's performance on economic growth should be seen in that context.
Japan Credit Rating Agency's upgrade of India to 'A-' from 'BBB ' illustrates the confidence the world has in India, Modi said, noting that the upgrade was the first such action in three decades.
"This shows that India's growth momentum, macroeconomic stability and the structural reforms of the last few years are giving the world comfort," Modi said.

OpenAI said today that it has found an AI-generated solution to one of the biggest problems in mathematics—a 200-year-old equation that describes the natural behavior of fluids like water and air.
The announcement appears to demonstrate the stunning power for AI to advance mathematics. But it has been marred by claims from another mathematician, Tristan Buckmaster, who says that OpenAI rushed ahead to solve the problem after learning of his and another mathematician’s progress on the problem, and also then tried to influence who got credit for the work.
The proof concerns the Navier-Stokes equation, one of the unsolved problems in the Clay Millennium prizes, which are each worth $1 million.
Sebastien Bubeck, a mathematician and AI researcher at OpenAI, said in a press briefing that the company began training a new AI model with advanced mathematical capabilities on August 28.
After reading rumors that Anthropic was making progress toward solving Navier-Stokes, Bubeck said the company decided to dedicate more resources to tackling the problem. The company had more than 1,000 agents tackle the problem over more than 50 hours before discovering that it had come up with a solution.
“I thought there must be a mistake somewhere,” Bubeck said. “And on Sunday morning we had the final solution, Lean-formalized and everything.” (Lean is a programming language that can be used to formalize mathematical proofs.)
OpenAI noted that solving this problem required using considerably more computing power than it had previously spent on solving mathematical problems. The amount required cost “in the millions of dollars,” said Mark Chen, head of research at OpenAI.
On Monday, Buckmaster, a mathematician at NYU, and Levent Alpöge, a researcher at Anthropic, posted documents claiming key advances in an area relevant to the Navier-Stokes problem. The pair says they used several AI models, including Claude and Codex, to complete their work.
Buckmaster also posted a statement claiming that, last week, he learned that OpenAI had become aware of his and Alpöge’s work and had started putting significant resources toward the problem. Buckmaster claims that he asked OpenAI leaders about whether the company had accessed the pair’s Codex logs. He says he was told the model “didn’t look up user data” but claims the company didn’t respond to questions about training. He then says that OpenAI offered several “proposals,” including one in which Buckmaster could publish a paper announcing the Navier-Stokes problem had been solved by an internal OpenAI model but without Alpöge’s name included.
Buckmaster, Alpöge, and Anthropic did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
In the briefing, Bubeck and other OpenAI executives denied that the company had ever inspected the pair’s Codex prompts in order to inform their work. “We, whether it’s the researchers or the agents, did not see any of their work until it was released publicly last night,” he said.
“I want to be extremely clear that we recognize the priority of Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster’s work on unforced Euler, and we have nothing but congratulations to them on this monumental achievement that they have made. To be clear, we did not use their prompt or proof to prompt our models or direct our agents,” said Bubeck.
OpenAI said today it wanted to recognize Alpöge and Buckmaster’s prior work. However, Ven Chandrasekaran, a mathematician at the company, also emphasized that their solution was significantly different in nature from the one produced by OpenAI’s model.
The spat over who gets credit for solving one of the biggest problems in math may rumble on for a while. As AI takes on more of the work involved with finding proofs, such fights could perhaps become more common.

- Published
Three men have gone on trial in Mexico for the alleged murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend in 2024.
The bodies of Callum Robinson, his younger brother Jake, and their friend Carter Rhoad from California - all in their early 30s - were found at the bottom of a well with gunshot wounds to their heads, days after they went missing during a surf trip in Baja California.
Prosecutors are seeking jail sentences of more than 200 years for the defendants, who also face charges of violent robbery and auto theft.
The parents of the brothers were in court on Tuesday in the coastal town of Ensenada, telling the media that it was "incredibly important and overwhelmingly difficult".
"We want the men accused of murdering our sons to see, in person, the human consequences of what happened," Martin and Debra Robinson said in a statement, according to Australia's national broadcaster, the ABC.
"Callum and Jake were not simply victims in a case file - they were our sons, deeply loved by their family and friends, with lives, dreams and futures that were brutally taken away."
On the opening day, the accused - Jesús "El Kekas" Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús - were moved to a smaller courtroom amid accusations that some witnesses had been intimidated by people associated with the defendants.
Dozens of witnesses are expected to give evidence during the four-week, judge-only trial.
The 2024 alleged killings of the Robinson brothers and their US friend shocked Australians as well as many residents of the normally peaceful town of Ensenada.
Despite high levels of cartel violence in the northern Mexican border states, tourists are rarely targeted for such violent attacks in Baja California's surf towns.
The ex-girlfriend of one of the accused, Ari Gisell, became the first person to be convicted over the tourists' killings last year and was sentenced to 20 years in prison for her role in their murders.
Mexican prosecutors are pursuing jail sentences of more than 200 years for each of the defendants, as well as an additional 168-year sentence for the alleged ringleader.
Prosecutors say the victims were killed due to a bungled robbery, while the defence argued there was not enough evidence to prove that theory.
Callum Robinson was a member of Australia's national lacrosse team and lived in San Diego where he was a professional lacrosse player.
His younger brother Jake had travelled from Australia for the surf trip and was due to start a job as a doctor when he returned while their friend Rhoad was killed a few months before his wedding.

Hegseth is shaking up the Pentagon as the US wages war - but at what cost?
- Published
The United States military is at the centre of a fight on two fronts.
First is President Donald Trump's attempt to prise the Strait of Hormuz from Iran's grip; the latest phase of his stalemated war in the Gulf which is drawing in US forces and equipment from around the globe.
The second is a culture war at home in which Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth is conducting a promised shake-up at the Pentagon, sparking bitter recriminations and a string of departures including the top civilian in charge of the US Army last week.
The upheaval has triggered questions that could shape the legacy of Trump's second term. Is the US military being stretched to a point that could risk global security? And are these shifts leaving America's extraordinary global network of alliances vulnerable?
Last Monday there was dramatic news from the Pentagon.
One of its most senior political leaders, Dan Driscoll, stepped down as US Secretary of the Army.
Driscoll is not exactly a household name in America, let alone outside it. But his departure mattered. It was the latest twist in a power struggle within the fortress-like walls of the Pentagon over the future of the world's most formidable fighting force.
Driscoll had clashed repeatedly with Hegseth over the nature and speed of military reform. His departure was the latest in a long line of top leaders removed or sidelined by Hegseth.
The level of concern became clear as one Republican Senator Thom Tillis - a frequent Trump critic - called for Hegseth to be fired. "I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country," he said.
"This is not good news. You know, for our nation, for the army," H.R. McMaster, who served as Trump's National Security Adviser during his first term, told CBS when asked about Driscoll's departure. "Secretary Driscoll was pushing… a modernisation agenda to catch the army up."
The backstory of Driscoll's resignation cut deep into issues about the readiness of the US Army. Driscoll wanted urgent modernisation by adding drones throughout ordinary army formations to make it adept for 21st Century warfare.
He said the Ukraine war had shown how the battlefield had changed, with cheap drones and anti-missile systems challenging the US military with its vast bureaucracy and expensive procurement processes.
Hegseth had in fact initiated much of this modernisation plan but subsequently came into conflict with Driscoll, according to reports, as well as with others advocating its rapid expansion.
A source familiar with last week's departure said Driscoll had raised concerns within the administration about army readiness and transformation, which Driscoll said Hegseth was "blocking" specifically by firing the generals responsible.
Jon Duffy, a retired Navy captain and former White House defence policy official, said Driscoll's resignation showed how far Hegseth had "hollowed out" the military leadership at a critical moment.
"You lose the [army] secretary, the chief of staff and other senior leaders driving modernisation, it creates a lot of uncertainty and it disrupts momentum," he said.
"That uncertainty at leadership levels has downstream effects on the force," added Duffy, who had a 30-year career and commanded US warships before joining the White House during the second Obama administration.
In public, Hegseth - a former Army National Guardsman and Fox News pundit - has spent much of his time calling for cultural change to the US military.
He has vowed to end what he called "woke" initiatives and scrap "stupid" rules of engagement he said constrained war fighters' "lethality". He tore up diversity programmes, banned beards and railed against seeing "fat generals in the halls of the Pentagon".
He removed or sidelined the top uniformed officers in charge of the Army, Navy and Air Force as well as at least two dozen generals, admirals and civilian defence leaders, including some of the US military's most decorated officers, often with little explanation.
One critic compares the changes in the top ranks to President Xi Jinping's political purges of the Chinese military which are said to have left serious deficiencies in command structure and readiness.
"We've been conducting a military purge as well, and that has real effects on the ability of our military to be able to discharge its responsibilities," Michael Schiffer, a former top Pentagon official who covered East Asia from 2009 to 2012 under the Obama presidency, told the BBC.
"The way in which [Hegseth is] shaking them up… is bringing on board an awful lot of risk without any apparent way to be able to address or ameliorate it," said Schiffer, who is now a senior fellow at the liberal think-tank the Center for American Progress.
Asked last week about Driscoll's departure, Vice-President JD Vance defended Hegseth, saying he was in "strident agreement" about the need for a culture shift after what he called 40 years of lost wars and "military misadventures".
"What Pete came in wanting to do was revive the warrior spirit in the United States of America," Vance said.

In a statement, the White House told the BBC that President Trump had "full confidence in Secretary Hegseth and the entire Department of War whose record of success in Operation Epic Fury, Operation Absolute Resolve, and Operation Midnight Hammer speaks for itself".
Trump has continued to back Hegseth, standing by him during controversies such as Signalgate and describing him in a phone interview with NBC News last month as "actually one of my best".
Ezra Cohen, a former Under Secretary of Defence during the first Trump administration, described Hegseth's reforms as "bringing in fresh thinking and a more forward-leaning attitude".
But the reported friction among the military leadership and the stalemate with Iran has raised questions about the future of the US military at a critical moment.
'Vulnerabilities in Europe'
Trump's order to launch strikes on Iran on 28 February led to a significant global redistribution of US military resources over the subsequent months. US weapons stored in Europe and Asia were transferred from those regions to replenish supplies in the Gulf.
Europe is now feeling significant "blowback", according to Professor Liana Fix, a Germany-based expert at the Council on Foreign Relations.
She said the lack of communication by the Trump administration with its Nato and European allies ahead of the attack on Iran left relations reeling and accelerated a strategic decision already in process to shift some US military resources away from Europe, particularly as Trump complained that his European allies weren't helping.
Prof Fix said in that context Russian President Vladimir Putin had escalated so-called "hybrid" attacks involving armed drones or sabotage attacks on Nato countries like Germany. Russia denies carrying out the attacks.
"What [Putin] is seeing is not a united stance from the United States and the Europeans to further increase pressure on Russia… he sees that they are weakening, that there are windows and openings of vulnerabilities in Europe," she told the BBC.
Last month, CIA Director John Ratcliffe paid a highly unusual visit to Moscow. He is reported to have delivered a warning to the Kremlin not to test Nato's resolve. But at the same time, one of Hegseth's top officials at the Pentagon, Elbridge Colby, was in Europe to push countries to spend more on their own defence.
Washington had announced a cut of 5,000 from a total 40,000 US troops based in Germany, while a Biden-era plan to deploy a US battalion with long-range Tomahawk missiles to the country was being dropped.
The drawdowns in Europe fit the Trump administration's strategy that predates the Iran war. It sees the Pacific region and Washington's rivalry with China as America's number one national security challenge.
But while the fallout from the Iran war has exacerbated Trump's irritation with Europe and accelerated some US military moves away from the region, it has not been to the immediate benefit of the US presence in the Pacific.
In fact, Washington has also pulled resources from there. Carrier forces were diverted from the Pacific to the Gulf, including the USS Abraham Lincoln and later the Japan-based USS George Washington.
The war is widely assessed to have left critical stocks of American ammunition badly depleted. The US fired about a third of its 3,000-strong stockpile of Tomahawk attack missiles, according to the Washington DC-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).
Its air defence munitions were burned up at an even higher rate, with nearly 1,500 Patriot interceptors - used to shoot down aircraft and cruise and ballistic missiles - fired out of a stockpile of around 2,300, according to the CSIS.
White House Principle Deputy Press Secretary Anna Kelly said America's "military might" was "stronger than it's ever been".
"The United States Military has more than enough munitions, ammo, and stockpiles to serve all of the Commander-in-Chief's strategic goals and beyond," she said.
Meanwhile Ezra Cohen, the former Trump defence official who is now a fellow at the Hudson Institute, described the president as having degraded Iran's conventional military threat.
Iran's proxy groups are weaker than ever, he said, and in many places they have been completely obliterated, meaning "the president now has additional options and forces in the region to strike other Iranian targets, including nuclear targets, at will".
The strikes might yet take place again. Thousands of troops, including the 82nd Airborne Division, were sent to the Middle East more than six months ago for a deployment that is now stretching into 2027 with no obvious end in sight.
Pictures last week of the USS Abraham Lincoln docking in Thailand with a rusting hull after a gruelling nine months at sea in the Gulf were pounced on by Iran. The regime tried to portray it as a symbol of America's spent efforts.
Hegseth, meanwhile, forcefully rejected claims of abysmal conditions on board. But the narrative war reflected the challenge for Trump and Hegseth as they fight to transform the Pentagon while waging a costly, protracted war.

A new wave of illegal fruity vapes?
STAT’s Sarah Todd was at a gas station in Ohio when she saw the advertisement for new flavors of Vuse Pro vapes: peach, berry, watermelon, and fresh mint. Companies aren’t allowed to sell new nicotine and tobacco products in the U.S. until they’ve been authorized by the FDA — but these products haven’t been. What’s the deal?
Sarah explains in her latest story: Some critics have said that the FDA basically invited companies to start breaking the law after softening its enforcement guidance earlier this year, according to some critics. And now that one major player in the industry has put unauthorized products on the market, it could spur other big manufacturers to do the same. Read more on what the impact could be.
A small but skyrocketing number of kids on GLP-1s
From 2019 to mid-2026, the number of children ages 8 to 11 without diabetes who are prescribed GLP-1 weight loss medications increased from 0.3% to 9.3%, according to a study published Friday in Pediatrics. That’s a 310-fold increase.
Researchers calculated prescribing rates by analyzing Epic data from across health systems. Among more than 3.5 million kids with obesity over those years, about 20,200 total received prescriptions. Most of the kids who were prescribed these meds had “severe obesity.” Girls were more likely than boys to receive a prescription, as were older kids and those living in wealthier communities.
An administrative gap delays access to new treatment
When the FDA approves a new drug, it’s supposed to make it easier for patients to access. But in the weeks immediately after approval, there’s a gap where the opposite happens: Early access programs — often called compassionate use — are immediately closed after a drug has been approved, but commercial insurance coverage often isn’t available for weeks as payers work through the technical steps required to start coverage.
Kelsey Solano and her husband Juan were in the middle of finishing paperwork to join Revolution Medicine’s early access program for its new pancreatic cancer drug when it received FDA approval. “He was considered an urgent request because his clinical status was really starting to change,” Kelsey told STAT’s Angus Chen. Without coverage, she had to set up a GoFundMe and raise her credit limit to get one week’s worth of the drug. Read more about the maddening limbo some patients have found themselves in while trying to get the first major pancreatic cancer breakthrough in decades.
Can dealmaking save rural hospitals?
Ahead of President Trump’s unprecedented Medicaid cuts — and the shortfall in federal funding that’s expected to come with them — rural hospitals are looking to cushion the blow by partnering with bigger, more stable health systems. Since the passage of the tax bill last year, the number of merger and acquisition deal announcements has been ticking up, STAT’s Daniel Payne reports.
And “for every deal that’s been announced, there are scores being talked about,” said Greg Maddrey, president of Chartis, a consulting group that works with hospitals. “There’s a lot going on under the surface.” Rural hospitals may be seeking out these deals, but lawmakers are skeptical. Research has shown that hospital prices go up in the years after a merger, and policymakers across parties have pushed for more regulation. Can hospital systems ensure that their doors stay open without falling into anticompetitive practices? Read more in the third installment of Unraveled.
1.66 million
That’s how many people died across the world in 2023 as a result of exposure to secondhand smoke, according to an analysis published yesterday in The Lancet Public Health. Overall, 2.71 billion people were exposed to secondhand smoke that year.
While the proportion of people exposed has decreased since 1990, the absolute number has stayed steady due to the rising global population, per the paper. And in some places, exposure rates are increasing: Exposure nearly doubled in sub-Saharan Africa in that time, and increased substantially in North Africa and the Middle East.
What it’s like to be a fat medical student
The anti-fat bias of the medical community is very well-documented. Even still, medical student Jessica Rosenblum was shocked by the way that doctors and trainees talked about fat people in front of her, a fat person.
“Sometimes, it feels like my identity as a medical student is a magic cloak obscuring my identity as a fat woman,” Rosenblum writes in a First Opinion essay. Other times, her fatness was all another person could see. The Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) has surveyed 1,252 paying guest (PG) buildings between September 7 and 9 as part of its safety assessment drive launched after the Satya Niketan building collapse, according to officials.

Greetings from Paris, where the 2024 Olympics balloon rises again
One of the highlights of the 2024 Paris Olympics was, for me, the sight at the opening ceremony of the floating cauldron held aloft by a giant glowing balloon. So I was thrilled to learn on a recent visit that the vasque — the cauldron — is still making regular appearances two years later, showing up all summer long in the nighttime Paris sky.
Along with hundreds of other spectators, I settled into a spot on the grass between the Louvre and Tuileries Garden to wait and watch on a warm August evening. A couple of hours before the balloon's liftoff from the Tuileries, the area was already packed.
At 9:30 p.m., a hush fell as the luminous balloon began its slow ascent. Some people broke into applause. As the balloon carrying the cauldron rose and bobbed a couple hundred feet overhead, many got busy taking photos and recording videos and selfies.
I snapped this picture, then put my phone away. No photo could match the wonder of seeing this. It put me in mind of the magic of a much smaller Parisian balloon, the one from the classic French film The Red Balloon. And I couldn't help but appreciate that in a season when skies across Europe have been marred by wildfire smoke and drones, here was a reason to look up in joy — an event of no purpose other than delight.

A wind-fueled wildfire forces hundreds from homes in Turkey as firefighters battle flames
Firefighters in Turkey are battling a large wildfire in Antalya's coastal province
ANKARA, Turkey -- Firefighters on Tuesday battled a wildfire in Turkey's Mediterranean coastal province of Antalya that forced hundreds of people from their homes and injured at least two people, the state-run news agency reported.
The fire broke out Monday evening in Antalya’s Aksu district and, fueled by strong winds, quickly spread into the neighboring Kepez district, Anadolu Agency reported.
Two people were hospitalized with injuries to their legs while six others affected by smoke were treated on site, the report said.
Authorities evacuated people from at least 254 homes in Aksu and Kepez and temporarily closed a highway between Antalya and the city of Isparta, located some 130 kilometers (80 miles) north.
As flames and heavy smoke threatened the area, more than 100 dogs were evacuated from an animal shelter in Aksu and taken to safety, Antalya Municipality said. Video footage showed veterinarians treating a dog affected by the smoke.
More than 2,000 homes in the region were affected by power outages, Anadolu reported.
The agency said at least five firefighting aircraft, 10 helicopters, 110 fire extinguishing trucks and 600 personnel were deployed to battle the blaze.
Firefighters were also battling wildfires in the nearby provinces of Adana and Mersin.

Over a decade ago, the Islamic State released a disturbing video that depicted its members lowering men locked in a cage into a swimming pool and drowning them. Today, that video has been reproduced as a SpongeBob SquarePants cartoon depicting fish in orange jumpsuits inside the cage, as SpongeBob lowers the cage into the water while Squidward films the scene.
The video, shared on TikTok, is part of what a new report from the Institute of Strategic Dialogue (ISD) calls “Slop Jihad,” a trend where young supporters of Islamic terror groups like ISIS and al-Qaida appear to use generative AI tools to create fan edits, cartoons, and memes designed radicalize a new generation of online backing.
This shift “signals a fundamental transformation in the aesthetics of jihadist propaganda online,” concludes the report, which was shared exclusively with WIRED.
“The principal concern is the growing volume and diversity of material,” says Adam Hadley, executive director of Tech Against Terrorism, a UN-backed counter terrorism organization that has also written a report about the Slop Jihad trend. “Highly stylized AI-generated content can make violent Islamist extremist material more accessible to younger audiences while reducing the visibility of conventional terrorist branding. Users may encounter perpetrator glorification inadvertently through fan edits, cartoons, memes, and other entertainment-oriented formats, after which engagement can drive algorithmic recommendations of related, more overt propaganda.”
Islamic terror groups have long demonstrated their capacity to adapt to new media environments to get their messages to a wide audience online, leveraging new and emerging technologies to aid recruitment and create a decentralized network of propaganda. This was seen in the early 2020s Alt Jihad movement, which sought to co-opt the aesthetics of the alt-right in the Islamic terrorism content.
These groups have also been making use of generative AI technology for a number of years. In 2024, the Islamic State-affiliated news program News Harvest began using AI-generated anchors to help disseminate propaganda videos quickly and cheaply.
But today, the look and feel of the content produced with generative AI is markedly different.
“This is new and it's still growing, it has not peaked by any means,” says Moustafa Ayad, the research chair in global Islamism and counter terrorism at ISD. “There's always been really shoddy content that's been produced in the support ecosystem, but it wasn't SpongeBob SquarePants as the Islamic State.”
Generative AI tools have also been utilized to quickly and cheaply turn official content from terror groups into animated videos. In one example, one TikTok account was turning the weekly al-Naba newsletter from ISIS into anime.
The Slop Jihad trend has seen some pushback from more traditional supporters who don’t like the new aesthetic. “There seems to be some animosity towards it, because they don't believe the producers of Slop Jihad are true believers,” Ayad says, referring to some reactions to the SpongeBob video. “But again, some accounts that have shared traditional official propaganda are sharing the newer videos. So there seems to be a love-hate relationship with the Slop Jihad content.”
For years now, TikTok has been central to Islamic terror groups online messaging campaign, taking advantage of the platform’s powerful algorithmic recommendations to spread their message. A report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development in 2024 found that TikTok was among the top 10 platforms used to spread terrorist and extremist content.
While Ayad did find a limited number of Slop Jihad videos on other platforms like Instagram and Facebook, the vast majority of the videos were found on TikTok. In total, he found 150 Slop Jihad videos from 71 accounts with more than 5.4 million total views on the platform. Ayad believes the prevalence of this content on TikTok is down to the platform’s For You Page algorithm “that is hyper-targeted to user interests.” He also credits the high level of general AI slop on the platform and “an existing entrenched ecosystem of jihadist support on the platform.”
TikTok contested the findings of the report. "This report's vague methodology reaches poorly evidenced conclusions and doesn't reflect how people use our platform,” a TikTok spokesperson tells WIRED. “We prohibit the presence of violent and hateful organisations, and we use a combination of advanced moderation technology, safety teams, and partnerships to proactively detect and remove violative content, as we keep TikTok a safe space for our community. All the content referenced in this report has been removed from TikTok."
Dozens of the videos identified by ISD for their report were deleted after WIRED shared them with TikTok.
WIRED shared the ISD report with several outside experts on Islamic terror groups' use of social media to radicalize followers, and all broadly agreed with ISD’s findings. “What is notable here is the ease with which generative AI allows a much broader and more decentralized set of users to remix jihadi figures and imagery and the extent to which that material can circulate across communities whose interest may be driven as much by violence, trolling, or notoriety as by actual commitment to jihadi ideology,” Aaron Zelin, a researcher who specializes in Jihadi extremism at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, tells WIRED.
While Ayad admits that some of the wilder Slop Jihad content may be difficult to identify as terror-related, much of it is very clearly supportive of terror groups and ideologies. TikTok has taken down some of the accounts Ayad was monitoring, but many of them have backup accounts in place and have signaled to their followers where they can find them in the case of a takedown.
“Some of the content is surviving for months at a time and continues to evade moderation efforts, whether it's their AI system that's meant to detect terrorist material or not,” Ayad says.

‘Channi has assured his full support to Congress’ poll efforts’: Sachin Pilot
Sachin Pilot told HT that all Punjab leaders have assured him they will work together to deliver results under Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge's leadership
Congress general secretary Sachin Pilot, who was recently appointed in-charge of Punjab, maintains that all senior party leaders in the state have assured him that they will work unitedly ahead of the crucial assembly polls. In an interview to HT, the senior Congress leader also spoke about his new role as well as the party’s prospects in the upcoming Punjab polls. Edited excerpts:
The Congress in Punjab faces sharp divisions between Charanjit Singh Channi and Amrinder Singh Raja Warring.
Punjab is very important not just for the Congress but for the country. This state is very dear to all of us including the Congress leadership. I have already met most of the top leaders in Punjab. They have assured that they will work unitedly. It will be my duty and responsibility to ensure that every leader and worker feels that he or she is a stakeholder in the collective future of the Punjab Congress.
Of course, there are minor differences of opinion. But we will fight this election with Mr Rahul Gandhi, the one person who has captured the imagination of the youth and all thinking people. It’s clear that Rahul and Priyanka Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge will lead the campaign. And everybody else in Punjab who has really toiled for the last one and a half years will be a major support to our effort when we lead the campaign.
Have you met Channi?
As I said, I have spoken to almost all the key leaders. All of them have assured me they will work collectively to deliver results under the leadership of Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge. People of Punjab want the Congress to be there. All of us want the Congress to win. I had a cordial meeting with Channi and he has assured me that he will offer his full support to the party’s efforts for the election. Please remember, the Congress had made him the only Dalit chief minister of Punjab. He remembers what Rahul Gandhi had done for him. In our meeting, he was very candid and assured that he will work shoulder to shoulder with the top leadership of the Punjab Congress.
You are set to face AAP, a possible coalition between Shiromani Akali Dal and BJP, and outfits such as Akali Dal (Waris Punjab De). How do you see it?
It will certainly be a multi-cornered election but the main contest will be between the Congress and the AAP. Of course, there is BSP, BJP, the two factions of the Akali Dal and some other smaller parties. But people of Punjab are looking for a stable alternative. It’s a border state and people know that religious divides or geographical disparities must not come in the way of giving a solid mandate. We also feel what the BJP has done in Delhi it was an open display of being anti-young people and anti-students. So, there’s a narrative now and I think Rahul Gandhi is at the forefront of that. Also, BJP doesn’t have a very strong footing in Punjab. They have been a junior ally of the Akali Dal. And even when they were together, they have lost many elections.
In the last election, the Congress won just two of the 69 seats in Malwa region. Channi himself lost both his seats. And there is a demand for a stronger Jatt Sikh leader.
When any party is in government, going into polls, person heading the government becomes a face. But as the opposition, it can’t just be one or two people. It has to be a full team. Look, Channi was given a chance towards the fag end of the term and he tried his best. I don’t want to use the last election as a benchmark. It was a wave election where a lot of people perhaps won who weren’t deserving. This election will see a fair decision.
AAP was untested and people gave them an opportunity. But in the last four and a half years, the AAP government has only served the interest of the party leadership. Today it is marred by controversies, arrests and corruption scandals. The Congress had a very good performance in the Lok Sabha elections, which indicates that the people want change.
What is Rahul Gandhi’s message to you?
His consistent message is that we have to work for the people of Punjab. The voters of Punjab expect the Congress party to live up to their expectation. He’s asked me to go and work on the ground and that he wants to spend time in Punjab. He’s very keen to start his yatra as soon as possible. Our teams are working to finalise the details of how to do it. Rahul and Priyanka Gandhi want the party in Punjab to work tirelessly, unitedly, collectively for the party and for the state.

GlobalEye gamble: Ottawa chose surveillance plane without knowing it met military needs
'There's gonna be trade-offs everywhere,' says government's point person on defence procurement
Ottawa had no guarantees that Saab's GlobalEye surveillance plane could meet military requirements when it began negotiations to acquire six of the Swedish manufacturer's early warning and control aircraft last spring, CBC News has learned.
Sources added that the most recent assessment of the GlobalEye came to the conclusion that the aircraft meets only a portion of the military's requirements and that modifications will be needed to achieve operational readiness.
Prime Minister Mark Carney surprised almost everyone in attendance at the country's premiere arms exposition last May in Ottawa, called CANSEC, when he announced plans to acquire the aircraft. He added the deal included a production line in the country for domestic and export markets.
Among those surprised was the commander of the Royal Canadian Air Force, who was in the room, say several defence industry sources.
- Stephen Fuhr was mocked for opposing the purchase of F-35s. Now he's in charge of Canada's defence procurement
- Air force's 1st new refuelling jet won't be delivered until late 2027
CBC News is not identifying the contractors because they don't want to endanger their relationship with the federal government. Four of them spoke confidentially.
At the time of the announcement, the air force had yet to inform potential bidders of its exact technical and operational needs for a new fleet of airborne surveillance aircraft.
In an interview, Ottawa's point person on military procurement said that the government must also weigh factors such as cost, jobs and geopolitics in major military purchases.
"Are the requirements important? Of course they are," said Stephen Fuhr, secretary of state for defence procurement. "It's not the only thing that needs to be considered here.
"We need to leverage this money to stimulate our own economy. We need to become more independent. We need to think about supply chains and relationships."
Carney's announcement on the GlobalEye forced the Royal Canadian Air Force to scramble to try and match what the aircraft can do with what it needed in terms of a surveillance plane over the Arctic, said several confidential sources.
It was only in late June — more than three weeks after the announcement — that Canadian military officials met with Saab to go over the specific kinds of features the plane needs.
There was one follow-up session in August where the GlobalEye's shortcomings were confirmed.
Carney has made it a priority to increase the speed of military procurement, but critics say the desire to leverage the economy — through the Canadian jobs the GlobalEye could bring — is trampling on defence needs of the country.
For example, the military is concerned that the plane, under its current design and configuration, doesn't have 360-degree radar coverage. There are also concerns about the range and frequency of the radar.
Saab has proposed modifications, putting additional radar sets in the nose and tail.
There are also concerns about the number of crew stations and connectivity equipment to plug the plane into the NORAD network, which would limit the GlobalEye's ability to offer a "control" function during operations that involve a series of military assets.
The military is also seeking a radar plane that can be refuelled in flight to cover the vast expanses of the Arctic, a feature that is not currently included on the GlobalEye.
Saab says it's responsive to 'customer demands'
In an interview earlier this year, Saab deputy CEO Anders Carp said the company is well aware of the Canadian military's expectations and that the company is ready to meet them.
Overall, the GlobalEye's sensors offer 360-degree coverage, but the main radar on top of the fuselage offers coverage in the 300-degree range, he said.
"We do have a program in place where we can place in a forward-looking and an aft-looking radar, should that be something that the customer demands," said Carp. "And the same will go for air-to-air refuelling."
Also in an interview with CBC News last spring, Saab test pilot Jussi Halmetoja spoke about the flexibility of the company's engineering process.
"We have a spiralling development process on how to improve our systems across the board at Saab, and depending on customer requirements, of course," Halmetoja said.
Fuhr added that sometimes, the government needs to opt for the "85 per cent solution," saying there is "nothing out there" that checks all possible boxes.
"There's gonna be trade-offs everywhere," he said. "So it's a function of balancing all those things to meet the moment."
Last spring, CBC News reported how Canada will have to ask the Trump administration to share a key piece of technology that allows fighter jets and early warning systems to communicate while maintaining stealth.
Experts doubt the United States will allow a high-tech data link used exclusively on F-35 fighters to be installed on either the early warning aircraft or the Gripen-E — if Canada chooses to buy that warplane.
None of Saab's U.S. competitors — L3 Harris and Boeing — were shown the air force's requirements, according to the confidential sources.
L3 Harris, headquartered in Melbourne, Fla., acknowledged in a recent interview with CBC News that it had not been privy to the Canadian surveillance plane requirements before the announcement.
- Canada ready to further distance itself from U.S. on military procurement
- Ottawa to spend almost $2B over 4 years to buy 190 Canadian-made armoured vehicles
Boeing, whose leadership is located in Arlington, Va., declined to say whether it has received an advance look, but a spokesperson added the company continues to stand ready to support the Canadian government.
The requirements form the basis of what the military needs to have in the aircraft — or any other piece of kit it is buying.
The process also helps the defence industry decide whether its product is the right fit. And if it is, the process sets the conditions to decide what kind of modifications might be required and eventually what the price will be.
The GlobalEye could end up being an extraordinary — but not unprecedented — end-run around decades-long procurement practice, says former senior defence procurement official Alan Williams.
The process, he said, is in place to prevent "governments making these decisions haphazardly."
Williams said it's important to distinguish between what the military says is absolutely essential in a capability and what is optional.
He also said he doesn't buy the argument that measures such as this are necessary to speed up procurement because there are existing authorities within existing legislation that allow the government to move swiftly.
"You don't have to go to these strange lengths in order to try to do things faster. Go through the front door, do things right and you can get the right result in a timely fashion," Williams said. "I think it really does undermine the process. And it makes us look, I think, very, very amateurish. It goes against the intent of the legislation."
Industrial policy vs. defence needs
Philippe Lagassé, a defence policy and procurement expert at Carleton University, said there is an obvious tension at play between Ottawa's focus on job creation and the military's long-standing alliance with the United States.
"It's important to recognize that military requirements are not handed down from on high in some platonic ideal. They are meant to reflect the government defence policy," he said.

"At the end of the day, the governments get to decide what they choose to prioritize and what they'd choose to emphasize."
Ideally, Lagassé said, Canada would have updated its defence policy and articulated "what the government believes the Canadian Armed Forces should be doing and with what kind of equipment."
That hasn't happened yet.
Lagasse also said, in an ideal world, there would be no "trade-offs between domestic industrial policy or defence policy."
Requirements don't give the military a veto over what the government intends to buy, he said.
"It means that the government has to come out and accept the operational risk that it's imposing" on the military, said Lagassé.
What happens if the trade-offs cost lives?
"I think that's the challenge, right? Who wears the operational risks that we're asking the Canadian Armed Forces to accept?" Lagassé said.

Mumbai: Maharashtra will focus on industry-oriented training, artificial intelligence-based skilling and a centralised placement system to improve the employability and industry readiness of engineering and polytechnic students, Higher and Technical Education Minister Chandrakant Patil said on Wednesday.
Technical Education Must Move Beyond Degrees And Diplomas
Patil said technical education should go beyond awarding degrees and diplomas and equip students with skills that match changing industry requirements and emerging technologies.
“Giving students only a degree or diploma is not the ultimate objective of education. They need to be made employable, industry-ready and capable of facing the opportunities and challenges posed by future technologies,” Patil said.
ISTE Initiatives Presented At Government Review Meeting
The minister was speaking during a review meeting on skill development, employability and industry readiness of engineering and polytechnic students in Maharashtra. Various initiatives proposed through the Indian Society for Technical Education (ISTE), including a Centralized Placement Platform, Centre for Future Skills and the ISTE-SmartBridge AI Skilling Initiative, were presented at the meeting.
The proposed centralised placement platform aims to bring employment, internship and apprenticeship opportunities onto a single platform. The initiative is expected to match students with opportunities based on their skills while improving coordination between educational institutions and industries.
Centre For Future Skills To Offer Training In Emerging Technologies
The Centre for Future Skills, meanwhile, has been proposed to provide students with training in emerging and advanced technologies. A presentation was also made on the ISTE-SmartBridge AI Skilling Initiative, which proposes AI training ranging from foundational to advanced levels for students.
Patil stressed the need for stronger coordination between education, industry and technology sectors to prepare Maharashtra's youth for a changing job market. He called for curricula, training and practical industry exposure to be aligned so students acquire skills relevant to employers.
The minister also directed officials to prepare a clear, outcome-oriented and time-bound roadmap for implementing skill-development programmes and take concrete decisions based on it.
The meeting was attended by Additional Chief Secretary of the Higher and Technical Education Department B. Venugopal Reddy; Maharashtra State Board of Technical Education Director and Director of Technical Education Dr Pramod Naik; Deputy Secretary Amol Mutyal; Institute of Chemical Technology Vice-Chancellor Prof Aniruddha Pandit; University of Mumbai Vice-Chancellor Ravindra Kulkarni; Shivaji University Vice-Chancellor Dr Rajnish Kamat; AICTE's Pratap Desai and other officials.
Patil said the government would focus on institutionalising such initiatives and ensuring their effective implementation, with the broader objective of taking engineering and polytechnic students from “education to skills, skills to employment and employment to an empowered future.”

In Summary
- The Poco M8x is the latest phone from Xiaomi’s sub-brand, Poco, and is targeted at the budget segment.
- The phone is the first in the Indian market to come with the new Qualcomm Snapdragon 4 Gen 5 processor and also boasts a massive 7900 mAh battery.
- At Rs 20,999, the Poco M8x packs a punch in everyday use. It cuts some corners in the display department, but remains a very good option for those wanting reliable performance on a budget.
Even as smartphone prices head north, a new budget contender has entered the Indian smartphone market. Xiaomi’s sub-brand Poco has launched the Poco M8x 5G. With a starting price of Rs 20,999, the smartphone is the first in India to be powered by the Qualcomm Snapdragon 4 Gen 5 processor and also packs in a huge 7900 mAh battery. It also packs in some good specs and some decent ones, but is that enough to help it deliver a performance that can make it stand out in a segment which is not as spec-forward as it once used to be? Let’s find out.
Table of Contents
Poco M8x Appearance and Design: Premium looks even at a budget price
The Poco M8x may be a budget smartphone but does not look like it. We received the Leather Green variant, and it is, without a doubt, the best-looking version of the device. There are plain-ish black and blue colors on offer too, but the combination of muted gold and that vegan leather back makes the Leather Green look very good indeed.
The back has a rectangular camera unit with rounded sides. This is slightly raised and comes with a matte gold finish and a shiny metallic gold outline around it. There are two large, dark camera lenses arranged vertically on the left side of the camera unit, while the flash is encased in a long, vertical pill-shaped island on the right. The Poco badge appears on the lower portion of the back, which is covered with textured green eco-leather goodness. This not only helps the phone stand out from the usual budget segment crowd but also keeps scratches and smudges at one arm’s distance. We are guilty of packing multiple gadgets in the same bag compartment, which often roughs them up, but the Poco M8x still looks brand new in spite of many such crowded trips.
The front of the phone is more regular-looking. It is all about a tall display, surrounded by bezels which can be termed “thick” now, for those who notice them. There is a punch-hole notch in the middle of the top of the display, which is home to the front camera. The sides of the phone also come in the same gold shade as the camera unit and house ports and buttons. The left side of the frame is completely plain, while the right side carries the volume rocker and the power/lock button, which doubles up as a physical fingerprint scanner as well. While it has been written off in almost every other smartphone segment, you do get to see the mighty 3.5 mm audio jack in the budget segment. The Poco M8x comes with one right on top of the phone, although the trademark IR blaster has been skipped. The base holds the hybrid SIM card tray, along with a USB Type-C port and a speaker grille.
The Poco M8x is a big phone, and this is immediately noticeable – it is 170 mm tall and 78.4 mm wide. It is relatively slim at 8.8 mm, but at 232 grams, it makes its presence felt both in hand and in pocket. While the phone feels very good in hand, one needs both hands to use. It is a pretty sturdy customer too – it comes with an IP64 rating which provides some dust and water resistance, while the screen has Corning Gorilla Glass 7i protection.
Poco M8x Spec sheet: Fit for its segment
Its design may look more premium than its price, but the Poco M8x’s spec sheet slots very well in the budget segment, or rather the new budget segment that has been defined by increasing component prices. It is the first smartphone in India to be powered by the Qualcomm Snapdragon 4 Gen 5 processor. This is paired with 4 GB and 6 GB RAM and 128 GB storage, which can be expanded up to 2 TB using a microSD card.
The display on the phone is big – a 6.9-inch HD+ LCD display (yep, those have made a comeback) with a 120 Hz refresh rate. There are two cameras on the back of the phone, one being the main 50-megapixel sensor and the other an “auxiliary” one, while the one on the front for selfies and video calls is an 8-megapixel sensor.
One of the major spec USPs of the Poco M8x is its battery. The phone comes with a large 7900 mAh battery, with support for 45 W fast wired charging and 22.5 W reverse wired charging as well. The Poco M8x comes with Android 16 out of the box with Xiaomi’s HyperOS 3 on top of it, with a promise of 4 years of OS and 6 years of security updates. In the sound department, it features stereo speakers and a 3.5 mm audio jack as well. Since it has an LCD display, the fingerprint scanner is on the side. All in all, these are good specs for the price the Poco M8x charges.
Poco M8x Performance: A consistent daily driver
The Poco M8x delivers the performance its spec sheet promises. The processor and RAM combination is budget-level, and the phone manages to get through everyday smartphone tasks with ease. Jumping from one app to another, social media scrolls, messaging, emails, photography, and calls are all handled without strain. Casual games like Tetris and Subway Surfers run with ease too. The phone is not designed to handle high-end games – we tried Genshin Impact, and not surprisingly, the experience was laggy even with tweaked settings.
The display is big, and the 120 Hz refresh rate does make the process of scrolling on social media a pretty smooth one. However, it is an LCD display with HD+ resolution, which makes the content feel a little less sharp, even though the colors do seem quite vibrant. This, combined with stereo speakers and a 3.5 mm audio jack, makes the Poco M8x a good device for those who like to watch content on their smartphones.
We had said waaay back in 2020 that the real home of a fingerprint scanner is on the side of the phone, so the fingerprint scanner placed on the side of the Poco M8x is something we actually liked. It worked smoothly and was easy to access. There is the option of using face unlock as well, which turned out to be impressively accurate and speedy, although it is supposed to be less secure than the fingerprint scanner. Call quality was good, and we did not face any abrupt call drop issues. In short, the Poco M8x is a terrific daily driver, handling everyday life and delivering entertainment with ease.
Poco M8x Cameras: Good main and selfie camera for the price
The Poco M8x comes with a 50-megapixel main sensor on the back paired with an auxiliary lens. The daylight performance of the main camera is pretty good. It captures basic shots well, with a decent amount of detail. The colors look a little muted as compared to the natural settings, but still turn out good enough for a quick social media post. You get a 2x digital zoom, which basically crops an image. The details do get compromised here, but it comes in handy when you need a closer look. The camera, however, struggles a bit if you push it out of its comfort zone.
It struggles to capture macro photos – you have to keep your hand very (very) steady to get a decent photo, and the portrait mode on the phone did not really add a lot of visible difference – the bokeh added was very light and almost negligible, which was disappointing. The low light performance of the phone is nothing too special either. As the light dims, details take a hit, and the colors remain muted here as well. There is a night mode which makes results a bit better, but low-light pictures in general take a second to process, and it is very important you keep your hands very steady for that second (there’s no OIS, remember). The phone comes with a number of modes like Document, Dual video, and Pro, that give users more shooting options and utility.
The front camera also performs surprisingly well for a modest-sounding 8-megapixel shooter, in terms of both color and detail. With beauty mode off, it can capture skin texture well, and colors seem good too. The portrait mode on the selfie camera actually delivers deeper bokeh than what we got from the primary camera. It does not catch edges very well (blurred out my ear once), but the photos are good enough for social media posts. There are a number of beauty filters, all of which do their job well. However, it follows the path of the primary camera and struggles with details and color in low light. The primary camera is capable of capturing full HD videos at 30 fps. Videos also turn out well in daylight but get noisy in low light. All said and done, we were actually surprised by the cameras on the Poco M8x, which performed well beyond our expectations (we still don’t know what difference the auxiliary camera makes, though).
Poco M8x Battery: Where the phone is BOSS
This is one department where the Poco M8x shines most brightly, and how. The phone comes with a massive 7900 mAh battery, and it is safe to say it just keeps going on and on. The combination of a low-resolution display, an efficient everyday processor, and a big battery is a terrific one. The Poco M8x comfortably lasted for two days of hectic usage, with hours of Instagram scrolls, YouTube, and some Modern Family episodes here and there, emails, messaging, WhatsApp, calls, sessions of Tetris, and some photography. The phone handled it all like a champ.
With a bit of careful usage, we even got it to last the third day. It is safe to say this is perhaps the best battery performance we have experienced in this segment. The phone comes with 45 W fast charging support and a 45 W adapter in the box, which took about one hour 15 minutes to go from 20 percent to full. But so big is the battery that even a 30-minute charge session can easily give you a full day’s battery. And as it comes with a 22.5 W reverse charging feature as well, it can double as a power bank for your other devices, including smartphones and wearables. This is pretty much the battery boss of the segment.
Poco M8x UI and software: A mixed bag of functionality and third-party apps
The Poco M8x comes with Android 16 with Hyper OS 3, and on budget devices, Hyper OS is a bit of a mixed bag. The first thing that hits you when you fire up the phone is the large number of third-party apps. It is a little overwhelming – there are even multiple casual games of the same type. Although there are also popular apps like Instagram, YouTube, YouTube Music, and LinkedIn, the interface can seem very crowded. Thankfully, these can be uninstalled, and we recommend doing so.
Now on to the good bits. HyperOS is otherwise quite functional and customizable. There are a number of personalization options – from icons to fonts, to themes and wallpapers; you can personalize them all to your liking. There are also features like interconnectivity that allow you to connect your device to other Xiaomi products and carry out functions over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, and you can also link your device to a Chromebook.
There are some basic AI features on the phone as well – Google Gemini for writing and other assistance, and features like Circle to Search. Of course, given its specs, we do not recommend pushing the phone too hard in the AI zone. Finally, the phone has an array of accessibility features (divided into general, vision, physical, and hearing), which aim to make the experience smooth for all users. Get rid of the bloatware, and the Poco M8x’s UI experience can be a pleasant one.
Poco M8x Price: In line with the new budget zone
The Poco M8x comes with a starting price of Rs. 20,999 for its 4 GB/ 128 GB version, while the 6 GB/ 128 GB version is priced at Rs. 22,999. Keeping in mind the rising prices of smartphones, the Poco M8x is quite fairly priced for the specs it offers. It does face competition, though.
One of its most notable competitors is the Samsung Galaxy M17, which starts at Rs 17,999 and comes with triple cameras on its back (50 MP+ 5 MP+ 2 MP), a 13-megapixel front camera, and most notably, a Super AMOLED Full HD+ display with a 90 Hz refresh rate. That said, its display and battery (with no charger in the box) and its Exynos 1330 processor are a step behind the Snapdragon 4 Gen 5 on the Poco M8x. There is also the Moto G37 Power 5G, which starts at Rs 19,999 and is powered by MediaTek Dimensity 6400, and has RAM that goes up to 8 GB, but comes with a smaller display and battery and also starts with a 4 GB/ 64 GB version.
Poco M8x Review Verdict: The big battery boss of the budget segment
For its starting price of Rs. 20,999, the Poco M8x is a pretty budget smartphone. It mainly shines in two areas: design (Green Leather variant) and battery. It also does well in other departments, and we can see many people liking its large display, good speakers, and main and selfie cameras (in good light conditions). It also delivers very consistent everyday performance and comes with a very functional OS as well. All of which make it a great option for those who are looking for a good-looking but reliable device with days of battery life.
