Mumbai, September 9, 2026: Maharashtra is set to introduce a Land Titling Act by December aimed at providing definitive ownership records for properties and significantly reducing land-related disputes and litigation, Revenue Minister Chandrashekhar Bawankule said on Wednesday.
Bawankule said Maharashtra would become the first state in India to enact such legislation, bringing the state’s property ownership system in line with practices followed in several countries. He said similar land titling laws are in place in around 80 countries, but no Indian state currently has a comparable system.
Definitive Titles For Properties
At present, documents such as 7/12 extracts, registered sale deeds and property tax records issued by municipal bodies or gram panchayats serve as evidence of transactions and possession, but do not provide conclusive proof of ownership. The proposed legislation seeks to address this gap by establishing definitive titles for properties.
Under the new system, property owners will receive a comprehensive property card containing details such as the location, measurements, valuation and ownership of the property. The card will also carry a QR code, enabling access to complete property-related information digitally.
Vertical Property Cards For Flats
The government is also planning to introduce a 'Vertical Property Card' system for flats and apartments. Under this mechanism, the share of land belonging to individual flat owners will be recorded along with details of the flat, including its area, dimensions and value.
Bawankule said delays and discrepancies in land measurement were among the major causes of property disputes and prolonged litigation. The government is therefore working to ensure that land measurement is completed within 15 days of an application.
Surveyors To Use Modern Technology
Around 500 licensed surveyors have already joined the initiative, while the government plans to deploy 100 to 150 licensed surveyors in every district. The surveyors will be trained and equipped with modern technology, including rovers, while drones will also be deployed for land surveys.
The minister said the government aims to reduce land-related litigation to around 10 per cent of its current level within three years by establishing definitive property records.

Measures To Protect Government Land
The Revenue Department is also strengthening mechanisms to prevent illegal sale or registration of government land. Following a recent incident in Pune, the registration system is being upgraded to automatically flag attempts to register government-owned properties.
Bawankule said the department had introduced around 104 Cabinet notes over the past 18 months to amend rules and laws and streamline revenue administration.

Warner Bros. TV Group isn’t acting like a studio with an uncertain future. Even as the fate of Warner Bros. Discovery remains up in the air — given the uncertain timeline of a Paramount Skydance acquisition — the studio has been on a development and production spree in recent months.
This summer the division, under chairman Channing Dungey, reupped its megadeal with John Wells — whose hit juggernaut for HBO Max, “The Pitt,” already won four Emmys last weekend and is expected to dominate the drama category at Monday night’s main ceremony.
Also, Variety can exclusively reveal that Matt Reeves and his 6th & Idaho production shingle (“The Penguin”) have reupped their overall deal with Warner Bros. TV. Reeves and company first signed on in 2020 to produce all TV projects with the studio. (“Matt has a true knack for getting into the psyche of his characters and he and his team have delivered some of the most compelling, thought-provoking stories over the years,” Dungey says.)
Popular on Variety
Other overall deals housed at the company include prolific creators like Greg Berlanti, Bill Lawrence, Chuck Lorre, Mindy Kaling, Lucia Aniello/Paul W. Downs and Jen Statsky.
Meanwhile, since January, the studio has landed 12 new series orders — most recently, the long-awaited revival of the “Manifest” franchise at Netflix, “Arrivals: A New Manifest Mystery.” Warner Bros. also lined up pickups for scripted series such as the DC-themed true-crime mockumentary “The People v. Gorilla Grodd” at HBO Max; the Brett Goldstein romantic comedy “Escorted” and horror drama “Stillwater” at Prime Video; the reimagined comic “Afterlife With Archie” at Disney+; and sitcom “I Suck at Girls” at Netflix.
Then there are the dozen series that have been renewed in recent months: “The Pitt,” “It: Welcome to Derry,” “Stuart Fails to Save the Universe” and “Rooster” at HBO Max, “Leanne,” “Untamed” and “Running Point” at Netflix, “Shrinking” and “Bad Monkey” at Apple TV, and broadcast hits “Memories of a Killer” (Fox) and “Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage” (CBS). At ABC, “Abbott Elementary,” the No. 1 broadcast comedy in multiplatform among adults 18-49, returns for Season 6 next month.
And if that’s not enough, the studio is also spending big on the upcoming “Harry Potter” series it’s producing for sibling HBO Max; and it’s behind one of the most anticipated new series on Netflix in the coming year, “Scooby-Doo: Origins.”
Dungey’s studio domain also includes unscripted fare (including new seasons of “The Real Housewives: New York City,” “The Real Housewives: Salt Lake City” and Season 30 of “The Voice”), syndication (“Extra” and “The Jennifer Hudson Show”) and animation (including recent orders for Genndy Tartakovsky’s “Heist Brothers” and Tubi’s “Yokoso Scooby-Doo”).
As head of WBD U.S. networks, her oversight includes top 10 networks TBS, TNT, TLC and Food Network, and launched the No. 1 new unscripted series with TLC’s “Suddenly Amish.” Also this year, Discovery’s “Shark Week” had its best ratings since 2019, while “Puppy Bowl” scored its best audience in eight years across multiple platforms.
“Certainly when I when I look up toward my boss and everything that’s happening on the corporate level, it’s a complicated time,” says Dungey. “But it is not impacting our day-to-day business in any real way… My focus is continuing to work with the best creatives, develop the best shows, find the best homes for them, and that’s all been happening.”
Variety spoke with Dungey about the state of the studio and cable portfolio, and what’s next.
Two seasons in, what have you learned from the success of “The Pitt?”
What we’ve discovered with “The Pitt” is two things: audiences really love the weekly drop. “The Pitt” isn’t alone in this. We drop “Ted Lasso” weekly, for example. I think that there is something about the event. I think you appreciate them more when you watch them one at a time as opposed to binge. But the other really significant thing is the idea that you have it on an annual cadence. People right now are losing their mind that we’re already putting out teaser trailers for “The Pitt” Season 3 when it feels like “The Pitt” Season 2 just ended. And that feels good to the audience. It keeps them engaged and it keeps them connected to these characters. When you’ve got 18, 20, 22 months between seasons, sometimes even longer, life goes on and you kind of forget. Like, “why did I like that show so much?” I am hopeful that more streamers will put effort into trying to bring shows back on an annual cadence.
How did the “Manifest” spinoff finally happen?
“Manifest” original recipe did very well on Netflix, and there was a desire to continue to explore stories and ideas within that universe. It took a little bit for [creator] Jeff [Rake] and team to nail the right way to approach the concept. Even though it’s taken a little bit of time, I think we’ve now built something else that has a really great long-running engine at its core.
How much does the new show play off the old one? Is it a continuation of the story?
It was very important to Netflix that people who never watched the original could dive in and appreciate it on its own. But if you were a hardcore fan of the original, there’s enough connective tissue and mythology and Easter eggs that reward you for having been a part of this universe for such a long time. That’s part of why it was a little tricky to figure out exactly how we wanted to build it.
Will there be any cameos from the original cast?
Possibly. There’s definitely room for some of that if we choose to. But at this point there aren’t any big plans to do that.
There’s been a lot of conversation lately about the difficulty with Season 2 drop-offs on some of the streamers.
It’s always been hard. Back in the day, I always would say, getting through Season 2 is always the toughest. Because things launch, they’re new, they’re exciting, you’ve got a plethora of stories to tell. Then you have to do that all over again in Season 2 … And then it’s a one-two punch if you take forever to bring it back and then you drop all the episodes and you watch it all in a matter of days. It’s hard to remain part of the conversation.
You were looking to replicate that regular “Pitt”-like cadence with the police drama “American Blue,” which was passed on by HBO Max. How’s the search going to find it a new home?
We still have a couple of bites. We have the finished pilot, and we have another five scripts done to follow it. So if one of these places picks it up, we’ll be ready to rock ‘n’ roll. And we also still have “How to Survive Without Me,” which is the other pilot that we did in contention at Max. That is also the “Pitt” model, but the relationship drama version. It’s Greg Berlanti doing what he did so well with shows like “Brothers and Sisters,” with Ray Romano and Josh Jackson and Kaley Cuoco.
What’s the word on that one?
We should be getting some word imminently. We’re waiting on another script to go into Max, and hopefully that’s the thing that says “greenlight, go.”
Most recently, Hulu canceled Mindy Kaling’s “Not Suitable for Work” after just a season. I know you’re looking to shop it around. How difficult is that? A few years ago a show like that would have been given a second season or would have quickly found a second home on another streamer.
Every platform has their needs and they know what’s going on internally. “Not Suitable for Work” is a tremendous show. I love that cast so much. I’m very hopeful that we land a second season somewhere else. But it’s tough, especially with comedy, you really have to develop that relationship with the characters, and it takes time.
As for “Ted Lasso,” does Jason Sudeikis have another three-season arc? How much of it is mapped out?
We haven’t heard any creative beyond the season that we are finishing editorial on right now. When you get to the end of this season, I think you can see that it could go either way. There’s definitely branching narrative that could continue forward, and if Season 4 becomes the end, then I think it’s satisfying in its own way too.
Is that a Jason call? An Apple call? Who are we waiting on to see if there will be a Season 5?
With this, it’s always a complicated conversation. I think you can say it’s a little bit of everybody.
With the success of “Stuart Fails to Save the Universe,” how far can you take “The Big Bang Theory” franchise? More series?
This is such a rare gift, right? To have a multi-camera comedy give birth to a single-camera comedy, then to a multi-camera comedy, and back to a single. I don’t think it’s ever been done before that hat trick in exactly that way, I’m really excited that we’re going to be doing a second season. I don’t know if Chuck has another idea in his back pocket for how to extend this universe further, but I’ll certainly be the first in line to hear it if he does.
Let’s talk about your expectations for “Harry Potter” as we get closer to Christmas. This is going to be unlike most launches that you’ve experienced.
Oh, 100%. I’ve never been a part of a of a show this big, in terms of the way this world has been realized. The opportunity that we’ve had to really bring the books to life in the fullest of ways because we’re not limited by a running time in that way has been really exciting and I think will be really rewarding for audiences.
What’s it like to be working on a project where you know it’s going to be going on for years? You can spread out costs and plot things out.
Casey and I joke about this. You feel sort of like you’re the people at the beginning of the marathon carrying the baton, and you’re going to run as far as you go, and then you’re going to hand it to somebody else. Because I mean, this is probably another decade from here. But it’s really been fun to be here at the beginning and to help bring this all to life.
Has any of the corporate uncertainty changed the way you can greenlight a show?
We have not run up against any of those problems or challenges in terms of programming. Certainly as a largely independent studio, we are still buying projects and selling them to all different platforms at all different times. I have not seen any impact in terms of the decisions that Casey [Bloys] and the team are making on the HBO Max side either. And in terms of what we’re doing with the U.S. Nets, most of that programming is done on an annual cadence. We’re well into our buying for ‘27 and ‘28 and all of that is moving forward.
What’s the biggest thing you’ve had to actually put on hold or adjust?
We haven’t really put anything on hold. I think that if this deal continues to go on, we may soon. With some of these longer-term overall deals, it’s not that you’re putting anything on pause, but if you’re going to be making a big long-term commitment, certainly we’re going to want to discuss that with our partners across the aisle.
Have you found that the threshold for green lights has changed at all in the business?
In terms of green lights and acquisitions around town, I think that most of the platforms that we work with, everyone is being a little bit more scrutinous about what they want to buy, what they want to invest in. There was a there was a period a few years ago where it felt like people were ordering everything straight to series off a pitch. And now it’s a little bit more like, “We’d like to see a couple of scripts, maybe three scripts. We want to hear the series pitch for the season before we commit.” And I think it just reflects the fact that everyone’s slates are a little more compressed than they were. People are being much more deliberate about the decisions that they make,
How would you describe the state of development in the industry right now?
It’s been pretty consistent. 2022, 2023 was the beginning of a little bit of a contraction in the business as a whole. And certainly around that time, broadcast got extra skinny. That impacts the number of projects that you’re developing. But I feel like since that time we’ve remained pretty level year over year.
How are budgets looking now? You’re producing what I imagine is one of the most expensive shows on television with ‘Harry Potter.’
I think everybody is being a bit more fiscally responsible than they were in that really boom, bonanza time. In the pre-COVID time it did feel like there was almost a freewheeling attitude toward it, especially from some of the streamers. I don’t think you feel that anymore. We’re spending what we need to spend to make the best possible shows at all different price points.
Sam Register is leaving as head of Warner Bros. Animation, Cartoon Network Studios and Hanna-Barbera Studios Europe. Are you able to fill that position, or do you have to wait for the ownership issue to be resolved?
That’s absolutely a role that we’ll be looking to fill. Sam built such an incredible team, and the creatives who have been working with Sam for so many years are all still in place. I do want to tap a new leader of the division. We shared the news with Paramount that Sam was going to be departing, but there is no impediment to filling that role.
Now that you’ve been in charge of the U.S. network for a while, how have your thoughts about the future of linear evolved? Can they continue to be programmed as cable networks or at some point do they become more seen as content engines for HBO Max and streaming platforms?
It’s an interesting question and I think it’s both — meaning, there is still a very loyal dedicated audience watching these cable networks on linear. We’re having ratings growth on Food. We launched two new shows, “24 in 24” and “100 Cooks,” that both broke through without having some of our big-name talent attached to them. So there is still a lot of real meaningful growth in linear. But we’ve spent a lot of time talking internally about the fact that in this current day and age, we can’t just think about these networks as linear networks. We do have to think about them as brands, and how can we extend and enhance these brands. So many of them have great consumer connection. Especially when you think about HGTV and Food. People are more likely to buy a can of paint if it has the HGTV logo on it. They’re more likely to download a recipe if it has the Food Network logo on it.
Do you ever think about where they might fit in and be integrated with the Paramount cable networks?
There are definitely some networks that they have that I think could work very nicely with some of ours. The opportunity for growth as you pull things together is potentially very exciting. I am hopeful that there will be a point where we can actually engage in some of these conversations. But for now, it’s all theoretical.
Have you had any conversations with David Ellison about the company, Warner Bros. TV and the cable networks?
I’ve had a couple of meetings with David, but more of a “getting to know you” on both sides and less of “Here’s the vision for the structure in the future.” It’s too early in the process for those conversations.
Would you like to remain a part of this company post-merger?
I love my team at Warner Bros. Television Group. I love our shows, our talent. And I’ve become very happy in my U.S. networks role, which was something that I didn’t see coming almost two years ago. The best-case scenario for me is something that allows me to continue to play around in both of these spaces.

The Cost Of India’s Convenience Economy Fuelled by massive capital and discounting wars, India’s instant service platforms are preparing for a mega festive season. But the gig workers are facing rigid targets and uncertain earnings. The Invisible Cost: For an instant help worker, a booking is only one part of their shift. The rest can involve waiting near high-demand communities, staying logged in to remain eligible for assignments and finding an affordable way to reach the next home. While the platforms depend on this proximity to promise quick service, workers claim that the time spent being idle often produces no income. Pay Promise Evolves: The instant help platforms initially marketed domestic work as a route to assured earnings. But gig workers now claim that compensation is increasingly linked to logged-in hours and tier-based performance. The issue is not merely linked to pay. Missed shifts, emergencies and a lack of bookings can make take-home income far less certain. Algorithmic Control: Ratings, availability and allocation systems also shape who gets the next booking. This pressures workers to accept jobs to avoid account suspensions or reduced payouts. Furthermore, workers also claim limited access to toilets, shaded waiting areas and secure resting places near customer clusters. Safety Question: For women workers, rapid order allocation can mean accepting jobs in unfamiliar locations with little room to assess safety concerns. With ratings, incentives and account access tied to responsiveness, declining a booking may carry a cost. There is also a complete absence of welfare benefits like paid period leave or emergency medical support. The Litmus Test: This festive season will test whether instant help platforms can build a business that values the workforce as much as customer convenience. Discounts may bring bookings, but retention will depend on fair pay and safety support. But as demand accelerates, will these platforms invest enough in the workers who make convenience possible? Even if you’re a casual consumer of MS NOW, formerly MSNBC, you know the names: anchors like Chris Hayes, Stephanie Ruhl, and yes, the one and only Rachel Maddow. The network has built a stable of talent who’ve amassed a massive number of casual viewers, plenty of fans … and more than a few obsessives.
Now, the network’s president, Rebecca Kutler, is looking to build that entire audience into something more akin to a fandom—turning casual viewers and fanatics alike, whether on TV or online, into paying members of an MS NOW media universe.
To do it, she’s launching an ambitious subscription program, called Membership, designed to connect MS NOW consumers much more directly to the Hayeses and Maddows of the world. Sure, plenty of news providers now offer subscriptions, WIRED included (and by the way, you can subscribe here). But what struck me about Kutler and Co.’s efforts was both their methodical approach—they surveyed 18,000 people before landing on a final offering—and their resolute focus on MS NOW’s deep bench of talent as the locus of their paid program. In a world where influencers are the new newscasters, and linear TV is in an inevitable decline, MS NOW is diving directly into the breach: applying the influencer playbook to build a sustainable business that’s future-proofed … at least until the next great audience pivot.
I caught up with Kutler at WIRED’s New York studios, just days before MS NOW’s subscription launch. We talked about turning TV talent into fandom magnets, beating Fox, and whether media consolidation is actually good news for the network.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
KATIE DRUMMOND: Rebecca, thank you so much for being here today. Start by telling me when you joined MSNBC. What’s the timeline?
REBECCA KUTLER: I think it was right before the midterms in 2022. I had grown up at CNN. I spent more than 20 years there. I left earlier in 2022, and some folks that I knew and really respected reached out from then MSNBC, and they talked about one of those jobs that has a lot of running room and is a little ambiguous, but in the best way. I thought, “Yeah, let's check it out.” I started at MSNBC, now MS NOW, running their digital businesses, basically all their nonlinear businesses.
It gave me a real opportunity to learn the place, but also think about what are the missed opportunities that we could take advantage of in the next few years.
At some point in your tenure, you took on the whole thing.
Yes.
What were those big challenges that you identified when you looked at the whole portfolio and thought to yourself, “What are we going to do here?”
One of the things that immediately struck me when I came over was the fandom.
I had worked in other newsrooms. I have friends who work in other newsrooms. I love the news and love what we do, but I had never worked at a place where the audience really sees themselves as fans, with a deep connection to talent.
When I joined MS, it was also at the same time Jen Psaki joined, and we had known each other a little from a previous life. So we went out into the field together and did a few pretty straightforward field reporting pieces. And I've walked through airports over my career with a lot of different anchors and newspeople, but I’ve never had the experience of walking through with Jen and seeing the [attention she got]. That's why she was a great fit for MS. She’s someone people were behind and were rooting for, and had a deep connection with.
When you think about Rachel Maddow and how she lands. You’re very close to this industry. If you talk to anyone in publishing and ask them where they would ideally like to debut their book, I think most of them would say The Rachel Maddow Show. There’s a reason for that: The audience loyalty and engagement with Rachel has been proven over decades.
It’s funny, when she shares a WIRED story on social media, the traffic to that story and the engagement on her social media around WIRED is crazy. I can tell you firsthand looking at the analytics, you can feel it.
I want to ask you more about talent in a minute, but that brings me to this Membership program you're launching. I'm going to read from the press release, which I very rarely do. You will offer “new opportunities for members to interact directly with the brand’s trusted journalists, exclusive community features to engage with each other, a new roster of contributors and experts, original creator content, new verticals that explore how news and politics impacts everyday life, and 24/7 access to livestreams and television programming.”
In layman’s terms, if someone’s a MS NOW viewer, they watch it on TV sometimes, they see it on social media, what should they expect from this? What are they getting that they’re not already getting by having cable TV?
I want to answer your question directly, but I just don’t want to assume your audience is the MS NOW audience. So if you'll allow me 30 seconds …
Give us your best pitch.
We launched as a new brand about a year ago. People traditionally see us as this cable channel, and that's great. We have a huge cable audience. We're actually right now the number two most-watched basic cable channel.
Who's number one?
Fox.
I see. OK. We might talk more about that later.
But that’s just one piece of our business. We have, right now, a digital business before we even launch what we're launching this week, that has more uniques than places like Axios, Politico, The Atlantic. People spend more time with us digitally than places like the Washington Post and NPR.
And on YouTube, we have been quite efficient at building out our presence in that space. We get more clicks on YouTube than ABC News, NBC News, and CBS News combined.
I say all of that to say we are starting from a position of strength. What we are excited about, and why we're launching this product, is all those digital things I just mentioned, we don't have a way to catch all those people if they’re not going to be watching cable.
Got it.
It’s taking our current superfans who watch us on linear and giving them more. So what are they going to get? They're going to get direct access to our talent. Seven days a week at noon and at 6:00 pm, if you are a member of the MS NOW community, you can hop on and directly interact with one of our anchors or one of our reporters.
On Monday it’s going to be Rachel Maddow, and then you go through the week. You're going to hear from Michael Steele, you’re going to hear from Jen Psaki, you're going to hear from Reverend Al Sharpton. You’re going to hear from the people that you know and love from watching them on MS NOW and have the opportunity to ask them your question directly, and not just interact with our talent, but also interact with each other.
When we started this process around a year and a half ago, we didn’t just sit in a conference room and think, “Hmm, let’s make another commodity news app.” Because let's be honest, a lot of that already exists. What we did was actually start from a place of product research. We went out to 18,000 people. We did surveys, we did in-person interviews, and we spent time taking that research and getting to where we are this week.
What I most want people to know is, what you see this week will look vastly different six months from now and a year from now if we're doing our jobs right. What we need to do is build and learn and test and add investment and expand where we need to, but not really think that we’re going to get it all right on day one, but give ourselves that latitude.
Is the goal to pull linear viewers onto digital, or is it to better engage the digital audience, or both?
It's both. All those people consuming us on YouTube, on digital, on social, in audio, 90 percent of those people do not regularly consume us on linear television. So a big function of this product is to say, “Hey, you’re watching YouTube videos all the time of Lawrence O'Donnell. Maybe you’re not someone who's going to be a cable subscriber. But can you come join our community in another capacity? Can we create a product that entices you to be part of an MS NOW community, even if you're someone who's reluctant to become a cable customer?”
I would say that, for the average person, if you ask them, “Fox News, MS NOW, who do those networks reach?” I would say Fox News reaches Republicans, and that’s who has it on TV, that's who’s going to that website. I would say MS NOW reaches progressives, Democrats, left-leaning people. Is that a stated goal for you, or do you want that tent to be bigger?
Is the audience for MS NOW different from the audience for Fox? Of course it is. There's probably a small amount of overlap, but not a lot, and that's OK.
For example, when I think forward to election night, I gotta say, I think there’s nowhere I'd rather hang out on election night than at our table with Rachel and Nicolle [Wallace] and Lawrence and Chris [Hayes] and Michael [Steele] and everyone.
What we try to do is be smart, respect our audience, and be a fun place, and a place where, again, Michael Steele is a big part of our election night. He was chairman of the Republican National Committee.
Right.
We have a broad range of views, but I think they all fall under that pro-democracy banner.
Are you competitive? Do you want to beat Fox? Do you want to see that number one?
Look, I am a pretty competitive person. I just see who our competition is as wider than that typical cable landscape.
I want to build a great product right now and have a large membership community, and I want to make sure that we are competing on every battleground.
That is yes, absolutely on cable, yes on digital, yes on YouTube, yes in audio. I think that because of the life that this brand lived under previous ownership, there were times when our wings were clipped a little from a business perspective, and that wasn't—if I was sitting in the seats of the leadership team at NBC, I might have made the same decisions.
When you’re working for the very large, very successful companies that NBCUniversal and Comcast are, they need to look at the whole company and figure out where best to invest their dollars. So what they did makes sense for them. But now we're lucky to be a part of Versant, and Versant has several pieces of their portfolio that generate a lot of cash.
What is Versant, for those who may not know?
Versant is the spinoff, so a spinout, of NBCUniversal. For folks that weren't following along day by day, around a year ago, NBCUniversal spun out a series of businesses. Those include what is now MS NOW, CNBC, brands like E!—you know, Live from the Red Carpet—and then golf.
We are now part of a company that is incentivized to invest the money that we earn as MS NOW back into MS NOW. We're just no longer part of a company that has to invest in theme parks and other things that, for that company, made a lot of sense.
I don’t think it’s a secret that cable news audiences are declining, and I’m going to ask this in the bluntest possible way: That’s an older audience, so what do you do when they die?
I am not blind to the long-term challenges. That’s why we are investing in digital. But do I think the cable business right now for MS NOW is quite healthy? I do.
Our average viewer watches nine hours a week.
That is a lot of MS NOW.
Do I wake up in a panic in the middle of the night? No. Do I know there are long-term challenges? Yes.
What do you wake up at night worrying about? Working in media and journalism is hard. It's a hard business, and these are really difficult transformations to try to undertake, and to undertake successfully. What's the hardest part of this for you right now?
What I wake up angsty about sometimes is I know we have this guest or that guest coming up, but how can we upgrade? How can we make it better? What is the better question? What is the better way in?
I might be old-school when I say this, but I think content always wins. Every single race.
I want to ask more about talent. You do have some real fandom magnets. I think one of the biggest challenges in publishing today, especially on digital, is that it is so noisy. There is so much competition. It’s not just news, but it’s everything on someone's Instagram feed. How do you encourage your journalists, your talent, to break through that in a digital context?
I'll just pick on Chris Hayes for a minute here. Because there’s almost no time that I talk to Chris Hayes that I don’t then hang up the phone or walk out of his office and think to myself, “That guy’s brain is huge.”
I think that’s the answer to the question of how do you break through? Every brand and every place in the media has to figure out what their breakthrough is. Look, there's people who want to break through by showing cat videos all day. People want to break through by writing outrageous headlines that aren’t really based in facts.
Yes.
Where I want MS NOW to break through is being brainiacs, is coming to the table with something that is intellectually interesting, that is showing me something or teaching me something or adding value to a news story in a way I hadn’t thought about it before, of drawing on their experience, decades of experience working in the room, being in the room where it happened.
What has the experience been like of transitioning some of the more TV-comfortable talent that you have, who are accustomed to doing a cable news show, and saying to them, “Now you do these interactive sessions with our audience, now you do TikTok, now you participate in these other parts of the ecosystem”?
One of my rules is: don’t do anything that feels weird for you. What I mean by that is, if you in your own life don’t use TikTok, I don’t recommend trying to become a TikToker. It’s going to land weird. We’ve seen it. So what I have encouraged our shows, our hosts, everyone in the MS NOW family, to do is don’t try to be everywhere. Don’t try to be everything.
I mean, a great example, Symone Sanders [Townsend] is fantastic at TikTok and Instagram because she grew up in those spaces and knows those audiences. That might not be the same for Lawrence O’Donnell. Lawrence O’Donnell is a huge hit on YouTube.
What has Trump 2.0 been like over there? Have you seen an audience bump? Have you seen fatigue? The challenge with the story of Trump 2.0 is that there are a thousand stories a day. How are you thinking about reaching your audience in a way that can grab them and hold them?
What I want our audience to know is that we are who we are, and we’re proud of who we are, and you can come to us on any platform at any time and trust that you are getting our best reporting and our best analysis without fear.
We haven’t talked about it yet, but as part of the spinoff, we had to build our own newsroom. What we tried to do is build our newsroom knowing the moment. We’re not trying to be commodity news. We’re trying to build an absolutely kickass DC newsroom, and I think we’ve done that.
MS NOW is one of the very few media brands in growth mode right now. It's impressive.
I'm curious about your take on the possibility of a merger between Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery, which would place CNN and CBS News under one owner. Would that consolidation be good for you? Does this help you even if the broader implications can be troubling?

The Mandya District administration on Wednesday assured to provide all necessary co-operation and police security to enable peaceful celebration of Gowri-Ganesha, but warned strict legal action against miscreants disturbing public order.
Speaking at a taluk-level harmony meeting in Nagamangala ahead of the festival, Deputy Commissioner of Mandya Kumar said no festival should be celebrated in an atmosphere of fear and apprehension. There should be no scope for incidents that could provoke communal sentiments in Mandya district, which is known for its spirit for communal amity.
He said some incidents that had occurred in the district over the past two years were a black mark on the system, he said while appealing to the public to remain vigilant and ensure that such incidents do not recur.
“Every member of society should act responsibly to ensure that activities disturbing harmony and communal amity are prevented,” he said.
While pointing out that “no one is above the law and everyone should respect the law,” Mr. Kumar said it is everyone’s responsibility to guide the youngsters, who are led astray, and prevent them from engaging in anti-social activities. “Everyone should take up the responsibility of counselling those intending to disrupt harmony,” he said.
Single window system
Making it clear that installation of Ganesha idols in public places requires permission, Mr. Kumar said the applicants need not visit the offices of different departments for this purpose.
“Officials from the police, revenue, fire and local-body departments will sit together at a single location, conduct inspections and issue permission within 24 hours under a single-window system,” he said.
The documents required for obtaining permission have also been simplified, and associations and members of the public installing Ganesha idols should cooperate with the district administration, he said.
Superintendent of Mandya district police V.J. Shobharaji, who also attended the meeting, said the date for installing and immersing Ganesha idols and the routes for processions should be finalised in consultation with the police department and followed accordingly. Necessary police security arrangements will be made based on these plans.
Ms. Shobharani said the use of DJs will not be permitted. Loudspeakers should be used within prescribed volumes in residential areas, she said.
In view of the safety of women and girls, CCTV cameras should be installed near Ganesha pandals. Necessary safety measures must be made mandatory during immersion to prevent any untoward incidents, she said.
Social media monitoring
The Superintendent of Police said trained personnel have been deployed at every police station in Mandya district to monitor social media.
She appealed to people to exercise caution while publishing posts, posters or reels on social media so that they do not violate the law or hurt the sentiments of any community.
The municipal officials were also directed to install electric lights, barricades and CCTV cameras during the mass immersion of Ganesha idols in the town.
She also instructed the authorities to deploy a crane and trained swimmers during the immersion and take precautionary measures to prevent any untoward incident.

Late last year, men in parts of Congo’s Tshopo province began whispering about something strange that was happening in nearby villages. At first, the stories sounded too absurd to travel far. A man in a market claimed his genitals had suddenly shrunk after brushing against a stranger. Someone else said it happened inside a taxi. In another village, people spoke about a man who returned from town convinced that the part of his body had disappeared altogether.
And then the videos started appearing, people gathered around phones watching clips of alleged victims speaking inside crowded churches while pastors stood beside them claiming they had been cured through prayer. Some videos spread through Facebook pages and TikTok accounts. Others moved from phone to phone through Bluetooth shares and WhatsApp groups, spreading across villages faster than official information ever could.
In many places, the rumours arrived before the authorities did. By the time officials in Tshopo publicly denied the existence of any mysterious illness, fear had already settled across parts of northeastern Democratic Republic of Congo, where rumours, churches, and social media had combined to create something more powerful than a simple falsehood. Men spoke cautiously around strangers. Communities became suspicious of outsiders. Stories changed slightly depending on who was telling them, but the central fear remained the same.
Something was stealing men’s bodies. In the month of October, the health workers travelling through the Isangi area of Tshopo province arrived in villages already consumed by weeks of panic. They carried tablet computers, questionnaires, and reflective jackets as part of vaccination-related field surveys, but in some communities those unfamiliar objects and routines were interpreted very differently by residents who had spent weeks hearing that outsiders were spreading a disease that caused men’s genitalia to shrink or disappear.
According to Reuters, at least four health workers were later killed after crowds accused them of spreading the supposed illness.
One of them was Dr. John Tangakeya. His wife later told Reuters that the family had spoken to him earlier that day because it was his birthday. The children were waiting for him to come home that evening so that they could celebrate together. Instead, news arrived that the health team he was part of had been attacked by mobs even as they tried to explain that their surveys had nothing to do with the rumours spreading in the province.
The World Health Organization(WHO)-backed Africa Infodemic Response Alliance, which monitors dangerous health misinformation across Africa, later linked at least 17 killings to the rumours, though some incidents could not be independently verified.
Long before social media existed, versions of this panic had already travelled across parts of Africa.
Researchers have documented similar episodes for decades in Ghana, Nigeria, Cameroon, Benin, and Congo itself, where rumours of “penis theft” or genital shrinking periodically triggered mob attacks against people accused of witchcraft or supernatural powers. In Ghana, during the 1990s, several people accused of “penis snatching” were beaten to death by mobs. In Kinshasa, in 2008, police detained more than a dozen suspected “sorcerers” after panic spread through the capital and led to attempted lynchings.
Anthropologists who study such incidents have often argued that the panic is not simply about superstition. In many places, fears around genital theft became tied to larger anxieties about masculinity, illness, vulnerability, power, and social instability, particularly in societies where spiritual explanations for misfortune remain deeply embedded in everyday life.
But something about the Congo episode felt different. Earlier, panic spread through markets, crowded taxis, churches, and radio broadcasts. This time, much of the fear moved online first, where videos featuring alleged victims and miracle cures circulated rapidly through algorithm-driven feeds before local officials fully understood what was unfolding on the ground.
Several churches in Kisangani hosted testimonies from supposed victims while Facebook pages and TikTok accounts reposted clips that gathered hundreds of thousands of views. Some videos remained online even after authorities publicly dismissed the claims as false.
Health officials later said the violence exposed a deeper crisis facing public health systems in parts of Africa, where distrust toward authorities has been shaped by years of political instability, misinformation, and memories of earlier health emergencies, including Ebola and COVID-19 outbreaks, during which some communities viewed outside medical teams with suspicion.
In villages where people had already spent weeks discussing the rumours among themselves, the arrival of unfamiliar health workers carrying devices and asking questions appeared, for some residents, to confirm the fears they already believed were true.
Months later, the rumours have still not completely disappeared.
Officials continue running radio campaigns and public awareness programmes aimed at stopping the spread of misinformation. Arrests have been made in some areas. But many of the original videos are still circulating online, resurfacing again and again across different parts of Congo, long after authorities declared that the illness itself never existed.

Gaurav Bhatia files ₹2 crore defamation case against CJP leaders, Saurav Das responds with ‘Greater Noida court’ quip
BJP spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia said that the “test of truth will take place where it should - in the court”.
Bharatiya Janata Party spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia filed a ₹2 crore defamation case against the entire leadership of satirical political outfit Cockroach Janta Party on Tuesday and said that the case will be listed for hearing before the Delhi High Court.
Bhatia shared a glimpse of the court document which names CJP national convener Abhijeet Dipke and co-conveners Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka as defendents.
“Tomorrow, every solid argument will echo in the court. The final nail will be hammered into the coffin of lies,” Bhatia wrote in a post on X, followed by a cockroach emoji.
In another follow-up post, the BJP spokesperson said that the “test of truth will take place where it should - in the court”.
“When accusations cross their limits, then the law draws its line. A ₹2 crore defamation lawsuit. Tomorrow, this defamation case will be listed for hearing before the Hon'ble Delhi High Court. No social media trial. No battle of statements. Only facts, evidence, and the rule of law. The test of truth will take place where it should— in the court,” read his post.
After Bhatia's post, Das took a jibe at him and quipped, "Hilte dulte Greater Noida court matt poch jana! (Don't reach Greater Noida court by mistake)” with a laughing emoji.
The case comes after a war of words erupted between Das and Bhatia last week . Saurav shared a post claiming the BJP spokesperson had called right-wing ‘influencer’ Swatantra Bhardwaj a “dimagi naxal”, following which, Bhatia said on Saturday that it was “fake” and asked Das to remove the post within 24 hours and offer an unconditional apology.
While Das later deleted the post and admitted that it was generated using artificial intelligence, he refused to apologise.
“Nonetheless, I challenge any leader in the BJP to repeat this line,” Das said.
After Das took down the photo, Bhatia warned that it he does not apologise, he will file an FIR.
“It took only 83 minutes for the post to be deleted. Unqualified apology still remains. Tomorrow will be a day of FIR if no unqualified apology is tendered. Can't spread propaganda and then just delete and run,” Bhatia wrote.
Bharadwaj is a right-wing influencer who claimed in an interview that he had “cracked the skull” of the student activist’s father during the June 23 protest and escaped arrest because of his political connections.
He was detained in Bulandshahr on Friday, hours after the CJP held a protest outside the Parliament Street police station demanding his arrest over the alleged assault.

Last month, Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon won the state’s Democratic Senate nomination in a major upset over her better-funded opponent, retired Army Lt. Col. Alex Vindman. Her victory was quickly slotted into a narrative about the Democratic Party’s insurgent progressive movement, which has triumphed in House and Senate primaries in Michigan, Colorado, New York, and elsewhere.
Can Democrats flip Florida in 2026?
Angie Nixon explains her playbook to be Florida’s next senator.
But while Nixon supports progressive policies, she argues there’s more to the story than a simple progressive-versus-centrist tale. She says that she out-worked and out-organized her opponent — and that Floridians across the political spectrum are hungry for change.
Vox’s Astead Herndon invited Nixon on a special pop-up episode of America, Actually to break down how she won the nomination, why she thinks there’s a path to victory in what many analysts believe is a solidly red state, and what she wants to get done as a senator if she prevails in November.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel.
Why do you think your victory took so many by surprise?
It took so many by surprise because people both tend to underestimate a Black woman — especially a progressive Black woman in politics — and then one who wasn’t able to raise as much money. But as a former single mom for 12 years, I know how to make a dollar stretch.
This win is attributed to good old-fashioned grassroots organizing. I am a former union organizer. I am a community organizer, and I know the importance of people power and talking to people and getting them energized about why they should vote and why they should see themselves in this country.
How much would you ascribe your win to the type of politics that you’re describing here versus the progressive policies that you championed? Should we take this as a sign that Medicare-for-all and “abolish ICE” have strong support in Florida?
It’s all of it, right? It is the hard work that we put into this race to raise awareness about who I am and the policies and positions that I stand for, which are policies and positions that the majority of hardworking, everyday people stand for.
Just because we want access to quality healthcare and affordable housing and fully funded public schools, they try to fear-monger and make it seem as though we are communist and we’re not.
We are not communist. We are people who want to put hardworking, everyday people in power so that they can determine and shape what our communities look like and what our economies look like. There’s nothing radical or extreme about that.
Democrats are still dismissing your chances to win a general election. Prominent pundits have said that Democrats should not invest in Florida, and that would amount to wasted money. Political forecasters moved the race in the Republican direction after your primary victory, arguing that the progressive politics makes it easier for Republicans to win in a state like Florida.
I wanted to ask about electability. Can you give me the case for how you can win a statewide race amongst such skepticism?
The same way that I was able to win a primary being outspent and out-raised 18 to 1. I am building a very unique, diverse coalition of people. We’ve had Republicans and independents that crossed over in the primary to vote for me in the primary. They also volunteer in our campaign. They’ve made donations.
We literally have a bunch of Republicans and libertarians who have been stating that they are voting for me because they like that I am no-nonsense. They appreciate that I am trying to put a check on what is coming out of Washington, DC, all of the cruelty and the corruption, and that is the winning message.
Look, we’re up against a woman, [incumbent Republican Sen. Ashley Moody], who allowed the theft of $10 million. She allowed money to be stolen from medically needy and low-income kids, to be diverted toward two citizen-led ballot initiatives that actually caused us to not have better health in our communities.
People are frustrated, and that’s all Ashley Moody has done — just look out for herself, her campaign donors and these billionaires. People are ready for elected officials to stop bailing out these big businesses [and] actually look out for everyday people.
In November 2023, you introduced a resolution to the Florida House calling for “the immediate de-escalation and ceasefire…in Israel and occupied Palestine.” It was rejected 104 to 2. And it earned you some bad blood with some of the members of the Florida Jewish Caucus. The chair actually said that the resolution was born out of ignorance and antisemitism.
Obviously, the Democratic Party base has shifted on that issue over the last several years. There’s been an open discussion about whether Joe Biden and Kamala Harris did themselves damage in the 2024 election by not breaking more explicitly with Israel’s actions in Gaza.
Do you think that was a mistake for Democrats?
I would say yes. I would say that we have to have really uncomfortable conversations amongst our different communities and we just have to talk. But I feel that they did do a disservice in regards to just going along with the AIPAC lobby.
You had mentioned that you don’t support sending any money or any weapons to Israel at this moment, but I also wanted to ask about things like BDS, the movement to boycott, divest, or sanction Israel. Is that something you support?
It is. I’m a Black woman who is a descendant of slaves, and who is the descendant of people from the civil rights movement, and I know how we used boycotts and we used protest to gain our civil rights for our community. So I’m fully supportive of that.
You repeatedly said that you don’t support defunding the police on your website. It says that you support demilitarizing the police. And that “real safety comes from good jobs, strong schools, affordable housing, and healthcare for all — not from more cameras, more cages, and more agents.”
What is the difference between that and defunding?
Whatever folks think the difference is. I’m not going to box myself in because I understand how they’ll try to cut and clip things with me saying certain words.
But doesn’t that sound a little bit like lessening the resources that go to police to focus on other things? I mean, that sounds a little like the same thing.
It sounds like I know that is my position. I want to defund Flock cameras because bad cops are stalking their ex-girlfriends and ex-boyfriends. And so to-may-toe, to-mah-toe. I literally said this before and that is what I am for. I’m not trying to get clipped in any kind of way.
Let me ask you this way. I appreciate the focus on root causes, and I think you’ve laid that out that that’s where you want the energy to go — that real public safety comes from focusing on the things that cause people to commit crimes in the first place, but those often take a long time to show effect.
If we’re talking about the root causes of crime, what is the message to someone whose community is unsafe right now that does not include policing?
What I would say is, making sure that we invest in making sure people have more jobs and we invest in community control of the police. I totally believe in civil review boards and that type of thing, but I believe in making sure that people’s most basic needs are met.
One of the things that I believe could help that right off the bat is things like universal healthcare, or at a minimum, extending the ACA subsidies so that we can drive down these healthcare premium costs. Or fully funding these programs that allow people to have access to first-time homebuyer programs.
I was a single mom for 12 years, and I took part in the first-time homebuyer program that was funded from the federal government. That trickled down to the state and then to the local government. That helped me with down payment assistance as well as closing costs and those types of programs. We need to put policies in place that are allowing people to be good.
We need to push for universal child care. For every $1 that is invested by the government, it puts $3 back into the economy so parents can get to work. They can be able to make sure that they have money to put their children in different programs. We need to invest in programs to keep our children off the streets.
There’s been so much effort to put you in one of the boxes that have defined the Democratic ideological battles — DSA versus establishment. I hear in this interview how that doesn’t neatly fit with what it seems like you’ve done in Florida.
Where do you think this campaign fits into the ongoing question of where do Democrats go next?
We’re coalition builders, we’re aggregators. Folks should know, I was a vice chair of a local Democratic Party. I was also the field director and the political director with the state party. I have never fit in a box. I was a union member and I also led a statewide organization that was straight-up progressive.
We need all these things to fight back against this Donald Trump regime. Look, this man is not going to leave willingly in 2028. He’s created a paramilitary force in the form of ICE that is getting away with shooting people and slaughtering them on camera while they’re masked without any accountability. They’re pushing to see how far they can go.
Granted, Black people have been getting slaughtered on camera without accountability for a while, but now they are doing it to people who aren’t just Black, who aren’t just Latino. They are banking on us being normalized with what’s happening.
First lady Michelle Obama says, “They go low, we go high.” I’m saying, “We get loud, we push back. We organize stronger and harder so that we can win and change this country and build a new vision for the next 250 years, where we have a Florida and an America for all.”

Whatever happened to kindness? Spoiler alert: Our readers prove it's alive and well
In recent years, NPR has explored how small interactions with strangers can do more than just brighten our days — they can improve our well‑being.
Our original story from 2023 traced psychologist Gillian Sandstrom's research back to her experience as a lonely graduate student in Toronto who exchanged a wave and hello daily with a hot dog vendor she passed on campus, even though she never once bought a hot dog. That brief exchange boosted her spirits so much that she began studying the power of "weak ties." Her research found what many people intuitively feel: Even the most casual encounters can boost mood, ease isolation and strengthen our sense of community.
Global health professor Kristin Jenkins of Cornerstone University in Grand Rapids, Mich., wrote to tell us that our story had inspired her to ask her students to intentionally engage with strangers and casual acquaintances. They enjoyed the assignment so much, they wanted to continue doing it! In sharing some of their experiences with NPR, they described moments that echoed Sandstrom's findings. A mechanic started "a wonderful conversation" about nursing school. A hospital worker felt more grounded during a stressful shift: "Something as simple as using someone's name or taking a few extra minutes to listen can actually mean a lot.". These short, simple interactions became reminders that kindness doesn't always have to be grand to be meaningful.
About This Series
We're looking back at some of our past global health and development stories to see "whatever happened to ..."
Now, we've invited readers to share their own moments of connection — small exchanges that lift their spirits and stay with them much longer than they expect.
One woman from California shared a story about her mother, who lost a year of school to polio as a child and has lived ever since with a twisted spine and chronic pain. Even so, for the past two decades, she and her dogs have made weekly visits to nursing homes and hospitals, bringing handwritten cards and goody bags to people who normally don't have visitors.
Another reader in Kenya told us that a quick question about an acronym on a man's T‑shirt while waiting in line at a bakery turned into a lively 15‑minute conversation. They both walked away smiling.
Finally, one open-hearted reader doesn't just limit kindness to other humans. "Even a simple greeting like 'Hello, brother' to a hawk or 'You are so beautiful' to a flower brightens my day."
And the stories kept coming, all reflecting a simple truth: small gestures matter. To keep a smile on your face, here are a few more:
A listening ear, a pack of tissues
It's no mystery that I enjoy talking to strangers. Everyone has a story, and I'm hear (see what I did there?) to listen to it. I actually dated a guy once that said, "Why do you have to talk to everyone?" I knew right then and there he wasn't the one.
When I stumbled across the NPR article, "Why saying hello to strangers can be good for you," I felt inclined to share a story that happened just today.
I work in corporate events, and part of my job includes operating registration desks. Consider me the Welcome Wagon! The role actually requires a lot of project management and organizational skills, but for the point of this story: I smile, check people in and print their badges. There is a lot of interaction with strangers, which I enjoy.
Toward the end of the day, a woman came up to my desk in tears. She was so embarrassed about what had just transpired in a meeting and decided to share with me. She explained she felt behind during the training course. She said the presenter did not assist her in a helpful way and was actually pretty crass. When she packed up her things and left the room early, the heavy door slammed behind her, making everything feel worse.
Out of everyone she could have walked up to, she chose me. I gave her a mini pack of tissues and listened. The woman talked about her struggles of being an older woman in a male-dominated tech environment and about how certain moments could make her feel invisible. I felt like I had a purpose right then to help her in the best way I knew how – just by listening. By the end of our conversation, I felt her mood shift and the heaviness lift. I even managed to get a smile out of her!
What she doesn't know is that she gave me something too. During our exchange, I felt like I was right where I was supposed to be, at the right time. I am proud that I carry myself in a way that makes others feel comfortable to approach me and share.
The article said people feel good after random encounters with strangers, and I would have to agree. I try to remind myself that we never know someone's full story, and a little grace — a smile, a quick hello, or a moment of listening — can really go a long way.
Michelle Sarnosky
Missouri
Puppy love
After moving from South Florida to a small town on Florida's west coast, I discovered the community was more closed-off than I was used to. But as I was out walking my puppy, neighbors — dog owners or not — would stop to talk. Within a month, my new husband, who had lived in this bedroom community for years, was amazed by how many new friends I was making for both of us!
Thank you for writing about this small but powerful way we can make a difference in each other's lives. It truly is a two-sided gift.
Anita Finley Derr
Florida
A stranger's hug
My older brother passed away unexpectedly on December 30, 2019. As my family gathered at my younger brother's apartment in downtown Philadelphia the next day, the mood was deeply heavy. We were all in shock — disbelieving and numb.
My dad was handling payroll for a small organization at the time and had to walk to the UPS on Chestnut Street to overnight some paychecks. I decided to go with him. When we entered the small UPS office and approached the counter, the woman working there made a pleasantry — I can't exactly recall, maybe something like "Oh, are you all together for the holidays?" I decided to be honest. I said in a somber tone that ended more in a whimper, "Yes… but also, unfortunately, my brother died yesterday.."
I will never forget her reaction. Her jaw dropped, she gasped, and she looked at my dad and asked "Your son?" When he said yes, she said nothing more. Without hesitation, she came around the counter and gave us both the most incredible, genuine hugs. She didn't know us at all, but she instantly recognized the weight of our indescribable pain in that moment.
There was something incredibly healing and meaningful about that moment. To feel seen by a stranger who cared enough to step forward — it mattered. I'll never forget this, and since then, I've often tried to pass on that type of compassion, whether to a stranger or friend.
Cordelia Biddle
Pennsylvania
A world of stories
I always chat with strangers, in elevators, walking along the street, waiting in lines. If you pay attention and listen, everybody does have a story to tell.
Donald Pederson
Maryland

Burundians rush to leave Kenya ahead of crackdown on unregistered traders
- Published
Hundreds of Burundians in Kenya are scrambling to process travel documents to leave the country ahead of the crackdown on unlicensed small businesses run by migrants.
Kenyan President William Ruto set Monday as the deadline for foreigners operating small-scale businesses to cease work, after the trade ministry said some exploited visa rules to work without the required permits.
Long queues were seen outside Burundi's embassy in the capital Nairobi after it said it would offer free emergency travel documents to citizens who want to go back home. Others are racing to buy bus tickets.
Kenya hosts hundreds of thousands of migrants from across East Africa seeking work and business opportunities.
Kenya's trade ministry said there had been "deliberate misuse of visa applications by some visitors", who arrived as investors or tourists but got involved in business activities that breached their declared status.
According to the United Nations refugee agency, there are around 16,000 Burundian refugees and asylum seekers in Kenya.
It is unclear how many are involved in small-scale trading or how many would be affected by the crackdown.
Burundians have been seen carrying all their belongings - from suitcases to mattresses - as they try to leave ahead of the crackdown, but some of them said they could not afford the cost of travel and urged the Kenyan government to extend the deadline.
Ruto's directive follows a similar crackdown in Tanzania last year and rising anti‑migrant sentiment in South Africa.
Burundi's Foreign Affairs Minister Edouard Bizimana said in a post on X that "Kenyans in Burundi were living peacefully but if the hate speech against Burundi continues things will certainty change".
"Kenya government is responsible for the lives of Burundians living in Kenya," he added.
His comments came after Ruto last week said that while Kenya remained open to foreign investment, it could not be "that a person comes from China or elsewhere to be a hawker or open a small shop".
He argued that investors should create jobs and expand production rather than compete with Kenyans in small businesses.
Ruto's comments sparked mixed reactions, with some critics describing them as a populist move that risked stoking xenophobia. Government officials deny the allegation.
Some foreign nationals say they fear for their safety, while police have warned Kenyans against targeting them.
Bizimana's post followed an urgent meeting he held with representatives of the East African Community (EAC), an eight-member bloc which promotes economic integration in the region.
Both Kenya and Burundi are part of the group. Kenyan representatives attended the meeting called by Bizimana in Burundi.
Bizimana said he had asked the Kenyan ambassador to convey to his government Burundi's concerns and to ensure that no Burundian was subjected to abuse.
On Sunday, a top official in Kenya's foreign affairs ministry said foreigners, with the required documentation, including "work permits and licences", could continue their activities.
"Burundian nationals and all East Africans - and Africans for that matter - are free to live in Kenya as long as they conduct their businesses or work according to the requirements of our laws, Permanent Secretary Korir Sing'oei said.
The government's clarification, however, did little to ease concerns among some foreign traders.
Alexis Ntinanirwa, the head of the Association of Burundians living in Kenya, told the BBC Great Lakes service that he was unhappy with Ruto's decision, but was urging Burundians to remain patient.
He warned that the issue could have wider regional consequences because Kenyans are also involved in small-scale businesses in other East African countries.
"This issue is not only going to cause problems for Burundians working in Kenya, but it is also going to cause problems in the region because there are also Kenyans doing these small jobs in our countries in Burundi, Tanzania and Uganda."
Ntinanirwa advised Burundians involved in hawking and other small businesses to avoid confrontation with police.

OroraTech partners with Eutelsat for infrared satellite monitoring from space
Sept 9 : German space technology company OroraTech said on Wednesday it had agreed with French satellite operator Eutelsat to deploy up to 96 infrared sensors on Eutelsat's future low-Earth orbit satellites and expand its ability to monitor wildfires, critical infrastructure and maritime activity from space.
Under the agreement, announced at the International Space Summit in Paris, OroraTech has reserved capacity for 48 hosted payloads with an option for a further 48.
The company said the deal would increase its observation capacity by nearly 500 per cent and expand what it describes as the world's largest commercial thermal imaging satellite network.
The sensors will be integrated onto Eutelsat spacecraft rather than launched on dedicated satellites, allowing OroraTech to scale up its coverage more rapidly and at lower cost.

HIV is no longer a word that frightens young people. For a generation that has grown up seeing HIV transformed from a feared death sentence into a manageable chronic condition, the virus no longer carries the deterrent power it once did.
But the fading fear of HIV is confronting Keralam with a new public-health challenge. Changing sexual behaviour, gaps in information and awareness, and growing substance use are increasingly putting young people at risk of sexually transmitted infections (STIs).
The numbers seeking care at the 23 District STI/RTI Centres (DSRCs) under the Kerala State AIDS Control Society (KSACS) have been rising steadily. However, these figures do not capture the full picture, as Keralam does not have routine STI surveillance across public and private hospitals. STIs also rarely figure in formal public health conversations.
World Sexual Health Day
On World Sexual Health Day (September 4), experts say Keralam needs more open conversations with young people about sexual health, safe sexual practices, consent and healthy relationships. Equally important is ensuring that youngsters know where they can seek confidential testing, advice and treatment without fear of judgement.
KSACS data compiled up to December 2025 show that attendance at DSRCs rose from 41,417 in 2023-24 to 63,129 in 2024-25. Another 51,243 people visited the clinics during April-November 2025 alone.
The proportion of DSRC clients undergoing RPR screening for syphilis also increased—from 55% in 2023-24 to 70% in 2024-25 and 79% during April-November 2025. The increase in screening means more infections are being detected, and the figures cannot by themselves be taken as evidence of a corresponding rise in prevalence.
Of particular concern is the increase among younger clients. Among those aged up to 19, clinic attendance rose from 1,547 in 2023-24 to 2,255 in 2024-25; another 1,910 had been recorded during April-November 2025. The proportion of newly detected HIV infections among those aged 15-24 also rose from 10% in 2022-23 to 15% during April-October 2025.
Change in societal attitudes
“There is a change in societal attitudes towards casual sex and today, the earlier message of abstinence that we used to give youngsters no longer works. Many youngsters are sexually active today and our only message to them is to remain safe, because their health is at stake,” a senior Health Department official said.
Being safe goes beyond HIV prevention. Condoms significantly reduce the risk of many STIs, including HIV, gonorrhoea and chlamydia, but do not eliminate the risk of infections such as syphilis, HPV and genital herpes, which can spread through skin-to-skin contact. HPV and hepatitis B vaccination, regular testing, timely treatment and reducing exposure to multiple or unknown partners are also important.
Consent and communication also need to be part of sexual-health messaging. Being safe means being able to say no, respecting a partner’s decision and discussing protection before sex.
Substance use among young people is another concern for sexual-health professionals, who say intoxication can increase risky sexual behaviour and impair the ability to make informed decisions.
Testing is crucial
“One of the most important messages we can give youth today is that testing matters, even without symptoms. Many STIs cause no symptoms, so someone can have and transmit an infection without knowing it. Testing becomes particularly important after a potential exposure or when starting a new sexual relationship,” said V. Sam Prasad, who heads AHF India Cares, an NGO working in HIV.
Keralam’s STI clinics are seeing a range of infections, with syphilis emerging as a particular concern. Doctors also report a resurgence of gonorrhoea, which they say is increasingly being encountered in clinical practice.
KSACS data show that clients found reactive for syphilis on screening increased from 1,206 in 2023-24 to 1,455 in 2024-25, with another 1,121 recorded during the first seven months of 2025-26.
Complicated infections
“We are quite concerned that some STIs are now presenting differently and with serious complications. We have had reports of neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis and cardiovascular syphilis, which are complicated and require long and intensive treatment,” a Health official said.
At STI clinics, young people diagnosed with an infection are encouraged to bring their partners for testing to prevent reinfection. They are also advised to complete treatment and undergo HIV testing, given the close relationship between HIV and other STIs.
Self-assessment tool
To encourage confidential testing, KSACS has launched a digital self-assessment tool through which users can privately assess their sexual-health risk. By scanning a QR code and answering questions about lifestyle and behavioural practices, users receive guidance on whether testing may be advisable, along with information on the next steps and the nearest STI clinic.

SAN DIEGO — When Kura Oncology decided to take aim at a protein involved in cell division and signaling, researchers reported a bonus finding: Targeting the protein, menin, didn’t just control the growth of leukemia cells, it also helped control blood sugar levels in animal studies. The biotech on Wednesday announced that it is turning that insight into a new company.
The new firm, Caspian Therapeutics, is launching with $50 million in financing to develop menin inhibitors for diabetes and other cardiometabolic diseases. The initial funding, led by BVF Partners and joined by Eli Lilly and members of Kura’s leadership team, among others, is meant to advance Caspian’s lead small molecule drug through an early-phase clinical trial in diabetes and support the development of a second candidate.
Kura will retain around 50% ownership of Caspian, and Kura CEO Troy Wilson will serve as executive chair of the new biotech’s board. Robert Spencer, who was most recently CEO of Neurommune Therapeutics and has previously led drug discovery programs at Merck, was named Caspian’s head.

The first foldable iPhone is finally here, and following its announcement, we got the chance to try the phone for ourselves. We’ve long been told that Apple would make a foldable iPhone once the tech was good enough — has it been worth the wait?
Hands-on with the foldable iPhone Duo
We’ve tried the first ever foldable iPhone at Apple’s launch event.
It definitely feels like something different. The inner screen has a decidedly matte finish that handled even some glare from the windows above the hands-on area well. The folding mechanism is smooth, and even IP68 rated, and the crease is almost impossible to find with my finger. The 5.4-inch outer screen looks petite by modern slab phone standards.
The real show happens when you open and close the phone — rather than just switching one screen off and lighting the other one up, there’s a gradual transition that happens and it looks as if the contents of the screen come into focus as it moves toward its final position. It’s a pretty nice touch. I also saw the phone positioned in laptop mode with Netflix on the inner screen, displaying controls on the bottom half before fading them away. There’s also the usual tricks in tent mode, where you’ll get StandBy even if you don’t have the phone plugged in. I’m very curious to see what that does to battery life.
Rumors that a foldable iPhone was in the works have been circulating since at least 2017, with Samsung releasing its first foldable two years after that. Since then, almost every Android manufacturer has entered the market, including Google, Motorola, Huawei, Xiaomi, Oppo, and more.
Over the last decade, Apple has been variously reported to be developing traditional book-style folding iPhones, smaller flip phone variants, and even larger foldable iPads, before it eventually settled on its final form factor. While early rumors suggested it would be like having two iPhone Airs side by side, the 1.4:1 aspect ratio is squatter, closer to a passport book when closed. That makes the 7.6-inch internal screen wider and better suited for watching videos in landscape than other foldables, but great for reading long scrolling pages or multitasking in portrait.
The dual main camera setup shoots 48-megapixel photos and includes a 2x optical zoom. It’s largely the same as the iPhone 18 Pro, but lacks the variable aperture.
