The anger was impossible to miss.
As television reporters walked into Delhi’s Jantar Mantar and adjoining protest sites to cover the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement, many were greeted with chants of ‘Godi Media Haye Haye’. Several journalists carrying microphones or wearing lanyards bearing the logos of prominent television channels — including NDTV, News X, ABP News, and Times Now — found themselves surrounded by protesters questioning their coverage of the movement. In some instances, reporters were heckled. In some instances, the confrontation turned physical: Times Now reporter Dev Kotak was roughed up by the crowd at Jantar Mantar, and video of the aftermath circulated widely. A Zee News reporter was filmed in Mumbai standing in the rain as youth protesters around him jeered.
The mood was most poignantly captured, perhaps, by a banner at the protest site. It contained the mugshots of six senior mainstream media journalist-cum-anchors: Arnab Goswami of Republic, Sudhir Chaudhary of DD, Chitra Tripathi of ABP, Anjan Om Kashyap of Aaj Tak, Amish Devgan then of News 18, and Rubika Liyaquat of Times Now Navbharat. Above their photos, the banner said, “India’s worst enemies — More dangerous that terrorists or anti-nationals”.
Taken together, the scenes that unfolded in Delhi raise the important question: Why did a large section of young protesters reserve some of their sharpest criticism not for politicians or police, but for television news channels?
Television Crew Faces Public Anger
The protests that erupted in Delhi in June-July brought together thousands of students and young people from across the country, turning a satirical political collective called the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) into the nucleus of a wider youth-led movement. What began as a mobilisation around the NEET-UG paper leak and concerns over the examination system expanded into a broader expression of anger against the government, with protesters demanding accountability from those in charge. The demonstrations grew in scale over weeks, drawing sustained public and media attention and eventually contributing to Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation.
As the protests grew, major television networks deployed reporters to cover the events. Instead of the routine interactions that often accompany live reporting, many ground reporters encountered open hostility from sections of the crowd.
Slogans of “Godi Media” were raised during a gathering in the national capital Delhi. pic.twitter.com/oyZpCVz0EY
— The Nawakadal (@thenawakadal) July 20, 2026
Videos shared widely on social media show protesters chanting ‘Godi Media Haye Haye’ — a phrase originally coined by journalist Ravish Kumar, roughly translating to ‘lapdog media’ — as reporters prepared to go live. In one video, a protester says he stopped a News18 vehicle from being damaged despite his own anger towards the channel. “I am a Muslim myself. I protected their vehicle from being damaged. Though I know this evening, they will again do a Hindu-Muslim debate,” he said.
GODI MEDIA IS DEAD!
Yesterday’s Massive Student Protest Delivered The Final Verdict:
Traditional Mainstream Media has COMPLETELY LOST Gen Z’s Trust!
Lakhs of Students who hit the streets got EVERY piece of Real Information from Social Media — not your Biased Propaganda Boxes.… pic.twitter.com/zLIOM5GXP1
— তন্ময় l T͞anmoy l (@tanmoyofc) July 21, 2026
As reporters started being identified by the brands they represented, some began using unbranded microphones instead. NDTV’s Shiv Aroor and Vishnu Som, and India Today’s Preeti Choudhry were among those.
The outbursts were not confined to a handful of isolated incidents. Numerous videos from different locations captured similar confrontations, while comments beneath those videos echoed the protesters’ criticism of mainstream television news. Smaller outlets perceived as pro-government were heckled as well, suggesting the hostility was directed at a type of coverage rather than at legacy television alone.
At the same time, several incidents crossed the line from protest into intimidation. Videos also emerged showing journalists being pushed, chased or physically heckled by sections of the crowd.
This andhbhakti of CJP is now crossing all limits. You can tell godi media to walk away, raise slogans, but you can’t physically push, grope or beat them.
Wonder whether these are genuine protestors or lumpen elements.https://t.co/Xo4bTJ1DgX
— 🍉 (@DelhiIsNotFar) July 21, 2026
In Kolkata as well, reporters of mainstream media outlets were allegedly pushed and shoved after a march on July 24 in solidarity with the Jantar Mantar protest.
Why Were Protesters Angry?
The central allegation against sections of legacy media seemed to be that they had stopped acting as the voice of the people and had instead become the voice of the establishment.
For many of the demonstrators, the resentment did not begin with the July protests.
Television news channels have failed, over the years, to hold the Union government to account over a wide range of issues that affect ordinary citizens’ lives — from examination paper leaks and irregularities in recruitment exams to unemployment, price rise, public health etc. This is precisely the role the media is expected to play as democracy’s fourth pillar. Most television news channels that have ample airtime for communal debates and polarising studio confrontations show far less urgency when the failures of the government directly affect the lives and futures of citizens.
The dissatisfaction was not simply about what television channels were reporting during the protests, but what they had consistently chosen not to report. For a generation facing an increasingly precarious education and employment landscape, the perceived reluctance of mainstream television to question those in power became a source of deep distrust.
Explaining the reasons for the anger against the mainstream media, AISA leader and student face of the Delhi protests Neha Bora said, “The hate that the government peddles comes to our drawing rooms, our WhatsApp groups and our very personal lives, within the four walls of our homes, through the Godi media. The Godi media and the IT cell are single-handedly responsible for the venom that runs through the veins of this country presently. Through systematic targeting and organised campaigns, they have made enemies out of citizens, neighbours and friends.”
Elaborating on how they had failed in their duty, she added, “The government is not a God-like figure. They are there to do a job; they have been elected to serve us. They will have to be questioned. The Godi media has systematically dismantled this idea. We are told not to question the government, criticise its policies or talk about the problems we face. If I say that the answer sheet in the Class 12 examination is not mine, the Godi media and the IT cell are going to call me a Pakistani.”
In May, Doordarshan anchor Ashok Srivastav called Class XII student from Delhi Vedant Srivastava a Pakistani. After receiving unexpectedly low marks in Physics, Vedant had applied for photocopies of his answer sheets through CBSE’s reevaluation process. When the copies arrived, he discovered that the Physics answer sheet uploaded by the Board was not his. He made an X account to post about his grievances.
“The disrespect that the youth has for Godi media stems from this — the recognition that this Godi media and its anchors, who scream at the top of their voices on TV screens, have fractured the democratic, secular fabric of this country,” Neha added.
Asked for her response to ground reporters being heckled, Neha said, “We recognise that there are ground reporters in Godi media who do honest work, and that is why we urged our people not to disrespect them. Our differences need not be expressed through violence. We don’t believe in mobs. But there is no denying that the mainstream media has become a BJP propaganda cell, it seems.”
The protesters’ criticism was also shaped by how they believed the movement itself was being portrayed.
Arnab Goswami, for example, in an apparent bid to discredit the protest and question its legitimacy, mentioned China, US, Bangladesh, Pakistan, BitChat, the deep state, Greta Thunberg, Jeremy Corbyn, and even John Cusack as conspirators behind the CJP protest.
In a podcast hosted by Navika Kumar, lyricist and screenwriter Manoj Muntashir Shukla called protesters anti-nationals.
As clashes broke out between protesters and police on July 20, ANI did not post a single news update throughout the day which mentioned injury to protesters.
In Kolkata, Zee reporter Ayan Ghoshal said while interviewing BJP leader Dilip Ghosh, “For the last 3 days efforts are on in Delhi to break India. PM has shown restraint. We know how Pak or Indonesia curbed students’ protest. Dead bodies were strewn on sreets. But no tough action here. They’re getting encouraged.”
The mainstream media drew criticism on social media for what protesters described as coverage that closely mirrored the official version put forward by the Delhi Police and the government. The channels, on the other hand, maintained that they were reporting developments on the ground.
You are the most vile, most pathetic, most disgusting person @sudhirchaudhary
I always agree to disagree, never hate anyone but you are really a bad person.
You are now labelling innocent students for your propaganda.
Shame on you! pic.twitter.com/lYj5cNlURk
— Arpit Sharma (@iArpitSpeaks) July 21, 2026
Rahul Shivshankar, editorial director of CNN News 18, amplified a video where RSS leader Atul Limaye called the CJP protest anti-national and “a weapon against the Constitution”.
It is worth noting that coverage of this kind carries risks beyond the newsroom. Framing a protest movement as anti-national, foreign-funded or a security threat can shape how the protesters are treated on the ground, by the state and by ordinary citizens alike. The Zee reporter’s on-air remarks, for example, were arguably not only biased, but amounted to incitement. Seen against this backdrop, at least some of the heckling and intimidation directed at reporters on the ground could be a reaction to this pattern of coverage.
A Widening Trust Deficit
The outpouring of anger at journalists points to a broader crisis of credibility confronting sections of India’s television news industry.
Alt News’s years of fact-checking work and media-watchdog journalism point to a pattern rather than isolated lapses: In the recent past, large sections of mainstream television media have functioned as an echo chamber for the government. The clearest symptom is the collapse of verification standards and rampant amplification of misinformation. During the India-Pakistan military escalation following the Pahalgam attack, several major channels aired unverified and outright false claims — old and unrelated videos and fabricated visuals presented as live combat coverage.
ALSO READ: Op Sindoor: As Indian media made false, outrageous claims, PIB looked the other way
Further in the past, we documented instances of mainstream media broadcasting misinformation targeting protesters and protest movements. During the 2024 farmers’ movement, Republic, News 18, India TV, Zee News, India Today, Navbharat Times — all ran a doctored video of farmer leader Jagjit Singh Dallewal without any context and amplified the misleading claim that he said Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s popularity graph had skyrocketed after the Ram Mandir inauguration and reached an all-time high.
More examples of such misreporting related the farmers’ protest can be found here and here.
It is worth noting that during the farmers’ movement of 2020–21, too, several mainstream television channels faced sustained criticism over their coverage, including banners at protest sites slamming Godi Media. Farmers accused sections of the media of portraying the agitation as foreign-funded or sympathetic to Khalistani groups rather than engaging with their demands. However, the scale and frequency of confrontations witnessed during the CJP-led protests appear significantly greater than what was seen during the farmers’ movement.
ALSO READ: The fictional strikes on the Karachi port and what it says about Indian media
A second, related failure is the normalization of communal debates on prime-time shows. On almost a daily basis, senior journalists anchor panel debates that are structured for conflict, with the hosts allowing and sometimes encouraging inflammatory rhetoric against minorities, because it drives engagement.
Check the thumbnails in the compilations from 2022 below. Each and every bulletin represented by these thumbnails was on communal issues. All on News 18:
Hosted by Aman Chopra:
Shows hosted by Amish Devgan:
The cumulative effect is to cloak hate-mongering as news content night after night. Several prominent channels have faced punitive action in the last few years for peddling communal propaganda on shows hosted by ‘star’ anchors. Related reports by Alt News can be found here, here, here, here and here.
After Operation Sindoor, when several mainstream channels aired unverified and absurd claims, including reports that India had attacked Karachi, the BJP’s official X handle shared a monologue by anchor Sushant Sinha defending the media’s coverage as part of a broader “information war” in national interest.
पाकिस्तान कभी नहीं सुधरेगा और हो सकता है कि युद्ध भी हो, लेकिन क्या ऐसे लड़ेगा भारत?
ऐसे भारत विरोधी तत्वों को पहचानिए, जिन्होंने #OperationSindoor के समय अपने देश, देश की मीडिया और देश की सेना का मजाक बनाया था…
हमारे जवान तो जंग के लिए तैयार हैं, लेकिन क्या आप मन से तैयार… pic.twitter.com/spQrwxqbTm
— BJP (@BJP4India) May 14, 2025
There could be no clearer indicator of the alignment of the mainstream media with the BJP government.
In a functional democracy, the public square is a space that should be open to everyone, equally, without fear, intimidation or violence. Whether that principle still holds in India is increasingly open to question. If sections of society — minorities, independent journalists and critics of the government — cannot live and function without fear of harassment, vilification or even incarceration, the mainstream media has played a significant role in creating and reinforcing that climate. And there appear to be few meaningful avenues for holding these media organisations accountable.
Structural Questions: The Nexus among Media, Corporate Power & the BJP Government
Structural factors help explain this pattern. Both the ownership and revenue models of India’s mainstream media organisations constrain their capacity for critical journalism. Several major outlets — including NDTV, IANS and News18 — are owned by large business conglomerates such as the Adani and Ambani groups, which have close ties to the Union Government.
The journalism produced by these organisations reflects those ties, more often than not. Television news, being capital-intensive, is also heavily dependent on government advertising and large corporate advertisers, who are often reluctant to fund critical journalism.
The incentive to toe the government line shows up not always as an explicit directive but more as a pattern of editorial choices: Aggressive coverage of opposition-ruled states, muted coverage of the same failures under the Union government or in BJP-ruled states; extensive coverage of minor opposition controversies, minimal coverage of major stories embarrassing to the ruling party. See here, here and here.
The closeness between media and corporate power was captured vividly when India Today anchor Rahul Kanwal was filmed tasting food meant for elephants at the Ambanis’ Vantara animal sanctuary, alongside Anant Ambani. For many viewers, the spectacle reinforced the perception of a media establishment more comfortable warming up to power than challenging it.
This was in March 2024. Exactly one year later, Vantara was in the news again. This time, after a South African wildlife coalition urged its government to investigate the transfer of wild animals to the Reliance-owned facility. A handful of Indian outlets reported the concerns, but within days, many of them took down their reports, leaving readers with ‘Error 404’ or ‘Page Not Found’ messages. The reasons for the removals remained unexplained. At least three media houses told Alt News that they had received threatening calls or emails.
In 2018, ABP News managing editor Milind Khandekar and anchor Punya Prasun Bajpai resigned after Bajpai’s show ‘Masterstroke’ fact-checked a claim made during a public interaction involving Prime Minister Modi. Chandramani Kaushik, a farmer from Chhattisgarh, had told Modi her income had doubled after she switched from paddy cultivation to processing custard apple. When ABP interviewed her, she said she had been coached by officials to make the claim. Senior anchor Abhisar Sharma was taken off air days later after e juxtaposed a Modi speech in Lucknow praising Uttar Pradesh’s improved law-and-order record with a shootout in the state on the same day.
Efforts to counter this nexus have had limited success. The Independent and Public-Spirited Media Foundation (IPSMF), set up with funding from Azim Premji and Nandan Nilekani to support independent journalism, has faced funding constraints in recent years and has been the subject of income tax investigations.
These dynamics are reflected in India’s global press freedom rankings, which have declined in the last two decades.
Reporters, like people in every other field of work, must be able to do their job without harassment or fear of violence. And physical retaliation can not become an acceptable response to disliked coverage. Once it is, it can easily be turned against any journalist doing legitimate reporting — not only those seen as compromised. But condemning those attacks should not foreclose an examination of the reasons behind the hostility.
The chants of ‘Godi Media Haye Haye’ were directed not merely at individual reporters standing in front of television cameras, but at institutions that many protesters believe have repeatedly failed to hold those in power accountable. Whether or not that perception is fair, the scenes from Delhi point to a widening gap between a section of India’s youth and parts of the country’s mainstream television news industry — a gap that did not emerge overnight, and is unlikely to close soon.

Satya Niketan Tragedy Aftermath: PG Staff Flees, DU Girls Denied Food & Face Harassment
In the aftermath of the building collapse involving the Hostel Days boys' hostel in Satya Niketan, female Delhi University students staying in an affiliated girls' PG face severe distress and harassment. With the owner arrested and the warden and caretaker absconding after turning off communication and disconnecting Wi-Fi, the residents have been left without essential management or assistance. Students report paying substantial security deposits and monthly rent of fifteen thousand rupees, yet they are being denied scheduled meals and asked to pay an additional four thousand rupees for food. Local religious institutions, including gurudwaras and temples, have stepped in to provide daily meals. Meanwhile, college faculty from Maitri College have provided temporary shelter in the college auditorium for stranded students. Faculty and students also revealed that PG owners in the area are refusing to refund deposits, denying media entry, and allegedly threatening occupants against reporting the unauthorised operations to authorities or police.

Chelsea agree £47.1m move for Monaco's Camara
- Published
Chelsea have agreed a £47.1m deal to sign Monaco midfielder Lamine Camara.
The 22-year-old is set to undergo a medical after Chelsea complete the sale of Enzo Fernandez to Manchester City in a deal that matched the £125m British transfer record.
Chelsea had been reluctant to complete a transfer for Monaco's asking price but they are believed to have dropped their demands when striker Folarin Balogun's move to Everton from the French club came into renewed doubt.
It was expected the Blues would continue with their current midfielder options despite sanctioning Fernandez's exit but an opportunity to sign one of their primary targets at a lower price was taken up.
They had also held talks with Roma's Manu Kone and another unnamed Premier League option.
The signing is not viewed as a like-for-like replacement for Fernandez, with Camara offering a different profile in midfield. However, Chelsea believe the deal will help maintain the strength of new manager Xabi Alonso's squad.
One of the club's aims this summer was to emerge from the transfer window with a stronger squad despite selling Fernandez to a direct rival.
Chelsea believe they have achieved that after signing Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa in a club-record £117m deal, centre-back Maxence Lacroix from Crystal Palace and, most recently, goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez from Aston Villa.
The club have also recruited strikers Emmanuel Emegha and Danny Welbeck, winger Geovany Quenda, midfielders Jordan Henderson and Valentin Barco, as well as full-backs Marco Palestra and Pep Chavarria.
Alonso's side have won all three of their matches this season, beating Fulham and Brighton in the Premier League, and have also reached the third round of the Carabao Cup with victory over Luton Town.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

Srinagar, Sep 09: Lieutenant Governor Vinai Kumar Saxena on Wednesday administered the oath of office to Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati as Chief Justice of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh.
LG Saxena- who has been appointed to discharge the functions of J&K LG during Manoj Sinha’s leave -administered the oath at the Shalimar auditorium of Sher‑e‑Kashmir University of Agricultural Sciences and Technology (SKUAST), Kashmir.

I Found the Best Kindles to Take Your Library Anywhere
Featured in this article
There’s a lot to love about a Kindle if you’re a reader. If you’re looking for the best Kindle, you really can’t go wrong with any of the models. These Amazon-powered ebook readers let you bring thousands of books anywhere and typically give a month of battery life per charge. You can subscribe to get unlimited books from Amazon or get free books from your local library. Our guide will help you decode the differences to find which Kindle is right for you.
I've owned all kinds of Kindles, from the newest Kindle Scribes to hand-me-down base Kindles without a front light. The latter came from a friend who noticed I had spent my entire postpartum summer glued to library books on my phone, and I still have it to this day. But after trying all of the latest Kindles, I can say it's easy to spot the best one.
Read on to find out my favorite overall Kindle and my favorite Kindles for specific uses and younger readers. You can also check out my other buying guides made for readers like me, including the Best Kindle Accessories, Best E-Readers, Best Digital Notebooks, and Best Gifts for Book Lovers.
Updated September 2026: I've updated this guide with details about Amazon's price hike and which Kindles saw an increase (hint: It’s most of them).

Why Are Kindles More Expensive Now?
Amazon raised its prices across its product categories, including Kindle devices. The price increases hit several current Kindle models, leaving only the recent Kindle Scribe models with the original price tag. Amazon declined to comment to WIRED, but a spokesperson told CNET the price hikes were due to rising costs in memory and storage components. It's interesting that none of the more powerful Scribe models needed a price update, but it's also a relief since all three of those models are significantly more expensive than a regular Kindle.
Here are all the increases, including Signature versions:
- Amazon Kindle (2024, 11th Gen): $150 (up $40)
- Amazon Kindle Paperwhite (2024, 12th Gen): $200 (up $40)
- Amazon Kindle Paperwhite Signature (2024, 12th Gen): $250 (up $50)
- Amazon Kindle Colorsoft: $290 (up $40)
- Amazon Kindle Colorsoft Signature: $320 (up $40)
- Amazon Kindle Kids (2024, 2nd Gen): $180 (up $50)
- Amazon Kindle Colorsoft Kids: $300 (up $30)
If you have your eyes on one of these Kindles, I'd wait until Amazon Prime Day or Black Friday to shop when they're on sale. It's likely the sale prices will only bring the Kindle down to be the price it was before, but better than paying more.
What About the New Kindle Scribes?
Kindle has three new Kindle Scribes that launched between late 2025 and June 2026. There's now the Kindle Scribe ($500), Kindle Scribe Colorsoft ($630), and the Kindle Scribe Without Front Light ($430). All three have a similar design and software experience, though the Scribe Colorsoft has a color screen and a shorter battery life—only eight weeks of reading time, compared to 12 weeks on the $500 Scribe and an impressive 16 weeks on the Scribe Without Front Light. Like the second-generation model, they're a great choice for note-takers and students, especially with the long battery life, but I still prefer the second-generation's price point.
All three models have a new, taller design with an 11-inch screen, slightly slimmer form factor, and updated stylus. They both also have a quad-core chip, a new homepage, and will support a variety of AI features, including AI search (along with some AI tools for summarizing books you're reading without giving spoilers, though those won't arrive until next year). Users can connect to Google Drive and Microsoft OneDrive to mark up documents, which the older model can't do.
Overall, I'd say they're good devices, but as long as the cheaper second-generation Kindle Scribe is available, I think it's the better buy. It has some AI capabilities, but no AI search, and has a different homepage design that matches a classic Kindle rather than the notebook-forward design the new ones have. Amazon said it'll get the same homepage this year, but I haven't seen it so far. I'm disappointed these new devices are so much more expensive; at that price, you might as well shop reMarkable's line of digital notebooks and get better features and accessories.
Accessories for Easier Reading
If you've ever had a long reading session that gives you hand cramps, these accessories might help. You can check out more options in our Best Kindle Accessories guide.
Cases and Covers
Amazon Kindles are, thankfully, not as fragile as a pricey smartphone, but you may still want to add a cover to protect the screen if you're frequently toting it around in a bag. These aren't padded for serious drops, but are some of the best Kindle cases I've found for daily protection from scratches and scuffs. Also, don't forget that the Kids' editions come with cases, so if you're buying one of those, you won't need a case.
About Those Older Kindles
Amazon doesn't release new Kindles often—the company usually takes a few years between models. Whenever a new one arrives, its predecessor's stock starts to dwindle. It's not that we don't recommend these per se, but I only suggest these if you can find them on sale for the right price. And don't buy too old a model, since Amazon has started pulling support for older Kindles.
Before making your purchase, cross-check the price against the latest model to make sure you're paying a fair amount less for the older device.
Kindle (2022, 11th Generation): This is the smallest of the lot at 6.2 inches tall and 4.3 inches wide, with a 6-inch screen. If you find tablets too cumbersome to hold with one hand, consider this one. With this model, Amazon doubled the storage to 16 gigabytes and upgraded the display to 300 pixels per inch (PPI) resolution (up from 167 PPI). It's tough to find, and I usually don't see it for less than $75 these days.
Kindle Paperwhite (2021, 11th Generation): This is the next step up from the basic model. It has a bright 6.8-inch screen with adjustable warm lighting, a fast page-turn rate, a USB-C port, and 16 gigs of storage. It's waterproof too. We like the Signature Edition, which also includes auto-adjust brightness and 32 gigabytes of storage. Don't recommend spending more than $100 if you can find them.
Kindle Scribe (1st Generation): The original Scribe is a great option for note-takers. It has a giant 10.2-inch screen for taking notes, marking up PDFs, or drawing, and numerous paper formats you can choose, like college-ruled or dotted. It also comes with the Basic Pen, which feels natural to write with and attaches to the side of the Scribe magnetically. It's only worth it for $230 or less, and I often see it for under $200 on eBay.
Kindle Kids (2022): This is an older kid-friendly model. It comes with a cover, a year’s subscription to Amazon Kids+, parental controls, and a two-year warranty, but the fact that it's only available secondhand means you'll likely miss out on the subscription window and may or may not still have a cover. Ideally, don't spend more than $70 on this one.
Kindle Paperwhite Kids (2021): This older Paperwhite version is a step up from the previous basic Kids models. It has a high-resolution 300-ppi display with an adjustable warm screen and is also waterproof. You shouldn't spend more than $110 on this one.
FAQs
Which Kindle Models Lost Amazon Support and Kindle Store Access?
As of May 20, 2026, Amazon stopped supporting Kindles released in 2012 or earlier. That means these models will not be able to get new books through Amazon's services or be registered to an Amazon account. You will be able to read books already on the device, though, and can manually download documents and books via USB cable and via software like Calibre.
The following Kindle devices are impacted:
- Kindle 1st Generation
- Kindle 2nd Generation
- Kindle DX
- Kindle DX Graphite
- Kindle Keyboard (3rd Generation)
- Kindle 4
- Kindle Touch
- Kindle 5
- Kindle Paperwhite 1st Generation
What’s the Best Way to Buy or Sell an Older Kindle?
Have an old Kindle lying around? Are you looking at a used one for sale? If you're trying to figure out what model it is, this Amazon page includes photos, specs, and release years for the entire lineup. Once you know which one you have, you may be able to trade it in for credit toward a newer model.
Most old Kindles probably still work, just with fewer bells and whistles. It's best to avoid Kindles with keyboards or any other physical buttons other than page-turn buttons. Some older models lost the ability to browse, purchase, or borrow new books directly from the device. However, you'll still be able to do this via Amazon on your computer or phone and have it sent to your Kindle, which is a better experience anyway. These models include the Kindle 2nd Generation (International), Kindle DX International, Kindle DX Graphite, Kindle Keyboard, Kindle 4th Generation, and Kindle 5th Generation.
How Do You Get Free Ebooks on a Kindle?
If you buy every single book you want to read on a Kindle, it can add up! But there are ways to save some money while reading as much as your heart desires. You may want to subscribe to Kindle Unlimited for $12 a month. You can only choose from the Unlimited catalog, but there are millions of titles there, including audiobooks and magazines. Start out with the 30-day free trial.
If you already pay for a Prime account, you're eligible for some free ebooks through Prime Reading. There are not as many options as with Kindle Unlimited, and in a lot of cases, you'll see both Unlimited and Prime options lumped together; you'll have to look closely to find the free ebooks. It's still something, and there are even a few magazines.
If you don't want another monthly subscription and don't want to continue giving your money to Amazon, take advantage of the ebooks available with your library card. Browsing a digital catalog is not as magical as spending an afternoon looking over every shelf in a library, but such is the ebook life (no one says you can't read both!). We have a detailed how-to on this that you should check out, but here are some of the takeaways:
- Get a library card for your local branch.
- Check your branch's website for its ebook offerings. Many libraries use a service called OverDrive.
- Download directly to your Kindle library. They'll automatically be removed when they're due back.
If you know someone else with a Kindle, you can lend books between your libraries, just as you would with a physical copy. Follow these instructions from Amazon if you want to share an ebook, but keep in mind that not all books can be loaned.
What Else Can a Kindle Do?
Kindles have helpful features you may want to take advantage of. Long-press a word or phrase to see its definition, highlight it, or take notes. You can also search the entire book for that particular word or phrase or translate it to or from other languages.
Word Wise shows short definitions in small text within the lines. Unfortunately, it's not available for all books, but when it is, you can turn it on or off and choose more and fewer hints. Clicking the short definition opens a longer one from Word Wise and the New Oxford American Dictionary or Oxford Dictionary of English (you can switch between the two), plus translations and a Wikipedia page, if applicable.
While reading, tap the top of the screen and click “Aa” to change font size or type—there's even a font called OpenDyslexic that helps make reading easier for people with dyslexia. You can control margin sizes and line spacing from that menu too.
When a Kindle is connected to a Bluetooth speaker or headphones, VoiceView Screen Reader (accessed through Settings > Accessibility) allows you to use gestures to navigate your device and reads aloud what you've pressed. It will also read a book aloud, though it doesn't sound nearly as nice as an audiobook.
Amazon owns Goodreads, so it syncs seamlessly to Kindles (press the three-dot menu > Goodreads). If you have a Goodreads account, you can review the Kindle books you've read or browse your bookshelf and recommendations. Long-pressing a word or phrase, in addition to what is mentioned above, opens up an option to share quotes directly to Goodreads.
There's a web browser too if you're connected to the internet (three-dot menu > Web Browser). It's not the best, so I'd reserve it for emergency searches.
How Do You Update a Kindle?
When Amazon releases a new software update, it will download and install to your Kindle automatically when it's connected to Wi-Fi. You can check if you're on the latest software by going to Settings > Device Options > Advanced Options > Update Your Kindle. If it's not on the latest software version, you'll see an update available and the Kindle will then prompt you to download and install it.
What Do I Do If My Kindle Colorsoft Has a Yellow Bar?
Following customer complaints in 2024 of a yellow bar at the bottom of the Colorsoft Signature’s screen and discoloration along the edges, an Amazon spokesperson confirmed to WIRED that "customers who notice this can reach out to our customer service team for a replacement or refund.” The company also said it’s “making the appropriate adjustments to ensure that new devices will not experience this issue moving forward.” However, there are still customer complaints about this issue, even with the new model out. We have not run into this issue while testing the Colorsoft, Colorsoft Signature, or Scribe Colorsoft.
Is This a Good Time to Buy a Kindle?
The best time to buy a Kindle is during a major sale event like Amazon Prime Day or Black Friday, because Amazon often has steep discounts. Amazon has always had sales on some (if not all) of its Kindles on past Amazon Prime Day and similar events, like Amazon Big Deal Days.
You can also wait for other sale events if you're not ready to shop yet. Kindles are often on sale for Black Friday and Cyber Monday, which will occur in late November. Other sales often happen from time to time, but these sale events have consistent Kindle deals, so they're a good time to wait for if you want a better price.
Are Kindles Good for Students?
Kindles are great for students, though the model they'll like best will vary on how they use it. If they want to pair it with a stylus for highlighting and be able to take notes, get a Kindle Scribe model. These models also have long battery life, making them great for students to use for weeks on end without worrying about charging. You can get some textbooks on a Kindle too, and send library books to them. For students who love to read but don't want to take a ton of notes, a regular Kindle or Kindle Paperwhite will be best for them.

Grand Canyon National Park announces flash flood recovery plan as search for Texas man continues
‘These last nine days have been the hardest days that my family has endured,’ the hiker’s wife wrote in a Tuesday Facebook post
Arizona’s Grand Canyon National Park announced a recovery plan for the canyon’s water system Tuesday as search operations continue following August’s deadly flash flooding.
River patrols are still trying to find one hiker along the Colorado River, which runs through the canyon, officials said in a statement.
Timothy Smith, a 53-year-old Texan and father of three, is the last person who remains unaccounted for after the flooding. He was supposed to return home Wednesday, his wife Carrie Smith wrote in a Tuesday Facebook post.
“These last nine days have been the hardest days that my family has endured,” Carrie wrote.
Park officials confirmed the deaths of Smith’s friends, 46-year-old John Guisti and 42-year-old Brent Rosenkranz, around the river on September 1.
The hikers were caught off guard by a deluge on August 29 that flooded the park’s Bright Angel Canyon and Phantom Ranch areas with five feet of water.
The fast-moving storm dumped nearly an inch of rain per hour there, forcing the dramatic helicopter evacuations of 80 people.
The flooding rain damaged 40 percent of the park’s main water supply system along the canyon’s South Rim, leading to water cuts for locals and forcing the closure of local hotels.
But now, the park says there is a path forward to restore water service - and it is expected to take weeks, instead of months.
Crews are working on a temporary pipeline to replace the one destroyed in the flooding. The new pipeline would have the same capacity as the previous pipeline, pumping approximately 500 gallons of water per minute.
“Engineers are in the canyon designing the temporary intake, the existing Transcanyon Waterline contract has been modified to support the work, and construction activities are beginning this week,” the park said.
The park is working with Arizona’s Department of Environmental Quality to meet federal water quality requirements and said teams were actively monitoring the system for leaks and unusual water use.
Officials also stressed that conservation remains “critical” while work moves forward. Every gallon saved by businesses, visitors and locals gives crews more time.
Bottled water is being passed out and handwashing stations and portable showers and toilets have been deployed throughout the community.
Tap water remains safe to use and there is no boil-water advisory in effect.
“Current conservation measures are offsetting approximately 137,000 gallons of potable water use each day, extending the amount of time available for crews to complete critical work on the water system,” the park wrote.

In Summary
- The CMF Buds Neo are the latest TWS from Nothing’s sub-brand, CMF.
- The new buds come in attractive colors, in true CMF tradition, and punch above their price point in terms of specs and features.
- At Rs 1999, the CMF Buds Neo are the most affordable TWS in CMF’s audio portfolio, and have also been called the most accessible entry point to the CMF ecosystem. They do face a lot of competition, though.
While it is hard being a new smartphone in this tech climate, we believe it is harder being a new pair of TWS. The number of new TWS, as well as increasingly competitive prices and features across a wide range of price brackets, make it quite a task for a new pair to make its mark in the tech world. The latest addition in this lineup comes from Nothing’s sub-brand CMF, the CMF Buds Neo. Priced at Rs. 1,999, the Buds Neo are positioned as the most accessible entry to the CMF ecosystem. They come with an impressive feature list and a quirky design. But is that enough to help the CMF Buds Neo make space for itself in the TWS market?
CMF Buds Neo Appearance and Design: Typically CMF, Geometry with some flair
CMF, like its parent company Nothing, speaks a very distinct design language. A language no one else in the industry has adopted (yet) – a very smooth blend of Nothing’s industrial design combined with CMF’s bright colored flair. The CMF Buds Neo speak this language. Their square-shaped case comes with soft, rounded edges that make it sit very comfortably in one’s hands. The top left corner has a tactile, round dial. This is not just a design touch but also has some utility – it can be used to attach a lanyard that will keep your Buds Neo from getting lost.
The buds come in three different colors: Black, White, and Dark Blue. The Dark Blue and White color options bring very vibrant color contrasts with green and orange ear tips and tactile dials, respectively, while the Black is all black. The white variant, whose white case comes with a super bright orange tactile dial, is perhaps the most distinct. There is a small ‘CMF by Nothing’ badge in orange on the front as well. The cases have a matte finish while the dials are glossy.
The case has a very tiny LED light on the front and a USB Type-C port on the back. Flip the case open, and you find the buds resting nicely inside, with a ‘Buds Neo’ branding slightly above the earbuds. The buds come with a typical TWS design – a bulbous head attached to a long pill-shaped stem. The eartips bring the pop of orange to the white buds, while the texture of the overall buds is a mix of glossy and matte.
There is a small glossy dot on the head of the stem of the right bud and a thick, slightly raised circle on the stem of the left bud. The buds are comfortable to wear and come with one set of eartips attached and two others in the box. We used the medium-sized eartips, and they fit snugly. Speaking of snug fits, the buds also attach magnetically to the case.
The CMF Buds Neo case itself is quite compact – it is square, with length and breadth both at 54.3 mm, and is a little thick at 23 mm. It weighs 50.3 grams, while the buds weigh just a little over 4 grams each. The case is very pocket-friendly, and the buds are light on the ear. The buds come with an IP55 rating, making them good enough for sweaty gym sessions, while the case has an IPX rating, making it splash-proof, which is handy (most TWS cases still do not have splash resistance).
The white case does get dirty very easily (it caught dirt marks in our bag), but all in all, the design of the CMF Buds Neo is very eye-catching and definitely something not-so-usual. If you are not into pops of color, you can choose the black variant. Those who want to be right between these two extremes can go for the blue variant, with its flash of green eartips and disk.
CMF Buds Neo Specs and Controls: Very impressive at this price point
The CMF Buds Neo come with impressive specs for their price. They have 12.4 mm dynamic drivers with a 20 Hz- 20 kHz frequency response, two mics per earbud (for a total of four), Bluetooth 6.0, support for AAC and SBC codecs, and ANC of up to 35 dB. There is also support for spatial audio, and you get six EQ presets. All of these features are accessible through the NothingX App. The case comes with a 460 mAh battery with support for fast charging, and each earbud has a 45 mAh battery in it as well. The buds support Google Fast Pair, Microsoft Swift Pair, and also Dual-Device connectivity.
Pairing the CMF Buds Neo is simple: you flip the case open, wait for the buds to appear in your device’s Bluetooth list, and select them. To get the buds in pairing mode to connect with other devices, you can simply tap and hold the stem of the buds for five seconds, then select them from your device’s Bluetooth list. The controls on the buds are basically a series of taps- double-tapping on either bud will take you to the next track or reject a call; triple-tapping will take you to the previous song, while tapping and holding will let you switch between ANC and transparency mode.
No action is assigned to the double-tap-and-hold, but one can assign it to increasing or decreasing the volume or summoning the voice assistant. Apart from the call functionality, these controls can be customized using the Nothing X app. Interestingly, there is no option to map a control to a single tap, perhaps out of concern for accidental touches.
CMF Buds Neo Performance: Good audio, decent ANC and very good calling
The 12.4 mm dynamic drivers on the CMF Buds Neo come with a titanium-coated PET dome and a flexible PEEK and PU surround. This, as per Nothing, adds a bass-ful punch to the audio while ensuring vocals do not get muddied. The buds certainly deliver on both these fronts. The audio is full-bodied, and while it does focus a bit on bass, it does not drown out the treble or vocals. It is not balanced in a way that would give an audiophile an eargasm, but we seldom see that at this price anyway. On the other hand, they will impress casual listeners in a heartbeat, delivering a thoroughly enjoyable experience in pop, Bollywood, R&B, and hip-hop, and similar genres.
The Nothing X app comes with six EQ presets, and each one offers a distinct sound profile, which sometimes is not the case in this price segment. There is also the option to create an EQ based on one’s own preferences. The buds provide a reasonably spacious sound, which is usually not very easy for TWS to achieve, especially at this price point. The sound obviously does not feel as immersive as some of the high-end audio gear available on the market, but for the price, it is a hit in our books. The vocals are sharp enough to listen to hour-long podcasts or watch content.
The CMF Buds Neo also come with ANC. There are four options – low, medium, high, and adaptive. We mostly stuck to the ‘high’ setting. It will not cancel out very loud noises, but the snug fit of the buds combined with effective ANC does kill environmental noise with ease. It managed to drown out noise in a crowded cafe very effectively. We could not hear our friend sitting across from us with ANC on. The transparency mode brings back awareness to what would otherwise be a very isolating experience – the conversation we were not able to hear earlier became clear with transparency mode.
The call quality of the buds is very good as well – a pleasant surprise at this price point. We did not have any issues hearing the caller and did not get any complaints about our voice quality either. There is a low latency mode for games, but we had to turn it on manually, which was a bit of a pain.
The controls of the CMF Buds Neo are easy to remember but take some serious getting used to. We often found we had to tap harder than we are used to in order to register a command. The buds also lack wear detection, which means the audio does not automatically pause when one takes the buds (one or both) out. While this is a feature not often found at this price point, its absence was inconvenient.
Battery is another strong suit of the CMF Buds Neo. The buds promise 11 hours of listening time with ANC off, with 52 hours of total playback with ANC off, including the case. With ANC on, the numbers become 5 hours for the buds, and 30 hours with the case. We found the buds’ actual performance to be close to these numbers. With mixed use (ANC/ transparency mode on and off) at 70 percent volume, the buds easily lasted for around 9 hours. The buds also have a fast charging feature in which 10 minutes of charging gives one 5.5 hours of play time with ANC off . However, there is no cable in the box, which is a bit of a letdown.
CMF Buds Neo App: NothingX remains as clean and easy to use as ever
The NothingX app is the perfect accompaniment to the CMF Buds Neo – simple, clean and easy to use. We did have some trouble adding our Buds Neo to the app, but after a little struggle, the buds were added to the list of our other CMF devices. There is one main page, and you can scroll down to access all the functions and features. ANC, Spatial Audio, controls, bass enhancement, equalizer settings, low lag mode, dual connection, and firmware updates can all be accessed through the app. One also gets the exact charge percentage left in each earbud, although rather oddly, not that of the case. The app is easy to use and remains one of our favorites.
CMF Buds Neo Review Verdict: Superb value for the price
The CMF Buds Neo come with a price tag of Rs. 1,999, which is quite competitive for the performance and specs they offer. The similarly priced OnePlus Nord Buds 3r bring a comparable spec sheet, as do the Realme Buds T200 Lite, but both come with Bluetooth 5.4, marginally less playtime, and are not even close to the Buds Neo in the design department.
The CMF Buds Neo are near-perfect entry-level TWS options. Their audio, ANC, and battery performance give them an edge over the competition, and the distinct design is the cherry on this TWS cake. If you do not want to burn a hole in your pocket and still want a good pair of feature-packed TWS, the CMF Buds Neo are the perfect pick.
- Distinct design
- Enjoyable audio
- Good ANC
- Super call quality
- Very good companion app
- Good battery life
- Controls take some getting used to
- No charging cable in the box
- The white coloured case attracts scratches and smudges easily

Suspected measles cases kill nearly 1,000 as Bangladesh struggles to contain outbreak
Bangladesh is struggling to tackle a measles outbreak that has killed almost 1,000 children this year despite a renewed vaccination campaign
DHAKA, Bangladesh -- Eight-month-old Rojatun Jannat Ramisa is struggling to breathe in a hospital in Bangladesh’s capital as her parents sit helplessly beside her. She's one of thousands of children sickened by a measles outbreak that's sweeping across the country and has killed hundreds of children following setbacks to the country's vaccine program.
Ramisa’s mother Ranu Akhter traveled hundreds of kilometers (miles) after doctors in eastern Bangladesh referred her to a specialized child hospital in Dhaka to seek treatment for the life-threatening condition.
“Fourteen days ago, when we were at the district hospital, there were other children being treated alongside my daughter. I saw that those children also had red rashes on their bodies, sores in their mouths and fevers,” Akhter told The Associated Press at Dhaka Shishu Hospital.
“It made me realize how widespread the measles outbreak is,” she said.
Every day, the death toll is rising.
Bangladesh has been racing to halt the outbreak's spread since March, when more than 100 children died in less than a month. By Tuesday, the death toll from suspected measles cases reached 999 since the start of the year, according to the government’s Directorate General of Health Services.
Since March, the country has recorded more than 166,000 suspected measles cases, including 19,835 laboratory-confirmed infections, according to the Ministry of Health.
The government launched an emergency vaccination drive in March together with the World Health Organization, the U.N. children’s agency and the Gavi vaccine alliance. It began with a focus on children from 6 months to 5 years old and later expanded nationwide in phases.
Measles is a highly contagious airborne disease that causes fever, respiratory symptoms and a characteristic rash. It can sometimes have severe or fatal complications, especially in young children, according to the WHO.
Two doses of a vaccine provide strong protection against measles, but the WHO says 95% of the population has to be vaccinated in order to stop the disease from spreading — which protects children like Ramisa who are too young to be vaccinated as well as immunocompromised people.
A few years ago, Bangladesh had measles largely under control, with a vaccination program that was credited for decades for protecting children and mothers from the deadly diseases of tuberculosis, diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus, poliomyelitis and measles. Between 2021 and 2025, the country recorded just 100 to 300 cases per year, down from 2,410 cases in 2020.
But in the last few years, disruptions to the vaccine program have left a growing number of children unvaccinated.
First the pandemic interrupted routine vaccinations, and then in 2024 the government largely missed a vaccination campaign previously carried out every four years.
Atiqul Islam, a neonatal and child specialist at Bangladesh Shishu Hospital and Institute, said during the pandemic period in 2021 and 2022, many did not take their children to get vaccinated.
“So, if you look at children who are now four or five years old, many of them missed their vaccinations. That created a gap. During the previous interim government, vaccines were also unavailable at many vaccination centers,” he said.
Bangladesh's current government, headed by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, said the failures in planning under ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and interim leader Muhammad Yunus left the country with shortages of vaccines and far behind on coverage.
The 2024 measles vaccination campaign was disrupted during the political upheaval that led to Hasina’s ouster. She left the country in the face of a mass uprising in August 2024, and was followed by Yunus, who led an interim administration that transferred power to an elected government after an election in February.
From exile in India, Hasina blamed the Yunus-led government for the disaster.
At Bangladesh Shishu Hospital, Islam said the situation has improved, but not enough.
The doctor said his colleagues are struggling to treat infected children who often arrive at the hospital with serious complications like pneumonia, diarrhea and encephalitis, or brain swelling.
“For the past six months, we have been treating measles patients continuously, and we are exhausted,” he said.

Singaporean man pleads guilty in US to massive crypto heist
- Published
A Singaporean man pleaded guilty on Tuesday to a racketeering conspiracy charge in the US for organising one of the biggest ever cryptocurrency thefts.
Malone Lam admitted to teaming up with friends to steal $245m (£181m) of bitcoin and laundering the proceeds.
The 22-year-old and his associates used the money to spend up to $500,000 a visit to nightclubs, according to the US Department of Justice (DOJ). It also said they bought a fleet of exotic cars, ranging in value from $100,000 to $3.8m.
Lam faces a maximum prison sentence of 20 years. US District Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly did not immediately schedule a sentencing hearing for him.
"If you build a cybercrime empire, we will find you, dismantle your operation, and hold you accountable," said US Attorney Jeanine Pirro said.
"This defendant led an international network that preyed on victims through deception, invaded their privacy, and stole hundreds of millions of dollars in cryptocurrency," she added.
According to court documents, the conspiracy began no later than October 2023 and continued to at least May 2025.
The co-conspirators - who came from California, Connecticut, New York, Florida, and outside the US - met via online gaming platforms.
The DOJ said Lam - who also went by the names Anne Hathaway, $$$, King Greavy - was the ringleader of the criminal enterprise, who identified victims and coordinated the roles of the different conspirators.
They tricked people into giving away confidential information as well as conducted occasional home break-ins to obtain details that allowed them to drain their victims' cryptocurrency wallets, the DOJ said.
The stolen cryptocurrency was also used to buy Hermes Birkin handbags, valued in the tens of thousands of dollars, which were thrown into crowds at nightclub parties, according to the DOJ.
Other items that the DOJ said the proceeds were spent on included high-end watches worth up to $500,000, luxury clothing valued in the tens of thousands of dollars, rental homes in Los Angeles, the Hamptons, and Miami, private jet rentals for travel and a team of private security guards.

New Delhi, Sep 9: The Centre on Wednesday extended by two more years, a scheme to allow its employees to visit Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Andaman and Nicobar Islands and the northeast region on leave travel concession (LTC).
In an order, the Personnel Ministry warned of appropriate action for any misuse of the LTC facility.
Eligible central government employees get reimbursement of tickets for to and fro journeys, besides paid leave, when they avail LTC.
The scheme allowing government servants to travel by air to northeast region, Union territories of Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh and Andaman & Nicobar Islands is extended for a further period of two years, with effect from September 25, 2026 till September 25, 2028, the order said.
All eligible government servants may avail LTC to visit any place in these regions against the conversion of their one home town LTC in a four-year block period, it said.
Government servants not entitled to travel by air are also allowed to travel by air in economy class by any airlines to these areas, according to the order.
"Fresh recruits are also allowed conversion of one of the three home town LTCs in a block of four years, applicable to them to visit NER/A&N/J&K/Ladakh. In addition, they are allowed one additional conversion of home town LTC to visit UT of J&K/UT of Ladakh in a block of four years," said the order issued to the secretaries of all central government ministries.
All the ministries and departments are advised to bring it to the notice of all their employees that any misuse of LTC will be viewed seriously and the employees will be liable for appropriate action under the rules, it said.
"In order to keep a check on any kind of misuse of LTC, ministries/departments are advised to randomly get some of the air tickets submitted by the officials verified from the airlines concerned with regard to the actual cost of air travel vis-a-vis the cost indicated on the air tickets submitted by the officials," the Personnel Ministry said.

Tributes flow in as Hong Kong mourns Tung Chee-hwa, pioneering first leader
Former business magnate faced difficult crisis during tenure, but officials and former colleagues praise his compassion and ‘brave leadership’
Hong Kong is mourning the death of Tung Chee-hwa, the city’s first leader after its return to Chinese sovereignty and a respected elder statesman, who died on Tuesday at the age of 89.
Tung was surrounded by his family when he “passed away peacefully” at 9.57pm, according to state news agency Xinhua.
Tributes and messages of grief poured in on Wednesday from across Hong Kong and mainland China, as well as from overseas, with top officials, politicians, business leaders and others praising his pioneering role as the first steward of the “one country, two systems” policy under which the city would be administered after the end of British colonial rule in 1997.
They remembered him for steering the city through its uncertain transitional years and laying the groundwork for its post-handover prosperity, and hailed his later role as an elder statesman who worked tirelessly to help improve US-China relations.
Beijing’s liaison office in Hong Kong issued a statement, describing Tung as a “close friend of the Communist Party of China”, an “outstanding contributor to ‘one country, two systems’” and a “renowned patriot”, while the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office sent a condolence message to his wife, Betty Tung Chiu Hung-ping.
The offices said Tung had made “major historic contributions” to Hong Kong’s smooth return to China, while crediting him with tackling complex political, economic and social challenges during the formative years of the special administrative region.
They also highlighted his work after leaving office, saying he continued to support successive chief executives and governments, promote closer ties between Hong Kong and the mainland and use his extensive international connections to foster exchanges between China and the rest of the world.

Anganwadis across UP were in disarray under previous govt, says Yogi; hikes honorarium for workers
Ayodhya, Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath on Tuesday claimed Anganwadi centres in the state were in dilapidated condition and utter disarray during the tenure of the previous government, also announcing a hike in honorarium for workers and helpers engaged at these facilities.
"Nine years ago, Anganwadi centres were in dilapidated condition and in complete disarray. They were plagued by the dishonesty of the erstwhile government, while it was Anganwadi workers who had to face flak. The nutritious meals meant for children did not reach Anganwadi centres.
"The meal services were operated by a liquor mafia, who had such reach and influence, that nobody dared to check him," Adityanath said, without taking any names.
He alleged that there were complaints over the quality of meals provided at Anganwadi centres during the tenure of the previous government, saying, they in collusion with the mafia had "ruined the system".
"Now, meal services have been freed from the mafia, while take-home ration services are being operated at 204 locations by women-led self-help groups," he said.
The chief minister was speaking at an event in Ayodhya, where he distributed appointment letters to newly-recruited Anganwadi workers and helpers.
He said before 2017, three to five-year-olds who came to Anganwadi centres, carried with them mats fashioned out of jute bags as there were no seating arrangements.
There was no drinking water at Anganwadi centres, and children were denied nutritious meals, he alleged.
"The Centre gave money, but there was an insensitive government in the state. It did not buy anything for these Anganwadi centres, and funnelled these funds to the mafia. Thus, Anganwadi centres had remained deserted," Adityanath said.
He further claimed that primary schools in the state were in "pathetic condition" under the previous government "without teachers, or students".
On the occasion, Adityanath announced a "gift" for the state's 2.91 lakh Anganwadi workers and helpers. He said the honorarium for Anganwadi workers will increase from ₹8,000 to ₹12,000, while that for helpers will increase from ₹4,000 to ₹6,000 per month.
Additionally, Anganwadi workers, helpers, and their families, will get cashless treatment of up to ₹5 lakh every year at empanelled healthcare facilities, government hospitals, and medical colleges, and receive three sarees every year, instead of two.
The chief minister also announced plans to make Anganwadi centres "smart", by providing smartphones to workers, the state government said in a statement.
Under the first phase of this initiative, 1.28 lakh smartphones have been provided for. Through these, data related to schemes can be recorded in real time and the work of Anganwadi workers can be simplified, he asserted.
Adityanath said when his government took charge in 2017, Anganwadi workers received a meagre honorarium of ₹3,000.
"Our government linked it with a performance-based system and increased it to ₹8,000. Now, it will be increased to ₹12,000," he said.
The honorarium of helpers was also increased from ₹1,500 to ₹4,000 earlier, and will now be increased to ₹6,000, he added.
Anganwadi workers and helpers played an important role along with auxiliary nurse midwives and ASHA workers during the COVID-19 pandemic, he said, adding that over the past nine years, more than 70,000 Anganwadi centres across the state have been given an organised structure.
Referring to Ayodhya, the chief minister said 10 years ago, there was little electricity in the area, no roads, facilities or cleanliness. "Ayodhya was in disarray, and anarchy prevailed.
"There was electricity for only three or four hours, sometimes during the day, sometimes at night, and a syndicate controlled power supply. Barring one or two districts, much of the state remained in darkness," he claimed.
"When we began constructing wide roads for Ayodhya, the Samajwadi Party opposed it, they agitated against building the railway station. When work on the airport here began, the Samajwadi Party protested against it," Adityanath said, terming the opposition party "anti-development".
He further said, "This is the same Samajwadi Party that opposed Lord Ram, and did everything to prevent the Ram Mandir from being built in Ayodhya. Once, these very people had ordered firing at devotees of Lord Ram.
"Yet, despite their opposition, the Ram temple movement did not stop, and eventually, the grand temple of Lord Ram was built here."
Lashing out at the opposition, he said those who divide society cannot be expected to unite it.
Highlighting the transformation of Ayodhya, the chief minister said, "Today, Ayodhya has four-lane roads, a grand railway station and an international airport named after Maharishi Valmiki. The railway network has expanded. The Ram Ki Paidi has been rejuvenated and Ayodhya has become a solar city."
Before his address, the chief minister inspected stalls set up by various departments at an exhibition at the venue, and officiated the 'annaprashan' of several children.
Around 12,000 Anganwadi workers and helpers were present at the Ayodhya event, while ministers, MPs, MLAs and Anganwadi workers joined various programmes organised across 75 districts, the statement said.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Republic of Korea have a long-standing partnership spanning over 75 years. As a result of their fruitful collaboration, there has been significant progress in health and development all around the world. The Republic of Korea has gone from being a donor-recipient country to a donor-country and is now a leader in global health and playing a critical role on the world stage.
Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General for External Relations and Governance (WHO) and Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination (Ministry of Health and Welfare, Republic of Korea), together with counterparts from WHO and the Government of the Republic of Korea. © WHO

Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination, Ministry of Health, led the Republic of Korea delegation and was joined by senior officials including Dr Young-Mee Jee, Commissioner, Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency, as well as senior counterparts from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety.
In addition, in line with WHO's work to enhance collaboration with parliamentarians, the WHO delegation also met with various Members of the National Assembly that are championing the global health agenda.

Curacao extend manager Advocaat's contract after turbulent year

Police arrest suspect in Germany power grid attacks after dayslong search
Police have arrested a suspect in connection with a series of attacks on power distribution systems across Germany
BERLIN -- Police arrested a suspect Tuesday in connection with a series of attacks on power distribution systems across Germany which had led to a massive, dayslong search.
A 48-year-old man was arrested near a power plant in Weisweiler, in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia.
The man, whose name and nationality were not given in line with German privacy rules but has been widely identified by local media as Daniel V., was in possession of explosives and offered no resistance at the time of his arrest, Cologne police said in a statement.
When the first acts of sabotage took place early last week at a substation near the Jänschwalde coal-fired power plant in Brandenburg in northeastern Germany, and then hours later, a short circuit knocked power lines out of service at the Bergheim power substation near Cologne, top security officials in both states raised alarm and said they couldn't exclude that the attacks were committed by foreign powers.
The incidents took place as the country was on high alert after the government blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 4 using a drone laden with explosives.
However, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Friday that the acts were believed to have been committed by a single activist in connection with climate extremism.
In addition to the first sabotage attacks near Jänschwalde and Bergheim, the man is alleged to have attempted, at several locations in North Rhine-Westphalia, and the eastern states of Brandenburg and Saxony, to use homemade rockets to shoot a thin wire across high-voltage power lines, thereby causing a short circuit.
Most recently on Monday police discovered several launch devices on a high-voltage power line near the Weisweiler plant — very close to the spot where police were able to arrest the man. Investigators also found a letter there claiming responsibility — in addition to several other letters they had found at other locations before, German news agency dpa reported.
In the letters, the man justified the attacks on the power grid as part of the fight against fossil fuels. Lignite is still being mined and used to generate electricity in all three of the states where the man allegedly committed or tried to commit attacks on power plants.
Police said Tuesday that near the place where they arrested the man, they also found a tent set up in the underbrush nearby, which contained additional explosive charges.
The items are currently being examined by a bomb disposal expert from the North Rhine-Westphalia State Criminal Police Office.
An arrest warrant had been issued earlier for the 48-year-old by the Cottbus Public Prosecutor’s Office.
Officers were at the scene in Weisweiler Tuesday to secure evidence and check whether any additional, as yet undiscovered, detonation devices have been set up in the surrounding area, police said.

Deaths in India due to second hand smoke increased nearly 50% in 2023, compared to 1990, even as death rates improved by about 30%, according to a global analysis published in The Lancet Public Health journal.
The estimates also suggest that while the population exposed to second hand smoke increased from 375 million in 1990 to 444 million in 2026 -- up by 18.4% -- age-standardised prevalence dropped from 43.2 per cent in 1990 to 30.6 per cent in 2023 in India.
Age-standardised prevalence is a statistical adjustment made to data to allow a fair comparison of prevalence across age groups.
An international team of researchers forming the 'Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023 Second-hand smoke Collaborators' estimated prevalence of exposure to passive smoking and the disease burden it contributes to across 204 countries and territories.
"In 2023, an estimated 2.71 billion people worldwide were exposed to SHS (second hand smoke), including 767 million children aged 0-14 years," the authors wrote.
Globally, exposure prevalence was 33.9 per cent in 2023. China, India, and Indonesia accounted for nearly half of the world's exposed population, with 664 million, 444 million, and 142 million people exposed, respectively, in 2023, they found.
However, "age-standardised prevalence was highest in southeast Asia, east Asia, and Oceania (48.4 per cent), with female individuals in some countries experiencing nearly 1.8 times the exposure prevalence of male individuals," the team said.
In India, absolute deaths in 1990 due to passive smoking were 2,17,700, while those in 2023 were 3,25,600 -- death rates or deaths per hundred thousand population, however, fell from 46.1 in 1990 to 30 in 2023, down by 35%, the findings show.
"The numbers mean that despite a fall in the adjusted rates, the absolute number of people exposed to passive smoking is still increasing. This can have long-lasting effects across multiple organ systems, not just the respiratory system," Neetu Jain, pulmonologist and senior consultant at Pushpawati Singhania Hospital and Research Institute, New Delhi, told PTI.
"Second-hand smoke exposure is associated with an increased risk of several diseases, including cardiovascular and respiratory conditions. The effects of passive smoking can also be particularly concerning in people with conditions such as coronary artery disease," she said.
Children were found to account for more than 12% of the world's health burden from second hand smoke, with lower respiratory infections causing the greatest burden, according to the study.
"Passive smoking is avoidable if smokers take steps to prevent exposing others to tobacco smoke. Smoking outside the home and away from enclosed spaces can reduce exposure to second-hand smoke, particularly among family members and children. Children are especially vulnerable because their lungs are still developing, and exposure to tobacco smoke can adversely affect their respiratory health," Dr Jain said.
"The effects tend to be greatest among those who are least aware of what passive smoking is and the health risks associated with it," the pulmonologist said.
"However, we should encourage smokers to quit and focus on bringing down smoking across the country through effective tobacco-control measures, including higher tobacco prices and taxes," she said.
