Between surviving an illness and returning to regular life, lies a journey of a thousand small victories. Physiotherapy helps people take those victories, one step at a time.
There is a moment after a heart attack or stroke that very few people talk about. It is not the moment the ambulance arrives. It is not the moment the doctors say the patient is out of danger. It is the moment when the hospital doors close behind you, you return home, and everyone expects life to slowly return to normal.
But what does ‘normal’ mean?
For someone who has had a stroke, it may mean learning to walk again, using an arm that suddenly feels unfamiliar, finding their balance, or simply getting out of bed without someone holding their hand. For someone who has survived a heart attack, it may mean taking that first walk outside without constantly wondering whether their heart can handle it.
And sometimes, the hardest part is not the physical limitation. It is the fear. “What if it happens again?” That question can stay with a person long after they have left the hospital. This is where physiotherapy becomes much more than a set of exercises.
What rehabilitation entails
We often imagine rehabilitation as someone working hard in a gym, lifting weights or walking on a treadmill. The reality can be much quieter.
For a stroke survivor, the first goal may simply be to sit upright without support. Then to stand. Then to take a few steps. For the family watching, it may seem like very little. For the person doing it, it may feel like climbing a mountain.
A physiotherapist is there for these moments. Not just to count repetitions or measure strength, but to help someone understand that progress does not always have to be dramatic. Sometimes, progress is one extra step. Sometimes, it is standing for ten seconds longer. Sometimes, it is being able to walk to the bathroom without asking for help. And sometimes, it is simply finding the confidence to try.
What patients go through
Imagine being someone who used to walk to work, play with their children, exercise regularly or climb four flights of stairs without giving it a second thought. Then you have a heart attack. Suddenly, your heartbeat becomes something you constantly notice. You begin questioning every sensation. Is this normal? Am I too tired? Is my heart rate too high? Should I stop?
That fear can lead people to become overly cautious and inactive. Cardiac rehabilitation can help break that cycle. With appropriate medical assessment and supervision, patients can gradually return to physical activity, improve their exercise capacity and learn how to manage their cardiovascular health with greater confidence. The physiotherapist’s role is not simply to say, “Push harder.” It is to say: “Let us understand what your body can safely do today—and build from there.”
Not only for the elderly
A stroke or heart attack is often imagined as something that happens late in life, after the age of 60 or so. But when it happens to a younger person, the shock can be enormous. Someone in their 30s or 40s may suddenly find themselves worrying about things they never expected to question. Will I be able to go back to work? Can I take care of my children? Can I travel? Can I exercise again? Can I return to the sport I love?
They may look perfectly healthy from the outside. But inside, they may be dealing with fatigue, weakness, uncertainty and fear about what comes next. That is why rehabilitation cannot simply be based on a person’s age or diagnosis. A younger patient may need to return to a physically demanding job. A sportsperson may want to return to competition. A parent may simply want enough energy to play with their children. Rehabilitation has to fit the life that person wants to return to.
The patient is not a diagnosis. This may be one of the most important things a physiotherapist learns. A medical report might say stroke. It might say heart attack. It might list numbers, test results and medications. But none of those words explain who the patient is. They do not tell you that the patient loves taking their morning walk. They do not tell you that someone has a child waiting at home. They do not tell you that being able to climb the stairs independently means more to that person than almost anything else. Good rehabilitation starts with a simple question: “What do you want to get back to?” The answer may be different for every person. And that answer becomes an important part of the treatment.
Preventive goals
Physiotherapy is also about preventing the next story. Rehabilitation should not only begin after a crisis. Physiotherapists also have an important role in helping people become more physically active, develop healthier movement habits and reduce preventable health risks. Physical activity is an important part of cardiovascular health, but exercise is not a prescription that can simply be copied from one person to another.
The right type, intensity and amount of activity depend on the individual. For someone recovering from a cardiac event, exercise may require appropriate medical guidance and monitoring of symptoms, heart rate, blood pressure and exercise tolerance. For someone recovering from a stroke, rehabilitation may involve improving balance, strength, coordination, walking and everyday functional activities.
The goal is not to push everyone to do more. The goal is to help each person do what is right for them—safely and consistently. The greatest thing a physiotherapist restores is not movement. It is the part of someone’s life they thought was gone forever.
We often say that physiotherapists help people move. But perhaps that does not quite capture the whole story. Physiotherapists help people return to the things that make life feel like life.
(Shanthi Dass is a sports physiotherapist and managing director of Synergy The Clinic, Chennai. synergytheclinic@gmail.com)

Buildings Department files 259 charges over work at fire-ravaged Hong Kong estate
Charges against two firms, four individuals relate to alleged use of substandard materials and failure to properly supervise repairs
Hong Kong’s Buildings Department has filed 259 charges against two companies and four individuals over major renovation works at the inferno-ravaged Wang Fuk Court, after investigations found non-fire-retardant materials were used and safety obligations were not met.
The department said on Wednesday that the charges included allegedly permitting or authorising the use of substandard materials or materials in breach of the Buildings Ordinance, as well as failing to properly supervise repair works, among other offences.
The two companies charged are the project’s consulting firm, Will Power Architects, and main contractor, Prestige Construction & Engineering.
The four individuals are Will Power director Wong Hap-yin and registered inspector Ng Yeuk, together with Prestige directors Ho Kin-yip and Hau Wa-kin.
In June, both firms, the four individuals and three others were already charged by police and the Independent Commission Against Corruption with offences including manslaughter, conspiracy to defraud, money laundering, attempting to pervert the course of public justice and tax evasion.
The Labour Department also laid 25 charges on Wednesday against related parties – the contractor, the project consultant and an individual – under the Factories and Industrial Undertakings Ordinance, in connection with the deaths of five contractors’ staff during the fire.
A Buildings Department spokesman said the department and the Housing Bureau’s Independent Review Committee “spared no effort in investigating the major renovation works involved” following the Wang Fuk Court blaze.

India has spent years celebrating founders who built companies from scratch. But what rarely gets discussed is what happens to the company, its shares and the family when a founder is suddenly gone. The recent tragic passings of prominent names in the Indian startup ecosystem, including Icertis’ Samir Bodas, Table Space’s Amit Banerji, Epigamia’s Rohan Mirchandani, Xpedize’s Regan Mithani and Whatfix’s Khadim Batti, have brought sharper focus on this question. An untimely founder death can leave behind more than grief — it can create a complicated trail of questions around ownership, unvested shares, succession and the future of the business. This is where estate and succession planning becomes critical. Putting the right provisions in place beforehand can help protect a founder’s family financially while giving the company a clearer path in their absence. “From a family standpoint, a founder may have created significant wealth. But when institutional investors come in, the founder’s shares are often subject to vesting clauses. If those agreements are not clearly worded, the family may not be able to recover the founder’s full stake,” said the founder of digital estate planning startup Yellow, Nikhil Varghese. While planning for one's demise could be uncomfortable for many, it is crucial to understand that estate and succession planning is important in several other situations. For instance, divorce, separation or disputes between cofounders can create questions around ownership and the division of assets. Therefore, this is less of a contingency plan and more of a governance issue that founders and investors need to address from the outset. So, What Happens When A Founder Passes? Preparation can only take one so far. Even with careful planning, what follows is hardly a speedy and straightforward process. “In the interim period, we have to give the family some time to adjust. Even if these principles are included in the documents, you can’t pick up the phone and say I’m going to enforce this right now. That’s not humane,” said Ashwini Thulsaram, a principal at 3one4 Capital, who leads the governance function for the VC firm. According to her, investors often assess whether a secondary transaction can be undertaken, while taking the preferences of the family or legal heirs into consideration. They also look at whether the legal heirs have the business acumen and the willingness to lead the company. “However, a secondary transaction is always a preference. This is because founders generally want to protect and create liquidity for their family,” she said, adding that a secondary could involve selling their stake to other investors at market value, at a certain discount, or at whatever price investors are willing to pay. These conversations could take 2-3 months. Generally, the immediate focus is to ensure that shares get bought at a certain price to ease the financial burden on the family, as per Thulsaram. More often than not, the company’s senior leadership team is prepared to step in and take over. How Can Founders Protect Their Legacy? While investors assist, it is the founders who should ensure the terms of the shareholding agreement match their needs. “Founders are often most focused on raising funds during their first round of investment. But if these issues are not addressed in the first agreement, those terms become the foundation for future rounds. It can then be much harder to negotiate better terms later,” Varghese cautioned. Understanding the vesting schedule and negotiating favourable terms requires the founder to have the right advisors. “Making a will is the basic thing that everyone should do but, for most startup founders, they should consider trusts to ringfence their liabilities,” Varghese added. A trust is a legal entity that holds assets on behalf of a beneficiary. It is a critical aspect of estate planning, especially when it comes to businesses, said Sandeep Nerlekar, founder of Terentia Consultants, an advisory firm that helps individuals, families, and businesses with their estate and succession planning. “Founders can hold wealth in different forms, including preference shares, CCPS, OCDs, NCDs and DVR shares. These assets can be transferred to a trust, creating a separate pool of assets and helping diversify the risk,” Nerlekar said. “This basically separates ownership from benefits. Then if liabilities come your way, they sit on your personal balance sheet and do not percolate into the assets held by the trust,” Varghese explained. Jurisdiction also becomes a major factor as Indian startups continue to attract capital from around the world. While India does not have any tax on inheritance or estate tax that applies to properties transferred on death, this is not true for the rest of the world. How Can Investors Prepare For The Worst Drawing from his experience, Bluegreen Ventures’ founding partner Anup Jain said investors are often left to manage their own crisis when a founder dies unexpectedly. This can involve supporting the founder’s family, helping the remaining founding team reach an agreement, and finding a suitable replacement with the right equity arrangement. “Life is uncertain. We plan to include succession planning provisions in all our deals going forward, because these concerns are not age-related. There are examples showing that tragedies can happen at any time,” Jain said. VCs also play an active role from the early stages of funding, ensuring that founders plan for potential risks and the future, said Thulsaram. When investors come on board, founders are generally subject to a vesting schedule wherein their equity unlocks at different stages after specified periods of time, similar to how ESOPs work. This helps keep founders aligned with investors while ensuring the company has greater stability if a founder exits. Exigency clauses are generally included by institutional investors when they participate in a deal. In case of a founder’s untimely passing, the term sheet might include provisions enabling the family to immediately unlock unvested equity, or allowing direct transmission of shares to nominees while bypassing the approval of other investors. “The terms for each situation vary by investor in terms of whether the family or a legal heir gets all the shares vested or only a proportion, or how many months get accelerated,” Thulsaram added. For India’s startup ecosystem, recent tragedies have shown why estate and succession planning can no longer be an afterthought. As startups grow larger and founder wealth becomes increasingly tied to company equity, planning for what happens next has to become an essential part of protecting both the founder and the business.

Srinagar, Sep 09: Renowned Bollywood actor and filmmaker Akbar Khan has hailed the first-ever film festival in Srinagar, saying the event has the potential to grow into an international cultural landmark and eventually compete with the Cannes Film Festival.
Addressing a press conference in Srinagar, Khan congratulated Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah and the organisers for what he described as a “spectacular opening festival”.
“The show was mesmerising, soulful and captured the rhythm and the purpose of this first-ever film festival in Srinagar,” Khan said, praising the musical performances at the opening ceremony.
He particularly recalled the performances of Dr Janas-e-R Akhtar, Rani and Falak, saying they “captured the mood of the festival” and “the heart of the beginning of such a beautiful initiative”.
Khan also praised Chief Minister Omar Abdullah's speech at the inaugural event, describing it as “very heart-rendering”.
“He was so prolific, recollecting the nostalgia of the Indian film industry, the Bollywood film industry, capturing chapter by chapter, moment by moment, how the people of Jammu and Kashmir love the units and the film stars and the directors and the producers who come and make the films here,” he said.
Recalling Bollywood's long association with Kashmir, Khan referred to films that helped establish the Valley as one of Indian cinema's most evocative locations.
He specifically mentioned Junglee, saying the famous “Yahoo” call by Shammi Kapoor
“had become a kind of a call of the Valley for every filmmaker to come and shoot”.
Khan said the festival had been organised in a location uniquely suited to bringing filmmakers and cultures together.
“I would say that there could not have been a better place than Srinagar to be the chosen city for such a grand first-ever film festival,” he said.
He predicted that the event would rapidly acquire an international profile.
“I feel from year to year this festival will grow from strength to strength and very soon would be in competition with the Cannes Film Festival and maybe even get better,” Khan said.
He argued that Kashmir's landscape itself could become one of the festival's greatest attractions.
“Because Cannes does not offer such an environment. Such a beautiful landscape,” he said. “It becomes a source of all filmmakers when they visit such a place.”
According to Khan, filmmakers attending the festival would not merely watch films from different countries but would also be inspired by Kashmir itself.
“Besides watching films of each other countries and different great directors, they also get inspired by the soul of Kashmir,” he said.
‘Cinema is the most powerful medium’
Khan placed particular emphasis on cinema's ability to build bridges across communities and countries.
“I would like to mention that cinema is the most powerful medium that makes bridges between nations and civilisations,” he said.
“It carries across borders, stories, civilisations, culture, people from different parts of the world who interact and meet and bring out, above all, their souls to understand each other.”
He said film festivals should therefore be judged primarily on artistic and cinematic merit.
“The greatest part of a film festival is that it should be judged on merits,” Khan said.
“Every film that is being chosen should be judged on merits, on its cinematic excellence, free of prejudice, free from the changing winds of ideology.”
He said filmmakers, actors, producers and singers should be allowed to present their artistic work without ideological interference.
“Actors, directors, producers, singers come on to a platform and present their artistic cinema, music, art, culture,” he said.
Khan also spoke at length about the responsibility of filmmakers when dealing with India's history and communal relations.
“I am very vocal. I respect every filmmaker. Every filmmaker has the right to present his film, his ideas, but never distort history. Never distort history to serve a purpose of creating disturbance, hatred [against] one another,” he said.
He added: “Cinema which spreads hatred should be discouraged in every nook and corner of the world, especially when it is designed for a specific propaganda.”
Khan said filmmakers could portray historical figures as heroes or villains, but should not manipulate history for a predetermined narrative.
“There are people who make films on villains and heroes and give the correct perspective as it is without dabbling it, without the historians and filmmakers diverting [it],” he said.
‘Kashmir has a very distinctive identity’
Khan also spoke about Kashmir's cultural identity, describing it as deeply rooted in Sufi traditions and communal coexistence.
“Jammu Kashmir is a very, very beautiful concept and identity. Kashmir has a very distinctive identity,” he said.
“Like every state has its lovely identity in different ways. But Kashmir has the Sufism involvement where people of all caste and creed are one.”
Describing Kashmir as “a secular centre which is mixed with warmth, love, affection”, Khan referred to Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs living together through its history.
He said India's civilisational diversity should be preserved and reflected responsibly through cinema.
“India is one of the greatest countries, a 5,000-year-old civilisation,” he said, before invoking the historical reigns of Ashoka and Akbar.
Khan recalled his own work on historical television productions, including The Sword of Tipu Sultan and Akbar the Great, saying his intention had always been nation-building.
“I first directed the first 22 episodes of The Sword of Tipu Sultan when my brother was struck by an unfortunate hand of destiny,” he said, adding that he later made Akbar the Great.
“At that time, Sulh-e-Kul was the religion of Emperor Akbar, where every religion comes under one umbrella. Peace for all, submission to all,” Khan said.
“I made that serial Akbar the Great again for nation-building. It brought harmony amongst the Hindus, the Muslims.”
Plans to bring Taj Mahal to Kashmir
Khan also announced plans to bring his film Taj Mahal: An Eternal Love Story to Kashmir for a premiere.
“My film Taj Mahal: An Eternal Love Story, inshallah, I will bring it to Kashmir to have a premiere of the film shortly and release it all over India again,” he said.
He said the film had already begun its international journey and recalled its screening in Malaysia.
“My film Taj Mahal has already started to take its first international journey on 6th February, 2006, where the Prime Minister of Malaysia had watched the film and he wrote a review, the same with the Minister of Culture,” Khan said.
He described the Taj Mahal as a symbol of love and said he wanted that message to reach audiences across the world.
“I want that this symbol of love, Taj Mahal, should sink into the minds and heart and soul of the people of the world,” he said. “It is the greatest message and Taj Mahal is one of our greatest monuments of pride before all the country.”
Khan concluded by thanking the organisers and praising Omar Abdullah and National Conference leader Farooq Abdullah for what he described as their commitment to an inclusive society.
“I have enjoyed every moment of my stay here with the warm hospitality of every officer, bureaucrat,” he said.
He described Farooq Abdullah as “one of the tallest leaders of a country” who believes in “the inclusive society, the love and harmony of a Brahman, of a Muslim, of a Christian, and a Jain”.
Khan said the presence of both father and son in Jammu and Kashmir's political leadership offered hope for the future.
“It is an amazing combination of a father and son and I am sure there will be great amount of peace, harmony, success and the people of Jammu Kashmir will soon be seeing a golden period,” he said.

Srinagar, Sep 9: Spanish filmmaker and producer Anna Saura Ramon on Wednesday described Kashmir as an ideal destination for filmmaking, praising its scenic landscapes, lakes, natural light and hospitality while calling for stronger cinematic ties between India and Spain.
Speaking to reporters on the third day of the inaugural International Film Festival of Jammu and Kashmir (IFFJK) at SKICC Srinagar, Saura, according to the news agency—Kashmir News Observer (KNO), said film festivals play an important role in promoting cinema and creating opportunities for filmmakers and audiences to discover films from different parts of the world.
"This is my vist to Kashmir and India. I hope to come again," Saura said, adding that she was looking forward to exploring Srinagar and experiencing the local culture.
On the scope for collaboration between Indian and Spanish cinema, she said there were differences between the two industries, but language should not become a barrier to stronger artistic relationships. "I think we can push for better relationships between India and Spain," she said, adding that there were opportunities for filmmakers from both countries to connect and work together.
Talking about Kashmir as a filming destination, Saura said the Valley had immense potential for filmmakers because of its landscapes, lakes and quality of natural light. "Of course, you have to promote Kashmir. There are great locations, good light for shooting and beautiful lakes," she said.
Saura also said she had already shared pictures of Kashmir with a friend, who suggested that the Valley could be explored as a potential location for filmmaking.
Asked whether she would consider casting Indian actors in a future India-Spain production, she said there was no reason why filmmakers could not work with actors from India. "There are lots of Indian-Spanish films that you will like," she said.
On the possibility of international studios and filmmakers coming to Kashmir, Saura said greater cooperation between governments and the film industry could help attract productions to the region.
"I am sure they will come and shoot here and make a movie," she said.
Reacting to IFFJK, Saura described it as a major initiative and expressed hope that the festival would have a long life.
"It is important for everyone," she said, adding that such festivals provide an opportunity to bring films and filmmakers from outside and expose local audiences to international cinema.
Saura also praised the atmosphere and hospitality in Kashmir, saying her first visit to India, particularly to Kashmir, had been a positive experience.
Saura is known for her work as a producer and director, including the documentary The Kid in the Photo.

The National Medical Commission’s plan to create a National Medical Register (NMR), is running into rough weather again as doctors are questioning why medical practitioners are being made to pay a fee and register again for entry into the NMR when their database is already available with respective State Medical Councils.
The question assumes significance as the Ethics and Medical Registration Board (EMRB) of the National Medical Commission (NMC) is moving to amend the Registration of Medical Practitioners and Licence to Practice Medicine Regulations, 2026.
The NMR is envisaged as a single, reliable national database that would make it easier to verify doctors’ qualifications and registration status and facilitate their practice across State boundaries. The system envisages a unique NMR identification number linked to every doctor’s State registration number.
The dispute now is over how this national database would be created -- is it the task of the State Medical Councils to provide the data for the creation of the NMR or should individual doctors have to put in application afresh, pay a fee and then await EMRB’s verification of credentials?
What the law says
Doctors point out that the NMC Act, 2019, already settles this. In Sections 31(1) , 31 (6) and 31 (7), the NMC Act says that the EMRB “shall maintain a National Register” of all licensed medical practitioners.; the State Medical Councils will maintain and update respective State Registers with the EMRB and that it will be the task of EMRB to maintain the National Register and ensure the electronic synchronisation with the State Registers.
“Nowhere in the NMC Act is it stated that it is the responsibility of registered medical practitioners to apply for NMR registration,” points out the Kannur-based doctor and RTI activist, K.V. Babu. Also, in a written reply in the Lok Sabha on August 5, 2025, the Union Health Ministry, quoting the NMC, had said that applying for NMR registration was voluntary.
Doctors therefore argue that the NMR should be populated from the verified data already held by State Medical Councils. “Our data is already with the State Medical Council and it just needs to be handed over to the EMRB. We fail to understand why the NMR database creation should be so complicated and why doctors are being put through the registration and verification formalities all over again,” says the State President of Indian Medical Association, Kerala, M.N. Menon
A registration backlog
The concern raised by doctors is genuine. Applications submitted by several doctors for NMR registration have remained pending before the EMRB for years, raising questions about the practicality of requiring every State-registered doctor to individually apply for national registration. According to the minutes of the NMC’s 17th meeting, fewer than 32,000 registered medical practitioners had applied for NMR registration by December 2025.
The cost angle
The issue also has a financial dimension. Doctors point out that they are already paying a substantial amount as registration and licensing-related charges to State Medical Councils. The registration fee that will be charged in the name of NMR will be another burden on doctors, Dr. Babu says.
Doctors have demanded that the NMC withdraw the proposed draft amendment and ask State Medical Councils to send its database to the EMRB for creating the NMR as well as the unique ID for doctors

Brazil Supreme Court removes federal police chief, deepening crisis at the top court
Brazilian Supreme Court Justice André Mendonca has removed the head of the federal police and the intelligence chief from their posts
SAO PAULO -- Brazilian Supreme Court Justice André Mendonca on Tuesday removed the head of the country’s federal police and its intelligence chief from their posts, deepening a crisis at the top court and drawing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's government into the turmoil ahead of October national elections.
Mendonca, an appointee of former President Jair Bolsonaro, said in his ruling that federal police Director-General Andrei Rodrigues, a Lula nominee, and the intelligence director of the force, Leandro Almada, headed an organization that allegedly produced six illegal reports on the justice's activities through the end of August.
Mendonca currently chairs two politically sensitive investigations: one into the collapse of Banco Master, which has ensnared several politicians, and another into alleged frauds in Brazil's pension system. The first has hit mostly figures of the country's opposition, while the latter has raised questions of wrongdoing by one of Lula's sons.
Brazil’s government did not immediately respond to a request from The Associated Press on whether it will appeal.
William Marcel Murad, the federal police's executive director, said in a statement that the director-general has the force's “full confidence” and that agents “will not be shaken by attacks.”
Lula is bidding for reelection in October against Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president who is currently serving his 27-year prison sentence at home for an attempted coup.
Mendonca’s decision to remove the federal police chief comes amid a major clash between him and fellow justice Alexandre de Moraes, who sentenced Bolsonaro to prison last year. Last week, Mendonca unsealed federal police documents that showed that Banco Master owner Daniel Vorcaro frequently sought de Moraes' legal advice before his arrest.
De Moraes had previously denied wrongdoing involving Vorcaro, though his wife provided legal services to Banco Master as part of a 130 million reais ($25 million) contract. Since Mendonca's decision to unseal documents last week, de Moraes is under pressure from politicians, the media and legal experts to resign. He is yet to make public comments about the case.
Brazil's main media reported last week that Mendonca was seeking a suspension for de Moraes from the court until it decides whether he should be investigated in the potential graft case. De Moraes, in turn, said in another ruling that Mendonca should be investigated by the court and potentially impeached by the Senate for interviewing Vorcaro in August without the presence of federal police agents or prosecutors.
On Monday, Brazil's Independence Day, tens of thousands of supporters of opposition presidential candidate Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro filled Sao Paulo's key artery, with many calling for de Moraes' removal. Demonstrators held a giant inflatable figure of Mendonca and wore shirts in support of the Supreme Court justice.

Japan is considering adding airport ground handling to the new Employment for Skill Development program, Immigration Services Agency officials said at a briefing Tuesday.
The government would shift 300 foreign workers from the Specified Skilled Worker program to the new system, which is scheduled to begin in April 2027, rather than increase the overall intake, officials said.
The shift would leave the combined projected intake under the two programs unchanged at about 1.23 million workers. The government estimates that the aviation sector needs 4,900 foreign workers in total, with 300 potentially moved into the new Employment for Skill Development category.
Agency officials said the proposed aviation expansion would cover airport ground handling, not aircraft maintenance.
The government is also considering changes to principal skills and industrial classifications in several other existing sectors, such as product manufacturing, construction and fishery, while keeping overall intake projections unchanged where additional demand is already reflected in existing estimates.
Separately, officials gave more details on the suspension of Certificates of Eligibility for Specified Skilled Worker applicants in the food-service sector. The number of workers had approached the 50,000-person ceiling, prompting the government to halt new certificates from April 13.
About 8,500 applications filed before the suspension remain under review. Applications to change one’s residency status are being prioritized, while certificates will be issued in filing order when departures or status changes create room below the cap.

Stories are nested within stories to steadily diminishing returns in “Company,” a perversely ponderous exercise in hide-the-genre that takes more than an hour to reveal what its game really is. Gathering little tension ahead of a ludicrous twist — one that puts proceedings in a new light while adding no great urgency to them — Casey Affleck’s second feature as writer-director feels altogether less assured than his 2019 debut, the somberly effective post-apocalyptic drama “Light of My Life.” This time staying behind the camera entirely, and handing a demanding lead role to his teenage son Atticus, Affleck again brings an earnest seriousness of purpose to this staggered tale of a mysterious stranger drifting into a household and holding it eerily rapt, repeated across three different eras. But for all the echoey narrative tripling here, the payoff is distinctly muted.
	
“Company” presents a significant challenge to the marketing teams of any distributors taking it on after its Venice competition premiere — though given the dull peculiarity of the film, coupled with a muted festival reception, said distributors are by no means a given. How does one pitch to audiences a film where its grabbiest story hook is also its most carefully guarded secret? Minus the surprise factor that certainly caught Venice journalists off guard, viewers going in with some idea of what’s coming will be even more perplexed by the coy obfuscation and molasses pacing of the film’s first two-thirds, which mostly present as the kind of melancholically revisionist period Western one might expect from the star of “The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford” and “The World to Come.” (And indeed his co-scripter Ron Hansen, writer of the former film’s source novel and the latter film’s screenplay.)
Popular on Variety
It begins in the year 1975, as Evelyn (Emily Alyn Lind), a quietly self-possessed, soberly dressed young woman, arrives on the doorstep of a well-to-do suburban home, in the midst of an almighty downpour. (Bob Dylan’s “Shelter From the Storm” is the opening soundtrack cue; it turns out to be lyrically on the nose in multiple ways.) Not recognizing the name Evelyn asks for, the man who answers the door says she has the wrong address, but invites her in to dry off; they’re having a Christmas party, and several of the guests are intrigued by the reserved, well-spoken stranger, who offers to regale them with a story.
In the recursive manner of the old “it was a dark and stormy night” chestnut, Evelyn’s story soon teases viewers (and listeners) with some déjà vu: Set in 1953, it tells of elderly rural widower Tom (a maximally grizzled Nick Nolte), who finds an enigmatic young woman, Alice (Caylee Cowan) collapsed in the snow near his cabin in the Colorado mountains, and brings her inside to warm up. In return for his hospitality, she offers to tell him a story — about Rebecca (Adelaide Clemens) and Emmett (Scoot McNairy), a hardscrabble Colorado farming couple in 1903, who find young drifter Caleb (Atticus Affleck) unconscious in the snow, and carry him home to recover.
This tedious roundelay of story introductions mercifully ends here, as the turn-of-the-century tale becomes the film’s primary focus, though fear not: Its principals still have plenty of stories to tell. Rebecca, a patient salt-of-the-earth type, is compelled by the surly, coldly withholding Caleb, and invites him to stay on as a hired hand. Emmett, wary from the start, would rather see the back of him, and his suspicions grow when word spreads of a series of brutal murders in the area. At this point, it’s impossible to discuss the film without any mention of its true identity, so potential viewers wishing to preserve the unspoiled viewing experience would be advised to stop reading here.
In all three timelines, a slightly unsettling stranger — clad in severe monochrome tailoring — is let into an unsuspecting home, and by the time bloody violence enters the equation, the clues check out: This is, like “Sinners,” a period heartland vampire movie that uses the mythic conventions of that genre to say something or other about the American spirit of community, or lack thereof. “Company,” however, peddles some wildly divergent vampire lore to ultimately announce itself as a fable on the nature of human, or inhuman, kindness: Its bloodthirsty raconteurs are capable of grace and mercy when treated with same, which is certainly a novel mythos within this rich and varied storytelling tradition, if not a terribly exciting one.
Caleb, at least, has a bit of attitude, and what tension “Company” generates largely rests on his still, pale-eyed, tacitly judgmental presence. In an extended verbal confrontation between him and neighboring farmer Kleinschmidt (a caustic, quick-on-the-draw Ben Mendelsohn, by several notches the ensemble’s MVP), Affleck and Hansen’s dourly lyrical dialogue finally crackles with something like foreboding. As Caleb, the younger Affleck — who resembles, in features and affect, the love child of Timothée Chalamet and Troye Sivan — occasionally lets his inexperience show, though there’s genuine mystery in his willowy insolence; only when he’s on screen does “Company” have a welcome whisper of danger to it.
Elsewhere, it simply plays as a protracted shaggy-dog tease with no sense of humor, and an inflated sense of its own poetry. Affleck continues to demonstrate promising filmmaking chops: He can conjure starkly mournful atmosphere aplenty, and the film is handsome in an appropriately ascetic, chambray-textured way. Yet perhaps the most puzzling thing about “Company” — more so, even, than its surprise vampires — is why it boasts a whopping eight DPs, including such accomplished, distinctive stylists as Masanobu Takayanagi (“Springsteen: Deliver Me From Nowhere”), Adam Arkapaw (“Macbeth”) and Marcell Rév (“White God”), as well as Affleck himself. If the plan was to give each of the film’s enfolded narratives its own characterizing aesthetic, that isn’t clear in the film’s earthy visual consistency. If it’s a tell of an addled or waylaid production, the final film doesn’t seem entirely worth the trouble. Many hands don’t make light work of “Company”; many tellers don’t make one good story.

Emergency slide deploys on Air Force One as Trump waits to board for Dallas convention
The president is scheduled to fly to Dallas, Texas, for the Republican midterm convention
An emergency inflatable slide deployed from Air Force One on Wednesday afternoon as President Donald Trump waited to board the aircraft at Joint Base Andrews.
At about 2:20 p.m., the slide rolled out onto the tarmac from the right side of the Qatari-gifted aircraft, opposite the side typically used by Trump to board, according to a White House pool report. Trump was seated nearby on Marine One at the time.
The president — who is scheduled to fly to Dallas for the Republican midterm convention — told reporters that “they were doing a check on the slide,” which he said “takes about 15 minutes.”
Asked by a reporter whether he’s sure that the aircraft is safe to fly, Trump replied: “Yeah, I am, or I wouldn’t be on it.”
The new Air Force One — a $400 million Boeing 747‑8 — was gifted to President Trump by Qatar’s royal family last year. After Pentagon-led modifications, Trump made his first flight aboard the aircraft in July.

From game show to Champions League - Sabah coach tells his incredible story
- Published
On Thursday, Valdas Dambrauskas will walk out at Old Trafford as manager of Sabah in the Champions League.
The Lithuanian's career will come full circle, some 20 years since he made his first steps into coaching with Manchester United Soccer Schools.
"This is beyond my imagination," Dambrauskas told BBC Sport. "To go through that tunnel on to that pitch.
"I've been many times to Old Trafford with the kids, and now I'm going to come as a coach."
This only scratches the surface of Dambrauskas' remarkable story.
It begins with an appearance on the Lithuanian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?, Dambrauskas using his modest winnings to move to London and forge a career in football.
It is a tale of casual jobs, a determination to succeed and a nomadic coaching career across Europe - which now brings the 49-year-old back to England in the Champions League with the Azerbaijani club.
How a gameshow gave Dambrauskas his break
As Sabah's players and staff celebrated reaching the Champions League two weeks ago, unbeknownst to Dambrauskas he was becoming a social media star.
It all related to that appearance on Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? in 2002.
Not because he was on the show, but how he spent the money he won.
"This is so long ago," said Dambrauskas with a wry smile. "A back-in-the-year story that really was forgotten.
"And now suddenly everybody is speaking about this."
Dambrauskas walked away with 4,000 litas (about £725). That might not sound like much, but it was six months' wages to the average Lithuanian.
For Dambrauskas, the real story should be his career and not a gameshow.
"Everybody now takes only this part, you know, about the money," Dambrauskas said. "But yes, it is a true story.
"My idea was somehow I will try to go on these [coaching] courses to gain the coaching badge, maybe go back one day to Lithuania and start to work as a football coach."
What began with Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? would map out his whole career.
'I was doing two, three, sometimes four jobs'
Dambrauskas says he had known since the age of 12 he would not make it as a player, but coaching would keep him close to football.
He arrived in London in August 2002 aged 25 on a student visa with limited English.
What followed would be eight years of hard work where he would coach for community projects, at a semi-professional club, within professional youth programmes - and hold down multiple jobs while raising two children.
In 2004 he enrolled on a course in sports science and coaching at London Metropolitan University, the first real step in his career.
Then he started out coaching by volunteering with the Access to Sports Project for deprived children in Finsbury Park.
He went on to work with London Tigers, a charitable community organisation which runs teams from junior level right through to semi-professional.
Starting out as a volunteer, across five years he progressed to manage the first team in non-league football in the Spartan South Midlands League, FA Cup and FA Vase.
Dambrauskas became the first Lithuanian to achieve a Uefa coaching licence through the London Football Association.
"I went on every possible course, every possible conference, London Football Coaches Association meetings," Dambrauskas said.
"Everywhere I could go just to gain some information, some knowledge, some extra diploma, extra course.
"That was very important for me and I took my chances."
He got his first break at a professional club when Manchester United Soccer Schools took a chance on him in 2004.
Dambrauskas spent five years coaching on residential courses in the UK and in Europe.
"That was the best thing that could happen in my life," Dambrauskas said.
"I went through three or four interviews. I will be forever grateful to [Foundation chief executive] John Shiels, the way he gave me this chance, because I didn't have experience.
"I'd never been in a place with so many great personalities as I got in the Manchester United Soccer Schools."
After a short spell with Fulham, Dambrauskas moved to Brentford. He credits academy director Ose Aibangee as one of the biggest influences on his career, pushing his limits.
All the while he was juggling home life and working multiple jobs to make ends meet.
"I was a gardener, a handyman, doing newspaper rounds at the beginning, also polishing floors in a pub," Dambrauskas said.
"So many jobs. Working in retail, and then as a sports development officer, then a sports development manager, and the central YMCA.
"I was doing two, three, sometimes four jobs."
As well as the trip to Manchester United this week, Sabah will complete their Champions League group games at Arsenal in January.
This also feels like fate for Dambrauskas - one of the buildings at London Metropolitan University on Holloway Road overlooked Emirates Stadium.
When asked about his time in England, Dambrauskas' face lights up.
"When I hear this word 'England', it for me sounds like opportunities," Dambrauskas said.
"It was really amazing. England gave me all this and I'll forever be grateful."
From England to 13 trophies in five countries
Dambrauskas was working three jobs - at Brentford, London Tigers and as a sports development manager - when the opportunity arose to coach full-time.
It meant leaving England to return to Lithuania, champions Ekranas appointing him assistant first-team and reserve-team coach at the end of 2010.
After four years at Ekranas he was named manager of Zalgiris Vilnius, Lithuania's biggest club, where his career really took off.
Dambrauskas won two league titles, three Lithuanian Cups and two Lithuanian Super Cups across three seasons - including a treble in 2016.
Then came a series of moves in which Dambrauskas took charge of eight teams over nine years in seven countries.
First RFS, with whom he won the Latvian Cup, and then Gorica in Croatia.
A third league title came with Bulgarian side Ludogorets Razgrad, along with another Super Cup and Europa League qualification.
Dambrauskas then returned to Croatia with Hajduk Split, a time which he described as "absolutely amazing" as the club won the Croatian Cup - their first trophy for 10 years.
Next up was a spell in Greece with OFI Crete, then Omonia in Cyprus - who qualified for the Conference League - and Diosgyori in Hungary.
Finally, in the summer of 2025, he arrived at Sabah, the 10th club of his career.
Dambrauskas completed the league and cup double in his first season, as the club won the title for the first time.
It took his trophy tally to 13 across five countries.
Next stop, the Champions League.
Champions League 'beyond imagination'
Dambrauskas had to navigate four knockout ties to get Sabah to the Champions League, and they are the only club to make it all the way through from the first qualifying round.
Welsh club TNS, Finland's KuPS, Danish side Aarhus and Israel's Hapoel Beer-Sheva were all knocked out.
The final qualifying game was as dramatic as Dambrauskas' own story.
Sabah were going out, then a goal by Tellur Mutallimov in the fourth minute of stoppage time sent the tie into extra time. They went on to win 5-2 on the night and 6-4 on aggregate.
"To go to the Champions League is something beyond imagination," Dambrauskas said.
"We have never qualified for the Conference League, we have never qualified for the Europa League. We have never passed more than two rounds in a row in one competition, and now suddenly we are here."
Sabah are based in the town of Masazir - 30 miles north of the Azerbaijan capital Baku - with a population of just 19,000.
Known as the Owls, Sabah were only formed in 2017 and on Tuesday will celebrate their ninth birthday.
Like many small clubs, their Bank Respublika Arena home, with a capacity of less than 9,000, does not meet Uefa regulations. Instead, the club are expected to play their matches at the Olympic Stadium in Baku.
Sabah will host Borussia Dortmund, Barcelona and Napoli, and face a trip to Villarreal - as well as the visits to England.
"It can be a very hard draw, and it can be a Sabah draw," said Dambrauskas, clearly excited by the prospect.
"You dream for this, to play in this competition, to play against those teams.
"So now is the time to show that you can handle it, to find a way to compete and we will try to do this.
"We have a good team, we have an ambitious team, we have hungry players who are really keen to show themselves."
Sabah president Magsud Adigozalov last week was full of praise for Dambrauskas' impact.
"His influence goes beyond tactics," Adigozalov told Report. "He has instilled a mindset and winning mentality in the team.
"Even in the most difficult moments, the team never abandons its game or fighting spirit, which is the result of the coach's work."
Twenty years ago, Dambrauskas looked out over the pitch at Old Trafford during one of his job interviews, dreaming that one day he would stand in one of the dugouts.
Now his coaching career will return to where it started.
"I lived in England when the battle between Manchester United and Arsenal was the biggest rivalry. Alex Ferguson and Arsene Wenger," Dambrauskas said.
"Now I'm going to come back as a coach in the Champions League and hear that anthem. It's really amazing."

CBS News accused of photoshopping image of new 60 Minutes lineup ahead of nerve-wracking launch
According to CBS, the promotional shoot took place in Grand Central Station’s Oyster Bar as a deliberate homage to network pioneers Edward R. Murrow and Walter Cronkite
CBS News is pushing back against online claims that a promotional photograph for the upcoming 59th season of “60 Minutes” was digitally altered or artificially generated.
The image, captured by photographer Mark Seliger at Grand Central Station’s Oyster Bar, features the program’s new lineup.
Following its publication, social media users highlighted several visual anomalies, drawing particular attention to reporter Lesley Stahl appearing to lean against empty space, overlapping feet that critics argued would compromise balance and an unclenched left hand gripping nothing.
“There’s a table behind her,” Jeremy Adler, the senior vice president of communications for CBS News, told The Daily Beast.
Seliger defended the portrait, noting the difficulty of getting a large group into a single frame.
“Bringing ten people together in one frame can be a challenge, but with this team there was an immediate chemistry and a real sense of connection,” Seliger said, according to CBS News. “You could feel the history of 60 Minutes, but also the energy of where it’s going. That’s what I hoped would come through in the photograph.”
The shoot location was intended as a tribute to network pioneers Edward R. Murrow, Walter Cronkite and Douglas Edwards, who broadcast from Grand Central when CBS maintained studios in the terminal between 1939 and 1964. According to the network, the historic studio was situated directly above the Oyster Bar, though “60 Minutes” did not premiere until 1968.
The backlash comes as the program prepares for its first full season under the leadership of Bari Weiss, whose appointment following the May departure of longtime executive producer Tanya Simon has drawn continuous controversy.
Critics have accused Weiss of censorship and shifting the program’s editorial stance, while the upcoming season launch features an interview with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Many users on X tied the picture's apparent glitches directly to ongoing frustrations with the broadcast's direction, with one calling it a “fake or poorly AI’d photo.”
User Darin Yates labeled the program “Liberal Propaganda and Fake News,” adding that “even your photo is fake.”
Other accounts questioned the staging entirely.
X user David Andersen asked, “Do they dislike each other so much they won't take a group photo?”
Commenters also zeroed in on specific physical awkwardness in the portrait.
“Is that a fake photo?” one user asked. “Lesley Stahl don't look right. Why on Earth would you use a fake photo ever and especially why for this?”
The Independent has contacted CBS News for comment.

‘It will be a photo you live to regret forever if you shake his hand at the 9/11 memorial,’ Laura Loomer, a right-wing provocateur, wrote on X
Right-wing provocateur Laura Loomer publicly urged Vice President JD Vance to refuse a handshake with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani at an upcoming 9/11 anniversary ceremony.
Loomer, an ally of President Donald Trump with a large social media following, made the plea Tuesday in a series of X posts laced with anti-Muslim rhetoric.
“I'm saying this from a place of concern: Mr. Vice President…Do not shake [Mamdani's] hand when you attend the 9/11 ceremony in New York,” she wrote. “It will be a photo you live to regret forever if you shake his hand at the 9/11 memorial.”
In a separate post, she wrote that the “most America First thing” Vance can do “on 9/11 is refuse to shake the dirty Muslim Mayor's hand.” She also baselessly characterized Mamdani as a “jihadist.”
“I'd rather chop my hand off than be caught in that photo,” Loomer added in a third post hours later. “I can't think of a worse photo opp.”
Vance is scheduled to travel to New York City Friday for a ceremony commemorating the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, which killed nearly 3,000 people. Like past mayors, Mamdani will be in attendance.
Mamdani, a democratic socialist and New York's first Muslim mayor, has faced calls from prominent Republicans to skip the anniversary event.
On Sunday, former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani, who was in office in 2001, told Newsmax that he opposes Mamdani attending the downtown event. “It offends me that he's coming,” Giuliani said before baselessly claiming that Mamdani supports a plot to “take us over” and compared him to al-Qaeda terrorists.
Earlier this month, former New York Governor George Pataki, who was in office during the attacks, told City & State that Mamdani should skip the event.
"With respect to the mayor, I think anyone who doesn't intentionally distance themselves from Hasan Piker, who has said that America deserved the attacks of September 11th, should not be there," Pataki told the outlet. Piker, a far-left streamer, is a vocal supporter of the mayor.
Conservative critics have also challenged Mamdani's appointment of Ramzi Kassem as the city's chief legal counsel, citing Kassem's past representation of a man whose brother-in-law was one of the 9/11 hijackers. The controversy intensified after The New York Post reported Saturday that, following the mayor's signing of an executive order designating September 11 as a "Day of Remembrance and Service," the ceremonial pen was handed to Kassem.
Mamdani, who has condemned the 2001 attacks as “horrific,” said he still plans to attend Friday's ceremony.
“I will proudly honor the families, the survivors, the first responders forever impacted by that horrific terror attack by standing alongside them at this year's 9/11 commemoration, reaffirming that we will never forget the solemn day felt by all of us who call this city home and, frankly, by all of us who call this country home,” he told City & State.
Also this week, he released over 170,000 pages of internal records that show officials misled people about the safety of the air around Ground Zero after the September 11 terror attacks.
“People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air,” Mamdani said during a news conference.
One prominent official who will not be in attendance on Friday is President Donald Trump.
According to The New York Times, the Republican president had initially planned to be there, but changed his mind after he was informed that no political speeches were allowed. After the story was published, Trump claimed that reporter Maggie Haberman had “made up the story.”
The president will instead commemorate 9/11 by attending a service at the Pentagon alongside first lady Melania Trump.

The Eiffel Tower has reopened after a one-day strike was called in response to the landmark’s management ordering female staff to keep out of sight at the request of a visiting religious group.
City Hall, which operates the Paris landmark, has apologised for breaching France’s republican principle of equality and ordered a full inquiry.
Workers at the tower walked out on Monday, closing the landmark to visitors, after female colleagues were sidelined and replaced during a visit organised by a Hindu religious group at the weekend.
In a statement, staff said they objected to “professional instructions that led to female employees being sidelined, replaced and made invisible because of their sex” during the visit.
“Some were asked to leave their posts and wait in separate rooms. In some posts, women were replaced by men. All female employees were instructed not to pass through or enter certain areas while the [Hindu] delegation was present,” they said in a statement.
Employees said they were shocked to find themselves in a situation that was “deeply contrary to the values of equality and nondiscrimination”.
“The Eiffel Tower is the symbol of France. We believe it must also be exemplary in the values it promotes and the way it treats staff,” the statement said.
The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) spiritual movement, whose members made the request in advance of a visit on Saturday, apologised.
“To our knowledge, nobody was refused access to the Eiffel Tower at any moment. Nevertheless, We offer our sincere apologies to anyone who may have been hurt or offended by this situation,” it wrote in a statement.
BAPS is close to India’s ruling Hindu nationalist party, Bharatiya Janata, and was in France to consecrate its first major temple in the country on Sunday.
The public-owned Eiffel Tower operating company (SETE) acknowledged that BAPS had requested that “interactions with women” be limited, and said it should not have accepted these conditions. “They are not in keeping with SETE’s values or the principles of equality between women and men and the neutrality that must guide the organisation of visits to the monument,” it said.
Emmanuel Grégoire, the mayor of Paris, has promised an investigation to “get to the bottom of this as soon as possible”.
He said moving female staff out of sight was unacceptable.
“These are not my values nor those the Eiffel Tower must represent,” he wrote on X.
Ariel Weil, mayor of the Paris Centre district and president of SETE, said he was unaware of the “shocking and unacceptable” conditions afforded the visiting group.
“I confirm again the Eiffel Tower’s commitment to republican values and gender equality,” he said.

Srinagar, Sep 9: The High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh has set aside the discharge of an accused in a UAPA case stating that secessionist sloganeering in a mob in the presence of the head of a banned separatist organisation prima facie falls under the definition of unlawful activity.
A division bench headed by acting Chief Justice Sanjeev Kumar set aside the discharge of Mohammad Yousuf Lone in a 2013 UAPA case by the Additional District and Sessions Judge (Designated Special Court under NIA Act) Kupwara.
"The sloganeering for secession, raised by an accused leading a mob in the company of the head of a proscribed separatist organisation, coupled with incitement of the public and violence against security forces, is capable, on a prima facie appreciation, of falling squarely within this definition," the bench observed in its order.
According to the case, a mob headed by Mohammad Yousuf Lone and Late Syed Ali Shah Geelani, chairman of the banned Hurriyat Conference, came out of Jamia Masjid in Kupwara on November 8, 2013, raised anti-national slogans against the Government of India, and pelted stones at police and security forces.
The separatist leaders also allegedly instigated the general public against the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Union of India, according to the chargesheet.
"The trial court has recorded, in a single sentence in paragraph 6 of the order impugned, that the facts 'do not fulfil the ingredients of Sections 2(o) of ULA(P) Act' without setting out the reasoning by which the specific statements or conduct attributed to the respondent in the chargesheet were tested against the statutory definition. This amounts to a bare conclusion rather than a reasoned finding," the high court said.
It said the material with chargesheet -- including the recorded slogans, the leadership role attributed to the respondent, and the resultant violence -- discloses a strong suspicion sufficient to put the respondent on trial, leaving the question of whether the charges are ultimately proved to be examined at trial and not foreclosed at the threshold.
"It is trite that an order of discharge must reflect application of judicial mind to the material on record, and that the findings at the charge stage, though summary, cannot be conclusory. However, it is abundantly clear from perusal of the order impugned that the same does not indicate that the specific contents of the chargesheet, the statements of the witnesses to the procession, the site plan, and the material, alleged to link the respondent to the incitement and the resultant violence, were tested against the ingredients of Section 13 read with Section 2(o) of the UAPA before the conclusion of non-applicability was recorded. On this ground, the order impugned is unsustainable and calls for interference," it added.
The court said it is neither making any definitive finding on the guilt or innocence of the respondent, nor expressing any opinion on the ultimate merits of the case.
"However, when specific material is brought on record that, on the face of it, discloses the commission of an offence and the complicity of the respondent, the trial court cannot act as a mute spectator and shut the doors of trial without assigning valid legal reasons," it added.
Allowing the criminal appeal filed by the state, the high court directed that the chargesheet be restored and the trial court proceed with the framing of charge against the respondent afresh after considering the material placed on record by the appellant.

Eye donation is said to be one of the most meaningful forms of donation, as a single donor can potentially restore sight to two individuals through corneal transplantation. India has made considerable progress in eye banking; the country currently has 396 functional eye banks, and corneal collections increased from 62,370 in 2022–23 to 69,848 in 2024–25. However, the need for donor tissue substantially exceeds its availability. There are approximately 2 million corneally blind people in our country, but only 40,000 corneal transplants performed per year.
Role of stakeholders
The government has a crucial role in strengthening the eye donation ecosystem through the National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment (NPCBVI). Government support includes funding for eye bank infrastructure and equipment, training of ophthalmologists and eye bank technicians, promotion of eye donation, and provision of corneal storage media. Government hospitals can further improve donation rates by establishing Hospital Cornea Retrieval Programmes (HCRP) and integrating eye donation into routine end-of-life counselling.
Non-governmental organisations and service organisations have an equally important role in creating awareness, dispelling myths, encouraging pledges and, most importantly, counselling families at the time of death. Organisations such as eye bank networks, Lions Clubs and other community-based groups can take the message of eye donation to schools, colleges, workplaces and rural communities.
Private eye hospitals and institutions can complement these efforts by establishing or strengthening eye banks, developing efficient corneal retrieval networks, maintaining high standards of tissue evaluation and preservation, and providing advanced corneal transplantation. Recent initiatives such as the expansion of the National Eye Bank at AIIMS, Delhi through partnerships with additional hospitals demonstrate the value of collaborative retrieval networks.
Building strong PPPs
Ultimately, the future of eye donation in India lies in a strong public–private–NGO partnership. Awareness must translate into timely family consent, consent into retrieval, and retrieved tissue into high-quality transplantation. Strengthening this entire chain will be essential to bring down the burden of corneal blindness and make the gift of sight a reality for many more Indians.
The goal is clear: to transform the gift of eye donation into the gift of sight. Every donated cornea carries a legacy of compassion—allowing one person’s life to bring light into another’s.
(Dr. Mohan Rajan is chairman and medical director and Dr. Sujatha Mohan is executive medical director, of Rajan Eye Care Hospital. drmohanrajan@gmail.com)

People are not happy about Flock Safety’s automated license plate readers and the cops that allegedly misuse them. If you’re one of those ALPR-haters, you can now take out your rage in the video game Grand Theft Auto V by installing Grand Theft Automated License Plate Reader, a mod built by artist Morry Kolman.
The mod installs 235 Flock cameras around the fictional Los Santos, a riff on the real-life city of Los Angeles. Players can smash and shoot down the cameras and get paid $600 for each one they destroy, which Kolman priced based on a teardown of a Flock Falcon Flex Camera by the Iowa-based civil liberties group Eyes Off of Cedar Rapids. The in-game cameras log every time a player destroys and drives by one, and players can render a photo album of their interactions.
In real life, vigilantes have allegedly wrecked Flock cameras in their communities using spray-paint, saws, bullets, and even flaming projectiles. An NPR analysis found that Flock cameras have been vandalized in at least 36 states.
“GTPLR is not an endorsement of the activities that it allows in the game in the same way that GTA is not an endorsement of the activities that are allowed in the game,” says Kolman, referring to the fact that GTA is largely about doing fictional crimes. “But I think there is a public appetite for some kind of cathartic release against these machines.”
In addition to being fun objects to destroy, the GTA cameras also operate as an extension of the police in-game. Passing by one of the 235 cameras while being chased by the cops prolongs the game’s cooldown period. Because of how dense the cameras are in some areas, it can make the game impossible to play.
There’s also a 5 percent chance that the cameras will trigger a random police response even if the player isn’t doing anything wrong, which Kolman says was inspired by news reports about innocent people being held at gunpoint because of ALPR errors.
“There are violent responses and really dangerous situations that are created by these cameras and their inaccuracies,” says Kolman.
Flock did not immediately respond to a request for comment for this story.
GTA V has been around for over a decade, and a rich modding community has built up around it (WIRED covered one back in 2015.) The long-awaited sequel, Grand Theft Auto VI, is slated to come out in November and will be set in a fictional version of Miami called Vice City.
Kolman doesn’t have specific plans to build a version of GTALPR for that, joking, “We'll probably wait to see what the people of Vice City and their local government have already installed around their map.”
In real-life LA, the Los Angeles Police Department suspended its use of Flock cameras this summer following a recommendation from the LAPD’s inspector general. The tide is turning in other places too—governors in both Texas and Florida recently took steps to curtail the use of Flock cameras in their respective states, and across the US, there were 131 Flock contract terminations in August alone, according to the anti-surveillance advocacy group Secure Justice.
For all the fun that fake-smashing surveillance cameras can be, Kolman seriously hopes that players can feel the “insidiousness and inescapability of the surveillance” through GTALPR.
“I know that you could read a thousand articles about why surveillance is bad and why Flock is horrible,” says Kolman. “Or I could make you feel how pervasive these Flock cameras are by having you try to drive around the map of Los Santos.”

Norway to bid farewell to King Harald V with funeral attended by royalty, dignitaries
Norway will bid its final farewell to King Harald V with a funeral paying tribute to the 35-year reign of the popular monarch who died on Aug. 28, aged 89
OSLO, Norway -- Norway will bid its final farewell to King Harald V on Wednesday with a funeral attended by royalty and leaders from across Europe and beyond, who will pay tribute to the popular monarch's 35-year reign.
Harald, who died on Aug. 28 aged 89, was Europe’s oldest monarch and had modernized the royal house, but refused to follow in the footsteps of other aging monarchs who have abdicated in recent times. His son immediately became King Haakon VIII and last week pledged an oath of allegiance to Norway's constitution in parliament.
On Wednesday, the coffin will be taken from the royal palace to Oslo Cathedral in a procession, followed by Haakon, other senior Norwegian royals, foreign guests and representatives of Norway’s parliament and others.
Ahead of the funeral, Norwegians have waited patiently to file past Harald's coffin as it lay in state in the chapel of the royal palace in Oslo. The queue was seven hours long at one point over the weekend.
Large crowds are expected in the capital for the funeral. The downtown area will be closed to vehicles and electric scooters, and police have instructed people not to bring bicycles, umbrellas or sharp objects. Large screens have been set up for people to watch the ceremony.
Among the guests expected to attend are the monarchs of Sweden, Denmark, Spain, the Netherlands, Belgium and Jordan. The heir to the British throne, Prince William, is also expected, as is Crown Prince Akishino of Japan. Presidents from a range of European countries will join them.
A minute's silence will be held across Norway at the start of the funeral ceremony. Eulogies will be delivered by Norway's parliament speaker and prime minister, and there will be a candle-lighting ceremony with representatives of different faiths.
After the funeral, Harald's coffin will be taken in a procession to the palace chapel at Akershus Castle, where the late king's ancestors are buried. After a private ceremony for the Norwegian royals, who will be joined by some of the foreign guests and senior Norwegian officials, it will be lowered into the crypt.
Norway’s monarchy traces its origins to King Harald Fairhair in the ninth century. When Norway regained its independence from Sweden in 1905, three-quarters of voters in a national plebiscite approved restoring the monarchy.
Today, the throne's role is largely symbolic and power lies with the elected government and parliament, but the Norwegian royal family retains a role in promoting the wealthy Scandinavian nation around the world.

ANI moves Delhi high court division bench in OpenAI case
The agency argued OpenAI had scraped, stored and commercially exploited its work, infringing its exclusive rights under copyright law.
News agency ANI has moved a division bench of the Delhi high court against a single judge’s order dismissing its plea to restrain OpenAI from using its content to train ChatGPT.
ANI’s appeal against the July 24 verdict was listed before a bench of justices V Kameshwar Rao and Manmeet PS Arora. However, it was adjourned to September 14 as the bench did not assemble.
ANI challenges Delhi HC ruling on OpenAI’s use of news content
On July 24, Justice Amit Bansal dismissed ANI’s plea, holding that OpenAI’s use of the news agency’s material for training its large language model (LLM) fell within the statutory exception of “fair dealing” under Indian copyright law.
The judge said the use qualified as “private use” under Section 52(1)(a) of the Copyright Act, 1957. The provision permits fair dealing of copyrighted material for private or personal use, including research, criticism, review and reporting of current events.
Also read: Delhi HC's OpenAI-ANI ruling: What it means for AI, copyright and publishers in India — so far
Justice Bansal, in his 135-page verdict, reasoned that the training data was accessible only to the AI model during the learning process and was not made available to the public for viewing or downloading.
ANI, in its appeal, argued that the injunction was denied without adequately considering OpenAI’s alleged admission that it had scraped, stored and commercially exploited the agency’s work. The agency contended that such acts infringed its exclusive rights under the Copyright Act, including the rights to store, reproduce, adapt and translate its original works.

Apollo Hospitals, Greams Road, has expanded its robotic-assisted orthopaedic programme with the use of an advanced robotic system for knee and hip replacement procedures.
The programme uses Mako SmartRobotics from Stryker, along with three-dimensional CT imaging and detailed pre-operative planning, to help surgeons assess a patient’s anatomy and plan bone preparation and implant positioning before surgery.

Arun Kannan, senior orthopaedic robotic surgeon at Apollo Hospitals, Greams Road, said the experience gained through the procedures had helped the team understand where robotic assistance could add value to joint replacement surgery. “The experience has helped us understand where robotic assistance can add real value and how best to use it for each patient,” he said.
Ilankumaran Kaliamoorthy, CEO, Chennai Region, Apollo Hospitals, said the adoption of advanced technology was part of the hospital’s efforts to support clinicians in surgical care.
As part of the milestone, senior orthopaedic robotic surgeons, Arun Kannan, Kornad Kosygan, Kunal Patel, Navaladi Shankar, Vijay Kishore Reddy, and Madhan Thiruvengada delivered keynote addresses.

Ola Electric’s FY26 annual report disclosed another suspected employee fraud at its wholly owned subsidiary Ola Electric Technologies Pvt Ltd (OET), with auditors reporting two such offences involving more than ₹1 Cr. According to OET’s secretarial audit report, the statutory auditors reported the two suspected employee frauds to the central government through e-form ADT-4 filings dated July 9, 2025, and June 4, 2026. While one suspected fraud was disclosed in Ola Electric’s FY25 annual report, the filing made in June 2026 appears to relate to a second case. However, the latest annual report did not disclose the employees involved, the nature of the suspected frauds, or the precise amount involved in either case. It is also unclear whether the “amount exceeding ₹1 Cr” refers to each offence or the two cases collectively. Queries sent to Ola Electric remained unanswered at the time of publishing. The story will be updated upon receiving a response. Inventory Weakness Persists The disclosure comes amid continuing concerns around internal controls at Ola Electric. Its statutory auditors issued a qualified opinion on the group’s internal financial controls, citing a material weakness related to the physical verification of finished goods and raw materials at OET’s plant and stores. As of March 31, 2026, the group had ₹251 Cr worth of raw materials and finished goods covered by the audit matter. Of this, inventory worth ₹153 Cr had not been physically verified during FY26 or subsequently up to the date of the consolidated financial statements. The issue echoes FY25, when auditors had flagged a similar weakness involving ₹362 Cr worth of electric two-wheelers and spare parts that had not been physically verified at stores and state distribution centres. Ola Electric had attributed the FY25 lapse to a temporary realignment of inventory processes under Project Lakshya and said it had found no financial impact or inventory misplacement. The company similarly described the FY26 observation as an isolated case. It said a redesign of its network operations in Q4 FY26 temporarily disrupted inventory processes, preventing management from undertaking physical verification at the end of the year. However, Ola Electric said its ERP system did not show any discrepancy and that physical verification was conducted before and after the network redesign. The company appointed TRC Corporate Consulting as its external internal auditor after the end of FY26. During the fiscal year, Ola Electric relied on internal resources to monitor and review its controls and processes. Workforce Churn Surges Ola Electric also reported a sharp increase in employee turnover during FY26. The turnover rate among permanent employees rose to 60% from 54% in FY25, while that among permanent workers surged to 105% from 29%. The company attributed the higher rate primarily to increased attrition among permanent workers and said the vacant positions would be filled or appointments made afresh. The increase followed multiple rounds of job cuts at Ola Electric. The company reportedly cut around 500 jobs in 2024, followed by more than 1,000 layoffs in March 2025. In January 2026, Ola Electric announced another restructuring exercise that was expected to impact around 5% of its workforce as it increased automation across its front-end operations. The restructuring formed part of Ola Electric’s attempt to move away from rapid expansion and build a leaner operating model following a weak fiscal year. The company’s revenue from operations halved to ₹2,253 Cr in FY26 from ₹4,514 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Meanwhile, net loss narrowed 19.5% to ₹1,833 Cr from ₹2,276 Cr in FY25. The revenue decline came as Ola Electric’s deliveries fell to 1.74 Lakh units in FY26 from 3.59 Lakh units in FY25. During the year, the company also continued to face criticism over delivery timelines, after-sales service, and regulatory issues. Ola Electric called FY26 a “year of structural reset”, during which it rationalised its retail network, cut costs, strengthened service operations, and focused on improving unit economics. More recently, the company opened its sales and service network to dealer partners, marking a shift from its earlier company-owned retail model. It is targeting more than 500 dealerships over the next few quarters, while its company-owned outlets will transition into product experience centres. Ola Electric also raised ₹780.2 Cr through a QIP in June. Earlier this month, its board approved another fundraise of up to ₹1,500 Cr, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals. Meanwhile, the company is expanding its battery cell business. It has “largely” completed the installation required for its 6 GWh cell manufacturing platform. In August, it launched the S1Z, its first escooter range powered by the company’s Bharat Cell LFP technology.

Watch: Pupils return to West Bank school behind barbed wire to protect against settlers
