Washington, Sep 09: The US military said it destroyed five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday in response to the latest attacks on its warships and Tehran hit back at American targets in Jordan, the latest burst of back-and-forth strikes that have lurched the sides back toward open hostilities in a more than six-month-old war.
Following the American strikes, Iran launched missiles toward US targets in Jordan, Iranian state-run media said.
Jordan's military said its air defence systems intercepted 18 ballistic missiles launched toward its territory and two others fell in places where no one lives.
It said it has no reports of casualties. Jordan is a staunch US ally that hosts American forces, making the kingdom's military bases a target of repeated Iranian strikes. US Central Command said it had no information to offer.
The latest strikes are part of a dual economic and military approach by President Donald Trump as he struggles to bring an end to the war.
The Trump administration on Tuesday also imposed sanctions on additional elements of Iran's aviation industry, targeting more than two dozen commercial and private airlines as well as foreign cargo service providers, in its new push to isolate Tehran from its remaining trading partners.
Both the US and Iran are seeking to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz, where about one-fifth of the world's oil passed before the war began. Rising energy prices are posing political problems for Trump and his Republican Party ahead of the November midterm elections. A barrel of international standard Brent crude briefly climbed as high as $99.46 on Tuesday.
The US forces also destroyed three Iranian oil tankers on Saturday after Iran's Revolutionary Guards tried to attack a US aircraft carrier and destroyer with ballistic missiles, warning that it would, “if necessary, destroy Iran's limited and exposed oil fleet”.
Iran later said it planned to announce a new “exclusion zone” near the Strait of Hormuz aimed at vessels intending to transit.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US will not allow Iran's attacks to go unanswered.
“Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships. And for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers. And I think you'll see that again today,” Rubio told reporters on Tuesday when asked about the latest attacks in Iran while on a trip to Colombia.
Danny Citrinowicz, an Iran expert at Israel's Institute for National Security Studies, warned that such back-and-forth strikes can only risk more retaliation and further impact on the global economy.
“There is no kinetic solution to the Strait of Hormuz problem,” he said on social media. “Every attempt to impose one only brings Washington and Tehran closer to an escalation that may become increasingly difficult to control.”
US Central Command said the military struck the tankers on Tuesday after the Revolutionary Guards targeted a Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days.
“The US warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed,” it said in a statement.
It said the Iranian tankers destroyed on Tuesday were the Kivik, Charminar, Horizon 1 and the Riesco in the Gulf of Oman. The US military also destroyed the vessel Derya, which was located near Kharg Island in the Strait of Hormuz. The statement said the crews of the five vessels were told to abandon ship before the attacks.
Iranian state television also reported the US strikes, saying US forces attacked Iranian oil tankers near the southern port of Jask and near Kharg Island in the Persian Gulf. It said the crews were evacuated.
An Iranian state TV reporter in Jask said an Iranian tanker was struck near the coast of Yekbeni. State TV later reported that the US military attacked a second tanker near waters off Jask. Separately, state television reported that another Iranian tanker was attacked in the Kharg Island anchorage area.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard Navy on Tuesday had warned crews of oil tankers near ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to immediately leave their vessels, saying the ships could be targeted in retaliation for US attacks on Iranian tankers. It accused Kuwait and Bahrain of hosting US forces and assisting in the attacks.
A US blockade of Iranian ports has squeezed the country's economy by limiting its oil exports, while the American military has been helping a limited number of ships transit on a route through the Strait of Hormuz off Oman. Tehran wants ships to follow a route that it chooses through the strait, which was considered an international waterway before the war.

Russell hindered or just Antonelli brilliance? - F1 Q&A
- Published
Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli climbed from 19th on the grid to win the Italian Grand Prix - his home race - in one of the great Formula 1 drives.
Antonelli extended his lead at the top of the drivers' standings to 66 points over team-mate George Russell.
Max Verstappen, in the Red Bull, finished third to complete the podium at Monza.
BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions before round 14 of the 2026 season in Madrid, Spain.
- Antonelli 'walks over water' for win that will go down in F1 folklore 
  - Published1 day ago
Why wasn't George Russell given the opportunity by Mercedes to pit under the virtual safety car in the Italian Grand Prix? I know he had the hard tyres on, but as the lead driver on track should he not have been at least given the choice? - Tom
In hindsight, it would be easy to think there would be some controversy around the decisions that were taken when the virtual safety car was called mid-race at the Italian Grand Prix.
In reality, though, there was not any.
At the time, George Russell was leading the race on the hard tyre and Kimi Antonelli was second on the medium, a few laps after the Mercedes drivers had been advised to call off their 'yo-yo' scrapping to allow them to optimise their pace and build a gap to Max Verstappen's Red Bull.
Without a VSC, the question was whether the mediums on Antonelli's car would last to the end - probably not - and what Mercedes would do about that.
With or without the VSC, the race result was up in the air.
The VSC changed the complexion of the race, but Russell, who had fitted hards at the red flag with the express intention of going to the end, said he had given no thought to changing tyres at the time.
"I didn't," he said. "I actually thought the guys behind me were going to stay out as well. But I'm sure the team were quite nervous on the pit wall watching our battle and were probably quite happy to send us on different strategies.
"And of course, when we had Max in the mix as well, from a team perspective, you're covering off both scenarios.
"If either of us were to pit, it was going to be Kimi. And that's why I was just a little bit annoyed with the timing of that VSC because I think it would have been tough for those guys on the medium to have competed with anybody on the hard tyre. But it takes nothing away from Kimi's drive."
At the time, Mercedes' strategy computers were saying staying out was the best option.
Team principal Toto Wolff said: "We didn't know what was the better strategy. At that stage, the system said that the one-stop comes out ahead. That two-stop was coming close to the end, but didn't catch it. That's what the software said."
All of which goes to underline the main takeaway - the sublime quality of Antonelli's drive.
He made remarkable progress up through the field from 19th on the grid, wasting no time in picking off cars in front, minimising any loss from overtaking to his overall race time.
He made this look easy, but as many other drivers proved at Monza on Sunday, overtaking another car of similar performance and immediately pulling away was anything but.
This was a performance for the ages - like Lewis Hamilton in Brazil in 2021, Max Verstappen in Brazil in 2024 or 2025, or Fernando Alonso in Valencia in 2012.
McLaren team principal Andrea Stella, who knows a thing or two about this sort of performance having worked with Michael Schumacher and Alonso, said: "While he had a very competitive car, we have to say that he beat a team-mate starting second on the grid.
"It's a very special day, very important for his championship. But for his career and for the fans, motorsport in general, this will be an iconic day. This will be remembered in the years to come."
Is Charles Leclerc's tendency to crash out of races starting to become a problem both for him and Ferrari? - Nathan
Charles Leclerc certainly did not have his best day in Monza on Sunday.
He was arguably too aggressive with Lewis Hamilton at the first chicane on the first lap, forcing his team-mate into the gravel and dropping him to 10th, and crashed out a lap later.
By then, he had also been passed by Max Verstappen, and his accident at Parabolica seemed to be influenced by the fact he was slightly wide into, through and out of the corner because he was defending an attack from McLaren's Oscar Piastri, although Leclerc himself said he thought that was not the cause of his crash.
"I wouldn't say that this is the issue," he said. "From lap one to lap two, I had a bit of a difference in power delivery. We'll look into it, but I don't want to comment too much before checking the data and confirming it 100%."
Having said that, does the allegation that Leclerc has a "tendency to crash out of races" stand up?
He has done it twice so far this year - the previous time was in Monaco, when he lost control at a restart on the broken track surface at Anthony Noghes.
But, unless I've missed something, you have to go back nearly three years to the one before that, when he retired with car damage after an incident-packed race at Zandvoort in 2023.
In that period, for comparison, Hamilton has done the same thing four times - Brazil and Netherlands last year, Austin in 2024 and Qatar in 2023.
Ferrari clearly have some things to sort out, however, in terms of their operations and general approach.
Hamilton is not happy about the way the team have effectively disregarded his - albeit slim - title hopes this year in favour of driver equality, and he said after dropping more points to Antonelli on Sunday that it was "far too late for those decisions to come".
The incident between Leclerc and Hamilton on lap one took place in the context of Hamilton saying after qualifying they had to "work as a team to try and topple" Mercedes.
Leclerc said of the first-corner incident: "I don't really know who is forcing that narrative that we are one against the other. I mean, honestly, Zandvoort there was way too many talks already.
"Here it's true, though, that we went too far. Lewis in Turn One, then Turn Two, I tried to do the tightest corner possible, but that was just not enough and doing it here is not good."
Hamilton was not impressed by the suggestion he had done anything wrong at Turn One.
When those remarks were put to Hamilton, he said: "He said what? I was ahead in Turn Two. By the ethics, I was ahead. There was no 'we' in it."
He added: "I don't race dirty. I've always raced clean and fairly and always left space."
Team boss Frederic Vasseur, who said he would talk to the drivers before discussing this in the media, has some smoothing out to do before this weekend's race in Madrid.
Aston Martin have had their major upgrades but were right at the back of the grid again in Monza. Have the upgrades just failed? - Colin
Aston Martin had a major car upgrade in Hungary two races ago, and a "spec two" Honda engine at the race before Italy in Zandvoort, on either side of the summer break.
There is no question the car upgrade worked. What was effectively an all-new car, apart from the rear suspension and gearbox, cut lap times by about two seconds.
Fernando Alonso made it into the second part of qualifying for the first time all year in Hungary, and drove an outstanding race to finish ninth on merit in the Netherlands, on a one-stop strategy, holding at arm's length the faster Alpine of Pierre Gasly and Racing Bull of Yuki Tsunoda in the final stint.
More upgrades are expected, in the form of a weight reduction around the gearbox, for either Madrid this weekend or Azerbaijan.
The Honda engine upgrade that made its debut in Zandvoort has been less impressive, which is why Aston Martin found themselves at the back again on the power-sensitive Monza track.
Trackside general manager and chief engineer Shintaro Orihara says Honda "observed a step forward in terms of performance from our metrics".
But if there has been one, it is small. Drivability of the spec two in Zandvoort was noticeably worse, too, although it had made a step forward in Italy.
The Aston Martin car seems to be a midfield-level chassis now, somewhere around the borderline of getting into the final part of qualifying, depending on circuit layout, if it had a competitive engine.
And on the chassis side, the team have a sense of direction that gives them confidence they can make another step next season.
With Honda, which still has comfortably the worst engine in F1, the upgrade has been less reassuring.
What is the new Madring circuit in Spain like in terms of power compared to all the previously visited circuits? Who is it expected to suit most of all? - Andrew
The Madrid circuit which makes its debut this weekend has been built from scratch.
The circuit layout has lots of corners, and it is expected to have a low power sensitivity, around the level of Zandvoort.
Medium-speed corners predominate. And overtaking is expected to be difficult - again, like Zandvoort, or even Hungary.
Given Lando Norris took dominant wins in the Netherlands and Hungary, some teams believe McLaren might be favourites heading into this weekend, but McLaren themselves are not so sure.
Hungary and Zandvoort have long-duration corners, where the McLaren excels. But the Madring corners are generally short duration, the exception being the long, banked Monumental, which is expected to be flat out.
McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said after the race in Monza on Sunday: "We still think that tracks like Baku and Madrid, where you have to be very precise with the trajectory, short corners, maybe they don't play to the best of our car.
"Yet, we have to say that in Zandvoort and Hungary we were in position to win races and here, while we were not, we know that it's a special race.
"Drag will be less important in Madrid. There is a much higher density of corners. We will definitely give it a go."
New tracks always throw up surprises. So, in short, while one can speculate about car and circuit characteristics all one wants, no one will actually know until qualifying on Saturday.

Lucknow, September 09: To address the shortage of doctors, particularly specialists, in the state and provide better, timely medical facilities to the general public, the Yogi government has taken a major decision in the public interest. CM Yogi Adityanath has decided to increase the maximum age limit for re-employment of retired specialist doctors of Provincial Medical and Health Services (PMHS) cadre from 65 years to 70 years. The government’s decision will increase the availability of experienced specialist doctors in hospitals across the state and strengthen medical services amid a growing population and increasing patient pressure. This step will be particularly important in providing timely, quality specialist medical facilities to poor and deprived sections.
Deputy CM and Minister for Medical and Health, Brajesh Pathak, stated, “Ensuring adequate availability of doctors, particularly specialist doctors, in the state is government’s priority. In view of the continuously increasing number of patients in the outpatient and inpatient departments of hospitals, this decision of CM Yogi Adityanath is an important step towards maintaining continuity in medical services.”
ACS Medical and Health, Amit Kumar Ghosh, informed that retired specialist doctors of the PMHS cadre will be re-employed against 500 non-cadre posts to ensure the availability of specialist doctors. Appointments will be made on a contractual basis through walk-in interviews. Re-employment will be made until the posts are filled by regular medical officers or for a period of one year, whichever is earlier. Thereafter, the tenure may be extended on a year-to-year basis based on work and conduct, merits and demerits, and a health certificate, but the maximum age limit will be 70 years. After regular appointment of specialist doctors, concerned non-cadre posts will automatically cease to exist. Under no circumstances will the total number of posts for re-employment exceed 500.
The re-employed specialist doctors will not be given any administrative post, nor will they be given a cadre designation. They will provide their services as ‘Consultants’ or ‘Paramarshi’. According to hospital requirements, they will also have to contribute to emergency and casualty medical services.
At the same time, provisions have also been made for the re-employment of specialist and MBBS doctors retiring from military service after completing their superannuation age, on the lines of retired doctors of the PMHS cadre. Meanwhile, the existing arrangement for the re-employment of MBBS doctors up to the age of 65 years after retirement will remain unchanged.
Private practice will be completely prohibited for re-employed specialist doctors. Doctors may recommend only medicines available in the hospital under government rules. If they engage in private practice or violate the prescribed conditions, the government may terminate their re-employment immediately.
According to the government, using the services of experienced retired specialist doctors alongside regular appointments will immediately strengthen the state's medical system. The Yogi government’s decision is seen as an important step toward increasing the availability of specialist medical services in government hospitals amid a growing population and rising patient pressure, and toward providing better healthcare facilities to the general public.

A video (here & here) is being shared on social media claiming that it shows a group of people reciting the Quran on a hilltop in Nepal during rescue operations amid the recent flash floods that occurred on 26 August 2026. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video showing a group of people reciting the Quran in Nepal during August 2026 Nepal flood rescue operations.
Fact: The video is unrelated to the 2026 Nepal flood rescue operations. It shows local villagers reciting the Quran during a massive search effort in Kyrgyzstan for a 6-year-old boy who was swept away by a river following a tragic car accident. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of the keyframes extracted from the viral video led to the same video (archive) uploaded on 25 June 2026 by a Kyrgyzstan-based Instagram page, two months prior to the Nepal tragedy. Additional footage posted by the same account indicates that the viral video is related to a rescue operation in Kyrgyzstan.
According to the media reports (here, here & here), on 23 June 2026, a passenger car fell off a cliff into a river in the Kegety Gorge in Kyrgyzstan’s Chuy region. While the adults and three children managed to escape, two children remained trapped. Rescuers initially recovered the body of a 12-year-old girl, while a 6-year-old boy was swept away by the strong current. The Ministry of Emergency Situations (MES) conducted an active, round-the-clock search operation.
The effort lasted for nearly four days and was joined by local and international volunteers. Reports indicated that local Muslim leaders recited the Quran and prayed for the safe return of the child. The operation concluded on 26 June 2026, when the boy’s body was recovered. Moreover, the viral video shows one of the rescue personnel wearing a chest badge belonging to the Ministry of Emergency Situations (MES) of Kyrgyzstan.
To sum it up, an unrelated video from Kyrgyzstan is being falsely shared as visuals of people reciting the Quran during rescue operations for the August 2026 Nepal floods.

For years, a claim has circulated online that MI5, the U.K.'s internal and domestic security agency, used Boy Scouts as messengers during World War I but replaced them with Girl Guides because the Boy Scouts were too loud and less reliable.
Girl Guides are a similar organization to the Girl Scouts in the United States.
For example, one Instagram profile posted a graphic featuring text that reads (archived), "The Boy Scouts were too noisy for British intelligence, so MI5 trusted its secret messages to teenage Girl Guides instead."
Other iterations of the claim have previously circulated on X, Facebook, Bluesky and Reddit.
According to an MI5 report about its "Organisation and Administration" between 1900 and 1919, the agency employed Boy Scouts to carry messages between officers starting in October 1914. However, the agency found the boys "very troublesome" because they would get into "mischief" during downtime on the job (Page 40) and instead hired Girl Guides, who proved more "amenable" than the boys (Page 41).
In a speech in October 2009, Jonathan Evans, who was the agency's director general at the time, described those same Boy Scout messengers as "feckless and noisy" and the Girl Guide replacements as "more reliable."
Given b
The MI5 report that mentions Girl Guides working for the agency is dated 1921 (Page 3). It is unclear when the agency released the report to the U.K.'s National Archives.
The section about Boy Scouts and Girl Guides says the agency sought out Boy Scouts because it needed messengers for in-house communication. However, the report adds (Page 40-41):
Boys were, however, found to be very troublesome. The considerable periods of inactivity which fell to their share usually resulted in their getting into mischief. When, therefore, the system of employing boys as coast watchers was introduced by the Admiralty, the boys employed by M.0.5. were advised to take up this work; outdoor work being much more fitted to their energy. Arrangements were then made to replace the Boy Scouts with Girl Guides and the results were most satisfactory. The girls proved more amenable and their methods of getting into mischief were on the whole less distressing to those who had to deal with them than were those of the boys.
MI5 was called M.O.5 until 1916.
According to the report, Girl Guides worked in the agency after September 1915 until January 1920 (Page 41).
Girl Guides in the U.K. commemorated the guides that worked for MI5 with a custom badge in 2023. The Girl Guides website says 90 guides, aged 14 to 16 years old, worked for the agency during World War I.
In "How the Girl Guides Won the War: An Extraordinary True Story and Social History of WWII Britain," author Janie Hampton described the Girl Guides' workday at MI5. Hampton wrote (Page 26-27):
Before a Guide could start work at MI5, she had to sign a contract confirming that she had permission from both of her parents and the Guide Captain who had recommended her. She pledged with her honour not to read the papers she carried, and was paid ten shillings a week for fifty hours of work, with only a short lunch break. The Guides' working day began at 9 a.m. and finished at 7 p.m., and as well as carrying messages they were responsible for keeping inkpots filled. Some were also trained to clean and repair typewriters.
The ten shilling note fell out of circulation in 1970 (Page 10) and was replaced by the 50 pence coin. A weekly pay of 50 pence in 1915, the first year the Girl Guides started working for MI5, was equivalent to £45.91, or roughly $62, in July 2026, according to the Bank of England.
The War Office also took Girl Guides to the signing of the Treaty of Versailles, which ended the state of war between Germany and the Allied Powers. Speaking about their work regarding the treaty, Hampton wrote (Page 29):
When the First World War ended, Guides were considered so reliable by the War Office that a contingent was taken with the British delegation to France. British Guides ran errands at the Palace of Versailles for the Paris Peace Conference in June 1919, and sixteen Ranger Guides were invited to witness the signing of the treaty.
For further reading, Snopes has previously investigated claims about Scouting America and the Girl Scouts of the USA.

India cruises to win over Japan in women’s junior Asia Cup
Skipper Anmol Ekka smashed six goals as defending champion India ended the pool stage with a 15-0 rout of Chinese Taipei, entering the men’s semifinals of the Junior Asia Cup hockey tournament in Mogi, China, on Wednesday.
The five-time champion finished at the top of Pool A with 10 points from three wins and a draw, while South Korea secured the other semifinal berth from the pool after edging Japan 3-2 to finish second with nine points.
Japan, Indonesia and Chinese Taipei bowed out of the title race and will now compete in the classification matches.
Aryan Xess opened India’s account in the 17th minute, before Prabhdeep Singh doubled the advantage a minute later. Gursewak Singh then made it 3-0 in the 22nd minute, giving India three goals in five minutes.
Anmol then got into action, converting a penalty corner in the 25th minute. Arjun Santosh Hargude added another in the 28th minute, before Anmol struck again from a set-piece in the next minute.
With India 6-0 ahead at half-time, it piled on misery after the break, earning two penalty corners within the opening three minutes of the third quarter. Anmol converted both to complete his hat-trick, while Ajeet Yadav found his name on the scoresheet in the 35th minute, capping another incisive Indian move with a composed finish.
With India firmly in control, Anmol continued his remarkable scoring run, converting another penalty corner in the 45th minute to bring up his fifth goal of the match and take India into double figures at 10-0 by the end of the third quarter.
The defending champion showed no signs of easing off in the final 15 minutes. Harpal joined the scoring spree with a field goal in the 48th minute, before Anmol completed an extraordinary individual performance by converting his sixth penalty corner of the match in the 51st minute.
Harpal then added his second goal, while Aryan Xess rounded it off with two goals to his name as India tore apart the Taipei defence.

Lok Sabha Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi's flight from Delhi made a go-around before landing at Lucknow airport on Tuesday due to weather conditions, aviation sources said.
Gandhi was on his way to Lucknow to proceed to his parliamentary constituency, Raebareli, for a two-day visit.
The Air India-operated Airbus A320 flight had a scheduled arrival at 3.30 pm but landed at Chaudhary Charan Singh International Airport at around 3.55 pm, the sources said.
"The flight had departed Delhi around 20-25 minutes behind schedule. On its first approach, the aircraft did not land due to light rain and low atmospheric pressure conditions and made a go-around," the source said, adding it's a "normal practice in such weather conditions."
"The aircraft landed safely around seven minutes after the go-around, following which passengers disembarked and proceeded to their respective destinations," the person added.
Upon landing, the Congress leader was welcomed at the airport by party workers and local leaders, including Uttar Pradesh Congress president Ajay Rai and Akhand Pratap Singh.
He then left for Raebareli by road.
Gandhi, who represents Raebareli in the Lok Sabha, reached the constituency towards evening. He was scheduled to meet party workers and locals, and a few groups.
On Wednesday, he will attend a district development coordination and monitoring committee (DISHA) meeting and review development works.

The Ruling National Conference (NC) and its ally the Congress traded barbs on Wednesday over the NC leadership’s decision to stand for all stanzas of the national song, Vande Mataram, after it was played at the inauguration of the International Film Festival Jammu & Kashmir (IFFJK) in Srinagar on September 7.
J&K Congress chief Tariq Hameed Karra, in a post on X, questioned Chief Minister Omar Abdullah and NC president Dr. Farooq Abdullah’s decision to stand for all stanzas of the song.
“National symbols, songs and traditions occupy a special place in the heart of every Indian. Their true strength lies in their ability to bind together a nation as diverse as ours. It is therefore a matter of concern that our alliance partners chose to sing the full version of Vande Mataram, disregarding the considered evolution of the song’s place in India’s national life, not merely during the freedom movement, but through the constitutional journey of the Republic thereafter. The adopted version represented a conscious balance preserving the historic ... ,” said Mr. Karra.
Mr. Karra’s post followed a social media statement by Congress General Secretary K. C. Venugopal, who posted the video of the Srinagar ceremony in which NC leaders stood for all the stanzas.
“The full version of Vande Mataram sits uneasily with the syncretic and pluralist ethos that our freedom fighters envisioned and nurtured for India. For us, the considered judgment of Mahatma Gandhi, Pandit Nehru, Sardar Patel, Subhash Chandra Bose, Rajendra Prasad, Acharya Narendra Dev, Maulana Azad, Sarojini Naidu and J.B. Kripalani — shaped in no small part by the counsel of Gurudev Rabindranath Tagore — remains paramount,” said Mr. Venugopal.
Honour freedom fighters
In the post, the Congress leader said, “With respect and humility, we would like our allies to honour the wisdom and judgment of our freedom fighters and stand with us in singing only the version of this beautiful and historic song that they adopted. That version was chosen deliberately, to keep the song from being communalised — a threat as real today as it was then. Upholding it is how we uphold the secular, inclusive character of our Republic.”
The Congress posts on social media platforms drew a sharp reaction from NC leaders. NC legislator Tanvir Sadiq shared videos of swearing-in ceremonies involving a Congress chief minister and asked Mr. Karra to comment.
NC spokesman Imran Nabi Dar said, “The NC’s official position is that it is not a votary of either the first two stanzas or six stanzas of the national song. However, it is a Constitutional obligation, and every holder of a Constitutional office has to accept it, whether it is the CM, a MP or anyone else.”
Referring to videos from the Congress-ruled states of Karnataka and Telangana, Mr. Dar said, “The chief ministers stand for all the six stanzas. However, we do not want to make this a controversy. We are not here to fight the Congress.”
Meanwhile, the Opposition Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) also criticised the NC. “On every key issue, Rahul Gandhi took a stand, his J&K ally NC caved and rolled out the red carpet for the BJP. No condemnation on the Waqf amendment Bill. No condemnation of SIR fraud. Justifying EVM rigging concerns. Accepted Vande Mataram’s addition. INDIA bloc in elections, BJP’s silent enabler in practice,” said PDP leader and legislator Waheed-ur-Rehman Parra.

The story so far: A rabies vaccine, that could be critical in preventing a fatal infection, has failed a mandatory potency test, after vials bearing the batch number of a genuine Abhayrab consignment were seized from an unlicensed premises in Delhi. The Central Drugs Laboratory (CDL), Kasauli, has declared the samples in question as “Not of Standard Quality” and “misbranded”, setting off an investigation into whether counterfeit vaccine was being manufactured or distributed.
Rabies is almost invariably fatal once clinical symptoms appear, while timely and quality-assured post-exposure vaccination can prevent complications and death. The immediate concern for investigators, therefore, is not only how the questioned vials came to bear the details of a genuine vaccine batch, but whether any person bitten by a potentially rabid animal received a product that lacked the required potency.
The samples, bearing batch number KE25012, were seized on April 22, 2026, during a joint enforcement operation by the Delhi Police Crime Branch and officials of the Delhi Drugs Control Department at an unlicensed residential premises in Mukherjee Nagar, Delhi. Four persons have been arrested in connection with the case, according to the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO).
The laboratory found that the questioned vials failed the prescribed potency test and differed from genuine reference samples in several respects. These included packaging, labelling, artwork, QR-code verification, cap colour and licence details.
Genuine batch or counterfeit? Where is the investigation going?
Indian Immunologicals Ltd. (IIL), which manufactures Abhayrab through its Human Biologicals Institute (HBI), has denied manufacturing the seized vials.
In a statement issued on September 4, the company said the genuine KE25012 batch comprised 83,370 vials, underwent the required testing and was released on November 7, 2025, through its authorised distribution network.
More significantly, IIL said the CDL identified 17 differences between the questioned vials and the genuine retention samples of the same batch submitted by HBI for batch release.
The company has submitted its manufacturing, quality-control, reconciliation and distribution records to CDSCO and has asked authorities to trace the source of the questioned vials and take action against those responsible. The CDL finding establishes that the seized samples were NSQ and misbranded. It does not establish that the genuine KE25012 batch manufactured by IIL was defective. IIL’s position is that its legitimate batch passed the prescribed testing and that the batch number may have been reproduced on unauthorised material.
What are authorities investigating?
Investigators now have to establish who manufactured the questioned vials, where they were stored, how they entered circulation and whether they reached patients through any part of the legitimate or informal medicine supply chain.
A particularly important question is whether anyone was administered the suspect vaccine. If so, authorities may have to determine the nature of the exposure, the treatment received and whether additional medical intervention is required.
The Drugs Controller General of India has asked State and Union Territory drug controllers to maintain strict vigilance over the movement, distribution and availability of Abhayrab bearing batch number KE25012 and to take appropriate regulatory action.
CDSCO has also stated that no part of the concerned genuine batch was exported to another country.
International counterfeit rabies products
The case follows a suspected counterfeit Abhayrab episode involving batch KA24014 in 2025. IIL had reported suspected counterfeit vials to authorities, following which health warnings were issued in some countries over the possibility that travellers to India could have received counterfeit rabies vaccine.
That episode highlighted the international dimension of counterfeit rabies products. Travellers exposed to rabies may begin treatment in one country and complete their vaccination schedule elsewhere. A falsified vaccine can therefore create a public-health concern beyond the country in which it was obtained.
In the present case, however, CDSCO has said no part of the genuine KE25012 batch was exported. The investigation will have to establish whether the questioned vials were entirely domestic and, crucially, whether they entered patient use.
Why rabies vaccine matters?
Rabies is a viral disease that affects the central nervous system and is transmitted mainly through the saliva of infected animals, usually through bites or scratches. Dogs account for up to 99% of human rabies transmission globally. Once clinical symptoms appear, the disease is virtually 100% fatal.
Yet rabies is preventable. Prompt post-exposure prophylaxis involves thorough wound washing, vaccination and, for appropriate severe exposures, rabies immunoglobulin or other recommended biologicals. Quality-assured PEP can prevent the virus from progressing to the nervous system.
This makes the quality of a rabies vaccine particularly consequential. For a person exposed to a potentially rabid animal, the vaccine is not routine preventive medicine; it is a time-sensitive intervention intended to prevent a disease that, once symptomatic, offers virtually no chance of survival.
India’s rabies burden
India continues to bear a substantial share of the global rabies burden. A recent ICMR-National Institute of Epidemiology estimate cited by WHO puts annual human rabies deaths in India at 5,726, alongside an estimated 9.1 million animal bites each year.
Globally, WHO estimates about 59,000 people die of rabies each year, with more than 95% of deaths occurring in Asia and Africa.
The suspected circulation of a misbranded rabies vaccine therefore raises a question that goes beyond counterfeit packaging or regulatory compliance: whether a person who believes they have received life-saving protection has actually received a vaccine capable of providing it.
What happens next?
The Union Health Ministry maintained that the immediate task is to establish the origin and distribution of the questioned KE25012 vials and determine whether any patient received them. Authorities will also have to establish the scale of any unauthorised manufacturing or distribution network.
For IIL, the laboratory comparison, together with its manufacturing and distribution records, will help determine whether the episode concerns a manufacturing-quality failure or the unauthorised use of its product identity and batch details.
For patients and healthcare providers, the case reinforces the importance of obtaining rabies vaccines through licensed hospitals, clinics and pharmacies and reporting suspicious products to drug-control authorities.
With rabies, the margin for error is exceptionally small. A genuine, potent vaccine administered promptly can prevent a fatal disease; a counterfeit product can create the dangerous illusion that protection has been provided.

Did a goat herder's lucky $200 nugget spark a gold rush in western Kenya?
- Published
A goat herder from a remote area of western Kenya has told the BBC his discovery of a golden nugget has sparked a gold rush, overwhelming his small village over the last few weeks.
When people found out that 33-year-old Manasse Lomachar had sold his three grams of gold for 36,000 Kenyan shillings ($280; £205) several weeks ago, he believes this led to thousands of prospectors arrived in Cheporor.
And it is true that what last month was just bushland and rough grazing ground near the village is now scarred by pits, mounds of earth and makeshift mining camps.
It is not clear if was Lomachar's lucky find or other recent discoveries that sparked the excitement. But local authorities estimate that about 10,000 people arrived at the height of the rush.
Even a small amount of the precious metal can transform the futures of these men and women - from Kenya and neighbouring Uganda - many of whose precarious lives rest on an unreliable farming income.
People do sometimes pan for gold in these parts - but rarely find anything significant.
Lomachar's says his discovery came about purely by chance. While he was searching for a missing goat he encountered a group of women panning along a riverbed.
"I joined them, and that's how [the village] realised there was gold in this area," he says.
Farmer and herder Patrick Lokolia, from neighbouring Napawoi village, joined the gold rush hoping to earn some extra money to support his family.
"I have children in school, and paying school fees has been a big problem for me," he tells the BBC wearing an old Chelsea football top and standing amid the mining activity.
Eighteen-year-old Abigael Chelengat says she had never mined before coming to Cheporor from a nearby district, but arrived hoping to find enough gold to pay her school fees and help keep her younger siblings in school.
Behind her hundreds of people work side by side, hacking into the rocky ground with hoes and shovels.
Others carry the earth to a nearby seasonal river, where mostly women crouch in the murky water, washing and sifting mud and sand hoping to detect a tiny trace of the element.
Some of the more experienced miners are deep in holes excavating the earth and drilling at rocks with the same goal.
Hope is kept alive by stories of those for whom the effort has paid off - like Lomachar.
Samuel Kiarie, the deputy commissioner of West Pokot county, says he thinks the rush began after two notable discoveries.
"Young men found what appeared to be a substantial amount of gold. The following day, women made another significant find in the same area," he tells the BBC.
Kiarie explains that women have been finding small quantities of alluvial gold along the same seasonal riverbed for years, typically earning $8-$23 a week.
But the uncovering of larger quantities at the beginning of August is what caught the attention of many people.
Kiarie reckons as rumours spread, the number and size of the discoveries were exaggerated - drawing in ever larger groups of people with little or no mining experience who hoped to replicate the reported early successes.
Since the initial rush, the number of prospectors has gone down to around 2,500 as some have given up the search.
While there is little doubt that some gold has been found in the area, questions remain about the size of the deposit in the earth and its commercial potential.
"I can confirm that small-scale gold traders told us they received an average of about 100 people every day," the deputy commissioner says - though whether the finds were actually gold is not known.
Individual discoveries reportedly range from amounts worth a few hundred Kenyan shillings to one find valued at approximately 78,000 shillings ($600).
West Pokot county borders Uganda, and communities on both sides have long-standing social and family ties.
Mugisha Godfrey, an artisanal miner from Busia in eastern Uganda, travelled to Cheporor after hearing about the discovery from a friend.
He immediately set out for the village spending about 100,000 Ugandan shillings ($27) to get there.
However, the living conditions in Cheporor are not favourable, he says.
"We sleep under the trees, and when morning comes, we continue working. Sometimes we work both day and night," Godfrey tells the BBC.
So far, he has found nothing. But he is not discouraged.
"We can't return unless we find something. Only when we have found what we need can we go back home," he says.
For others, the gold rush has created opportunities without requiring them to dig.
More than 200 businesses have emerged around the site, according to local officials, selling food, water and other essentials to the village's new population.
Irene Ameja travelled from neighbouring Baringo county to cater to the crowds. She sells bottled water, soft drinks, bread, milk and other foodstuffs.
"I am hoping that when I leave, I will have made enough money to continue with my business and expand it," she says.
But the rapid growth of the settlement has also exposed the area's lack of basic services.
"This is a forest and we are in the middle of the mountains," she says. "We don't have clean water to drink or even to bathe."
For women, she adds, the challenges become greater after dark: "You have to find somewhere safe to stay because most of the people sleeping here are men."
Local officials admit the influx has placed enormous pressure on an area with little infrastructure, no piped water and limited sanitation.
Public health officials have been deployed to monitor conditions and help prevent disease outbreaks.
The authorities say they have also increased security patrols amid concerns over sexual violence and the vulnerability of women and girls at the site.
Officials are also worried that children could be drawn into mining activities as schools prepare to reopen in September.
Measures are being put in place to discourage young people from remaining at the site once the new school term begins.
Those still searching are increasingly turning to deeper excavation.
Several truckloads of material have already been transported to nearby Ortum town for processing, with the authorities awaiting the results.
Until then, the size and commercial viability of any mining remain uncertain.
For Lomachar, the answer is not to stop the mining, but to make it more organised.
He wants the government to help local miners establish safer and more effective ways of finding and extracting the gold.
"We would ask the government to help us with things like metal detectors, which could help us find out whether there are other minerals here, so that our community can develop," he says.
He points to the homes nearby as evidence of the area's poverty.
"If you look around, there are hardly any houses with iron-sheet roofs; most are just thatched houses."

There isn’t much that we Indians agree on these days. GDP numbers are no exception. Last week, India released glowing GDP numbers for the latest quarter – 7.8% growth – higher than the forecast 7%. It sparked a furore.
Subhash Garg, a former finance secretary under Narendra Modi’s government and now a critic, reframed what Modi called a “herculean feat” as mere smoke and mirrors. According to Garg, the government revised last year’s current-price GDP downwards to inflate this year’s number – he believes the real growth is only 2.6%.
The assertion, made on a television channel, immediately went viral. A flurry of op-eds and hot takes have been published since. Supporters of the government, predictably, rejected the claims. Those who have questions agree on a more fundamental problem: a lack of transparency and statistical credibility in India’s economic data. So why is there no consensus?
Over the past decade, critics say, the government has systematically hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure, weaponising economic data for political gain and creating a trust deficit. Methodologies have been changed, crucial surveys have faced long delays and there have been attempts to suppress inconvenient findings.
In November, the International Monetary Fund rated India’s national accounts data a ‘C’ on a four-point scale, the second-lowest grade. In its report, the IMF said some of the methodologies are outdated, including relying on an old base year, unexplained discrepancies between GDP calculated from the production and expenditure side, as well as a lack of seasonal data.
India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous. There might have been disagreements on the quality of estimates but their independence was widely accepted. That trust appears to have eroded in recent years.
“There seems to be a systematic effort by the government to hide the truth,” said R Nagaraj, an economist who taught at the Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, adding that some of the other contested datasets include employment numbers, poverty numbers, health data and consumption data. “Over the last 10 years, the government has changed the methodology for many of these, raising questions. They have apparently also removed critical officials who headed some surveys. All of this adds to the scepticism.”
In one of the most prominent examples, from 2019, a Business Standard journalist revealed that the government had not published an official report showing unemployment at a 45-year high of 6.1%. Two expert members of the National Statistical Commission resigned in protest. The government initially denied it, calling it a draft. The figures were only released months later.
Then there is the census, which for the first time since independence, was delayed in 2021. Economists say relying on outdated demographic data means, among other things, inequitable allocation of welfare entitlements. (The first phase of the latest census finally began in April 2026.)
Nagaraj has witnessed some of this first-hand. He served on a subcommittee in 2014 whose report forms a part of the GDP. “The [numbers] we had discussed in the committee and what came out in the final report were different. So, I had to raise a red flag,” he said. The difference was notable: one figure in the published report had been inflated by 108%.
But government economists reject the ongoing criticism of the GDP numbers. Shamika Ravi, a member of the Economic Advisory Council to the prime minister, described it as a “noisy and very ill-informed debate” arguing that political leanings, not data, are behind the criticism.
The IMF rating was expected, she said. “The IMF rating of ‘C’ is the same rating that China has for its statistics. Several large developing or just developed economies have data issues.” Revisions to its calculations that the government was accused of having manipulated, she added, were precisely the sorts of changes the IMF had recommended.
The sticking point, as some including India’s former chief statistician Pronab Sen have pointed out, is the trustworthiness of the underlying data used.
Complicating this debate is the reality for many Indians. This year, young people have taken to the streets in frustration. Protests, which first began over leaked examination papers, have crystallised into a broader reckoning over systemic failures in education, jobs and the promise of a better future.
Almost 40% of graduates under 25 are unemployed, a recent report by Azim Premji University concluded. An estimated 87 million (8.7 crore) Indians between 15 and 29 are neither working, studying, nor doing skill training, a government thinktank reported last month.
That is why we should care about data quality, economists say. Incorrect data means bad policy. As economist Reetika Khera wrote in her recent book, Freebies or Rights: “Data shines the light to guide policymaking and is important for informed public debates.” As evidence, she points to gaps in basic statistics such as urbanisation and literacy numbers due to the delayed census. The consequences, she argues, are not abstract. Because the government still relies on outdated population numbers to decide who gets food subsidies, she estimates approximately 100 million (10 crore) people who should be covered are being deprived.
The controversy is making waves further ashore. In Sri Lanka, where second-quarter GDP figures are expected, the Daily FT newspaper wrote: “One hopes Sri Lankan policymakers and experts are not watching the theatrics in India with watering mouths and dreaming up smart arguments. Spare us such theatre!”
What else we’re reading about
Lollapalooza | British pop star Olivia Dean is to perform in India for the first time in January when she headlines Lollapalooza 2027 in Mumbai. Limp Bizkit is another headline act at the two-day event. Indian artists on the lineup include Ricky Kej (performing with Stewart Copeland) and Aditya Gadhvi.
The price of gold | Prime Minister Narendra Modi asked Indians once again to refrain from buying gold and travelling abroad. He had first made an appeal to self-reliance in May, in part to conserve India’s declining foreign exchange reserves amid a rise in import prices and global energy shocks.
Census 2027 | The new and expanded questionnaire for the 2027 census is raising concerns, reports Scroll’s Anant Gupta. The questionnaire asks respondents for details about their identity documents, as well as their parents’ religion and place of birth. Several of these questions were part of the controversial National Population Register that has remained in abeyance since 2020 and was controversial due to fears that the data might be used to target minorities through a citizenship registry.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Singer Prateek Kuhad (@prateekkuhad), whose latest album, Full Moon Chamber, was released in July, shares an indulgent treat: “I’m a big fan of artisanal Indian chocolate makers. I really like Manam, Carra and Naviluna, and there are many others. Although India has been growing cacao [commercially] since the 1960s, its craft bean-to-bar movement is more recent. Even a plain chocolate bar from one of these makers can be remarkably complex and delicious. More people outside India should know about it and try it.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
4,756,000
One-third of the electorate in Delhi, about 4.76 million voters, have been deleted from the draft voting list as the Election Commission carries out a contentious revision of its rolls across states. So far, about 130 million names have been dropped from draft rolls in 30 states and union territories, the Indian Express reported.
Vibe check
Earlier this year, Shakira’s concerts in India was postponed. But Rajasthani folk musicians the Ismail Langa Group (@ismaillanga_official) decided the music had to go on, in their own way. Their mashup of the Colombian star’s Hips Don’t Lie with the traditional folk song called Moruda has got everyone grooving (42m views and counting).
It took two months to pull off, says creative director Jagirdar RV. Most artists in the group, aged between 23 and 60, don’t speak or read English and learned the lyrics by rote. The song choice was simple, he said, because it “has a very nice vibe which matched our vibe”.
It’s been a breakout year for the group, which had a semi-final run on India’s Got Talent and are becoming known for taking folk songs to gen Z audiences on Instagram. They are working on their next English mashup – just not spilling which song, yet.

A food safety officer has become a social media star in India - why?
- Published
The images are hard to ignore.
Cockroaches scurry across kitchen floors. Spider webs cling to walls. Spoiled vegetables rot in corners, while food counters show signs of pest infestation.
One might assume these scenes belong to a struggling restaurant. But the photos are from a members-only club in Mumbai - India's financial capital and the capital of its richest state Maharashtra.
They are among dozens of photos and videos that have gone viral since May, after Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration (FDA) began a series of inspections at restaurants, cafes and other food businesses across the state.
At the centre of the crackdown is 51-year-old civil servant Tukaram Mundhe, the state's new food commissioner.
Since taking charge in May, Mundhe has overseen thousands of inspections and says food safety laws must be enforced regardless of a business's size, influence or reputation.
His department has suspended the licences of several quick-commerce warehouses and sent notices to Bollywood celebrities for doing advertisements suspected of indirectly promoting restricted products.
"These actions are taken in public health interest. We will continue to take them against violations," Mundhe told the BBC.
The campaign has made Mundhe a recognisable face across India, rare for a civil servant.
Videos of his inspections and press briefings circulate widely on social media, where reels and podcasts have turned him into an unlikely celebrity.
But the spotlight - and the controversy that often comes with it - is nothing new to him.
An officer in the Indian Administrative Service, Mundhe has more than two decades of experience and has been transferred so often that reports say the number exceeds his years in service, though he declines to confirm it.
"I have stopped counting my transfers," he told the BBC.
Admirers see the transfers as evidence of his uncompromising style. Critics argue that this confrontational approach has put him at odds with colleagues and elected representatives.
In the past decade, Mundhe has won praise for his handling of the Covid pandemic outbreak during his time as Nagpur city's municipal commissioner and earlier for his work on water conservation in Maharashtra's drought-prone regions.
"When he was transferred out of Nagpur during the pandemic, thousands showed up outside his home to bid him farewell. It took him an hour just to reach his car," says Shafi Pathan, a journalist who's written Mundhe's biography in the local Marathi language.
But his food-safety crackdown has brought him the most attention yet.
The scale of India's food-safety problem is serious and numbers presented to the parliament in July offer a glimpse of just how widespread the issue is.
Of 223,808 food samples tested across India in 2025 and 2026, nearly one in five, external were found to be "non-conforming" - which means the samples were either unsafe, substandard or mislabelled.
And Mundhe has responded with an unusually aggressive enforcement drive.
By the end of July, his department had carried out more than 3,100 inspections across the state - a number he expects has since crossed 4,000.
Around 300 licences had been suspended and more than 1,000 improvement notices issued. A new complaints portal had also received more than 16,000 complaints in its first three months, Mundhe said.
"Hygiene has always been a problem here," Pawan Agarwal, former chief of India's food regulator, told the BBC. "What Mundhe has done differently is make it visible".
Consumers have responded positively to that visibility, Agarwal says. Unlike in India's conventional system, where food safety cases and consumer complaints can take years to move through regulators and courts, enforcement actions are now playing out in public.
The campaign has also made Mundhe a social media star - he now has more than 3.8 million followers on Instagram.
However, even as consumers welcome the speed and visibility of his actions, many in the food industry are less enthusiastic.
Restaurant associations allege the official has been bypassing a statutory process, while courts have termed some of his actions "high-handed".
Under India's food safety laws, businesses are usually given time to fix violations before regulators suspend or cancel their licences. Regulators can suspend licences immediately only in urgent public health situations but must record their reasons.
"While compliance is non-negotiable, high-handed approaches - like public naming-and-shaming, instant suspensions over minor procedural or rectifiable issues and treating administrative oversights with harsh penal measures - create panic rather than reform," said Niranjan Laxman Shetty, legal chairman of hospitality association Indian Hotel and Restaurant Association.
Responding to the criticism, Mundhe said his raids are lawful and that suspensions are only for extreme cases. However, some businesses have publicly claimed that they've been shut over minor violations, without warning or a chance to improve first.
His actions have also faced legal challenges. In some cases, courts have overturned licence suspensions, ordered compensation for affected businesses and criticised the regulator's approach.
In August, for instance, the Bombay high court ordered, external Mundhe's department to pay 500,000 rupees ($5,291; £3,893) in compensation to a sweets shop whose licence remained suspended even after a reinspection found it 98% compliant with the law.
The court said the regulator's intentions were "laudable" but that it had "gone overboard".
The judges also raised a question - was the regulator applying the same scrutiny to government establishments as it was to private businesses?
Within a day of that criticism, Mundhe's team inspected canteens in the state's high court complex and flagged violations.
For Mundhe, it is proof that the rules apply equally to everyone.
"Had the food business operators or establishment complied with existing regulations, I would not be needed to take those actions," Mundhe told the BBC.
He also insists that they are not trying to shut down businesses but only ensure safety.
"We are not here to close down or suspend every licensee," he said at an event last week. "We are here to ensure food is safe, food is not substandard, it is not misbranded and it is good for consumption."
The restaurant inspections - which dominate social media - are only a part of his work.
Mundhe has enforced bans on using newspapers to wrap food, synthetic dyes and banned analogue paneer - non-dairy cottage cheese substitutes.
Its focus has now shifted to schools. The department has ordered canteens, hostel kitchens and midday meal suppliers to obtain proper licences, and banned the sale of food high in fat, sugar or salt within 50m of schools.
But the bigger question is what happens once Mundhe moves on to his next post.
"The efforts of Mundhe have created a nationwide awareness about food safety, both amongst businesses and consumers, which is desirable - but not sustainable," says Agarwal.
The challenge is to build systems that outlast an individual officer, he adds.
For now, however, the effects are being felt even on the streets.
Yuvraj Yadav, who sells sandwiches in a Mumbai suburb, says he used to wrap them in discarded newspapers, despite concerns that chemicals in the printing ink can leach into food. He recently switched to greaseproof paper after hearing about the ban.
"We started this a few months ago after newspapers were not allowed for packing as it's bad for health," he says.

Messi agrees to buy second Spanish club
- Published
Spanish second-division side Eldense say Argentina great Lionel Messi has reached a "preliminary agreement" to become the club's majority shareholder.
Eldense will become the second Spanish club Messi has invested in, having bought Catalan side Cornella in April.
The 39-year-old former Barcelona forward currently plays for Inter Miami and recently retired from international football after Argentina were beaten 1-0 by Spain in the 2026 World Cup final.
Eldense said: "A preliminary agreement has been reached with Lionel Messi for the acquisition of the shares currently owned by Grupo TH Soluciones, which would make him the club's majority shareholder.
"The transaction is currently subject to the completion of the remaining legal and contractual procedures, including the due diligence process, as well as the required authorisation from the Spanish National Sports Council (CSD)."
The club, based in Alicante, have two points from four games this season and, sitting 20th in La Liga 2, parted ways with head coach Claudio Barragan earlier this week.
Cornella are in the fifth tier of Spanish football and in April said Messi's ownership "reinforces his close ties to Barcelona and his commitment to the development of sport and local talent in Catalonia".
BBC Sport has approached Messi for comment.
He left Argentina for Spain when he was 13 and made his first-team debut for Barcelona aged 17 in October 2004.
He went on to score a club record 672 goals in 778 games before he left for French club Paris St-Germain in 2021 prior to joining Major League Soccer side Inter Miami in the United States in 2023.
Messi's former Real Madrid rival Cristiano Ronaldo, who plays for Saudi Pro League side Al-Nassr, bought a 25% stake in Spanish side Almeria in February.

Editor’s note, September 6, 8 am ET: We’re bringing you some of our best-loved Your Mileage May Vary columns while Sigal Samuel is on parental leave. The one below was originally published last year.
My students think it’s fine to cheat with AI. Maybe they’re onto something.
To save the humanities, we need to rethink our assumptions about AI — and education.
This unconventional advice column offers you a unique framework for thinking through moral dilemmas. It’s based on value pluralism: the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other. Submit your own question here.
I am a university teaching assistant, leading discussion sections for large humanities lecture classes. This also means I grade a lot of student writing — and, inevitably, see a lot of AI writing too.
Of course, many of us are working on developing assignments and pedagogies to make that less tempting. But as a TA, I only have limited ability to implement these policies. And in the meantime, AI-generated writing is so ubiquitous that to take course policy on it seriously, or even to escalate every suspected instance to the professor who runs the course, would be to make dozens of accusations, some of them false positives, for basically every assignment.
I believe in the numinous, ineffable value of a humanities education, but I’m also not going to convince stressed 19-year-olds of that value by cracking down hard on something everyone does. How do I think about the ethics of enforcing the rules of an institution that they don’t take seriously, or letting things slide in the name of building a classroom that feels less like an obstacle to circumvent?
Dear Troubled Teacher,
I know you said you believe in the “ineffable value of a humanities education,” but if we want to actually get clear on your dilemma, that ineffable value must be effed!
So: What is the real value of a humanities education?
Looking at the modern university, one might think the humanities aren’t so different from the STEM fields. Just as the engineering department or the math department justifies its existence by pointing to the products it creates — bridge designs, weather forecasts — humanities departments nowadays justify their existence by noting that their students create products, too: literary interpretations, cultural criticism, short films.
But let’s be real: It’s the neoliberalization of the university that has forced the humanities into that weird contortion. That’s never what they were supposed to be. Their real aim, as the philosopher Megan Fritts writes, is “the formation of human persons.”
In other words, while the purpose of other departments is ultimately to create a product, a humanities education is meant to be different, because the student herself is the product. She is what’s getting created and recreated by the learning process.
Have a question you want answered in the next Your Mileage May Vary column?
Fill out this anonymous form! Newsletter subscribers will get my column before anyone else does and their questions will be prioritized for future editions. Sign up here!
This vision of education — as a pursuit that’s supposed to be personally transformative — is what Aristotle proposed back in ancient Greece. He believed the real goal was not to impart knowledge, but to cultivate the virtues: honesty, justice, courage, and all the other character traits that make for a flourishing life.
But because flourishing is devalued in our hypercapitalist society, you find yourself caught between that original vision and today’s product-based, utilitarian vision. And students sense — rightly! — that generative AI proves the utilitarian vision for the humanities is a sham.
As one student said to his professor at New York University, in an effort to justify using AI to do his work for him, “You’re asking me to go from point A to point B, why wouldn’t I use a car to get there?” It’s a completely logical argument — as long as you accept the utilitarian vision.
The real solution, then, is to be honest about what the humanities are for: You’re in the business of helping students with the cultivation of their character.
I know, I know: Lots of students will say, “I don’t have time to work on cultivating my character! I just need to be able to get a job!”
It’s totally fair for them to be focusing on their job prospects. But your job is to focus on something else — something that will help them flourish in the long run, even if they don’t fully see the value in it now.
Your job is to be their Aristotle.
For the ancient Greek philosopher, the mother of all virtues was phronesis, or practical wisdom. And I’d argue there’s nothing more useful you can do for your students than help them cultivate this virtue, which is made more, not less, relevant by the advent of AI.
Practical wisdom goes beyond just knowing general rules — “don’t lie,” for example — and applying them mechanically like some sort of moral robot. It’s about knowing how to make good judgments when faced with the complex, dynamic situations life throws at you. Sometimes that’ll actually mean violating a classic rule (in certain cases, you should lie!). If you’ve honed your practical wisdom, you’ll be able to discern the morally salient features of a particular situation and come up with a response that’s well-attuned to that context.
This is exactly the sort of deliberation that students will need to be good at as they step into the wider world. The breakneck pace of technological innovation means they’re going to have to choose, again and again and again, how to make use of emerging technologies — and how not to. The best training they can get now is training in how to wisely make this type of choice.
Unfortunately, that’s exactly what using generative AI in the classroom threatens to short-circuit, because it removes something incredibly valuable: friction.
AI is removing cognitive friction from education. We need to add it back in.
Encountering friction is how we give our cognitive muscles a workout. Taking it out of the picture makes things easier in the short term, but in the long term, it can lead to intellectual deskilling, where our cognitive muscles gradually become weaker for lack of use.
“Practical wisdom is built up by practice just like all the other virtues, so if you don’t have the opportunity to reason and don’t have practice in deliberating about certain things, you won’t be able to deliberate well later,” philosopher of technology Shannon Vallor told me last year. “We need a lot of cognitive exercise in order to develop practical wisdom and retain it. And there is reason to worry about cognitive automation depriving us of the opportunity to build and retain those cognitive muscles.”
So, how do you help your students retain and build their phronesis? You add friction back in, by giving them as many opportunities as possible to practice deliberating and choosing.
If I were designing the curriculum, I wouldn’t do that by adopting a strict “no AI” policy. Instead, I’d be honest with students about the real benefit of the humanities and about why mindless AI cheating would be cheating themselves out of that benefit. Then, I’d offer them two choices when it comes time to write an essay: They can either write it with help from AI, or without. Both are totally fine.
But if they do get help from AI, they have to also write an in-class reflection piece, explaining why they chose to use a chatbot and how they think it changed their thinking and learning process. I’d make it shorter than the original assignment but longer than a paragraph, so it forces them to develop the very reasoning skills they were trying to avoid using.
As a TA, you could suggest this to professors, but they may not go for it. Unfortunately, you’ve got limited agency here (unless you’re willing to risk your job or walk away from it). All you can do in such a situation is exercise the agency you do have. So use every bit of it.
Since you lead discussion sections, you’re well-placed to prompt your students to work their cognitive muscles in conversation. You could even stage a debate about AI: Assign half of them to argue the case for using chatbots to write papers and half of them to argue the opposite.
If a professor insists on a strict “no AI” policy, and you encounter essays that seem clearly AI-written, you may have little choice but to report them. But if there’s room for doubt about a given essay, you might err on the side of leniency if the student has engaged very thoughtfully in the discussion. At least then you know they’ve achieved the most important aim.
None of this is easy. I feel for you and all other educators who are struggling in this confusing environment. In fact, I wouldn’t be surprised if some educators are suffering from moral injury, a psychological condition that arises when you feel you’ve been forced to violate your own values.
But maybe it can comfort you to remember that this is much bigger than you. Generative AI is an existential threat to a humanities education as currently constituted. Over the next few years, humanities departments will have to paradigm-shift or perish. If they want to survive, they’ll need to get brutally honest about their true mission. For now, from your pre-paradigm-shift perch, all you can do is make the choices that are left for you to make.
Bonus: What I’m reading
- I went back to Shannon Vallor’s first book, Technology and the Virtues: A Philosophical Guide to a Future Worth Wanting. If there’s one book I could get everyone in the AI world to read, it would be this one. And I think it can be useful to everyone else, too, because we all need to cultivate what Vallor calls the “technomoral virtues” — the traits that will allow us to adapt well to emerging technologies.
- A New Yorker piece about AI and cognitive atrophy led me to a 2024 psychology paper titled “The Unpleasantness of Thinking: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Association Between Mental Effort and Negative Affect.” The authors’ conclusion: “We suggest that mental effort is inherently aversive.” Come again? Yes, sometimes I just want to turn off my brain and watch Netflix, but sometimes thinking about a challenging topic is so pleasurable! To me, it feels like running or weightlifting: Too much is exhausting, but the right amount is exhilarating. And what feels like “the right amount” can go up or down depending on how much I practice.
- Astrobiologist Sara Imari Walker published an essay in Noema provocatively titled “AI Is Life.” She reminds us that evolution produced us and we produced AI. “It is therefore part of the same ancient lineage of information that emerged with the origin of life,” she writes. “Technology is not artificially replacing life — it is life.” To be clear, she’s not arguing that tech is alive; she’s saying it’s an outgrowth of human life, an extension of our own species.

A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows a girl in Ladakh being abducted from her home by Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) workers on the instructions of Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leader Vinay Kumar. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows a Congress supporter in Ladakh being abducted by RSS workers.
Fact: The video shows a Jaranan performance. Also known as Kuda Lumping, Jaran Kepang, or Jathilan, Jaranan is a traditional Javanese dance. The video does not show a Congress-supporting girl in Ladakh being abducted by RSS workers. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify the claim, we conducted a Google search using relevant keywords but did not find any police reports, credible news reports, or records about Vinay Kumar or RSS workers abducting a Congress supporter in Ladakh.
We then conducted a reverse image search of key frames from the viral video, which led us to the same video (archived) uploaded on the Instagram handle tubagusjakaa on 29 August 2026. The post featured similar visuals, and its caption read, “Mendem Jaranan”. The post also included hashtags such as #jaranan, #mendemjaranan, #kerasukan, #mbekes, #kudalumping, and #jatilan.
Jaranan, also known as Kuda Lumping, Jaran Kepang, or Jathilan, is a traditional Javanese dance from Indonesia in which performers dance while using flat, horse-shaped props made from woven bamboo, often accompanied by traditional gamelan music. The performance traditionally depicts horsemen or warriors and, in some forms, includes spiritual or trance elements in which dancers are believed to enter an altered state and perform unusual acts. It is performed both as cultural entertainment and as part of traditional or community events, and is regarded as an important part of Javanese cultural heritage (here, here).
The account that uploaded the video has also shared similar videos featuring people performing the same art form.
To sum up, a Jaranan performance video from Indonesia is falsely shared as a Congress supporter in Ladakh being abducted by RSS workers.

Since May 2025, the Delhi government has been setting up Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (AAMs), which serve as primary healthcare centres, across the Capital. In phases, they replaced the Aam Aadmi Party government’s Mohalla Clinics, which are no longer operational. While many staff members were absorbed into the AAMs, some say they have not received their final salary dues and have been told that the budget for the payments is “under consideration”.
There were 553 Mohalla Clinics. So far, the Delhi government has set up 415 AAMs and aims to establish 1,100 in all. The centres were envisaged to provide additional services such as maternal and child healthcare, routine immunisation, free screening for non-communicable diseases and nearly 80 types of free diagnostic tests.
However, some former mohalla clinic staff who were not absorbed into the AAMs are still awaiting their dues. Dr. Amit Gupta, who worked at a mohalla clinic near Mandawali metro station, said he is owed ₹78,000. He said interviews for AAM posts were open to all staff and some were selected. He is currently practising at his own clinic.
‘Budget under consideration’
In an email to an east district health official, Dr. Gupta wrote, “It is very unfortunate that our salaries for January and February are still pending”.
He received a response from an official on August 27, seen by The Hindu, stating that the file had been transferred to the respective cell and that “the approval of budget is under consideration”.
Another senior Health Department official said, “Many of them have been retained by AAMs and have received their salaries till date. If there has been any negligence, we will look into the matter”.
Two staff members retained at AAMs told The Hindu that they had been receiving their salaries. Those who spoke of pending dues were among the staff not retained.
Pending dues
Mohalla Clinics employed four staff members each: a doctor, a pharmacist, a multi-task worker and a lab technician. AAMs have a similar staffing structure, though the number of personnel varies with the size of the centre.
A former multi-task worker at a mohalla clinic in the east district said, “I am trying to get a job in the AAM but the vacancy has not risen yet. We have been told by supervisors that the funds have not been released for our last salaries. I have been without a job since March, when the Mohalla Clinic shut.”
Another doctor said that, besides salaries, which were linked to the number of patients seen, staff had not received other dues, including cleaning and costs incurred in transporting medicines for the final month. “Authorities have said that they are doubtful that it will come through but we are still waiting.” The doctor said she was ineligible to apply to the AAMs because the age limit was 55.
Last year, Mohalla Clinic staff protested outside the Secretariat, demanding that they be retained at AAMs. Selection tests have since been conducted and several former staff members have been appointed. Some have approached the Delhi High Court over the matter, which is to be heard on September 8.
