In Summary
- The Redmi Turbo 5 sees the Redmi brand return to a higher price point. It had earlier released the K series in this segment.
- The Redmi Turbo 5 follows Redmi’s classic formula of offering very good specs at surprisingly affordable prices. Its highlights are a powerful chip and a large Silicon Carbon battery.
- Priced at Rs 41,999, the Redmi Turbo 5 is one of the best options for those looking for something close to a budget flagship in an era of rapidly rising prices.
Redmi is mainly known for its budget-friendly devices, mostly in the mid- and lower-mid segment. It has occasionally released slightly more expensive devices, most notably in its K series, but has then gone back to the comfort of the Redmis and Redmi Notes. Now, as phone prices get on an upward-heading escalator, Redmi is getting back into the higher price zone with the Redmi Turbo 5. It comes with a starting price of Rs. 41,999, and while that may seem a bit on the premium side for a Redmi smartphone, it brings an equally premium spec sheet to the table. But can it help Redmi stretch beyond Note-land? Let’s find out!
Table of Contents
Redmi Turbo 5 design and appearance: Classy, yet not-so-loud appearance
The Redmi Turbo 5 does not come with a radically new design – it looks very similar to its cousin, the Poco X8 Pro. And that is a good thing. The phone has all the design elements that make up a trendy smartphone in today’s day and age – a tall, display dominated front which is surrounded by razor thin bezels, a flat back with two circular camera rings jutting out just a little parked on the top left side, and has those flat sides that have become an essential part of a modern day smartphone’s anatomy.
While not out of the box, the Turbo 5 still has a few distinct design touches that catch attention, the kind that are not obvious or scream for attention, but do not get lost completely either. The right side of the back comes with a thick vertical strip filled with very dainty checkered patterns, and the cameras seem like two independent lenses stacked together, but there is a subtle capsule outline encasing them. The two camera lenses also have LED rings inside them, which is a nice conversation starter.
We received the Turbo White variant of the smartphone, which has a red Redmi logo near the base of the back. The cameras and the power/lock button also come with a very distinct red accent. These subtle touches make the design of the Redmi Turbo 5 give it a personality of sorts, making it stand out in the crowd. The back comes with a matte finish, which keeps smudges and scratches at bay and keeps the phone relatively clean. The metallic frame (a pleasant surprise at this price) is home to a handful of features as well. The top carries an infrared port while the base holds a SIM card tray, a USB Type-C port, and a speaker grille. The left side is bare while the right one bears the volume rocker and the power lock button.
Although relatively light for the size of the battery it carries (more about that later), the phone is not exactly light. It weighs 204 grams, and you can feel the weight in hand and even when the phone is in your pocket. At 157.5 mm, the Redmi Turbo 5 falls somewhere between large (160 mm and above) and compact phones (153 mm and below). It is 75.2 mm wide and, at 8.18 mm, is impressively slim, again considering the size of its battery. It is quite a sturdy phone with Gorilla Glass 7i protection on its front and back, and with IP68 and IP69K ratings for dust and water resistance, which means it can easily survive a fall in the water.
At first glance, the Redmi Turbo 5 might seem routine, but give it more attention, and little details start to pop up, and you start appreciating it for its classy, yet not-so-loud appearance.
Redmi Turbo 5 Specs: Ticks a surprising number of boxes
At a time when brands are cutting spec corners, the Redmi Turbo 5 ticks a surprising number of boxes. The phone is powered by a MediaTek Dimensity 8500 Ultra processor, which is considered to be in the budget flagship zone, and is paired with 8 GB and 12 GB RAM options and 256 GB of storage. What’s more, the 12 GB RAM variant comes with LPDDR5X RAM, and the storage on both variants is UFS 4.1. On paper, this is a very powerful setup for the price, which can not only run your everyday smartphone tasks but even handle high-end gaming.
The phone comes with a 6.59-inch AMOLED full HD+ (2756 x 1268) display with 120 Hz refresh rate and a peak brightness of 3500 nits, which can actually cover as much as 25 per cent of the display, instead of being isolated to a tiny section. Photography is handled by a dual camera setup on the back comprising a 50 megapixel Sony IMX882 main sensor with OIS, and an 8 megapixel ultrawide sensor, while a 20 megapixel sensor on the front handles selfies.
The Turbo 5 also packs in some very impressive battery numbers – it brings a sizable 7540 mAh Silicon Carbon battery (a rarity at this price, actually at any price) with support for 100W charging and 27W reverse charging. Also on board are stereo speakers, an in-display fingerprint scanner, and an IR blaster. Like all Redmi devices, the Turbo 5 also runs on Android 16 topped with Xiaomi’s HyperOS 3. Xiaomi promises four years of software and six years of security updates.
In sheer spec terms, this is one of the best specced devices out there in its segment. Some might find the display a little small, but the power of that processor and the RAM and storage options will attract gamers on a budget.
Redmi Turbo 5 Performance: A smooth, powerful operator
The Redmi Turbo 5’s speedy processor+ RAM+ storage set up, reflects in its performance as well. The phone sails smoothly through everyday duties. It moves from app to app smoothly, handles multi-tasking without a hiccup, keeps going through intense social media scrolls, and binge sessions on OTT. The phone can also handle high-end games like Call of Duty and BGMI at 120 fps for long-ish sessions. Although it does get warm while going through power-hungry tasks, the temperature comes down quickly enough.
The AMOLED display with a 120 Hz refresh rate does not disappoint. It delivers a very rich contrast with vibrant colors and is bright enough not to dull down against a very harsh sun either. The 120 Hz refresh rate kept scrolling through social media breezy. The in-display fingerprint scanner works smoothly as well. This, combined with the loud and clear stereo speakers, makes the phone a multimedia master. We did not face any call drops or connectivity issues with the phone either.
Redmi Turbo 5 Cameras: One sensor show (censor the others)
Cameras are not the forte of the Redmi Turbo 5. There are three sensors on the phone, but all the photography weight rests on the 50-megapixel main sensor’s shoulders. This performs well in daylight conditions, capturing a good amount of detail and producing sharp images, so much so that the photos look decent even after a little zoom-in. The colors seem slightly more vibrant than reality but never to a point of looking unnatural. The details do take a very marginal hit in low light, but the presence of OIS helps, and Night mode on the device also improves results a fair bit. A number of other modes are built right into the native camera app, which offer a lot of scope for creative photography.
The 8-megapixel ultrawide sensor is capable of capturing a wider area, but it does not really do an impressive job. The colors remain nice and vibrant, but the details take a nose dive, resulting in images that look noisier, especially when compared to the main sensor. Matters only get worse as the light dims down. The sensor is usable and will allow you to take some quick snaps for social media in good light conditions, but do not pin your photography hopes on it. The 20-megapixel sensor on the front delivers social media-ready snaps but has the tendency to smooth out skin texture even with no ‘beauty mode’ on. The colors also lean towards being a little oversaturated, but you can get good casual snaps, and video calls are handled well.
The main camera supports 4K video at 60 fps, but the other two cameras are limited to 1080p at 60 fps. The video performance of the main camera sensor is good in daylight and even in low-light conditions, but the others miss the mark a bit. Overall, the 50-megapixel camera is the star of the Redmi Turbo 5’s camera show, while the other two are just supporting staff.
Redmi Turbo 5 software and UI: Very nice HyperOS, but loaded with third-party apps
The Redmi Turbo 5 runs on HyperOS 3. Now, HyperOS has been one of the most intuitive, simple, and functional Android skins since its MIUI days, and while that still largely remains true, the phone comes loaded with a plethora of third-party apps. This really makes the experience feel very cluttered and might even seem overwhelming to those new to the UI. Most of these third-party apps can be uninstalled, thankfully.
That said, features like Xiaomi Interconnectivity that not only allow you to connect your smartphone with other HyperOS products but with other gadgets as well, letting you create a hybrid ecosystem, give HyperOS its productivity edge. Top this with add-ons like Hyper Island (similar to Dynamic Island on the iPhone), and AI features like AI Translate, writing assist, call transcription, and a range of customizations, and HyperOS comes across as a very functionality-forward UI. The LED rings around the camera sensors that light up when you get notifications or calls were actually very handy, even while being a nice party trick as well.
Redmi Turbo 5 Battery: Lasts for days, gets charged in a jiffy
The phone’s massive 7540 mAh battery can see you through even the heaviest work days. Emails, messaging, gaming, photography- we did all of that and more with the smartphone, and it still had some juice left even after a day. If you are someone who does not push their device as much, the phone would easily see off more than two days on a single charge. It comes with 100W fast charging support with a 100W brick in the box, which means you get a fully charged phone in slightly over an hour, while the phone goes from 0-50 percent in about 30 minutes. This makes the Redmi Turbo 5 a device that will not only last for day(s) but will also get charged in a jiffy. The reverse charging feature is quite handy too and charges our TWS at a very decent speed.
Redmi Turbo 5 Price: Typically Redmi!
The Redmi Turbo 5 is available in two RAM variants – 8 GB and 12 GB, while the storage remains 256 GB for both options. Although the phone was initially launched at Rs 37,999, this price has since been revised, given rising costs of inputs. The 8 GB/ 256 GB version of the phone is now priced at Rs. 41,999, while the 12 GB/ 256 GB version is priced at Rs. 46,999.
It might have a much higher starting price than the Redmi Note series, but the Redmi Turbo 5 brings a solid spec sheet to the table at a price tag that is typically Redmi. While there are other devices in its price range, at the time of writing, none quite match its price-to-spec equation.
Perhaps the one that comes closest is its own cousin, the Poco X8 Pro, which comes with a similar processor and a similarly sized display at Rs 39,999, but has a smaller battery. Devices like the OnePlus Nord 6 come with a comparable Qualcomm Snapdragon 8s Gen 4 chip, but are more expensive at Rs 46,999, while the recently launched Vivo S2 brings a sleeker design and bigger display to the table at Rs 39,999 but loses out in terms of processor muscle.
Redmi Turbo 5 Review Verdict: A phone that does everything well
It might come with a higher price tag, but the Redmi Turbo 5 is a typical Redmi smartphone in more than one aspect. It delivers a very consistent performance across multiple segments, making it one of the most reliable and powerful options at its price point (typical Redmi!). Its gaming and general performance are both quite smooth; the main camera delivers good snaps, its battery is perhaps its biggest USP, and the display combined with the stereo speakers make it an entertainment master. The price tag is a little higher than some might expect, but the Redmi Turbo 5 is a device for those who are looking for a very good everyday phone that does almost everything well.
- Smart design, sturdy build
- Gorgeous display
- Very good speakers
- Long battery that charges swiftly too
- Good gaming and multimedia performance
- Smooth overall performance
- Ultrawide camera is average
- Bloatware in UI

EU warns of new menace 25 years after 9/11 as online youths seek violent thrills
Jihadist groups still pose a major threat to Europe, but 25 years after the 9/11 attacks a new menace driven by young people online is emerging
BRUSSELS -- A quarter of a century after the Al-Qaeda attacks on the United States, jihadist groups still pose a major threat to security in Europe, but a new menace has surfaced that is driven mostly by young people online and the authorities are worried.
The exact size of the network behind what is being called nihilistic violent extremism is unclear. But police investigators from nine European countries found about 4,340 URL web addresses linked to “The COM,” as the online community has become known, during a campaign to disrupt it in June and July.
“It’s violence for the sake of violence,” European Union Counter-Terrorism Coordinator Bartjan Wegter told The Associated Press in an interview, ahead of the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks on New York and Washington in 2001.
Overall last year, 45 terrorist attacks were reported across 10 of the 27 EU countries, although none of them were major, mass-casualty incidents. About half were foiled or failed, but six people were killed. A total of 486 people suspected of terror links were arrested in 21 member countries, according to the EU police agency Europol.
Jihadist groups — often guided or inspired by networks outside Europe — were behind 24 of the attacks and accounted for more than 70% of the arrests.
Of all those taken into custody, around one third were aged under 18, mostly boys.
Europol does not keep statistics on nihilistic violent extremism because definitions of it differ and acts can fall into the category of ordinary criminality as well as terrorism.
But in Finland in 2025, a 16-year-old boy stabbed three female student colleagues. He allegedly shared a “manifesto” in WhatsApp groups, recorded the attack on Snapchat, and asked on social media for someone to save and give him the video after his release.
In the “manifesto,” he said that he wanted to do something “significant” and “exciting.” No political motive was given for his rampage, according to an EU document on the emerging threat of nihilistic extremist violence.
“It’s very much a fascination with violence. It’s violence as a means of asserting oneself, as a means of gaining status in those online communities,” Wegter told AP. “There’s not a direct link with ideology.”
In Italy last year, a 15-year-old boy planned a murder to gain notoriety online, authorities there said. He kept images and videos of assaults, murders, school shootings and child pornography on his smartphone.
Wegter said these kinds of incidents, which have been on the rise for two to three years, are not isolated but organized by online networks that are “often driven by young people, for young people often involving young boys.”
He said that they “lead to offline violence. We’ve seen stabbings, a young individual stabbing an elderly person for no reason whatsoever.”
Such attacks are tough to prevent or track. They often involve “young individuals who will not have a criminal record, usually, who don’t leave any footprints other than online perhaps, but then it’s often behind encrypted walls and communities,” Wegter said.
High on the list of groups authorities’ radar is 764, which was founded by an American high school dropout, Bradley Cadenhead. He’s serving an 80-year prison sentence for child pornography and sex offenses, but the group still functions.
In Germany last year, a 20-year-old man believed to be a leading 764 member faced 123 charges over acts of “an unimaginable level of brutality and inhumanity,” including murder, rape and the sexual abuse of children, the EU document said.
Unlike 25 years ago — when extremists, mostly from Saudi Arabia, entered the United States and trained to become deadly pilots — the terror threat facing Europe today is mostly organized online.
“The online environment, for all the good things it brings, it is still too permissive,” Wegter said. He described it as “a petri dish for the connection between different threats.”
Privacy advocates insist that people have a fundamental right to communicate without unjustified intrusion. They accuse the authorities and some companies of undermining protections through spyware and other methods.
But Wegter said that “our law enforcement must be equipped with the instruments and tools to deal with the threat as it exists today.” He noted that 85% of investigations take place in the digital environment. “It means that we have to adjust ourselves to that.”
For the Dutch diplomat himself, it means talking more to authorities and organizations in other countries, notably those that such groups use as a rear base. “Because what happens outside our borders impacts on our security,” including what’s being amplified online, he said.
Europol said criminals are exploiting images and audio to create and edit propaganda, including through deepfakes, memes and GIFs. AI-powered bots were also used to boost recruitment and promote terrorist ideologies, while AI-driven app were used for research to prepare attacks.
“The kind of violent content, violence inciting content, propaganda, manuals, tactics, everything that is available, is very much amplified by AI,” Wegter said.

Argentina to file criminal case against oil company operating in Falklands
- Published
The Argentine government has said that it would file criminal charges against oil company Navitas Petroleum for operating in seas off the Falkland Islands.
The move came just days after Argentine President Javier Milei said he would sanction oil companies drilling in the British overseas territory in the south-west Atlantic Ocean.
Sovereignty of the archipelago remains disputed between the UK and Argentina more than 40 years after a British military task force ejected Argentine forces which had invaded the territory in 1982.
The simmering dispute heated up last week, when Milei said in a speech to the nation that the "winds of change" favoured Argentina's claim to the Falklands.
Milei has, in the past, been criticised by Argentine veterans of the 1982 conflict for being "too soft" on the Falklands, which Argentines call Las Malvinas.
In his speech on Thursday evening local time, Milei restated his government's position on the territory, saying "the Malvinas are Argentine, historically and legally... there's no debate about that."
The president described drilling for oil in the archipelago as a "clear and urgent danger" to Argentine sovereignty.
He also dismissed the result of a 2013 referendum in which 99.8% of the islands' residents voted in favour of the Falklands remaining a British oversees territory.
Milei argued that they were living on land which had been "usurped" by the British and therefore "have no legitimate right to self-determination".
The British government dismissed Milei's speech and stressed that its position on the Falklands was "unwavering".
Hopes that Milei's primetime speech may have been a blip and that he would return to his previous stance of strengthening diplomatic ties with the UK were crushed on Monday, however, when his office announced it would file criminal charges against Navitas Petroleum, several of its subsidiaries and their executives.
Navitas, which is listed in Tel Aviv, holds a 65% stake in Sea Lion, an offshore oil project set to start production in the North Falkland Basin in 2028.
The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.
In Monday's statement, Milei alleged that drilling in the area would violate Argentine law banning resource exploitation without approval from the Argentine authorities.
"The state will continue to pursue actions deemed necessary to counter any act which breaches the sovereign rights of the Argentine Republic," the statement insisted.
Navitas has not yet responded to this latest statement but said last week that Milei's remarks were "not expected to have a material effect on the development activities of the Sea Lion Project, including the timetable for completion of the Project's development".
Rockhopper, which owns a partial stake in the Sea Lion project, has also not yet commented on Milei's statement.
Both companies have in the past stressed that Sea Lion holds valid licences from the Falkland Islands.

Shehzad Poonawalla hits back at Rhiya Ahir's ‘uncle’ jibe as Bigg Boss spat escalates: ‘Your IQ matches Rahul Gandhi’s’
Rhiya Ahir, came into the spotlight after a viral video of her stopping a police van during the CJP protests went viral.
Shehzad Poonawalla and Rhiya Ahir engaged in a war of words on social media platform X after the former BJP spokesperson mocked the Mumbai-based model for not being able to enter Bigg Boss 20, while taking a jibe at her “IQ and knowledge”.
Ahir, who came into the spotlight after a viral video of her stopping a police van during the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protests went viral, lost a public-voted spot on the reality show, which went to Punjabi actress Love Gill.
Poonawalla had targeted Ahir in a reel, wherein he also criticised a journalist, claiming the model had wanted to use the platform to “spread anti-national and anti-Sanatan ideas.” He further took a jibe at the “left-wing ecosystem” and leader of opposition in Lok Sabha and Congress MP Rahul Gandhi.
Replying to the video, Ahir urged Poonawalla to “leave women alone”, while referring to him as “uncle” and claiming he was “twice her age.” The former BJP spokesperson hit back later, saying he was 38 years old, and saying Ahir's “IQ and knowledge matches Rahul’s.”
‘From ₹140 to Soros subscription package’: Poonawalla
The controversy began after Poonawalla posted a video targeting Ahir, journalist Sherwani and Rahul Gandhi. Taking a jibe at Ahir, Poonawalla said, “…To get a scripted photo go viral and getting a popular mandate to enter Bigg Boss…there is a big difference between these two.”
Poonawalla claimed that the model had the backing of the “left-wing ecosystem” and “anti-Modi YouTubers”. “She thought that instead of ₹140 subscription, she would now sell Soros subscription package on prime time using the viral photo,” the former BJP spokesperson said in his video. Poonawalla further slammed Rahul Gandhi, saying Ahir was also seen sitting with the Congress leader. “Rahul Gandhi, who has lost 99 elections, cannot make Congress win a single election, what support will he get for you?” Poonawalla said.
He alleged that Ahir “wanted to use the platform to spread anti-national and anti-Sanatan ideas.” “But the people changed the script – whether it is a democracy or a voting platform, remote control is in the hands of the people,” he added.
Ahir's ‘twice my age’ remark, Poonawall's ‘maths’ response
Responding to Poonawalla, Ahir said he was “twice her age”, while adding, “I would just request you to go do politics with people of your own age and men like you. Not little girls.” She said she had no affiliation with political figures, and claimed that Poonawalla's script had been used by “50 other cheap influencers.”
“Say something credible. “Someone who doesn't respect the Indian Army.” Show up with proof. Where have I ever disrespected the Indian Army or any professional or any institution or religion or anyone for that matter?” she questioned, while sharing an interaction with her competitor Love Gill, who Poonawalla had praised in his video.
“This is what she spoke about me on national television - “I was thinking that if they had not stopped the driver, she would not have been here today.” And I replied, “The purpose of my life was being fulfilled there.””
Poonawalla, in response to the post, clarified his age, while also taking a jibe at Ahir's “maths”. “You are 28 - you are not a “young girl” and I’m 38 so technically I’m not twice your age( clearly maths was never your strong point at school)- anyway you are confusing me another 56 year old- Rahul Gandhi!” Poonawalla said. Replying to her remark about not knowing him, the former BJP spokesperson said, “I’m sure you don’t know about me. That’s ok. After all your IQ & knowledge matches Rahul’s and we saw that right when you were asked about Vande Mataram…”

Mumbai has seen a surge in H1N1 (swine flu) cases over the last three months, as the number of cases have jumped to 441 this year from 62 during same period last year. This marks a 612% rise, while for malaria the cases have seen a 20% rise.
According to Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC)’s monsoon data for June, July, and August, 441 cases of H1N1, and 4,485 malaria cases were recorded between June and August as compared to 3,733 last year.
To curb the surge of swine flu, BMC has been screening suspected H1N1 patients, and prescribing Oseltamivir. Further, surveys are being conducted in the affected regions, where the H1N1 positive cases have been located.
The BMC said suspected H1N1 patients are being screened and treated with oseltamivir wherever required. Close contacts of infected patients are being monitored for 10 days, while door-to-door surveys are being conducted in affected areas. BMC also clarified that they have prepared ventilators, PPE kits, reserved beds and medicines to manage patients for hospitalisation.’
Mumbai’s E-ward, K-West ward, G-South ward, F-South ward, and H-West ward have so far recorded the highest cases of malaria. To combat the vector-borne disease, BMC has increased the field-level monitoring in most affected areas. They have surveyed 52,197 potential breeding sites for malaria control. Anopheles mosquito breeding sites were detected at 8,055 locations, along with 12,55,469 potential mosquito breeding sites for dengue control, and Aedes mosquito breeding at 27,352 areas.
Decline in monsoon related illnesses.
Mumbai saw a decline in dengue cases,leptospirosis cases, COVID-19 cases, Chikungunya, and Gastroenteritis. According to BMC data, COVID-19 cases dropped drastically by 77% this year, as 151 cases were recorded compared to last year’s 668. For dengue the fall has been by 20% — 1,563 patients recorded this year in June, July, and August. For chikungunya, cases have dropped from 370 to 46, a decrease of 87%.
Leptospirosis cases declined by 37% — from 406 to 255, while gastroenteritis cases dropped from 2,197 to 1,954, this year.

Citing the 'Deep State,' Trump overhauls the intelligence community
John Sipher spent nearly three decades at the CIA focused on the Russians, a core part of the agency's mission. That changed dramatically after the al-Qaida attacks on Sept. 11, 2001.
"Frankly, tracking and hunting terrorists, finding people, finding a needle in a haystack was not something that we trained for," said Sipher, who served in Moscow and later ran the agency's Russia operations at CIA headquarters.
The CIA and the larger intelligence community had to adapt quickly.
"We did that by by learning, and actually even developing new technologies, computer power, data collection, drones, communications, means to defeat networks, terrorist networks."
There were real successes, such as locating Osama bin Laden in 2011 and destroying his group, al-Qaida, and later, dismantling the Islamic State.
More broadly, the Department of Homeland Security was created, and now has a quarter-million employees, making it the second-largest government agency, trailing only the Pentagon. Military and intelligence budgets soared.
By most all accounts, the U.S. is safer at home. The country has not been hit on U.S. soil with anything remotely comparable to the 9/11 attack, which killed nearly 3,000 people.
Trump targets the "deep state"
Yet 25 years later, U.S. national security industry is undergoing another dramatic change.
President Trump is waging an ongoing campaign against the so-called "deep state," which he describes largely as national security officials trying to undermine him.
"We will clean out all of the corrupt actors in our national security and intelligence apparatus, and there are plenty of them," Trump said in announcing his plans for his second term.
Critics say Trump is tearing down the national security infrastructure with no clear vision of what comes next, aside from protecting the president's personal interests.
"Since the re-inauguration of Donald Trump, the architecture of American national security is being destroyed, just like the east wing of the White House," said author Tim Weiner, who's covered the U.S. intelligence community for decades. This includes a book last year, The Mission: The CIA in the 21st Century, that examines the CIA since 9/11. "Trump has deliberately swung a wrecking ball through American national security and has in great part worked to dismantle the systems set up after World War II to protect the United States.
Weiner said Trump consistently selects loyalists with limited experience to lead national security agencies.
"The people he has put in charge, [Pete] Hegseth at the Pentagon, Kash Patel at the FBI, John Ratcliffe at CIA, are sycophants," said Weiner. "They will tell the president what he wants to know rather than what he needs to know."
Cutbacks at home, strained relations abroad
While many officials have been dismissed under Trump, some left on their own.
Steven Cash held multiple national security posts — at the CIA, the Senate Intelligence Committee and the Department of Homeland Security.
He resigned when Trump began his second term.
"I could not in good conscience keep working for a president who was going to take what I was working on and what others had spent careers working on, and turning it against Americans, which is exactly what he has done," Cash said.
Cash now leads the Steady State, a private group of more than 400 former national security officials. They were career officials who served in both Republican and Democratic administrations, but are now highly critical of Trump's policies.
Cash believes the intelligence community made important advances over the past quarter-century, particularly in information sharing. But he acknowledges it's been an imperfect process.
The post of director of national intelligence, or DNI, was created to coordinate the work of what are now 18 separate intelligence agencies.
"The original idea was it would be very small," Cash said. "We sort of joked that the new DNI would get a deputy, he'd get a big conference table with 18 chairs, and the biggest, best coffee machine he could find. And other than that, he'd get nothing."
The office quickly swelled and is often criticized for not functioning as intended. There are periodic calls for the office to be abolished.
Trump cut back the office, along with other national security agencies, as part of his larger government reductions.
Cash said these moves have gone way too far.
"We took a dive off the cliff in 2025. All the gains, I think, are gone, and we are in the process of destroying our intelligence community," he said.
Shifting agendas
U.S. successes in fighting terrorism have made it less of a priority these days, leading to cutbacks, according to Marc Polymeropoulos, a former CIA officer who spent much of his career in the Middle East.
"Counterterrorism is getting second fiddle to the threats from China and Russia, and the current administration's focus on the border and narco-trafficking means a shift of resources to the Americas," said Polymeropoulos. "I am afraid that counter-terrorism will not be a priority until a mass casualty event, and then it very much will be once again."
John Sipher says one of the most damaging ideas that's taken root is that career intelligence officials actively take sides in partisan politics.
"We have allowed our partisan anger, and specifically the Trump administration, to create this narrative that there's a deep state and that the intelligence services work for one party or another. I think it's a real danger," he said.
Tim Weiner said the damage has also been inflicted abroad as Trump repeatedly antagonizes U.S. allies.
"The CIA in particular relies or depends on intelligence sharing with friendly and not so friendly foreign intelligence services," Weiner said. "It it is still only 20,000 people, and they cannot cover the entire world. They need the British. They need the Dutch. They need the Saudis. They need help."
That help, he says, is much harder to come by today than in the aftermath of 9/11.

For a diehard fan of Donnie Darko, meeting director and screenwriter Richard Kelly is a thrill in itself. But to first encounter him as a silhouette in a darkened movie theater is to feel almost like a character in one of his films—unmoored by indefinite space and physics, questioning your altered perception.
It’s a hot Friday in mid-August when I sit down with Kelly, 51, at Santa Monica’s Aero Theatre, a beloved repertory venue that makes a key appearance in Donnie Darko, his remarkable debut feature. Released in October 2001 with virtually no marketing due to the tragic events of 9/11 weeks prior (the plot hinges on a plane accident), it couldn’t get a toehold at the box office. But in the months and years that followed, the film became a hit on the home video market and gained a fervent cult fandom thanks to its unique supernatural mystery.
To mark its 25th anniversary, the movie will enjoy another limited theatrical run, beginning on October 2, the date that launches mentally disturbed suburban teenager Donnie Darko (Jake Gyllenhaal) on a surreal journey that may or may not lead to the end of the world. Kelly has just finished recording an intro for the new 4K restoration, and snippets of it play without sound on the big screen as we talk.
“My memories of this film run the entire spectrum from fear to love,” Kelly jokes, alluding to the corny pop psychology peddled by Patrick Swayze’s self-help guru in the film. This occasion, Kelly says, is all about the “love,” as he couldn’t be more grateful to “all the people who have continued to support” his work.
That camp should be pleased to hear that on December 15, Kelly will publish his mammoth first novel, The Philosophy of Time Travel, available for preorder now. The 800-page volume picks up right where the movie left off and is intended to set the stage for a film sequel as well. “It’s been very inspiring for me to remain focused on continuing the journey that began 25 years ago, on my own creative terms,” Kelly says. “This film has defined my entire career, but at the same time, it's set a benchmark in the sense of the movies that I want to continue to make.”
Here, the auteur revisits the unforgettable dreamscape that put him on the map, and considers the artistic possibilities still ahead.
On when he realized Donnie Darko was becoming a cult hit:
There was one specific moment, I think in March of 2002, when I was in New York City. I was walking through the East Village, and I walked past a pizza restaurant called Two Boots, and my poster for Donnie Darko was hanging in their window. I saw the poster and I was like, “What's going on? This is bizarre. Why does a pizza restaurant have a movie poster?” I went inside and I asked the manager, and he said, “Well, we have a little theater in the back, the Pioneer, and we're playing your movie every Saturday night at midnight—and it's selling out.”
I showed up the next Saturday night at about two in the morning, when the movie was finishing. I expected there’d be maybe 10 people there, and he wasn't joking, it was sold out, and there were people with camcorders and lights in my face, and Michael Musto from the Village Voice was there. I was just completely bowled over by the fact that there were people who cared, who were really, really connecting with the movie. That was the moment I knew that it wasn't over, that the movie was going to have a second wind.
On how Drew Barrymore and Jason Schwartzman saved the screenplay from Hollywood purgatory:
It all started with Jason Schwartzman. He attached to play Donnie, and by virtue of his attachment, the script got sent around to a whole new round of people. It had been circulating for about a year, and the story was, “Oh, the writer won't sell it. He wants to direct. It's his first movie, it's too ambitious. It's just a writing sample, he's never gonna get that movie made. He won't let anyone else take it away from him.”
Then the script got sent to Nancy Juvonen, who’s partners with Drew Barrymore [at Flower Films]. She read it and flipped out and wanted to meet me, so we went down to the set of Charlie's Angels. We went into Drew Barrymore's trailer, and she was finishing the script, and we just immediately hit it off. I'm like, “Drew, would you like to play the English teacher, Mrs. Pomeroy?” And she's like, “Will you let my company, Flower Films, produce the movie with you? And I'm like, “Of course.” She had a one week window in August of 2000 before she was going to do a Penny Marshall film called Riding in Cars with Boys. We had to meet that deadline and get Drew to shoot her out in one week.
Jason Schwartzman had a scheduling conflict, and then in walks Jake Gyllenhaal. So it all happened really quickly. Nancy and Drew really deserve an enormous share of the credit in getting this whole thing off the ground—and Jason Schwartzman, too. Had he not attached, I would not have a career.
On having real-life siblings Jake and Maggie Gyllenhaal anchor a fictional on-screen family.
I heard from Joseph Middleton and Michelle Morris Gertz, our wonderful casting directors—they told me that Jake has an older sister, her name is Maggie Gyllenhaal, and she's a brilliant actress. She had only appeared in one movie thus far, Cecil B. Demented, a John Waters film. I think she had a tiny cameo, but she had done a lot of theater and was obviously an enormous talent, like her brother, and once I realized there was a possibility of getting her, I was just like, “We have to get Maggie. It will anchor the family with real siblings, and Maggie will be this great foundation for Jake, and for the whole cast, and she was just so essential.” Sometimes the cards are dealt in your favor in terms of who's available, who is interested, and so much of filmmaking is just the timing. It’s a miracle that any movie gets made.
On giving Seth Rogen his first film role (as a high school bully):
He had done Freaks and Geeks, and he was a standup comedian, performing in comedy clubs. Seth was one of these prodigy kids, really wise beyond his years and ahead of the game. He was maybe 19 years old when we shot the movie, the same age as Jake—incredibly observant, very articulate and funny young actor and writer and comedian, he was already pursuing all these different avenues. I felt like we had access to all the cool LA kid actors, because we shot in Los Angeles, it was the summer of 2000, and there was a commercial [actors] strike where all of the commercials were dark.
On creating the 1980s setting of Donnie Darko.
When we were doing the ‘80s, it was the year 2000, and we were capturing 1988, which is completely insane. That's 12 years. So you subtract 12 years from 2026 and we are in 2014, which seems completely insane to do a period piece about 2014, because things don't look that different than they did in 2014—but the disparity between 2000 and 1988 aesthetically was pretty significant. The cars looked completely different, the TVs looked different, the clothing looked different.
In terms of the ’80s aesthetic, we wanted it to feel subtle, we didn't want a lot of big ’80s hair, and we didn't want someone wearing a “Beat It” Michael Jackson jacket. We didn't want it to be kitschy. April Ferry, our incredible, Oscar-nominated costume designer, who we lost a few years ago, was so wonderful in bringing the ’80s fashion for Mary McDonnell and Beth Grant—you see them with the shoulder pads and the different ’80s suburban costuming.
On the movie reference from his original script that didn’t make it to the screen:
In the original script, Donnie and Gretchen went to go see C.H.U.D., just because I thought it was a funny ’80s horror movie. Linda McDonough, who was an executive at Flower Films, was trying to track down the licensing permission for the movie C.H.U.D. as we were approaching the shoot date here at the Aero Theatre, and she was getting nowhere. It was one of the big studios, and there was some woman in charge of licensing at that studio who was just like, “You're never getting this.”
You would think we were trying to license Lawrence of Arabia or Citizen Kane. They wanted so much money, and we were three days from shooting the scene, and we didn't have a movie to show. Linda, to her enormous credit, said, “Richard, I am friends with the producers at the studio that owns The Evil Dead, they own the negative. Sam Raimi is a great guy, and they will let us have the poster to show at the front in the lobby of the theater. They'll let you show any clip from The Evil Dead you want, the music, you can have it basically for free.” It was like a deus ex machina in the form of Sam Raimi. That led to the whole Evil Dead sequence in the movie, that was so perfect. Then we were able to do the marquee with The Last Temptation of Christ—we weren't showing a clip from the Scorsese film or the poster, just showing the title. That's an easier ask.
On the influential soundtrack of post-punk and new wave music:
I wasn't thinking that deep. I was just like, “I love this song.” Like, “Head Over Heels” [by Tears for Fears] was written into the script because I knew that when Donnie and his friends jump out of the school bus, when Donnie's feet hit the pavement, that first big piano note of “Head Over Heels” starts. When the camera flies through the window and you see all the kids sitting down and Drew Barrymore gathering the class together … “Time flies.” I had to get from the feet hitting the pavement to when they said, “Time flies,” and I had to edit the song down. It was just me doing a music video and loving that song and the vibe and the energy of it.
I have to give an enormous amount of credit to Manish Raval and Tom Wolfe, my music supervisors, who really expanded the canvas of the music in the movie to include Joy Division and Echo and the Bunnymen. It really did form a cohesive musical narrative. We were very fortunate, because no one was really trying to license a lot of that music in the year 2000.
The one song that we could not get—if you go back and watch the dailies, the Sparkle Motion dance scene was choreographed to Pet Shop Boys, but that was a no-go, we could not afford it, so we replaced it with Duran Duran.
On the dialogue that has had a surprising impact—such as the line “Sometimes I doubt your commitment to Sparkle Motion,” as delivered by actor Beth Grant:
It's so ridiculous. You never know it's gonna connect. Literally that's gonna be in my obituary, that line of dialogue, the only thing people remember that I wrote. Beth Grant is the best.
On what the social media reaction would be like if Donnie Darko came out today:
I can't even wrap my head around it. Online discourse is terrifying, and you kind of try to stay away from it. Any filmmaker that gets too caught up in online discourse, that can only have a negative impact on one's art. You have to be cognizant of what's going on in the world, but I think you need to curate your own art as the artist. We need more of that, art that is purely what the artist wants to say.
But I'm emboldened and excited about the younger generation going back to the theaters and reading books. Launching a book, the enormous amount of work that's gone into writing a novel—it's very gratifying to get to the finish line on something like that because you realize how a novel can help be the engine for something that is very difficult to get made because of the budget.
On the newer films and filmmakers to catch his eye:
Like everyone else, I saw Obsession. I thought it was terrific. Incredibly well done for such a small budget. The performances were great. I love Ari Aster's work. I love Jane Schoenbrun's work. I've not seen [Sex and Death at] Camp Miasma, that's next on my list.
On the movie he most wants to make (besides a sequel to Donnie Darko):
There are so many scripts I've written and projects that have hit roadblocks for various reasons. I would love to get my Rod Serling biopic made. That is a very ambitious project that tells the life story of Rod Serling using a fantasy and science-fiction language, in conjunction with his daughter Anne Serling and her memoir about her father. It's an expensive movie to make, given the fantasy elements and the period elements and the scope. If there are big influences, they would be Defending Your Life, the Albert Brooks film, A Matter of Life and Death by Powell and Pressberger, and All That Jazz by Bob Fosse.

'Hunted,' 'shattered,' 'scared': How victims say Canada's most prolific voyeur has altered their lives
Some images still online, despite efforts police say they've taken
The 15-year-old wore her school uniform, unaware a stranger followed as she walked with her mother and brother through Victoria's Mayfair Shopping Centre.
A cellphone video would later show a voyeur trailing the family, before getting close enough to slip a camera beneath the girl's pleated skirt.
When police told the girl's mother, she faced a dilemma: tell her daughter, or keep it to herself?
"Learning my daughter's image had been taken and posted on child pornography websites was devastating," she wrote in a victim impact statement read in court earlier this year.
"I have carried significant stress over how I want to tell her and how she will cope with the information once she learns the truth."
The teen is one of 652 women and children filmed in what officials claim is the largest case of voyeurism ever reported in Canada.
Yin Yeung Derek Chan spent six years secretly recording victims throughout communities on southern Vancouver Island, filming through house windows and prowling malls and well-known stores in the heart of downtown Victoria.
In the year prior to Chan's 2024 arrest, the voyeur was creating more than a video a day, uploading footage and photos of victims to social media, porn sites and a personal website that had over a million views before it was taken down.
Chan was sentenced to four-and-a-half years in prison in May — but many of the photos and videos remain online. Only a fraction of the victims have been identified.
Despite wide reporting of the sentencing, many questions remain about the police investigation and the impact of Chan's crimes.
CBC News has spent months gathering court records, listening to audio of courtroom proceedings and reaching out to Chan's victims.
In her victim impact statement, one woman said watching the video Chan took of her "shattered" her sense of safety.
"Seeing myself through the eyes of someone who had been hiding, watching, deliberately capturing me without my knowledge or consent — it made me feel hunted," she said.
"This crime did not end when the recording stopped."
Chan used delivery job to access victims' homes
Chan came to Canada from Hong Kong as a child. Although Chan's lawyer said the 39-year-old identifies as gender fluid, police referred to Chan using male pronouns and some victims say they saw a man hovering nearby, phone in hand.
Crown prosecutor Paul Cheeseman said Chan worked as an Uber Eats delivery driver, using the job to access apartment building laundry rooms.
"[Police] found thousands of pairs of women's underwear in his house and a number of them were used," Cheeseman told the court.
"So it appears he was stealing women's underwear while he was doing these videos and deliveries."
Chan has a history of secretly recording women; in 2019, Chan was caught filming a woman in a changing room at a Forever 21.
During Chan's recent sentencing, the voyeur apologized to victims but offered little insight into a pattern of prolific offending. The judge said Chan compared it to the rush of "stealing a chocolate bar from a store" and attributed the crimes to "warm weather” in an earlier proceeding.
Saanich police have repeatedly declined to specify where Chan filmed victims, in spite of calls from B.C.'s attorney general to help potential victims know if they could be affected.
According to the court records, more than 400 victims were targeted at Value Village in Victoria, while about 80 were filmed at local Walmart locations. Others were recorded at Greater Victoria businesses, including Indigo Books, Munro's Books, Shoppers Drug Mart, Michaels, Mayfair Shopping Centre, Hillside Centre, and the Bay Centre mall.
A few were sunbathing at what is believed by police to be Willows Beach in Oak Bay.
Five people were recorded through the windows of their homes and apartments, at addresses in the James Bay, Fairfield, and Hillside neighbourhoods of Victoria.
Police also found about 100 hours of other videos Chan recorded of other women at gyms and malls that "don't rise to the level of criminal voyeurism," Cheeseman said.
'A part of my innocence was taken from me'
One victim told CBC News that Saanich police contacted her in January 2025 after an officer she knew recognized her in a video seized from Chan's home.
Until she saw the video, she didn’t know Chan had snuck up behind her in an Indigo Books to film up her dress — though she remembers seeing the voyeur.
"Him being so close to me was like the most icky feeling and thing to think about, like, how did I let someone get so close to me without noticing?" said the woman, whose identity is protected by a publication ban.
"It made me scared to think of, like someone could get that close to me without realizing, like what else could they have done to me?"
For a time after she found out, the woman says she was too afraid to go out alone in public, even to the grocery store.
Just weeks ago, a man in line at a dollar store started talking to her.
"I just like, shut down in my body," said the woman.
In victim impact statements, other women told the judge who sentenced Chan that they have difficulty holding down a job, struggle with mental health, and have changed the clothes they wear.
Some spend money on Ubers to avoid public transit. One victim said she got off a bus and walked almost an hour, because another passenger had a phone camera pointed her way.
The women said Chan's crimes have affected relationships, eroded their ability to trust others, and left them feeling powerless.
"I feel as though a part of my innocence was taken from me," wrote one victim, who was 17 and days out from her high school graduation when Chan filmed her.
Another victim was underage when Chan recorded her working as an employee at a mall. The incident triggered past trauma and she began to isolate herself. Her grades at a local college suffered, and she had to withdraw.
She said she was unable to maintain a job due to intense anxiety and fear in public spaces.
The woman said she gets counselling and financial support from WorkSafeBC, but the $4,900 she receives a year isn't enough to make ends meet.
"My life has been delayed and derailed, and my future seems uncertain," she said in her statement to the court.
"This offence did not just take away my sense of safety, it took away my independence, my ability to support myself, and my financial stability."
Some recordings still online
Cheeseman said Chan was well known in the online voyeurism community for posting videos, which were downloaded and reposted by other users.
"Mr. Chan has made it available for the entire world to revictimize these people," he said.
While police have gotten some recordings removed from Chan's personal website and Flickr, the prosecutor said officials have faced challenges in getting others taken down.
A search of the username Chan used to upload many videos and images of the victims shows many are still easily found online on social media and porn websites.
One of these posts, on Reddit, is tagged "NSFW" — the site's label for explicit content.
Comments on this post, shown in court, ask Chan where to find the videos.
"We're all eager and ready to pay or something man you gotta bless us you got the finest bitches on camera," writes one user.
"Will u sponsor me?" Chan writes back to another, telling a third user the videos are "only open to payers."
Reddit did not respond to questions from CBC News about the post.
Saanich police did not answer questions from CBC News, but Deputy Chief Const. Damian Kowalewich said in a statement that "the scale of this case was unprecedented and the impact on victims cannot be overstated."
"We recognize that once material has been distributed online it may not be possible to remove every copy, which remains an ongoing concern for many victims and represents an additional layer of victimization."
'None of it was your fault,' woman tells other victims
On May 21, the day of Chan's sentencing, Saanich police published a notice announcing the case publicly for the first time.
The victim who spoke to CBC News says it felt strange to see everyone discussing something she'd only told a few of those closest to her, especially as police promised to update her before the case became public — which she says they did not.
At first, she said it felt scary to read what people thought online about the case. But with time, it began to feel validating.
"It kind of made me feel like I was able to then be like, you know what, this was really messed up, and this happened to me, and I am allowed to feel violated by this situation, and I should allow myself time and space to have those feelings," the woman said.
"It doesn't devalue who you are … you didn't do anything wrong to put yourself in this situation, and none of it was your fault."

The national capital is all decked up with posters and illuminated installations ahead of the BRICS Summit 2026.
The BRICS Leaders' Summit is scheduled to be held at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi on September 12-13 at Bharat Mandapam. The official theme for this year is “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability”.
The high-profile Summit, scheduled for 12–13 September 2026 at Bharat Mandapam, brings together leaders of BRICS Member and Partner Countries, as well as Outreach Invitees.
Quick answers to key questions
The theme of the BRICS Summit 2026 is 'Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability'.
Key leaders attending the BRICS Summit 2026 include Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and leaders from South Africa, Egypt, Indonesia, Iran, and Ethiopia.
Delhi Traffic Police has implemented a detailed traffic management plan, controlling or diverting traffic on over 35 roads to ensure smooth transit for foreign delegates while minimizing public inconvenience.
Major topics at the BRICS Summit 2026 will include strengthening multilateralism, inclusive global governance, and the theme sessions on resilience, innovation, and sustainability.
The BRICS Summit 2026 is significant for India as it is hosting the event while serving as the BRICS Chair, enhancing India's role in global governance and its diplomatic influence amid expanding regional dynamics.
India is the BRICS Chair for the 2026 edition.
Initially established as the BRIC alliance comprising Brazil, Russia, India, and China, which convened its first Foreign Ministers' meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York in 2006 and held its inaugural summit in Yekaterinburg, Russia, in 2009, the group expanded to BRICS following South Africa's admission in 2011.
The grouping has since undergone a transformative expansion, welcoming Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE as full members in January 2024, followed by Indonesia in January 2025.
Today, featuring 11 full member states alongside an expanding array of partner nations, the alliance commands significant global economic and diplomatic influence.
Delhi Traffic Police has finalised a detailed traffic management plan in preparation for the upcoming BRICS Summit.
Speaking to ANI on the arrangements, Additional CP (Traffic) Dinesh Kumar Gupta confirmed that extensive security and mobility protocols are being implemented across the capital to ensure smooth transit for foreign delegates while minimising public inconvenience.
“BRICS Summit will be held at Bharat Mandapam in Delhi on September 11, 12 and 13. Heads of Nations, foreign delegates, heads of organisations and VIPs will arrive. So, we have charted out a detailed traffic arrangement,” Gupta said.
Delhi Police has already identified more than 35 roads where traffic will be controlled or diverted as part of the summit arrangements. The restrictions will primarily affect central, south and adjoining parts of Delhi, with temporary stoppages expected during the movement of VIP motorcades.
The event will bring together heads of state, foreign delegates, heads of international organisations, and key dignitaries.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi will host the summit.
Russian President Vladimir Putin will attend the Summit. This would be his second visit to India in under a year, following the annual bilateral summit in New Delhi in December 2025. Modi renewed the invitation to Putin in person when the two leaders met at the SCO summit in Bishkek on 31 August.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to attend, though China has not formally confirmed his participation.
If Xi visits, it would be his first trip to India since the 2019 informal summit in Mamallapuram with Modi. A Modi-Xi bilateral meetingon the sidelines is widely anticipated.
The Chinese leader's delegation could run to around 400 officials, roughly double the 2019 contingent, according to some media reports.

Breakfast-cereal boxes are a window into both the politics of food and American culture. As a particularly timely example, since Robert F. Kennedy Jr. took office last year as secretary of health and human services, he has called for the removal of artificial dyes from breakfast cereals. On Fox News in 2024, he lamented that the bright colors in Froot Loops are “literally poisoning our kids.” (How exactly these dyes interact with human health is complicated.)
Cereal companies responded right away. General Mills announced last month that it had transitioned its entire U.S. portfolio of cereals—including Trix and Lucky Charms—to all-natural dyes made from fruits, veggies, and spices. Kellogg had previously announced plans to do the same by the end of 2027. Target stopped selling any cereals with artificial colors earlier this year.
For the Make America Healthy Again movement, the removal of artificial dyes is a big win. But cereal still comes with a major concern for many consumers. Nearly all ready-to-eat breakfast cereals sold in the United States—and especially those marketed to children—are presweetened.
The initial loading of breakfast cereals with sugar has been attributed to a single person: Jim Rex, a heating-equipment salesman who lived in Pennsylvania in the early 20th century. As the story goes, Rex was appalled by the spoonfuls of sugar his kids added to their breakfast cereals and set out to create a version that would not induce such behavior. His brilliant contribution: a glossy honey coating on puffed wheat, a cereal he named Ranger Joe Wheat Honnies in 1939.
It didn’t take long for Rex’s strategy to backfire. By 1949, Post had launched Sugar Crisp. Kellogg introduced Sugar Pops in 1951, Sugar Frosted Flakes in 1952, and Froot Loops in 1963, each among the company’s all-time best sellers. General Mills launched Sugar Smiles in 1953. The next year, the company added sugar and artificial colors to its Kix cereal, thus creating Trix.
In 1950, such presweetened cereals represented just 5 percent of all cereals sold, but by the mid-1970s, kids accounted for almost 40 percent of all cereal consumption. In 2014, the Environmental Working Group estimated that kids could ingest about nine pounds of sugar a year just by eating a serving of cereal every day.
Advocates for children’s health have long complained about the high sugar content of breakfast cereals. In the early 1970s, Congress held hearings to highlight cereal’s inadequate nutritional quality. Cereal companies objected, arguing, correctly, that grains are nutritious. But they also responded by trying to make their products appear less sugary.
They began by removing the S-word from cereal names, and some substituted honey for sugar on the theory that people perceive honey as more wholesome and nutritious. In the 1990s, companies hit on another clever strategy: If they used multiple sugar types, they could list grains first on a product’s ingredients but sprinkle sugars throughout the list. Cereals looked healthier, but when Consumer Reports compared the sugars in 27 breakfast cereals in 2008, it found that many were still 50 percent sugar by weight. Rumors circulated that federal agencies were working to set nutrition standards for foods advertised on television programs aimed at children younger than 12, which would likely spell trouble for sugary cereals.
In 2009, General Mills pledged to reduce sugar in its most popular kids’ cereals—most of which had at least 12 grams a serving—to single digits. Its pledge would apply to 10 cereals, including some of its most popular, such as Lucky Charms and Cocoa Puffs. The results were mixed. By 2012, General Mills had reached the single-digit goal for Cinnamon Toast Crunch, Cookie Crisp, and more. Some of this success was due to decreased serving size. And the best General Mills could do for Lucky Charms was 10 grams of sugar in a three-quarters-cup serving—which the company found to be the minimum sweet spot for kids’ acceptance. The project had encountered a harsh reality: Kids like sugar, and companies remove it at their peril.
Sugary cereal is not just a consumer concern; it is also a matter of government nutrition policy. Since 1980, the federal Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) has limited the sugars in cereals it will cover to six grams an ounce, about half of the amount in typical cereals aimed at kids. WIC can be a lucrative business for cereals that qualify, so the limit has induced companies to take two actions. The first is to formulate new cereals with less sugar specifically for the WIC market. In 2006, for example, General Mills introduced a new kid-targeted cereal, Dora the Explorer, “lightly sweetened cinnamon corn puffs,” with six grams of sugar in a 27-gram serving—an amount that meets the WIC standards.
The second is to petition to change how sugar in cereals is counted. When the six-gram rule went into effect, in the early 1980s, Kellogg immediately objected. Its Bran Flakes met the WIC standards, but Raisin Bran did not; it contained 12 grams of sugar an ounce, seven from the raisins. Kellogg argued that raisins are healthy and pointed out that WIC was encouraging women to add raisins to their diet to increase their iron intake. For decades, despite Kellogg’s persistent efforts, the U.S. Department of Agriculture did not budge. But times change. In 2024, USDA issued its third comprehensive update to the WIC food package since 1975. The agency retained the six-gram limit but specified that it applied only to added, not total, sugars. It said the policy change was justified to align with listing “added sugars” on food labels and with the government publication Dietary Guidelines for Americans, and to create a “more permissive standard for products containing naturally occurring sugars.”
The distinction between natural and added sugars has continued under Kennedy. The new dietary guidelines, released in January, declare that no amount of added sugar is recommended for healthy eating. At a press conference announcing the new guidelines, Kennedy told reporters, “Today, our government declares war on added sugar.”
Current breakfast cereals have less sugar than they did years ago, but it’s hard to remove completely. Some amount of sugar is still needed to mask the bitter taste of added vitamins. Sugar also helps cereal flakes, puffs, and Os hold their shape in milk. Less sugar is better for kids’ health, but more is better for structural integrity—and taste.
For a truly healthy cereal, look to a time before Jim Rex. The most nutritious option will have one ingredient: wheat or oats. Even if you add your own teaspoon of sugar, it will be only four grams.
This article has been adapted from Marion Nestle and Lisa Sutherland’s new book, Sugar Coated.

Smaller ball for women makes it 'harder to do my job'
- Published
England will play Australia, Canada and New Zealand in the next three weeks and, like all the world's top women's players, they have some new equipment: a smaller ball.
During September and October's WXV Global Series, World Rugby is trialling a size 4.5 ball - about 3% smaller than the size five used in the men's game, but the same weight.
Their introduction has not been without controversy and for England hooker May Campbell, responsible for throwing the ball in at the line-out, told BBC Sport it can go "a bit skew-whiff".
One of England's kickers, Helena Rowland, has found a much bigger margin for error with the smaller ball, saying: "If you get it slightly wrong, the difference is massive."
The fly-half says England players have noticed passes "dying", falling to the floor earlier than expected, "which they wouldn't have done previously".
Not all feedback has been negative. Wales wing Lisa Neumann is a fan, saying "it's changed the game" for her passing because of improved grip on the ball.
The thinking behind the trial is that the smaller ball will suit women's physiology and improve their skillset. In other sports, like basketball, women use a smaller ball, and in athletics sprint hurdles are lower for females.
But Rowland says she has never felt "hindered" by playing with the same size ball as in men's rugby.
'Harder to do my job'
Players with a specific skillset may find the change harder than others. Hookers must throw in at a line-out, scrum-halves are the most frequent passers and fly-halves the most regular kickers.
Rowland explained: "We've learned for however long how to kick with a size five.
"So I've had 13-odd years of doing that and training my routine and trying to nail that and get as much consistency as I can.
"So it's about, I suppose, trying to pack all those years of training and all those kicks into a four- or five-week block to get used to it, to then go out on to the world stage."
Rowland added that she has not "necessarily seen any positives", saying: "I know some of the girls have said that from an offload perspective, it's maybe made them more confident.
"But for me, it hasn't. I don't think there's enough of a change in the ball for me to be able to be running around with it in one hand and offloading left, right and centre.
"I haven't necessarily found any of the positive impacts. I've just found it a bit harder to do my job."
A World Rugby spokesperson said everyone involved in the WXV Global Series, including players, coaches and match officials, would have their views taken into account "with equal value" through surveys.
- Smaller balls for women's rugby 'worst decision ever' 
  - Published6 May
John Mitchell, England's head coach, has said "it's too early" to judge the impact of the smaller ball, and conclusions would have to be drawn after the world champions' opening three Tests in September.
Some England players were given a size 4.5 ball to practise with in the off-season and Campbell says "there's no point in complaining about it", given every side in the WXV Global Series will be in the same position.
But she adds: "I feel like a lot of us don't know how it's going to change the game, and kind of the reason behind it changing and the data behind it.
"It's just this decision has kind of just happened that we're now trialling it at the top level."
Inconsistency in shape
One area of concern for the England players is the ball changing shape.
Campbell says they "played around" with how much the ball was blown up, adding: "In previous weeks it was actually a bit fatter, and then this week it definitely feels smaller."
Rowland agrees, saying: "There needs to be a bit more done in terms of how the balls are made. We had some new balls today versus the ones we've had for the last three weeks [and the difference] is massive.
"If you've been training with an old ball that's fat to then go into a game and it's a completely different shape, actually that makes a massive difference as well, which I think is something that you don't necessarily find so much in the size five."
The ball has already been trialled in the Under-18s and Under-20s Women's Six Nations as well as the HSBC Sevens Series.
Rowland says she would "love to see the data on if it actually has made a difference".
It seems a fair request, and is one that BBC Sport put to World Rugby, but we did not receive any data.
A spokesperson said: "The balls haven't been used in the international XVs environment yet so there isn't directly comparable data to share with players either directly or via their unions.
"Once we've built up a large enough data set of player responses, match official responses and game data, we'll publish the results, so it'll be available to players, unions, the International Rugby Players Association, coaches, match officials, the media and everyone else."
Some players are frustrated as they feel they have become guinea pigs on the global stage. To compound that frustration, they will then return to their clubs where the league season will be played with a size five ball once again.
BBC Sport asked World Rugby when the trial period is likely to conclude, and were told: "We'll be able to assess our position on women's 15s once the international window has started.
"This will allow for completion of the WXV tournaments and full analysis in early 2027. The evidence to date suggests that further exposure produces greater results."
While it looks like players and coaches will get to see the data in early 2027, any wider outcomes or decisions might take longer.

On the eve of Apple's highly anticipated folding iPhone, Samsung isn't feeling threatened. Instead, the folding smartphone pioneer says the competition is “absolutely welcome.”
That's according to Hee-Cheul Moon, head of Samsung's Advanced Mechanical R&D Group, who sat with WIRED on a virtual Zoom call with Seungki Choi, head of Samsung's Smartphone R&D Group. Before the talk veered toward Apple, the pair spoke about how the company managed to shave 75 grams off the weight of its latest Galaxy Z Fold8 in the 7 years since it debuted the original.
Weight is integral to a folding phone's success. If the device is too chunky and heavy, you're less likely to want to use it. Over the past two years, folding devices from Honor, Google, and Samsung have rapidly gotten lighter, which each iteration featuring thinner designs. It may be why Samsung saw preorders for its latest folding handsets increase 30 percent globally versus last year's models, with the Fold8—the device with a new smaller shape that’s easier to hold—accounting for nearly half.
“Seeing these other brands entering the market, we feel very proud of ourselves that the value that we pioneered with this new category of foldables is being acknowledged and recognized,” Moon says through a translator.
When I asked what advice the company had for Apple ahead of its folding debut, Moon says, “The key to providing the highest customer value in this market is all about the weight of the device. As you know, it's not easy." Apple's folding iPhone, rumored to be called the iPhone Ultra, is expected to weigh between 230 and 241 grams (the iPhone 17 Pro Max weighs 233 grams), heftier than Samsung's latest.
Samsung has made notable strides this year in making its main Galaxy Z Fold8 smartphone lighter than top-end candybar-shaped smartphones. The single-screen Galaxy S26 Ultra weighs 214 grams, but the Fold8 is merely 201 grams, thanks to its smaller, passport-style shape. The company says its own customer data and YouGov survey data from 2024 show that bulky designs were a chief concern for people uninterested in folding phones.
The company says it analyzed every single component in the latest Fold8 and Fold8 Ultra—approximately 270 components and more than 180 auxiliary parts—from circuit boards and antennas to tapes and fastening components.
The team looked everywhere to cut weight. For example, it redesigned the printed circuit board to remove unnecessary circuits and improve component layout, reducing the space requirement. Samsung says it even eliminated 15 auxiliary parts and machined the internal display support plate down to roughly 0.2 millimeters. To keep that thinner panel durable, Samsung developed its “Flex Titanium” screen—a titanium alloy film roughly one-third the width of a human hair designed to maintain surface flatness and keep the crease from worsening over years of folding.
You'll also notice Samsung's primary folding phone no longer has three cameras on the back. Instead, it's powered by a dual-camera system, a main camera and an ultrawide—there's no more telephoto. For those who still demand high-end zoom and a 200-megapixel primary shooter, Samsung points to the larger Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra, framing the Fold8's camera cutback as an intentional concession to deliver that lightweight, passport-style design.
Apple's folding iPhone is also expected to have a wider and shorter passport-style shape, and it's likely to have a similar camera setup. Both Apple and Samsung made similar concessions last year chasing ultra-thin-and-light smartphones.
Choi says this came down to user feedback as Samsung's customers wanted a folding device that was “effortlessly portable” yet could be unfolded for an immersive multimedia experience. “We continue to always monitor the voice from the market, and we are open to any possibilities,” he says. We spend most of our time consuming multimedia with our smartphones, and the Fold8's new shape is specifically tailored for media, with less obvious letterboxing than previous Folds.
Yet chasing that slim, lightweight profile leaves foldables exposed where traditional flagships excel: durability and ingress protection. Most candybar smartphones sport an IP68 rating for dust and water resistance, meaning they'll be fine even after spending some time at the bottom of a pool, but the Galaxy Z Fold8 series is still stuck at IP48—it can get wet, but dust will cause problems. Dust notoriously forced Samsung to delay the launch of the first Galaxy Fold in 2019, as little specks could get through the hinge and damage the screen.
Google's folding Pixels are the only models with an IP68 rating. Still, even with the higher rating, dust can pose a problem, according to Elizabeth Chamberlain, iFixit's director of Sustainability. The repair company's teardowns show that dust can get inside the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, making the hinge sound “crunchy” and causing what could be a serious liability over time.
“We still haven't seen a solution for that,” Chamberlain tells WIRED. “Repair is still a problem for foldables.” iFixit's recent teardown of the Galaxy Z Fold8 gave it a 4/10 for repairability. “The hinge is buried under all the other components, and the hinge is the thing most likely to get damaged,” Chamberlain says. She did give Samsung props for its new adhesive system that makes battery removal easier.
Moon reiterated that Samsung's Folds have the “best-in-class” dustproof and waterproof performance in the industry, and that the company isn't just “chasing the numbers for the sake of it.” He also emphasized that despite the Fold8's slim profile, internal components are far easier to detach and service than earlier iterations.
That tension between engineering finesse and long-term durability is what Apple is stepping into. While Samsung enjoys a boost in Fold8 preorders, the broader foldable category was staring down a double-digit decline after five consecutive quarters of losing steam.
Nabila Popal, senior research director at the International Data Corporation, says this niche market is stabilizing, and the upcoming iPhone is expected to help the category grow nearly 13 percent year over year—the only bit of growth in the smartphone market right now. Drew Blackard, Samsung's senior vice president of Mobile Product Management, previously told WIRED that more competition will help bring visibility to the category.
Popal says foldables are more durable and dependable now, arguing Apple is entering just as hardware anxieties have eased.
Chamberlain isn't convinced the category is truly mature. “I want a phone that is durable and repairable, and I think it's highly unlikely that Apple will have solved the hinge problem,” she says.
Even with the durability question unanswered, Samsung's engineers believe they've finally landed on the right formula. When I asked what device everyone in the room was using, a sea of Galaxy Z Fold8 models appeared in the air. Moon held up both the Z Fold8 and the Fold8 Ultra, smiling and saying, “We use the Fold8 Ultra also.”
