'I'm not a robot' - Kerr responds to criticism before Ingebrigtsen reunion
- Published
Great Britain's Josh Kerr says he is "very happy" to see Jakob Ingebrigtsen back competing - but he is "not going to lose" when they resume their fierce rivalry at this weekend's World Athletics Ultimate Championship.
Their long-established war of words was recently reignited when Ingebrigtsen criticised Kerr's decision to miss last month's European Championships, where the Norwegian marked his return from long-term injury by winning 5,000m gold.
The men's 1500m at the inaugural Ultimate Championship in Budapest this weekend will have added edge after Ingebrigtsen, 25, labelled his rivals a "bunch of cowards" at last week's Diamond League Final.
Speaking to the media before the championship, Kerr was reluctant to directly address Ingebrigtsen's recent comments towards him but admitted their presence would bring "a lot more energy" to the event.
"When you boil it down, I'm very happy that he's back racing," said Kerr, 28.
"I think it's great for our distance. He's one of the best 1500m and 5,000m runners of all time.
"I'm not going to lose, but I'm excited to go out there and race."
Kerr added: "A championship 1500m or 5,000m is very different to what he's used to right now, coming off a long-term injury.
"So I first foresee some struggling from his side."
Although interest in their absorbing rivalry has transcended the sport, Kerr and Ingebrigtsen have not gone head-to-head for two years.
In their last meeting, at the Zurich Diamond League in September 2024, Ingebrigtsen placed second and Kerr fifth - one month after the Briton was edged to Olympic gold by American Cole Hocker, and Ingebrigtsen missed out on a medal.
It is around the major championships where one of the sport's most compelling storylines of recent times has truly developed, both on and off the track.
Their frequent exchange of words has built hype between exhilarating showdowns. Ingebrigtsen won Olympic gold five years ago. Kerr took the world title in 2023. Hocker stole in as they fought to outdo one another in Paris.
Making a winning return after 11 months out with an Achilles issue, Ingebrigtsen said he was "very" disappointed by Kerr's absence from the Europeans and claimed that athletes who choose to miss major competitions are "ruining" the sport.
Kerr had long made clear those championships were not part of his 2026 plans, focusing instead on smashing the 27-year mile world record in London and winning Commonwealth gold in Glasgow this summer, after reclaiming the world indoor 3,000m title in March.
Kerr's preferred approach to each season is to identify three or four big dates in an attempt to avoid injuries and inconsistent performances.
"These next three years are going to be some of the biggest in my career. I'm not going to get greedy," said Kerr, whose world title defence was ended by a calf tear 12 months ago.
"The first question I was asked after running the mile world record is 'when are you going to go after the 1500m record?', and it's just not that simple.
"I'm a human being at the end of the day. I'm not a robot. I think if you want to have a career that's 10-12 years long then you can't [race all the time]."
The World Athletics Ultimate Championship will take place at the stadium where Kerr beat Ingebrigtsen to world 1500m gold three years ago.
Because of their limited racing, neither Kerr or Ingebrigtsen qualified for the event and were instead granted exceptional invitations by the sport's governing body.
On accepting the invitation, Kerr said: "I think having the best athletes - maybe not the best in-form athletes, like with me and [Ingebrigtsen] getting invited - that have shown up on consistent championships, can make the most exciting race.
"I know that the rest of the 1500m squad are wanting to have a go with both of us. I think it'll end up being a fantastic race.
"I think we're bringing a lot more energy to the race by being in it."
The keenness of their competitors to make a statement will have been sharpened considerably after Ingebrigtsen called his rivals "cowards" and "losers" last week.
The Norwegian, who faded to fourth in the Diamond League Final after attempting to front-run the 1500m, was angry at his rivals - particularly Hocker - for their reluctance to push the pace.
"I think I will run circles around them in not so many months," Ingebrigtsen told FloTrack.
He later offered something of an apology when he admitted there was "maybe a little too much adrenaline and emotion" involved when he made those comments, but added: "I will always call things as I see it."

Babies born to mothers with anaemia have smaller brains, particularly in key regions linked to movement, learning and the regulation of emotion, according to a study.
Researchers said the differences, first detected at the age of one, could lead to cognitive problems when children started school.
More than a third of pregnant women worldwide have anaemia – a condition typically caused by iron deficiency in which the number of red blood cells in the body is lower than normal. Symptoms include fatigue, shortness of breath and dizziness. Rates are highest in sub-Saharan Africa and south Asia.
Researchers from King’s College London in the UK, and the University of Cape Town in South Africa, followed more than 300 mothers and their babies in Cape Town, scanning the brains of the infants several times between the ages of three months and two years.
On average, the total brain volume of babies born to anaemic mothers was 4% lower than that of babies born to non-anaemic mothers – despite all the anaemic mothers being diagnosed only with a mild version of the condition.
Differences were recorded in three specific regions of the brain: the putamen, caudate nucleus and corpus callosum.
“All three of these brain regions are implicated in key neuropsychological functions,” said Jessica Ringshaw, first author and researcher at King’s Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience (IoPPN) and the University of Cape Town, citing processing speed, emotion regulation and executive function as examples.
The gap between the groups of babies widened over the first two years of life – the corpus callosum, for instance, was about 4% smaller at 12 months in the group whose mothers had been anaemic but 6% by 24 months.
Earlier research in South Africa looking at toddlers and school-age children found comparable differences in brain volume.
“These aren’t children who are catching up, where the brain differences are disappearing over time,” said Ringshaw. “They are still there when the children are six years old and going to school, and when these things might then start translating into more noticeable cognitive difficulties.”
The findings offer a potential explanation for earlier studies showing that children born to mothers with anaemia scored less well on tests of development, she added.
The mothers with and without anaemia were otherwise very similar in terms of factors such as household income and food security, Ringshaw said, making her confident that maternal anaemia caused the differences the team observed.
The results reinforced the importance of tackling anaemia in women of reproductive age, Ringshaw said. “We should be screening for anaemia and iron deficiency, particularly during pregnancy,” she said, recommending the use of oral or even intravenous iron supplementation where appropriate.
The causes of anaemia were complex and could include infectious diseases, she said, with the study finding higher rates of anaemia in women living with HIV, “so having our iron interventions, but also appropriate infection management in conjunction with that [is important]”.
While the World Health Organization lists reducing rates of anaemia as a priority, progress has stagnated over the past two decades.
“Now more than ever, anaemia needs to be placed at the forefront of public health efforts if we are to ensure that children are not only surviving but thriving,” said Ringshaw.
The research, published in the journal Brain Communications, used special new MRI scanners that are cheaper and more portable than the conventional machines used in hospitals.
It compared images taken using the traditional “high-field” MRI machines with those taken by the portable “low-field” options, and found the latter were sensitive enough to detect the same differences in the brains of babies born to anaemic mothers.
Steve Williams, professor of neuroimaging at King’s, said: “This study has proved that our novel technology can measure the impact of malnutrition on the developing brain, at scale, in some of the most challenging environments. This will provide an early, sensitive assessment of planned interventions.”

Good morning, everyone, and welcome to another working week. We hope the weekend respite — longer than usual thanks to a holiday on this side of the pond — was relaxing and invigorating. An experimental Novartis drug for a rare neuromuscular condition failed to improve muscle function in a pivotal study, its second major trial collapse in a matter of days, STAT writes. The two study flops will likely stoke concerns about its pipeline and acquisition strategy as it navigates a major patent cliff, though the company did see a victory with a multiple sclerosis drug last week. The stock was down by as much as 10% in early trading in Switzerland. The Phase 3 HARBOR trial was testing the drug del-desiran in a condition called myotonic dystrophy type 1, known as DM1, which causes progressive muscle stiffness and weakness.
Novo Nordisk stopped two trials of a drug that aims to tame inflammation as a way to improve cardiovascular health, another blow for the approach, STAT notes. The company said it had halted the HERMES and ATHENA trials of its drug, ziltivekimab, after a data monitoring committee found they were unlikely to succeed. Novo informed trial investigators on Friday. The move follows the earlier failure of the drug in the ZEUS trial, which showed that the medicine, despite lowering markers of inflammation, did not reduce the risk of major clinical complications, including deaths and heart attacks.

U.S. military says it destroyed 5 Iranian oil tankers after attacks on Navy warship
WASHINGTON — The U.S. military said it destroyed five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday in response to the latest attacks on its warships and Tehran hit back at American targets in Jordan, the latest burst of back-and-forth strikes that have lurched the sides back toward open hostilities in a more than 6-month-old war.
Following the American strikes, Iran launched missiles toward U.S. targets in Jordan, Iranian state-run media said. Jordan's military said its air defense systems intercepted 18 ballistic missiles launched toward its territory and two others fell in places where no one lives. It said it has no reports of casualties. Jordan is a staunch U.S. ally that hosts American forces, making the kingdom's military bases a target of repeat Iranian strikes. U.S. Central Command said it had no information to offer.
The latest strikes are part of a dual economic and military approach by President Donald Trump as he struggles to bring an end to the war. The Trump administration on Tuesday also imposed sanctions on additional elements of Iran's aviation industry, targeting more than two dozen commercial and private airlines as well as foreign cargo service providers, in its new push to isolate Tehran from its remaining trading partners.
Both the U.S. and Iran are seeking to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz, where about one-fifth of the world's oil passed before the war began. Rising energy prices are posing political problems for Trump and his Republican Party ahead of the November midterm elections. A barrel of international standard Brent crude briefly climbed as high as $99.46 on Tuesday.
The U.S. forces also destroyed three Iranian oil tankers on Saturday after Iran's Revolutionary Guards tried to attack a U.S. aircraft carrier and destroyer with ballistic missiles, warning that it would, "if necessary, destroy Iran's limited and exposed oil fleet." Iran later said it planned to announce a new "exclusion zone" near the Strait of Hormuz aimed at vessels intending to transit.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. will not allow Iran's attacks to go unanswered.
"Iran continues to try to hit U.S. naval ships. And for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers. And I think you'll see that again today," Rubio told reporters Tuesday when asked about the latest attacks in Iran while on a trip to Colombia.
Danny Citrinowicz, an Iran expert at Israel's Institute for National Security Studies, warned that such back-and-forth strikes can only risk more retaliation and further impact to the global economy.
"There is no kinetic solution to the Strait of Hormuz problem," he said on social media. "Every attempt to impose one only brings Washington and Tehran closer to an escalation that may become increasingly difficult to control."
U.S. Central Command said the military struck the tankers on Tuesday after the Revolutionary Guards targeted a Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days. "The U.S. warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed," it said in a statement.
It said the Iranian tankers destroyed on Tuesday were the Kivik, Charminar, Horizon 1 and the Riesco in the Gulf of Oman. The U.S. military also destroyed the vessel Derya, which was located near Kharg Island in the Strait of Hormuz. The statement said the crews of the five vessels were told to abandoned ship before the attacks.
Iranian state television also reported the U.S. strikes, saying U.S. forces attacked Iranian oil tankers near the southern port of Jask and near Kharg Island in the Persian Gulf. It said the crews were evacuated.
An Iranian state TV reporter in Jask said an Iranian tanker was struck near the coast of Yekbeni. State TV later reported that the U.S. military attacked a second tanker near waters off Jask. Separately, state television reported that another Iranian tanker was attacked in the Kharg Island anchorage area.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard Navy on Tuesday had warned crews of oil tankers near ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to immediately leave their vessels, saying the ships could be targeted in retaliation for U.S. attacks on Iranian tankers. It accused Kuwait and Bahrain of hosting U.S. forces and assisting in the attacks.
A U.S. blockade of Iranian ports has squeezed the country's economy by limiting its oil exports, while the American military has been helping a limited number of ships transit on a route through the Strait of Hormuz off Oman. Tehran wants ships to follow a route that it chooses through the strait, which was considered an international waterway before the war.

As Baar Baar Dekho completes 10 years, its song ‘Sau Aasmaan’ continues to be remembered by listeners. Composed by Amaal Malik, sung by Armaan Malik and Neeti Mohan, and penned by Kumaar, the romantic track was among the popular songs from the film’s album.
Sau Aasmaan Turns 10: Amaal Malik, Armaan Malik and Neeti Mohan reflect on ‘Baar Baar Dekho’ song˝
The song’s upbeat sound, along with Katrina Kaif and Sidharth Malhotra’s on-screen chemistry, added to its appeal. A decade after its release, the makers and singers have looked back on their experience of creating the track.
Amaal Malik recalled working on the song and said, “‘Sau Aasmaan’ was great fun to compose for Baar Baar Dekho. Armaan and Neeti brought such amazing energy to this peppy romantic number, and Armaan and I have some wonderful memories from recording it. Azeem Dayani’s vision as the music supervisor and Kumaar’s beautiful lyrics played an important role in bringing the song together, while Nitya Mehra’s incredible vision elevated it visually and gave it a distinct identity. It’s one of the most beautifully shot songs, and I’m so happy it has remained a favourite with audiences for 10 years. Even today, hearing it takes me straight back to those recording days — it still feels like a little musical road trip!”
Neeti Mohan also spoke about her connection with the song, describing it as a track that continues to evoke happy memories. She said, “‘Sau Aasmaan’ has always been very close to my heart. It has that rare quality of making you want to pack your bags, fall in love and just get away somewhere beautiful. Recording it with Amaal, Armaan and Kumaar was such a lovely experience because the song had such a natural, breezy energy to it. Katrina Kaif and Sidharth Malhotra’s chemistry showcased a perfect dreamy, carefree romance. Even after ten years, I’m amazed by how beautifully the song has stayed with people. I love it when the song plays for dance performances by kids or at weddings. It’s one of those songs that takes you back to a nostalgic, happy memory.”
Armaan Malik reflected on the challenges of creating the song and how it has remained relevant over the years. He said, “Baar Baar Dekho and ‘Sau Aasmaan’ will always hold a very special place in my heart. I still remember the excitement around the song and how much fun it was recording it with Neeti. Creating a proper danceable Bollywood love song with that breezy, summery, almost EDM-esque sound is actually quite challenging because you want it to feel big and euphoric without losing the romance and soul of the melody. Amaal composed the song beautifully, and I think he really nailed that balance. The combination of his composition with Kumaar’s writing created something that felt fresh for its time, but still had that timeless Bollywood emotion at its core. Azeem Dayani’s music supervision and creative contribution also added so much to the song and helped elevate the overall sound. Ten years later, it’s honestly incredible to see the kind of love ‘Sau Aasmaan’ still gets. There’s something very special about making a song that becomes a part of people’s memories, and I feel very grateful that this song has done that for so many people.”

Following the collapse of a building in Delhi's Satya Niketan that claimed seven lives, the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) initiated surveys across 1,100 properties in 12 zones and commenced demolition of unsafe structures. MCD teams deployed hammer action to pull down the fifth floor of an adjacent weakened building that housed a paying guest facility. A local resident stated that basement pillar work was underway during heavy rain when the building caved in. Questions have been raised regarding civic negligence, past notices, and delayed emergency response before MCD initiated clearing and demolition operations.
Apple has officially launched the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, skipping a base iPhone 18 model for now. The iPhone 18 Pro starts at 1,199 US dollars, while the 18 Pro Max starts at 1,299 US dollars for the 256 GB variants, marking a 100-dollar price increase across models. Official Indian pricing is currently awaited. Alongside the smartphones, Apple introduced AirPods 5 with an open-ear design, the Apple Watch 12, and the Watch Ultra 4, with anticipation also building around Apple's first foldable phone.
A portion of an under-construction building collapsed in the Kudasan area of Gandhinagar, Gujarat, prompting an immediate rescue operation. The incident occurred around 9:30 PM when a concrete slab gave way, trapping several labourers beneath the debris. Fire department personnel and emergency response teams reached the site to clear the rubble and rescue survivors. At least 12 labourers have been safely pulled out and shifted to a local hospital for medical care, while search and rescue operations continue for others feared trapped.
In an interview with India Today, former Labour Secretary Sumita Dawra shared insights on bureaucratic accountability following the Satya Niketan building collapse in Delhi. Commenting on the suspension of civic officials, Dawra stated, "Suspension may not be a punishment, but it, reflects, it indicates visible action." She stressed that suspensions must be followed by swift investigations, proper inquiries, and the fixing of culpability. Dawra noted that addressing systemic issues requires examining violations across the entire chain of command, from junior engineers to senior supervisory authorities. Emphasizing the need for institutional deterrence, she said, "There should be exemplary punishment so that it's a warning for the system." She also highlighted the importance of leveraging modern technology, such as GIS mapping and municipal tax data, to monitor structural deviations and flag unauthorized constructions early.
In an interview with Maria Shakil on India Today, former Intelligence Bureau Special Director Yashovardhan Azad addressed systemic administrative failures and accountability lapses in Delhi's municipal governance following urban tragedies. Azad asserted that municipal commissioners and senior bureaucrats must be directly held accountable for rampant illegal constructions and safety oversights. Emphasizing top-level responsibility, he stated that "the buck should stop right at the top" and suggested issuing charge sheets to the municipal commissioner and housing development secretaries rather than only suspending junior personnel. He highlighted how councillors and local politicians exert pressure on junior engineers, protecting illegal establishments and avoiding structural oversight. Azad argued that IAS officers frequently escape disciplinary measures due to undefined culpability and close alignments with ministers. Calling the situation an absolute collusion between the political class and bureaucracy, he demanded systemic reforms to restore civic safety and administrative accountability across the capital.

It was at the 1992 Olympics in Barcelona when the mutterings about a new "secret weapon" started.
Dozens of Great Britain athletes had been taking a new product that increased muscle mass and improved athletic performance – a "wonder pill" that didn't fall foul of any doping rules.
They were talking about creatine.
Now found in tubs and bags on many supermarket shelves and tagged in your social feeds, it is the supplement of choice for millions of people and one of the most scientifically researched.
But back then, when it came on the scene at the very top of British elite sport, there were suspicions and stigma around the use of any substance described as 'performance enhancing' – even if it was legal.
From the minute an athlete wakes, to the moment they go to bed, they are thinking about how they can optimise their performance and recovery.
Today, creatine is just one of a long list of supplements taken by elite athletes in this pursuit of marginal gains. Some help with muscle size and strength, while others correct deficiencies in the diet.
"There are various reports in the literature of some studies that say maybe up to 90% of athletes take supplements. I often jokingly say that means 10% are lying," says Prof Graeme Close, professor of human physiology at Liverpool John Moores University.
"The sports teams that I've worked in, I think that's probably closer to 100% of athletes will be taking some form of supplementation."
So, what do supplements actually do and why do athletes take them? And in the world of strict liability, where elite athletes are solely responsible for what they put in their bodies, how do they make sure they stay clean?
While experts like Close advocate for seeking to meet nutritional needs through food in the first instance, it may not always be possible or practical to do this - and that is where supplements come in.
Take, for example, creatine, which is found naturally in meat and fish.
"You would need the best part of a kilogram of raw chicken a day to get the amount of creatine you need," says Close. But it is unsafe to eat raw poultry because of the food poisoning risk from harmful bacteria.
Creatine is a natural compound in the body produced in the kidneys, liver and pancreas. It is a quick source of energy for muscles, which is especially important for short-duration, high intensity activities such as sprinting.
Its big break as a supplement came in the 1990s when two scientists who had been researching it for two decades shared their findings with Steve Jennings, whose Maxim sports nutrition company supplied products to the British Olympic team.
During the 1992 Barcelona Games, investigative reporter Doug Gillon had learned of a 'secret trial' involving British athletes and seen a box of their Ergomax C150 – effervescent creatine tablets. He wrote that if the scientists' claims - that creatine could improve explosive athletic performance by 1-3% - were true, then "sport may never be the same again".
In terms of sport supplements and nutrition, he was right. By the time of the next Olympics in 1996, an estimated 80% of athletes were taking creatine, and since then it has become mainstream, with research suggesting there may be cognitive benefits as well as physical.
According to the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, the creatine breakthrough of the 1990s had "launched a new era in sports nutrition" and "sparked exploration into other supplements".
The global dietary supplements market size was valued at $209.5bn (£154bn) in 2025 and is projected to grow to $431.7bn (£317.4bn) by 2033, according to Grand View Research., external
Close, who oversaw nutrition for last year's British and Irish Lions rugby union tour, sees supplements as the "final piece of the jigsaw" rather than a starting point.
"What we're talking about is small margins of benefit, where actually these athletes who focus on the food, I think what you often find is that they've got the big-ticket items right," he says.
"So they're seeing great performance benefits because their overall diet is immaculate.
"They might be missing out on the one per-centers, but they've really nailed the 99 per-centers. And they often do better than those who chase the one per-centers but have not given enough attention to the 99 per-centers."
Australian cyclist Nicole Frain agrees, adding: "I'm a pretty big believer that they are called sport supplements. They are there to supplement the things you already do right.
"I don't think supplements are the answer to fix my problems.
"You need to be eating a balanced diet, training well, sleeping right, recovering well, hydrating – all of those things – before we add in all of the extras."
Close puts protein powders top of the list of supplements taken by athletes he works with, followed by creatine and vitamin D.
Protein powders maximise muscle repair and contribute to muscle growth, while creatine is a quick source of energy for muscles and important in short-duration, high-intensity activities like sprinting. Vitamin D, meanwhile, is essential for bone health and supports muscle function.
Other popular supplements include carbohydrate gels, which Close says were key in the first sub-two hour marathon run earlier this year by Kenyan long-distance runner Sabastian Sawe.
"As sport nutritionists we were all fascinated at what the fuelling programme was, and it was the sports drinks and gels that played a huge part of that fuelling," Close says.
"There was a calculation done of what it would take to break the two-hour marathon, and that did involve making sure that over 100 grams of supplemental carbohydrate were ingested per hour.
"And the reports coming out of the recent sub-two-hour marathon was that it was 110 grams of carbohydrate per hour that was achieved."
Supplements can improve performance, but there is an uneasy ring to describing them as 'performance enhancing' because of the association with banned substances and anti-doping rule violations.
So what determines whether something is on the World Anti-Doping Agency's (Wada) banned list?
"For Wada to put anything on the list, it's got to hit two out of three criteria: dangerous to health, performance enhancing, and against the spirit of sport," Close explains.
"So just because something enhances performance, if it's not dangerous to health and not against the spirit of sport, Wada will not touch it.
"So creatine is a good example.
"Though something like an anabolic steroid, where it's against the spirit of sport to be injecting yourself for a performance benefit, it's dangerous to health and it's performance enhancing - that hits all three."
But taking a supplement still carries anti-doping risks.
"No guarantee can be given that any particular supplement is free from prohibited substances," UK Anti-Doping advice states, urging athletes to "be vigilant" in using them.
And if you test positive for a prohibited substance, consuming it unintentionally can result in the same four-year ban as if you deliberately took it.
There are supplement-testing programmes which batch test products before they are sold to make sure they do not contain any Wada-prohibited substances.
One of those is Informed Sport, which says as many as one in 10 supplements is contaminated with ingredients and compounds prohibited in sport and points to a study carried out by the Anti-Doping Knowledge Centre that showed product contamination was responsible for 8% of all anti-doping violations between 2005 and 2022.
While Informed Sport is a very well used system among athletes, Wada makes it clear that quality assurance schemes can reduce but do not eliminate the risk of an anti-doping infringement.
If you do accept the risk, you need to be organised to keep track.
In the case of Great Britain rower Heidi Long, it takes a spreadsheet.
"I've recorded the batch number of every product that I've taken and its expiry date because if you take it after the expiry date the Informed Sport [certification] is no longer viable," she says.
Close says he has also done site visits to factories to see where the supplements are made to check the manufacturing processes because "the risk of failing a drugs test is huge".
There are risks to the general population too, he adds, saying: "You can be buying supplements off the internet that are made in somebody's garage and you've got no idea of the manufacturing processes."
He points to studies on creatine products which have found there is no creatine in them and so "you're completely wasting your money" and that in the worst case scenario it may contain substances that are dangerous to your health.
"So it is really important that the message is that while they can play a small role, the safety considerations are the key factor," he says.
There is, however, more than one way for an elite athlete to chase a competitive edge – and some are going back to basics.
For every trending supplement, there is an unprocessed, wholefood alternative – from the anti-inflammatory benefits of turmeric, staving off cramp with pickle juice or consumption of high-nitrate foods like beetroot before competition.
It is what Close calls a "food-first" or "food-only" approach and something he says every athlete should use as a starting point.
The latest to have its moment in the spotlight is an ancient Ethiopian grain called teff.
Used for thousands of years in traditional east African diets, teff is now making its mark globally in performance nutrition.
In comparison to other popular grains like wheat, rice and quinoa, teff has a high mineral content and is rich in calcium, iron and vitamin C. Naturally gluten-free and good for the gut, it is also unique for being a 'complete' protein, meaning it provides all nine essential amino acids required for human nutrition.
These superfood credentials have caught the attention of some of the world's best athletes over the years, from Olympic champion marathon runner Haile Gebrselassie to seven-time Grand Slam singles champion Venus Williams, and it is now becoming a more common sight on UK supermarket shelves.
British boxer Fran Hennessy was introduced to teff by her nutritionist and it is now part of her daily routine.
"I've never looked back," she says. "What I'm putting in my body is good fuel and energy and teff has so much. It energises you so much before a workout and it gives you the fibre you need."
As well as boosting her performances, Hennessy credits teff with being key to recovery.
She says: "Each meal I'm having there's a reason behind and everything that's in it there's a reason behind... I know what I'm putting in my body is fuelling me, recovering me, energising me."
Cost is another consideration when athletes are deciding on supplements.
"The supplement industry is really expensive," says Long. "And we're definitely not made of money. So I think it's really picking and choosing when you want to put that investment in."
She says it makes sense to have more supplements around racing time "when the performance is super critical and very time dependent".
"[But] on a daily basis if I can get the protein intake from my dinner and a glass of milk or yoghurt and breakfast then actually I was going to be eating that food anyway so it's not as expensive."
And then there is taste.
"I would much rather enjoy a coffee in the morning with friends or while I'm working rather than have one of the gels," she says. "Some of the gels ... you'll end up holding your nose when you take it.
"I guess it's just like the enjoyment of what you're taking, you know, it's nicer to eat food than it is to take supplements."

Labor Day sales are the last gasp of summer DIY season, and it almost always means steep discounts on tools and batteries—especially as retailers clear inventory space for the holidays. The Home Depot Labor Day sale goes pretty hard this year, bolstering the usual battery of BOGO deals, as well as end-of-season grill discounts.
Alas, not everything is a winner. The smart home and home-security deals I've seen for Home Depot are either not great deals—or they're on older models or services like Ring that WIRED doesn't recommend for privacy reasons. Check out WIRED's Best Tech Labor Day Deals of 2026, or the Best Amazon Labor Day Deals, if this is what you're after.
But here are the best deals on tools and grills that I've found for 2026's Home Depot Labor Day sale, or check out my colleague Kat Merck's Labor Day deals guide to getting an excellent tool starter kit for less than $400. You can also browse Home Depot's Labor Day deals by category, but fair warning: There's a lot to sift through.
Home Depot Labor Day Grill and Griddle Deals
The steepest Labor Day price cuts are often on grills and griddles. At Home Depot, the best deals are on Traeger's stock of pellet smokers that offer easy temperature control, but maybe a little less smoke than charcoal or wood cookers. These have the side benefit of maintaining utility through the cool months. In the temperate, four-season Pacific Northwest, I actually far prefer fall to summer as a grill and smoker season.
Discounts include a cool hundo off the basic model of Traeger's Woodridge smart pellet grill, whose bigger, upgraded version, the Woodridge Pro (8/10, WIRED Recommends), was WIRED's previous top-pick pellet smoker. Its no-fuss operation and cleaning, sophisticated temperature control, and absolute beastly capacity set it apart. But Home Depot's steepest discount is on Traeger's standby, entry-level Pro 22 smoker. We have not tested this recently, but after a dozen years it's a near-classic, and $390 is the lowest price it's seen all year.
Other deals among WIRED-recommended grills include $50 off a couple of Weber's durable, last-you-forever standbys—the Weber Kettle and the Weber Spirit E-210. I and fellow WIRED reviewer Scott Gilbertson tend to love these two models precisely because they are basic, durable, reliable, and low-cost. The Weber Kettle, especially, can be upgraded with smart features into a temp-controlled, smart-charcoal beast.
This $50 off deal tends to be the standard Weber deal. But the price already starts out affordable, and so the sale price amounts to an excellent value on a grill that's likely to be with you a while. If you'd like your kettle in green, you can get it for half off, a mere $100.
Home Depot Milwaukee Tool Deals
Buying power tools is all about picking an ecosystem (and a battery pack). WIRED reviewer Scott Gilbertson favors Milwaukee for its intersection between reliability and value, and for tentpole sales Home Depot usually offers free battery packs or buy-one-get one deals.
One of the best and most versatile tools Gilbertson recommends is Milwaukee's excellent impact driver ($179). Lucky you: During the Labor Day sale, this comes free with the purchase of the portable M18 battery you'll need to operate it wirelessly. If you've already got a Milwaukee battery, the BOGO still holds for an assortment of tools including an oscillating multi-tool that's also one of the more underrated tools in the DIYer home kit.
Home Depot Ryobi Landscaping and Tool Deals
Ryobi is the brand that former WIRED reviewer Parker Hall has consistently recommended for yard and landscaping tools, in large part because of their service philosophy. In many regions including mine (the Pacific Northwest), Ryobi keeps a local repair technician on retainer to come and fix your mower or blower, instead of making you ship your machine to a repair center somewhere. This is clutch, even if you won't have to use the service often.
Home Depot is offering its usual BOGO battery deals on Ryobi's landscaping tools, including the heavy-duty leaf blower ($159) you're going to need sooner than you expect.
For entry-level tool kits, my colleague Kat Merck also recommends this shockingly low-cost starter power tool kit from Ryobi—which is not going to make you the envy of any job site, but offers great value and torque for the money. This set offers a ½-inch drill/driver, an impact driver, a circular saw, and an LED light. There's also another discount kit with a sander, drill/driver, and circular saw.
Home Depot DeWalt Tool BOGO
My editor, Kat Merck, is a DeWalt devotee. But the DeWalt Deals are a bit more specialized this season. There's still a few good BOGO offers, though, especially if you're in the market for a circular saw or angle grinder, or a hammer drill kit to carve holes into masonry.

The suspected murderers of two Australian surfers and an American at a Mexican surfing hotspot have gone on trial, two years after the killings in a suspected robbery.
Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, respectively, and 30-year-old American friend Jack Carter Rhoad were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast when they were shot dead in Baja California state.
They had been camping in a remote beachside area when they were allegedly attacked in April 2024.
Their bodies were found dumped in a cliff-top shaft several days after they went missing.
They bore gunshot wounds to their heads. Three men are on trial over their killings.
The Robinsons’ parents traveled to the port city of Ensenada for the start of the proceedings on Monday.
Bereaved mother Debra Robinson stared at the accused before bursting into tears in the courtroom.
“It’s about representing our sons, being here for them. I know they want us to be here,” her partner, Martin Robinson, had earlier told reporters.
“We want to find out what happened. We want to find out why.”
Authorities allege the men were murdered during an attempt to steal their pickup truck, which was found burned near their bodies.
Three witnesses appeared before the court on Monday, including the stepson of one of the defendants, who described his stepfather as violent.
Testifying from an adjoining room with his face concealed, he said he accompanied the accused to the crime scene, waiting nearby when the “commotion” began.
“I heard a lot of noise,” he said, explaining that he had run away but rejoined the group after they called him.
He said they warned him that “the same thing that happened to the gringos would happen to him” if he said anything.
The crime sparked outrage and grief in Australia and the US, where the surfers’ friends and families galvanized a major search on social media for their bodies.
Callum Robinson played professional lacrosse in the US. His brother Jake was pursuing a career in medicine.
Rhoad was killed a few months before he was set to marry.
Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organized crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity doesn’t usually affect tourists.
Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.
Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were murdered in 2015 while traveling through the northwestern state of Sinaloa in the north-west. Their bodies were later burned.

Images from this year’s Ocean Photographer of the Year competition, presented by Oceanographic Magazine and Blancpain, featuring some of the best coastal, drone, and underwater photographs selected from more than 15,000 entries
Winner, Female Fifty Fathoms Award. An American crocodile moves through the mangroves of Cuba, a habitat that provides shelter for crocodiles feeding, breeding, nesting, and raising their young.
Finalist, Adventure. Three surfers converge on the same wave at Teahupoʻo, French Polynesia, after a paddler is thrown from his board. The tow-in surfer immediately changes course, grabbing the cameraman to avoid a collision.
Overall Winner, Ocean Photographer of the Year 2026. An adult seahorse pictured with newly born juveniles in the shallow seaweed-filled waters of Moorea, French Polynesia. While it is not known whether these seahorses are related, their arrangement creates the impression of a farewell, as if the tiny seahorses have gathered around their father after he has released them into the world.
Finalist, Fine Art. A hinge-back cleaning shrimp rests against a pink barrel sponge in Bali, Indonesia; its eye are sharply focused while the surrounding colors dissolve into a soft blur.
Winner, Female Fifty Fathoms Award. A mother humpback whale and her calf glide through Tonga’s warm, sheltered waters. The calf stays close to its mother at first, then becomes curious, swimming in playful circles and approaching the camera. The mother remains calm and watchful, guiding her young when it comes too close.
Finalist, Conservation Impact. Three gentoo penguins stand beside the rusting remains of the former Hektor whaling station at Whalers Bay, Deception Island, Antarctica. Once a center for Antarctic whaling, the site is now being reclaimed by wildlife and the harsh polar environment.
Finalist, Adventure. Sunlight pours through cracks in an iceberg in East Greenland, illuminating the seabed like a natural theater. Created by a storm just days earlier, these openings allow light to reach an underwater world usually hidden in darkness.
Finalist, Wildlife. A New Zealand fur seal tears apart a rough skate in the waters of New Zealand, while seabirds gather for the scraps. Unable to swallow such large prey whole, the seal throws the skate repeatedly to break it into smaller pieces.
Second Place, Fine Art. A common octopus reveals its intricate suckers, textured skin, and watchful eye in the waters of Blue Heron Bridge, Florida. Known for its rich marine life, this shallow dive site provided the setting for a close encounter with one of the ocean’s most intelligent animals.
Third Place, Human Connection. A teenager stands at Bronte Ocean Pool, Sydney, as a powerful swell sends waves crashing over the closed bathing site. While the conditions forced beaches to shut, people watched the waves from behind the fence. A group of locals climbed into the closed area and stood on the edge, waiting for the waves to crash over them and sweep them across the pool.
First Place, Conservation Hope. A great hammerhead shark, known as Tamataroa in French Polynesia, is photographed at 55 meters depth in Tiputa Pass, Rangiroa Atoll, during a population survey. This image represents the moment an anonymous shark becomes a known individual. Through photo identification and laser-calibrated video photogrammetry, scientists can track sharks over time to measure their size, sex, and population trends.
Finalist, Conservation Hope. A Hawaiian monk seal rests with her week-old pup on Kaimana Beach in Waikīkī. Mothers nurse their pups for around six weeks without feeding, losing up to a third of their body weight while the pup grows before becoming independent.
Finalist, Conservation Hope. At sunrise, a traditional fishing village shares the coastline with rows of oﬀshore wind turbines stretching across the sea, on Nanri Island, Fujian, China.
First Place, Conservation Impact. A whale shark is surrounded by divers and snorkelers in the Maldives, revealing the overwhelming pressure that crowded wildlife tourism can place on marine animals. With almost 50 people visible in the frame, this image captures the reality behind some popular wildlife encounters: an animal seeking space while people compete for a closer view. It challenges us to rethink how we experience and protect the species we admire.
Third Place, Conservation Hope. A male white-spotted puﬀerfish creates an intricate spawning nest in the sand. The fish carefully shapes a two-meter-wide radial pattern using only his fins. Built over several days, this structure and its subtle details reveal the extraordinary eﬀort this small fish invests in reproduction.
Finalist, Ocean Unseen. A pygmy seahorse, no larger than a grain of rice, clings to a delicate hydroid in the reefs of Raja Ampat, Indonesia. Perfectly camouflaged, these tiny animals are rarely seen, even by experienced divers.
Finalist, Conservation Impact. A silky shark circles helplessly after taking bait from an illegal longline, its fate sealed by a steel hook and heavy line designed to prevent escape. Photographed less than 48 hours after Baja California’s seasonal shark-fishing ban ended, the image reveals a hidden reality unfolding far from shore. A small group of pilot fish remains beside the shark, highlighting how the loss of one animal can ripple throughout an entire ecosystem.
Finalist, Human Connection. From above, moored fishing and tourist boats bloom across the sapphire-blue sea, like the petals of a flower. Fringed by golden coastal vegetation, the shoreline becomes an abstract pattern that is diﬃcult to recognize from ground level.
First Place, Ocean Unseen. A ribbonfish rises vertically through the dark waters of Osezaki, Japan. Its long, silver body and delicate fins are adapted for life in the open ocean. This image was captured during a winter blackwater dive. Around the ribbonfish, a swarm of salps—small jelly-like animals that feed on tiny particles in the ocean—provides a glimpse of life moving through the deep sea.
Finalist, Conservation Hope. Animal care workers perform daily physiotherapy on Norah, a juvenile harbour porpoise undergoing rehabilitation at SOS Dolfijn in the Netherlands. Rescued after being stranding on the Dutch coast, Norah was treated for multiple serious conditions, including pneumonia and severe muscle spasms. This image captures the intensive care required to return her to the sea.

Quantum cybersecurity startup QNu Labs has raised ₹200 Cr (around $21 Mn) in its Series A1 funding round co-led by the state-backed National Quantum Mission and Speciale Invest, along with participation from Sony Innovation Fund, Gaja Capital and Artha Ventures, among others. The Bengaluru-based startup plans to use the fresh capital across R&D, sales and go-to-market strategy, and forging partnerships. Cofounder and CEO Sunil Gupta told Inc42 that the startup will also invest in internal processes, IT and automation as it moves from a technology development phase into a “proof-of-scale” business. The latest fundraise takes QNu Labs’ total capital raised to ₹375 Cr. Prior to this, QNu Labs raised ₹60 Cr in its Series A funding round. The investment comes at a time when QNu Labs is expanding beyond its existing cybersecurity portfolio. The startup has built a new platform, QShield 2.0, focused on the discovery and assessment of cryptographic assets as enterprises begin preparing for quantum-safe migration. It is also working on security solutions for drones and satellites, with its drone security technology already undergoing pilots. Gupta said QNu Labs expects the offering to cater to the defence sector. Additionally, the fundraise will also help QNu Labs meet the matching requirement for its RDI project. After being awarded a ₹150 Cr project under the government’s Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund, QnU was required to raise a matching amount from its side. The fresh capital will help it meet this requirement, with the startup saying it has already signed the final term sheet for the project. Founded in 2016 by Gupta and Srinivasa Rao Aluri, QNu Labs is building cybersecurity products aimed at protecting data and communications against quantum computing-led threats. It currently offers solutions based on quantum random number generation (QRNG), quantum key distribution (QKD) and post-quantum cryptography (PQC). It claims that its quantum-safe VPN is currently its most sought-after product. It has around 180 employees as of now. Underlining the necessity of the fund raise, Gupta said quantum tech is moving closer to mainstream adoption, with India targeting 2029 for the transition. “Now the common understanding across the globe is that this tech will become mainstream in the next 2 to 3 years,” he said. The startup is also strengthening its international expansion, with a presence in Australia and the US and partnerships in other markets. While it sells hardware and software in India, its international business largely focuses on subscription-based platforms for enterprises across sectors such as banking and healthcare.

When grazier Peter Lake moved to the Clarence Valley in the New South Wales northern rivers region in 2007, he knew was “buying in flood country with … eyes open”.
His cattle farm, about halfway between Yamba and Grafton, borders the Coldstream River and has flooded five times since 2009.
“Out of 130 acres … in a major flood we would have maybe 15 acres that were flood-free,” he said. Lake has systems in place to prepare for such events, including moving cattle to the dry paddocks, where they would also store fodder to feed the animals.
But the amount of safe ground is shrinking: in the historically big flood in 2022, “we only had just a few acres of flood-free land”. Because of both drought and frequent floods, “we just haven’t been able to successfully grow a fodder crop for some years”.
“If we’re going to have more frequent and more severe major events … we need to change the way we think about how we manage,” Lake said. “If rising sea levels impact on us, it’ll just this make property less and less viable.”
Agricultural damages are among $855.1bn in economic losses projected Australia-wide by the end of the century due to coastal flooding, according to a Climate Council report released on Thursday.
The report forecasts that more than 267,000 coastal properties and 2m hectares (4.9m acres) of Australian land will be damaged by flooding by 2100 as sea levels rise.
Queensland (93,157 properties), NSW (71,210) and Western Australia (51,366) are the three states with the greatest number of homes at risk.
The Gold Coast, Brisbane and Melbourne are the metropolitan areas expected to be worst affected.
The Gold Coast, the country’s most exposed urban area, faces $84.4bn in projected economic losses, while in Melbourne, losses are concentrated in low-lying areas around Port Phillip Bay and the Yarra River.
The Climate Council report is based on mapping coastal flooding by 2100, taking into account both sea level rise and storm surges under the climate scenario known as RCP4.5 – which projects a 2.7C increase in global temperature by the end of the century, similar to expected heating based on current policies worldwide.
It was co-authored by Prof Tom Kompas at the University of Melbourne, whose modelling of the economic impacts was also published in the peer-reviewed journal Scientific Reports and drew upon localised projections at 239 hotspots around Australia.
Kompas said the costs – an estimated $274.3bn in property losses and $580.7bn in land use damages – were a conservative estimate, and did not take into account the additional impacts of coastal erosion or significant ice sheet melt.
He said due to the scale of agricultural losses, there was a food security issue potentially coming as well: damage is projected to affect 619,713 hectares (1.5m acres) of farming land.
Sea levels have risen, on average by more than 22cm globally since 1900, with human-caused global heating the dominant cause of the rise since 1970. An additional 14cm rise is expected in Australia by 2050, increasing the frequency of permanent inundation and tidal flooding.
Kompas said that while reducing greenhouse gas emissions to limit global heating was of paramount importance, “we have to start planning and responding and adapting now”.
“The nice thing about the work is it shows where the hotspots are and what … assets will be impacted. So we can start to plan for how to deal with that.
“The first thing, of course, is not to build on flood plains, which is common still.”

Google picks Finland for its largest single investment in Europe
- Published
Google will buy up to half the electricity produced by one of Finland's nuclear power plants as part of a record €13bn (£11bn; $15bn) investment in the country's AI infrastructure, the company announced.
The US tech giant said the package would fund three new data centres, expand an existing site and support energy projects to power growing demand for AI services.
"This is Google's largest single investment in Europe and a testament to Finland's leadership in responsibly building AI infrastructure," the company said on Wednesday.
"Google's decision is a clear testament to our strengths," Finland's Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said in a statement.
As part of the deal, Google signed a 22-year contract with Finnish utility Fortum to buy up to 50% of the output from the Loviisa nuclear power plant.
Earlier this week, TikTok announced a $1bn investment in Finland to build a new data centre in Kouvola, pointing to the country's "strong digital infrastructure, clean energy mix, robust data governance and skilled tech talent".
Finland has emerged as an attractive location for data centres because of its cool climate, plentiful low-carbon electricity and relatively uncongested power grid. The colder temperatures can reduce the energy needed to cool facilities packed with computer servers.
Technology companies are racing to secure power supplies as the AI boom drives demand for vast networks of data centres.
The Google investment is expected to support more than 37,000 jobs during construction and boost Finland's GDP by €3.6bn a year, according to Google. Construction is set to take place in 2027 and 2028.
"The value of the data economy extends far beyond direct investment into spurring innovation, research and development," Orpo added.
"Deepening our collaboration with Google will deliver lasting benefits for both parties."
Google will build new data centres in Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala, while expanding its existing facility in Hamina, which it established after converting a former paper mill in 2009.
The infrastructure will help support products such as its AI chatbot Gemini, alongside services including Search, Maps and YouTube.
Google said the investments also covered "clean energy projects, and dedicated nature and community funds to support local biodiversity, education, research, and workforce development".
"Google is proud to deepen our roots in Finland," said Ruth Porat, president and chief investment officer of Alphabet and Google.
"This investment underscores Google's commitment to grow our presence responsibly, pairing the expansion of our technical infrastructure with new energy capacity, grid enhancements, and energy affordability initiatives," she added.
Earlier this year, Google's parent company Alphabet raised its global spending plans to as much as $205bn as it sought to expand computing capacity for AI services.
The agreement with Fortum provides long-term financial certainty for the Loviisa plant, which currently generates about 10% of Finland's electricity.
Fortum said Google's commitment would support an investment programme aimed at extending the life of the nuclear station and increasing its generating capacity.

Lonnie Bunch Protected the Smithsonian From More Than Trump
As pressures bore down on an American institution, its secretary held firm.
Americans may not realize for many years just how lucky they were that Lonnie G. Bunch III led the Smithsonian Institution from 2019 to 2026. Bunch has announced that he will step down at the end of this year. He insists that the timing is his own, and we should do him the honor of believing him—notwithstanding the immense pressure the administration has applied to the Smithsonian generally and Bunch personally since Donald Trump returned to office last year.
Bunch, 73, would likely have chosen to retire earlier if not for his sense of duty—his conviction (which few dispute) that he was the best person to guide the Smithsonian through a turbulent period. The Smithsonian is the world’s largest museum, education, and research complex. It’s also “part of the glue,” as Bunch himself said shortly after taking office, “that holds the country together.”
Since his appointment as the Smithsonian’s top official—its 14th secretary and the first historian and Black man to hold the position—in June 2019, Bunch has been the glue holding the Smithsonian together. Through a combination of principled stances and deft political skills, he has kept the sprawling institution on mission and aligned with its public. Chief Justice John Roberts, who serves as the Smithsonian’s chancellor, said in a statement that Bunch has “pursued excellence in the telling of our nation’s story” and that the Smithsonian has “benefited greatly from his wisdom, vision, and leadership.”
Bunch is a fighter, but a smart one. He has often struck me as a master of institutional jiu-jitsu—a leader who knows instinctively when to hold the line, when to yield, and how to convert yielding to the advantage of the institution he has done so much to advance and protect. “When you’re Black in America,” he told The New York Times earlier this year, “you’ve got to figure out how to get through, right? You’ve got to figure out how to build allies, when to stand firm, when to bang the table. So in some ways, all of that prepared me for this moment.”
Bunch has worked at the Smithsonian since 1978, interrupted by stints at the California African American Museum in the 1980s and the Chicago Historical Society in the early 2000s. His tenure as secretary included the upheavals of 2020 and 2021, when—after the killing of George Floyd and amid the coronavirus pandemic—activists on the left were accusing museums across the country, including the Smithsonian, of being bastions of white privilege, colonialism, and cultural theft. Bunch remained calm and compassionate in the face of these critiques, compromising when appropriate, but never giving in to bullying.
It surely helped that his greatest achievement prior to becoming the Smithsonian’s top official was planning, raising funds for, and launching the National Museum of African American History and Culture. The museum, which opened to great fanfare in 2016, has been hugely popular. Under Bunch’s leadership, the museum balanced a forthright, profoundly moving description of slavery and its long aftereffects with exhibits that bear witness to the extraordinary flowering of African American culture, celebrating a panoply of achievements by Black Americans across many fields of human endeavor.
The Smithsonian was founded by an act of Congress in 1846. During the Civil War, it created a controversy by refusing to host a lecture series presented by abolitionists. The institution’s leadership eventually relented, but Frederick Douglass, the most prominent abolitionist of the day, was still not permitted to speak. At the 2019 ceremony installing him as secretary, Bunch referred back to those days: “Today we are here speaking in a place as an African American, where Frederick Douglass could not speak, but we are a different institution.”
Bunch’s leadership, and the Smithsonian’s resilience, has been severely tested since Trump’s return to power. Efforts by the institution to tell what Kim Sajet, the former director of the National Portrait Gallery, described as “a fuller, more American story” and “one that fosters connection, reflection and understanding” came into conflict with White House officials who felt that the “fuller story” being told was overly focused on moral failure, hypocrisy, and oppression.
The new administration was quick to target the Smithsonian. Some of what gave Bunch moral authority during the Biden years now threatened to work against him.
In March 2025, an executive order noted that the United States had witnessed “a concerted and widespread effort to rewrite our Nation’s history.” The Smithsonian, it stated, had, “in recent years, come under the influence of a divisive, race-centered ideology.” Trump announced that he was firing Sajet. The Smithsonian regents asserted that only Bunch had authority over such personnel decisions, but she resigned anyway.
More recently, the administration has ramped up pressure on the Smithsonian, demanding an overhaul of its presentations to rid them of perceived liberal bias and attempting to force its hand with explicit threats, such as pulling funding and erecting warning signs in front of the National Museum of American History. (Although it is independent, the biggest share of the institution’s budget comes from the federal government.)
Bunch has had to figure out how to handle these various assaults without allowing the Smithsonian’s mission to be compromised. He has said plenty on the public record—all of it sage and diplomatic, yet consistently firm on questions of principle. I can only imagine what private conversations he has been having on a daily basis.
Thanks to the double whammy of COVID and activist pressures, few leaders of any prominent organization have had a fun time since 2020. But Bunch has been the leader of an enormous—and enormously important—institution that’s explicitly in the business of (among other things) telling the American story at a time when the question of how to tell that story has become so fraught and divisive.
What to do in such circumstances? Perhaps Americans could all begin by just agreeing that the pandas in the National Zoo (which is part of the Smithsonian) are very, very cute. And then, perhaps, that the Apollo 11 command module in the National Air and Space Museum—the one that carried Neil Armstrong, Michael Collins, and Buzz Aldrin to the moon and back—is really cool. If so, perhaps they can next agree that Bunch, during his tenure at the helm of the Smithsonian, has been the exact combination of resolute leader and compassionate and good-humored public servant that America needed him to be.

Several videos have gone viral on social media following the devastating flash floods in Nepal on August 26, 2026. Some users shared a video claiming that after the disaster, the world’s largest Shaligram, said to be more than 170 million years old and weighing 30 tonnes, was found in Muktinath.
In this context, Zee News put out a report with a screenshot from the viral video and, along with the hashtags #Nepal, #Flood and #Shaligram, wrote: “Viral Video: Floods have revealed a secret, a 170-million-year-old Shaligram has been found.”
Shaligrams are naturally formed stones traditionally found in Nepal’s Kali Gandaki River, and revered by Hindus as representations of the deity, Vishnu.
Right-wing X user Amitabh Choudhary (@MithilaWaaala), who has been found spreading misinformation and comminal propaganda several times in the past, shared a video and wrote: “Stone older than dinosaurs. Worlds largest Shaligram weighing 31 tonnes is revered as Form of Bhagwan Vishnu has been found in Nepal.”
Kisi ne sahi hi kaha hai, “शुरुआत भी वही, सफ़र भी वही, और अंत भी वही।”
Stone older than dinosaurs !!
Worlds largest Shaligram weighing 31 tonnes is revered as Form of Bhagwan Vishnu has been found in Nepal 🇳🇵 pic.twitter.com/GIv851LJbV
— Amitabh Chaudhary (@MithilaWaaala) August 29, 2026
X user Shashank Shekhar Jha, who claims to be a Supreme Court lawyer, and others such as @Nalanda_index, @CodexZeroTR, @Krishnavallabhi, @bhaktSenapati, along with several Facebook and Instagram users, too, shared videos and photos with similar claims.
Fact Check
To find out the truth behind the viral claim, we performed a relevant keyword search. This led us to reports published on June 30, 2026, by Himalaya Times and Online Khabar featuring images of the giant sculpture seen in the viral video.
The reports stated that a 22-foot-tall Shaligram sculpture in Nepal’s Mustang district was gradually becoming a centre of religious faith. According to the reports, sculptors from the Nepal Academy of Fine Arts carved a huge rock on the banks of the Kali Gandaki River in Jomsom in Gharpajhong rural municipality area and created the 22-foot-tall Shaligram replica between April 20 and May 4, 2026.
During our investigation, we found a report by a website called Desh Sanchar. According to the report, the 22-foot-tall sculpture had been unveiled on the evening of May 28, 2026, after religious rituals on the banks of the Kali Gandaki River.
We also located a video uploaded on April 23, 2026 on the Facebook page, Nepal Raibar, in which artists could be seen carving a rock to create a Shaligram statue.
We also geolocated the Shaligram statue shown in the viral video. It’s located on the Kali Gandaki River, opposite ‘Thakkhola Lodge & Jimihendrix Restaurant in Jomsom. When we compared Google Street View images from 2025 with the viral video, we found that the 2025 image only showed a large rock.
This makes it clear that the Shaligram statue shown in the viral video is not a natural or ancient stone. Rather, it is a statue created by carving a rock.
We also tried to look for the sources of all the variants of the now-viral visuals. We found the original version of the video and the screenshots shared by Zee News on the Instagram account of a user named Durga Prasad Poudel. It was posted on June 2, 2026.
View this post on Instagram
Similarly, we found the second viral video uploaded on June 30, 2026, on the Instagram account of a user named Rijan Dongol.
View this post on Instagram
The third viral video was shared on June 8, 2026, on the Facebook account of a user named Arjun Singh. Its caption reads: “A huge 22-foot-tall Shaligram statue is located on the banks of the Kali Gandaki River in Jomsom, Mustang. This monumental work, inaugurated by Jagadguru Shankaracharya Mahaswami Vidushekara Bharati, attracts a large number of pilgrims and stands as a major spiritual and cultural site in Nepal.”
Thus, all three viral videos featuring the Shaligram statue have been available on social media since June 2026. They have absolutely no connection with the recent disaster in Nepal in August.
Overall, the claim by Zee News and other users that after the recent disaster in Nepal, the world’s largest Shaligram, more than 170 million years old and weighing 30 tonnes, was found in Muktinath is completely misleading. In reality, the 22-foot-tall Shaligram statue seen in the viral video was created by carving a rock on the banks of the Kali Gandaki River in Mustang district, during April–May 2026. The videos of the Shaligram statue circulating on social media are also from June 2026 and have no connection with the recent disaster in Nepal.

NEW DELHI: The Delhi Police investigation into the Satya Niketan building collapse has revealed the sequence of renovation work that allegedly weakened the structure before it came crashing down, officials said on Wednesday.
According to the investigation, renovation work was carried out at the building around 10 days before the incident on the instructions of Mahesh Gupta, news agency ANI reported.
Police said the work involved levelling the basement with the ground floor, for which around three truckloads of construction debris were filled into the basement.
On the day of the collapse, a wall on the ground floor was allegedly removed to create additional space for a shop.
The structural changes, coupled with the additional load in the basement, allegedly affected the building's stability, leading to the collapse, police said.
Labour contractor Sanoj Kumar, 35, who was allegedly hired for the renovation work, was apprehended from Kasganj in Uttar Pradesh and subsequently arrested in the case.
During questioning, Sanoj allegedly told police that Mahesh Gupta paid him Rs 2,800 per day for carrying out the renovation work, ANI reported.
The investigation also revealed that the building was being used as a paying guest accommodation.
PG operator Shudhanshu Lovneesh, 31, was arrested by police.
Police said Shudhanshu and his associate Shubham Tyagi had taken four floors of the building on lease in August 2025 for Rs 1.05 lakh per month.
According to police, the property was taken at a comparatively lower rent because of its dilapidated condition.
Investigators have alleged that Shudhanshu was aware of the renovation work but remained negligent despite knowing that the changes could affect the building's stability.
Mahesh Gupta, Sanoj Kumar and Shudhanshu Lovneesh were produced before a court, which granted two days of police custody.
Further investigation is underway.
Seven people were killed after the five-storey building collapsed in Satya Niketan on September 6.

Late last week, word started leaking that the National Institutes of Health (NIH) had reached an agreement with the Department of Defense that would see part of the NIH’s budget used to fund research at the Department of Defense. So, on the Friday just prior to a US holiday weekend, the Department of Defense released a copy of the agreement and confirmed that it had been signed roughly a month earlier. The move is striking for a number of reasons, ranging from the existing budget disparities between the two parties involved to the fact that the money would be used for projects that the current NIH leadership has explicitly rejected.
The agreement itself sets up a system where the NIH would transfer money to the Department of Defense to fund staff and projects that would “support the advanced development of medical countermeasures against pandemic influenza, chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) threats, and emerging infectious diseases.” The money would come out of the budget for the NIH’s National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, or NIAID, to which Congress has allocated $6.6 billion in 2026. The agreement is set to run for a decade.
Left unspecified is just how much of the NIAID budget will be spent on Defense projects. Reporting by Nature suggests that the Department of Defense was looking for up to a third of its total budget but was being told to settle for about 10 percent. There’s obviously an enormous disparity between the budgets of these two agencies, given that the 2026 Defense budget is roughly $1 trillion. That budget is under considerable strain, however, due to the open-ended nature of the conflict with Iran. The deal has also been announced at a time when the NIH has been struggling to issue sufficient grants to use the money that Congress allocated to it.

Canada is set to impose retaliatory tariffs on billions of dollars’ worth of American imports early on Tuesday, escalating a trade fight with its largest trading partner as tensions between US president Donald Trump and Canadian prime minister Mark Carney intensify.
The tariffs, which take effect at 12.01am on Tuesday, will range from 15% to 50% and apply to products covering C$27.6bn in imports from the US. The measures will target sectors including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics – industries that have been most affected by US tariffs.
The retaliatory tariffs come “as a result of the United States’ decision to impose a 50% tariff on $27.6bn of Canadian goods effective August 22”, the Canadian government said.
“Canada’s counter-measures do not apply to US goods that are in transit to Canada on the day on which they come into force,” it added.
Tensions between Canada and the US have intensified in recent weeks, with Carney last week urging the Trump administration to “start being serious” as the trade dispute has increasingly spilled into broader diplomatic tensions.
Trump and senior US officials have repeatedly criticized Canada and its leadership, while Trump has taken a series of symbolic digs at Canada including signing an executive order renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America” – which Canadians have rejected.
US vice-president JD Vance has also reportedly mocked Carney, apparently saying the Canadian prime minister “comes in and puffs his chest out and says: ‘I’m going to, like, out-tough Donald Trump.’”
Last month, Trump announced a new 50% tariff on cars and raw materials from Canada. He accused the country of “ripping off” the US “for years”, adding: “We don’t need Canada, they need us!”
Carney said last month Canada would not accept a US trade deal that weakened French-language protections, saying American negotiators viewed the measures as an “irritant”, while “in Quebec, these are rights”.
Quebec has long maintained laws aimed at protecting French and preserving its distinct cultural identity. Those measures have become a sticking point in the trade talks between the two countries, with American negotiators raising concerns about rules they say can disadvantage US businesses.

Trump’s Smithsonian vendetta, briefly explained
After a resignation announcement, what comes next for the Smithsonian?
Welcome to The Logoff: The head of the Smithsonian Institution will resign after weathering nearly two years of attacks by President Donald Trump.
What’s happening? Lonnie G. Bunch III, the secretary of the Smithsonian, announced on Tuesday that he will step down at the end of 2026 after more than seven years in the role.
Bunch’s retirement isn’t entirely about Trump; he’s 73 and has already served longer as secretary than his two most recent predecessors.
But the president, who has waged a relentless campaign against what the White House has described as “improper, divisive, or anti-American ideology” at the Smithsonian, is indisputably part of the story. As Bunch put it to the New York Times on Tuesday, “at a certain point, I’d like to wake up in the morning and not look at my cellphone.”
What has Trump done to the Smithsonian? Since last spring, Trump has gone after the Smithsonian system for promoting “narratives that portray American and Western values as inherently harmful and oppressive.” He has threatened its funding, forced out the director of the National Portrait Gallery, and attempted to meddle with its exhibits. His ability to successfully make changes has been limited by the Smithsonian’s structure — but a new secretary could give Trump far more control.
The president also, unsurprisingly, wants more Trump: administration officials have reportedly pressed for a new Portrait Gallery exhibit focusing on the president.
What’s next? Trump doesn’t officially have a role in selecting Bunch’s successor, who will be chosen by the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents — but that board does include Vice President JD Vance and multiple Republican members of Congress, so he might as well.
Trump will surely want to install a loyalist, which means — as the Washington Post’s art and architecture critic Philip Kennicott explained on Tuesday — that the Smithsonian’s fate could depend on the ability of the rest of the board, and especially its chancellor, Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts, to resist.
And with that, it’s time to log off…
