Your food may be safe. Its packaging is another story.
A sweeping new study shows why you should ditch plastic food wrapping whenever possible.
Most people decide if it’s safe to eat an old tub of yogurt in the fridge or canned tuna in the back of the cupboard by checking its sell-by date. But no label indicates that pesticides, phthalates, PFAS, or other hazardous chemicals could be seeping from those containers into your food.
Of more than 15,000 chemicals that come in contact with food, a new peer-reviewed study found that 1,222 pose serious health risks such as cancer and reproductive harm. And the vast majority — 87 percent, or more than 13,200 — lack enough accessible information to even estimate their risks.
The fact that there’s not enough publicly available information for independent scientists to assess the safety of chemicals that can contaminate food is “the elephant in the room,” said study co-author Jane Muncke, managing director at the nonprofit Food Packaging Forum Foundation, which led the research, published Tuesday in the journal Environmental Science & Technology.
Consumers trust that when regulators allow chemicals in products like food packaging, it’s because it’s been through safety testing, Muncke said. “But that’s not the case,” she said. “And it doesn’t make sense.”
The team has done a “very, very good job” highlighting how little is known about the risks of substances that affect everyone, said Maricel Maffini, an independent chemical safety and regulation expert who was not involved in the study but has collaborated with Muncke in the past.
Because the study focused on a list that people in industry and regulators regard as reliable, it’s looking under the proverbial lamppost, Maffini said. While there’s plenty of information suggesting that many of these chemicals should not be on the market or should have stronger regulations, she said, there’s so much information beyond that list that’s missing.
In previous work, Muncke and her team identified more than 15,000 chemicals used in food processing or packaging from lists of substances approved by regulators in the United States, China, Japan, and countries in Europe and South America or that had been identified in studies. In the new paper, they analyzed that “jaw-dropping” number of chemicals, Muncke said, to flag the most problematic.
To maximize the utility of their priority list, the team used only data obtained from governmental and regulatory agencies linking a chemical to human health hazards such as cancer, reproductive harm, or ability to concentrate in the body.
That yielded a priority list of 1,222 chemicals that they ranked into four tiers, with the highest to lowest evidence of human exposure from food-contact materials. Ninety-four chemicals known to seep into food and detected in breast milk, blood, or other human samples were assigned to Tier 1, the highest priority for regulators and companies to consider phasing out.
These chemicals include liver- and immune system-damaging PFAS “forever chemicals,” which make food wrappers grease- or water-resistant; the likely carcinogen styrene, used to produce takeout packages and refrigerated dairy food containers; hormone-disrupting phthalates, added to make plastics like those that hold vegetable oils flexible; and bisphenol A, added to hard plastics and can linings and a poster child for endocrine disruptors’ ability to impair development at low doses.
Studies have found these and other chemicals leaching from containers into a diverse array of food and beverages, including water, infant formula, orange juice, ice cream, yogurt and cream, oils, cake, and fatty foods.
The next highest priority list, Tier 2, included an additional 264 hazardous chemicals that leach into food but have not been detected in biomonitoring studies. At least, not yet.
Recommendations to protect consumers
Experts with the Food Packaging Forum say regulators can take simple steps to reduce people’s exposure to harmful chemicals found or used in food-contact materials, starting with moving away from evaluating one chemical at a time.
- People are exposed to multiple synthetic chemicals simultaneously through food-contact materials, textiles, personal-care products, air pollution, and more. Regulators should introduce a “mixture allocation factor,” which creates a safety margin that accounts for the combined effects of multiple chemicals in a single exposure.
- Chemicals should be regulated in groups. If there is sufficient evidence that individual chemicals in a group with similar structures and properties are hazardous, then all members of that group should be pulled from the market or not approved until proven safe, as the European Union did in its 2023 proposal to restrict PFAS as a group.
- Modify rules for material safety to ensure that what escapes from products is safe under different use conditions and expand screening of toxicity to include chronic disease outcomes like diabetes, infertility, and harm to the immune and nervous systems.
- Determine if chemicals or materials like glass or stainless steel classified as inert leach into food. If they don’t leach, they’re not a priority for in-depth chemical analysis. Inert materials that can be reused should be the policy goal.
The chemicals in Tier 1 provide the most reliable evidence that materials that come in contact with food are a source of people’s exposure to these chemicals, Muncke said. The chemicals are in people, they’re in food, and they’re in food-contact materials, she said. “What more proof do you want?”
Inside Climate News asked the American Chemistry Council and Food Packaging Coalition, trade groups that represent the chemical and food-packing industries, if their members would release hazard information about the chemicals they use and phase out those known to be hazardous. Neither responded, but the Food Packaging Coalition maintains that packaging is designed to prevent the transfer of its components to food and to ensure that they are safe and suitable for their intended use.
The paper offers a practical and transparent roadmap for using the best available evidence to prioritize food-contact chemicals for regulation, said Sara Lupolt, an expert on exposure assessment at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, who was not involved in the research.
Though not addressed in the paper, she added, more research is needed to determine which foods and chemical combinations result in more chemicals moving into food.
Plastic chemicals in baby food
Many of the chemicals that migrate into food are so-called non-intentionally added substances, (NIAS). Their identity is often obscure because existing tools can’t identify every chemical in use, especially when researchers don’t know what to look for because producers keep proprietary chemical ingredients secret.
Muncke is particularly concerned about babies’ exposure to plastic chemicals in pouches that hold juices and pureed food. Earlier this year, her team found evidence that more than 330 chemicals leach from pouches, including nearly 80 known to be hazardous. They presented the findings at an event at the House of Lords in the United Kingdom in June.
A greater volume of chemicals gets into baby food because the ratio of packaging to food is much greater in a small serving size, Muncke said. And the pouches are sterilized using heat, which drives chemicals to migrate and forms microplastics.
Several peer-reviewed studies, including a 2023 Chemosphere study, also found chemicals, including NIAS, in baby food packaged in pouches. The paper’s authors believed the NIAS, which lacked adequate information to assess risk, were impurities and raw materials from producing plastic. “Infants may be constantly exposed to NIAS via consuming pouched food products,” the authors warned.
For the 87 percent of chemicals that lack hazard data, it’s primarily a question of the data not being public, said study co-author Helene Wiesinger, a chemist and Food Packaging Forum scientific officer.
That delays regulatory action, Wiesinger said, because governments and independent scientists must first figure out which chemicals are safe. She believes a product or chemical should not be allowed on the market until a company can prove that it’s safe.
At a minimum, chemicals that have structural similarities with others known to be hazardous should be priorities for regulation, the paper argues. Seventy percent of the more than 4,200 chemicals the team classified into 38 priority groups — including PFAS, phthalates and organophosphates (used as flame retardants and pesticides, among other applications) — lack enough data to assess potential harms.
Just because something isn’t yet known to be hazardous doesn’t mean it’s not hazardous, Wiesinger said. Time and again, chemicals found to present unreasonable risks are replaced with others that have similar properties and ultimately similar risks.
“We hope this work provides practical guidance on how to at least not make the very obvious mistakes,” she said.

Brennan rules Seville sprint as Visma claim seventh Vuelta stage win
SEVILLE, Sept 9 : Matthew Brennan turned Seville's grand avenues into another Visma-Lease a Bike runway on Wednesday, powering to his fifth stage win of this year's Vuelta a Espana as the Dutch team's remarkable run of success continued.
The 21-year-old Briton, making his debut in the race, again proved untouchable when the peloton wound up for the final sprint, beating Jordi Meeus into second place while Magnus Cort Nielsen finished third.
Visma have now won seven stages in the race, with Brennan's five victories added to Wout van Aert's two, underlining their dominance of the Vuelta's flat and rolling stages.
Enzo Paleni, Sinuhe Fernandez and Fredrik Dversnes attacked shortly after the start of the 185-km stage, although Dversnes quickly dropped back. Paleni and Fernandez pressed on and built a lead of more than five minutes around the halfway mark.
Visma, driven for long spells by Steven Kruijswijk, kept the breakaway within reach, with Cofidis also contributing as they worked for Bryan Coquard.
A brief acceleration by Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe split the bunch inside the final 50 kilometres, but the peloton soon regrouped. Paleni and Fernandez still held a lead of 1:50 with 25 kilometres remaining before Fernandez took the intermediate sprint at San Jose de la Rinconada.
Paleni then attacked alone with 15 kilometres left, but his lead shrank rapidly and he was caught inside the final three kilometres.
UAE, INEOS and Uno-X all tried to shape the run-in, but Brennan timed his effort best to seal another emphatic win.
Overall leader Enric Mas finished safely in the bunch to retain the red jersey for a ninth successive stage, leading Felix Gall by 2:06 and Primoz Roglic by 2:10.

Two people have been pulled out alive from a hydropower tunnel in Nepal nine days after deadly flash floods buried the projects in deep mud and left them trapped.
The workers were rescued during an ongoing operation at the Trishuli 3A tunnel, a hydropower project in one of the areas worst affected by last week’s floods, according to the army spokesperson Brig Gen Raja Ram Basnet.
Sanjay Shah, a foreman, was the first to be rescued and was taken to the army barracks in Trishuli. Another person, identified as Kabir Maharjan, a project supervisor, was also pulled from the tunnel. They were recovered from a depth of 170 metres (558ft) inside the tunnel, Basnet said.
A senior police official confirmed that a body had also been recovered from the tunnel. By Friday afternoon, police confirmed they had halted the operation as they had found no more signs of life.
Nepal’s army released images of Shah being pulled from the small dark entrance of a tunnel. He emerged covered in mud but conscious and was carried from the site on a rescuer’s shoulder.
Speaking to army officials after he was rescued, Shah’s first question was: “What day is it?”
Shah said he had been in the tunnel’s control room at the time of the flood, alongside about 40 to 45 others. “Since I was in the control room, my responsibility was to save everyone’s lives,” he said. “After such an accident, I couldn’t just run away by myself. I had to save everyone.”
He said that after realising there had been a major accident, he raced through the tunnel telling people to run and save themselves. “In doing so, I lost time. In the end, I couldn’t get out myself,” he said.
To keep himself calm in the darkness of the tunnel, Shah said he spent his time chanting mantras. He said that while trapped, he had heard the voices of three or four others.
“We were communicating by shouting to each other from nearby. There could also be people inside the powerhouse. Some of them may not have been able to escape,” he said.
Officials said the two men had been flown to a hospital in Kathmandu. Shah was said to be stable but Maharjan was in a critical condition and had been transferred to intensive care.
Speaking over the phone from the rescue site, Amrit Thapa, deputy superintendent of the armed police force, who is part of the seven-person search and rescue team, said they had managed to crawl the length of the tunnel looking for survivors. They were accompanied by a team from the Nepal army.
“The team crawled through areas for about 10 to 15 metres and reached the main section,” said Thapa. “When we went to the final point, we found a body on the remaining upper level.”
Thapa said that “except for two sections, the entire tunnel was filled with debris. After checking everything, we did not hear any further voices. We also searched the entire powerhouse area, but so far, nothing else has been found.”
Most of the hydropower projects along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers were destroyed when a surge of water, debris and mud came coursing down the valley last week, triggered by the collapse of a melting glacier on the border between Nepal and China-controlled Tibet.
At least 1,287 people were killed in the floods and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.
Rescue efforts have increasingly centred on the hydropower tunnels, where authorities believe workers may have survived for more than a week in air pockets. So far, more than 270 people have been rescued across several projects.
Large boulders and flood waters had deluged the hydropower tunnels, blocking off the entrances, and some were buried deep in mud. At the Upper Trishuli 3A facility, it took rescue workers almost six days to find the tunnels.
Army and specialist teams have been working round the clock to try to clear debris from the tunnel entrance. At least 557 workers are missing from the hydropower project along the Trishuli River, with about 115 believed to be trapped in the main tunnel, according to the Independent Power Producers’ Association of Nepal.
Families of those missing in the tunnels have been gathering at hospitals in Kathmandu and at the Nepal electricity office for nine days, desperate for answers about their relatives.
Standing outside the hospital, Bidya Dangol, the sister of Maharjan, described his rescue as a “miracle”. “I haven’t been able to see him yet, but I am incredibly happy,” she said. “I cannot even put into words how happy I am. We had almost given up hope.”
In total, local authorities estimate about 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects high up in the Himalayas, with about 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels.
Rescue efforts have also focused on Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant, where Nepali authorities said they were confident that 46 workers trapped in an underground chamber in the plant were still alive.

Regarding your editorial (The Guardian view on child marriage: girls should not be wives, 26 August), every year, 12 million girls are married under the age of 18, while more than 70 million more are estimated to be at risk of child marriage between 2025 and 2030. Yet, as international development budgets face unprecedented contractions, traditional field programming alone cannot keep pace.
At current funding levels, international funding for ending child marriage amounts to less than $1 per girl at risk per year – a level of investment that cannot match the scale or urgency of the problem
Ending child marriage requires dismantling the patriarchal norms that perpetuate it. Over eight years of participatory research across Bangladesh, India and Nepal – engaging 350 grassroots partners – our team validated a cost-effective alternative: narrative edutainment. Field-testing a film-driven intervention yielded a striking 49.4 percentage point shift in community attitudes, proving visual storytelling can transform entrenched behaviours where policy alone stalls.
Through our film project, we are establishing a scalable model combining cinema, school toolkits, community screenings and policy briefings to reach 100 million people across south Asia, with a clear blueprint for expansion into sub-Saharan Africa.
Child marriage inflicts a staggering $175bn economic cost worldwide yearly. In an era of scarce global funding, investing in scalable-impact film assets is an urgent necessity. This vital tool can break the cycle of poverty and protect millions of young girls.

Story so far: The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has stepped up action against food companies using “100%” claims on their products, saying such claims can give consumers an impression of absolute purity or completeness that may not match what is actually inside the packet.
The move comes as food regulators are paying closer attention to how products are labelled and advertised. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has also asked food businesses to stop using “100%” claims on food labels, packaging and promotional material.
The key question is: can a company claim “100%” when the product does not actually contain 100% of that ingredient? The CCPA’s orders offer some clues.
What has the CCPA found?
In June 2026, the CCPA imposed a ₹1 lakh penalty each on Mrs. Bectors Food Specialities, which markets English Oven products, and Storia Foods and Beverages for misleading “100%” claims. The companies were also directed to stop using the claims on their packaging, websites and digital platforms.
In the case of Mrs. Bectors, one of its bread products was marketed as “100% Atta Bread” and “100% Whole Wheat Bread”. The company, however, admitted that the bread contained 87% whole wheat flour.
Mrs. Bectors argued that “100% Atta” was meant to convey that wheat flour was the only grain used in the bread. The CCPA did not accept this explanation. It said that “100%” is an exact numerical expression and should not be used loosely or approximately.
The Authority also took into account the use of “Zero Maida” alongside “100% Whole Wheat Bread”. Taken together, these claims could give consumers the impression that the bread was entirely made from whole wheat flour.
What about ‘100% Juice’?
The Storia case involved a similar concern, but with beverages.
Storia marketed one of its products as “100% Tender Coconut Water” and “100% Natural Tender Coconut Water”. However, the ingredient declaration listed water and 9.6% coconut water concentrate, followed by the words “Equivalent to 100% Coconut Water” and “Reconstituted”.
The CCPA found the prominent “100% Tender Coconut Water” claim misleading because an ordinary consumer could understand it to mean that the product was entirely natural tender coconut water.
The CCPA raised a similar concern over Storia’s fruit beverages marketed as “100% Juice”. These products contained water as well as specified quantities of fruit pulp or juice concentrates.
For example, the pomegranate variant contained water, 4% pomegranate juice concentrate and 10% apple juice concentrate. The mango variant contained water, 16% mango pulp and 12.5% apple juice concentrate.
Can the fine print save a claim?
The CCPA’s orders suggest that putting the correct information in the fine print may not be enough if the prominent claim creates a misleading impression.
Consumers typically see the front of a packet before reading its detailed ingredient list. The CCPA has therefore looked at the overall impression created by the packaging and advertising, rather than assuming that a detailed ingredient declaration automatically corrects a prominent claim.
This approach was also seen in the case of McVitie’s Wholewheat Marie biscuits.
The biscuits contained 19.5% whole wheat flour, while refined wheat flour accounted for 52%. The CCPA found that the prominent use of the word “Wholewheat”, along with wheat imagery on the packaging, could lead consumers to believe that the biscuits were predominantly made from whole wheat.
Pladis India, the manufacturer, argued that “Wholewheat” was part of its registered trademark and pointed to a disclaimer on the packaging.
The CCPA, however, said that being a registered trademark does not put a company outside consumer-protection laws. Nor, it held, can a disclaimer necessarily cancel out a prominent representation that may mislead consumers.
What is the FSSAI’s stand on ‘100%’?
The FSSAI too has taken note of a noticeable surge in the use of the term “100%” across food product labels and promotional platforms.
In May 2025, it advised Food Business Operators (FBOs) not to use “100%” on food labels, packaging or promotional material. It said the expression was not defined under the existing food regulations and could create a false impression of absolute purity or superiority.
The FSSAI had earlier taken a more specific position on packaged juice products. In June 2024, it directed food businesses to remove “100% Fruit Juice” claims from labels and advertisements where the juice was made by reconstituting concentrate.
The FSSAI’s action primarily deals with food safety, standards and labelling requirements. The CCPA, on the other hand, looks at whether companies are misleading consumers through their advertisements or product claims.
Under Section 21 of the Consumer Protection Act, the CCPA can order a false or misleading advertisement to be discontinued or modified. It can also impose a penalty of up to ₹10 lakh on a manufacturer, which can rise to ₹50 lakh for every subsequent contravention.
What does this mean for food companies and consumers?
The recent orders show that the ingredient list is not the only thing that matters. The CCPA can also look at how a product is presented on its packaging and in advertisements.
For companies, this means that product names, claims, images and disclaimers may all be considered when assessing whether it could mislead consumers.
For consumers, the front of a packet may not always give the complete picture. The ingredient list can help show what the product actually contains.

In one interview published by a credible source, Rush said about Trump, "He's a worker. He's up all night." In another interview Rush said Trump "does try to eat healthy, but people don't get to see that part of it. They just see the part that we want to show on social media."
Tabloid news outlet TMZ paraphrased a comment it ascribed to Rush as, "Trump was always friendly and complimentary to the staff," but didn't present it as a direct quote. We have reached out to Rush for confirmation and will update this story accordingly.
In late August and early September 2026, numerous Facebook posts purported to quote Andre Rush, a former White House chef, praising U.S. President Donald Trump for his work ethic, healthy diet and friendliness to the White House staff.
Snopes readers sent us examples of the post in which three separated quotes were attributed to Rush. Below are the various sections of the post the alleged Rush quotes in bold (emphasis ours):
Chef Andre Rush. Nearly 20 years working inside the White House kitchen. Four Presidents. Clinton. Bush. Obama. Trump.
A man who observed all of them from extremely close range — not from a press conference, not from a campaign rally — but from the most personal place imaginable. Their kitchen.
Because you can say anything in a speech. You can put on a performance at a rally. You can create an image for the cameras. But inside a kitchen — at unusual hours — when food is being prepared and nobody important is paying attention — that is where the real person can reveal themselves.
And here is what Chef Rush reportedly revealed — something the media reduced to one sentence before moving on.
When he was asked which President was the most difficult to cook for — he said Trump.
But not for the reason you might expect.
"He's a worker. He's up all night. It wasn't a lot of morning breakfast."
Up all night.
The kitchen was prepared. The meals were ready. And Trump simply wasn't there to eat them.
Because he was working.
[…]
The chef could never predict when Trump would walk through that kitchen.
Because Trump's schedule wasn't organized around meals.
It was organized around America.
And when Trump DID come through the kitchen?
"Always friendly. Always complimentary to the staff."
Not once — during all those years — did Trump make the kitchen staff feel unimportant.
Never a cruel word. Never an unreasonable demand. Never the kind of behavior powerful people sometimes display when they believe nobody significant is watching.
[…]
And then Rush said the part that completely broke me.
"He does try to eat healthy. People don't get to see that part. They just see what we want to show on social media."
For years, the media showed you Trump eating McDonald's. The Diet Coke. Image after image that could make him appear careless.
But his own chef — the man who actually prepared his food — said publicly that Trump tries.
That the real picture is different from what people see online.
Although placed in a highly embellished context above, two of the highlighted quotes about Rush's experience working in Trump's White House were taken from credible published sources. The alleged quote about Trump's friendliness was actually a paraphrase of remarks attributed to Rush by TMZ, a tabloid news outlet.
Snopes reached out to Rush via Instagram to confirm these quotes and will update this story accordingly. Until then, we rate this claim a mixture of true and undetermined information.
Other parts of the post are elaborate descriptions that may or may not have derived from things Rush actually said. For example, we have not found evidence that Rush said, "Not once — during all those years — did Trump make the kitchen staff feel unimportant." Nor did we find proof that Rush said Trump never said a "cruel word" or made an "unreasonable demand."
Rush worked as a chef at the White House for nearly 20 years, cooking for former presidents Bill Clinton, George W. Bush and Barack Obama, as well as during the first Trump administration. In a 2021 interview with Mashed, a cooking and food service publication, he spoke about Trump's meal habits:
He's a worker. He's up all night. It wasn't a lot of morning breakfast. Actually, all of them [the presidents], it was very different in comparison. Food wasn't a high priority, when I say that, I mean on the administration side of it — on that administration side of it for his term. Nothing's wrong with that if you know what he ate and how he ate during the day, which has been all over from the burgers to everything overcooked or taco salads. … I would have to say burgers would be the number one if I had to put [it] into perspective, as he'd call it the American food.
In a 2024 interview with Politico, Rush described Trump's eating habits:
He gets so much flack about the unhealthy side of him. He does try to eat healthy, but people don't get to see that part of it. They just see the part that we want to show on social media. I mean, Bill Clinton ate just as many burgers as Donald Trump did.
In a 2024 interview with TMZ, Rush allegedly said Trump was always friendly and complimentary with the staff. However, TMZ did not directly quote Rush and appears to have paraphrased his words:
Rush made sure to note Trump was always friendly and complimentary to the kitchen staff … which the chef is sure will continue — even if the cooks have to covertly slip veggies into his meals.
Snopes has previously reported on rumors about Trump's diet and health, including the claim that he uses a button in his office to order Diet Cokes.

Quick Answer
One UI 9 focuses on control, privacy, and usability with customizable Quick Settings, a redesigned media player, per-app network blocking, unified call history, network speed indicators, PIN-protected shutdown, bypass charging, and dual-camera video recording.
One UI 9 is Samsung’s latest update based on Android 17, which was launched with the Galaxy Z Fold8 and Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra. As for its slab phones, the One UI 9 update is still in beta for the Galaxy S26 series and was recently made available in the US, India, and South Korea for older models like the Galaxy S25 series, Galaxy Z Fold7, Z Flip7, and even the Galaxy S24 series. Samsung has already confirmed that the One UI 9 stable update will soon reach the Galaxy S26 series, but the exact date isn’t confirmed as of yet. One UI 9c isn’t a massive overhaul but is focusing heavily on privacy, aesthetics, and usability. Here are the top new features of One UI 9 that you will get on eligible One UI 9 phones.
Table of Contents

Here is the complete list of Samsung devices that are slated to receive the Android 17 One UI 9 update:

| Rugged devices | Galaxy XCover7, Galaxy XCover7 Pro, Galaxy Tab Active5, Galaxy Tab Active5 Pro | 
New One UI 9 features
While we await the One UI 9 Android 17 stable update on our phones, here are the new features that you should know about:
Highly customizable Quick Settings panel
Samsung has tweaked the Quick Settings panel a lot after the One UI 8 update. Now with One UI 9, the company will take things further and introduce a highly customizable Quick Settings panel. While at first glance, you will notice a familiar Samsung identity, the visual tweaks make it more ergonomic and pleasing to the eye. Samsung introduced thicker, more tactile sliders for volume and brightness, making them easier to adjust quickly with your thumb. Additionally, the dark mode toggles and volume settings have also been undocked from these sliders, which gives the interface a much cleaner and less cramped look.
However, you will notice that with One UI 9, you will be able to resize the brightness and volume sliders to a compact 2×1 grid size. This is fantastic for those who want to get more quick setting toggles on a single page. You also get dedicated new toggles for accessibility features such as “Select to speak,” which reads aloud what is displayed on your screen.
Redesigned media player
The media player Quick Settings tile has also been refreshed. Noticeably, the album and podcast get new circular toggles for play/pause, rewind, and skip. The visualizer waveform on playback now dynamically extracts hues and colors from your currently playing album art. This gives your lockscreen a visual overhaul and a rich look.
Network restriction controls
Let us face it. We have been in this situation so many times where we download an offline game, a calculator app, or even a flashlight tool, and are suddenly bombarded with full-screen ads. These ads not only waste a lot of time, but sometimes they are so intrusive that you cannot close them, or they force you to purchase the pro version. One UI 9 fixes this and introduces a feature that power users have been begging for.
Network Restriction Controls is the new setting that is buried within the main Settings app; you now have a master kill-switch to block specific applications from connecting to the internet entirely. This is a massive win for privacy and data management. If an app does not strictly need an external internet connection to function, you can cut its Wi-Fi and mobile data access with a single turn of a toggle. This will stop ad-filled apps from quietly phoning home with your personal data in the background.
A unified phone app
Calling is no longer limited to standard cellular calls. You now make calls on WhatsApp, Google Meet, or message family members on Viber. But the problem with all this is that all of your call logs are scattered across various apps. WhatsApp calls will be available in its app, Google Meet’s call history is available in its app, and so on. You have to switch between apps just to view the call history.
One UI 9 fixes this issue and introduces a unified phone app. It fixes the headache by merging all of your calling applications into one centralized feed inside the Samsung Phone app. Now, when you open your dialer, your WhatsApp calls, Google Meet calls, and standard carrier calls all live in one neatly organized timeline.
Status bar enhancements
If you are someone who loves keeping a close eye on the device’s performance, then One UI 9 brings a highly requested feature: a native network speed indicator in the status bar. While this has been a staple on many Chinese smartphone brands, Samsung models will finally get a built-in way to see real-time download and upload speeds. It is an incredibly useful diagnostic tool to quickly see if your Wi-Fi is acting up or if you are getting the correct speed with it or not.
Note that you still need to make use of the Good Lock “Quickstar” module to enable it. But it is well worth the two minutes if you want to keep an eye on your internet speed. Plus, Samsung has also adjusted the size of the status bar pill area, basically the area that shows background activities like active calls or screen recordings. The pill is noticeably larger now, which allows it to display more content.
Everyday usability and multitasking tweaks
When it comes to multitasking, Samsung has always been the king. The One UI 9 update brings a few quality-of-life improvements that only help get things done much easier.
- Browser Windows in Recents menu: After using Google Chrome for years, I ditched it for Samsung Internet Browser as my default. One UI 9 brings a massive usability bump, as you can now configure individual browser tabs to show up as separate cards in your phone’s Recent Apps menu. This way, you don’t have to open the Samsung Internet Browser app just to close these tabs. You can do that from the Recent Apps menu.
- Mandatory PIN for shutdown: Smartphone theft is a real concern. Just the other day during a stroll around Hyde Park, my phone was almost snatched by a thief. While my phone was not stolen, thieves, when they get their hands on a phone they usually turn it off to stop tracking immediately. One UI 9 adds a crucial security layer, and you now you need to enter your PIN, password, or biometric data before the phone lets you restart or power off your phone.
- Clearer Routines: For those who use Samsung Routines to automate their device, they will be happy to know that Samsung has finally added plain-English explanation text for all the presets. You no longer have to guess what a specific routine means.
- Floating Bars return: Throughout various first-party apps, Samsung has brought back floating action bars. This gives you a cleaner gesture area at the bottom of your screen, good for those who customize their home screen.
- Bypass Charging: Mobile gamers are getting a new Bypass Charging feature. With this, the phone will route the power directly to the processor rather than charging the battery. This will reduce heat and protect your battery in the long-term.
- Dual Vertical Video: Samsung’s Camera app is packed with features, but One UI 9 adds some more elements to it, especially tailored for social media creators. You can now record vertical video using both the front and back camera simultaneously. The phone will record the footage in a 1:1 square aspect ratio.
Final thoughts
One UI 9, based on Android 17, may not be the biggest visual overhaul update that you might be expecting, but that was already done with the One UI 8 update. Now, with the latest update, Samsung is aiming to give users more control. It is a mature, polished, and thoughtful update that makes every Galaxy device a little bit more intuitive. More details will come about the update after the stable update is pushed.

India is ageing, and the most recent official figures show how quickly this is happening. The National Family Health Survey - 6 factsheets, released in August 2026, indicate that the proportion of Indians aged 60 years or older has reached 12.9%, up from 11.8% in NFHS-5, some four years earlier. This represents a small national increase, and while significant, is not the most interesting aspect of what the data reveal.
The more important conclusion is that India is not ageing as one country. Keralam, which was already the oldest state, now has 20.7% of its population aged 60 and over; Goa is at 17.2%, Himachal Pradesh at 16.4%, and Tamil Nadu at 16.3%. On the other hand, Bihar and Uttar Pradesh had their proportions of elderly people increase by only 0.4 and 0.3 percentage points, respectively and remain young by any measure. There is also the case of Ladakh, where the percentage of people over 60 rose from 8.9% to 14.6% in four years, a 5.7 percentage-point increase, which is greater than the increase Kerala achieved over the same period.
It is impossible to apply a single national template to such different populations. In States that are already ageing, there will be increases in the demand for care of chronic diseases, geriatric services and long-term care. Although younger States have more time ahead of them, that time is exactly when preparation should take place. Putting off action until the elderly population is large enough to be seen when looked at as a group, means responding to demographic change rather than predicting it.
What the fact sheets cannot tell us
The NFHS-6 State and national fact sheets include 101 key indicators. The only one of these relating to older Indians is the proportion of the population aged 60 and over; all the other information that could tell us about their health is either included in age groups that are too broad to be of any use or is given in a form that does not allow linkage to individuals.
When it comes to hypertension and high blood sugar, the two main indicators of India’s burden of non-communicable diseases, both conditions are recorded for adults aged 15 and over. Thus, a 25-year-old and an 85-year-old are placed in the same statistical category. Based on the available fact sheets, there is no way to know how common hypertension is among the elderly in India, how this prevalence differs from State to State, or whether the States ageing most rapidly are also experiencing the steepest increase in chronic disease among older adults.
When it comes to nutrition, the gap is even more apparent. Body mass index is reported only for adults between the ages of 15 and 49, and not because older adults were measured and then left out of the tables. They were never weighed. Height and weight are recorded only for women up to 49 and men up to 54. The population whose nutritional and functional status matters most as a society ages does not appear in the data at all.
With regard to health insurance and financing indicators, they are provided at the household level. These indicators tell us whether a household has coverage, but they tell us very little about whether the older person in that household is financially protected when their healthcare needs become intensive and long-term.
There is a deeper design issue underneath this. NFHS interviews women up to 49 and men up to 54. Above that age, Indians appear in the survey only as a line in the household roster and, if selected, a blood pressure cuff and a glucose reading. So even where we have a measurement for a 70-year-old, we have very little to explain it with: nothing on their tobacco or alcohol use, whether they are on treatment, whether they sought care, whether they still work. The elderly are enumerated. They are not interviewed.
This does not mean that NFHS-6 is a flawed survey; it is, in fact, one of the most valuable sources of information on population health available anywhere in the world, and it was intended to track overall population health rather than to answer all the questions raised by an ageing society. But as India’s age structure changes, so must the information system used to formulate health policy.
The evidence is older than the policy
This is no longer just a theoretical issue: since the Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB PM-JAY) has been extended to all citizens aged 70 and over, the government has now assumed responsibility for financing the health of a very large number of elderly people.
To serve that population adequately we need to know more than simply how many people are eligible. How many live with chronic diseases? How many need help with everyday activities? How much are they paying out of pocket? Only on the basis of this information can we tell whether the money and the services are being directed towards the right needs in the right States.
India possesses the necessary equipment to deal with these questions. The Longitudinal Ageing Study in India, conducted by the International Institute for Population Sciences, was designed precisely for this purpose. In its first phase, it included more than 73,000 adults aged 45 and over, gathering information on their health conditions, their use of and expenditure on healthcare, economic circumstances, social networks, functional health, and biomarkers. It is a major piece of infrastructure.
The problem is that the first wave covers the period 2017 to 2018. For a policy programme being expanded this year, a baseline that is eight years old cannot be considered up-to-date evidence. Once data has been collected, it loses relevance over time, and this decline in value is most rapid in cases where the underlying population is changing quickly.
Staying current
When a gap in data is identified, the reflex is to call for a new survey. That is the wrong instinct here. India already runs two surveys. The NFHS gives a regular, broad picture of population health across the country. The LASI does a deep dive into ageing and its social and economic consequences. They were built to do different jobs, and turning the NFHS into a second LASI would be expensive and would damage what it already does well.
What is needed is more modest. Keep the ageing data current, rather than letting a decade pass between one wave and the next. Report the numbers by age where the NFHS already collects them, particularly for hypertension and blood sugar. And design the two surveys so they can be read against each other, instead of sitting in separate silos.
An ageing India will have to do more than simply count its older population; it will also need to find out what their requirements are, where these needs are appearing first, and whether the health system is able to meet them. With regard to the first of these questions the data are now fairly good, but with respect to the others we are still making guesses.
(Tanya Singla is a research student, tanyasingla.india@gmail.com, and Megha Jacob is an assistant professor in the department of economics at Jesus and Mary College, University of Delhi, mjacob@jmc.du.ac.in; Karan Babbar is an assistant professor of economics at XLRI Jamshedpur. phd17karanb@iima.ac.in)

The US Army says that its special battalion focused on drone warfare and lessons from Ukraine was always meant to be a temporary experiment, not a lasting element of the force.
The Unmanned Assault Battalion was created last fall as an experimental unit in the 173rd Airborne Brigade specializing in drone tactics. The 3rd Battalion of the 504th Parachute Infantry Regiment was tasked with testing uncrewed systems and developing battlefield lessons the Army could apply more broadly.
When news broke last month that the service intended to phase out the battalion's drone-focused mission and return it to airborne infantry, with a focus on traditional warfighting, the move prompted questions about why the Army was ending the experiment and concerns about its wider approach to drone warfare.
At an Army modernization media roundtable on Wednesday, Army officials said that the shift had been planned from the beginning and presented how they intend to spread lessons on uncrewed aerial systems across the service.
"They were never flagged to be a permanent centralized drone unit," Alex Miller, the Army's chief technology officer, told reporters.
"In fact, we pushed back on having something like a drone corps since its inception because our theory of the case is, if you centralize that in one place, what you lose is the ability to actually scale that learning and send that out to the rest of the Army," he added.
The plan, Miller said, was for the battalion to test uncrewed technologies and learn tactics in the six to seven months before they received their full infantry battalion equipment. Then, the Army would disseminate those takeaways across the service and the troops from the battalion would return to their role as airborne infantry.
When The Wall Street Journal first reported the change, an Army spokesperson said the service was committed to "drone dominance" but did not comment on future plans. The Journal reported that no end date was specified when the battalion's drone role was established.
At the time, an Army spokesperson told Business Insider the unit's findings would inform force design and future experimentation.
The reporting on the plans to phase out the battalion's drone mission raised concerns among defense analysts and lawmakers, who questioned what the decision signaled about the Army's commitment to drone warfare, the service's willingness to learn from Ukraine's warfighting experiences, and broader Pentagon priorities for uncrewed capabilities.
"We have deep concerns that eliminating this specialized drone unit will limit our ability to learn from allies, particularly the Ukrainian Armed Forces, and hinder our efforts to modernize drone warfare at the speed necessary to compete on the modern battlefield," US lawmakers wrote in a recent letter to Army leadership.
The letter added that "this specialized unit was a prudent response in a moment when the character of warfare is changing faster than a conventional formation's ability to adapt."
The Army didn't explain publicly that the drone mission was always intended as a short-term experiment when the planned change first drew criticism weeks ago, but officials said Wednesday they wanted to clarify.
"We're sort of combating this narrative that we set something new up, and then we killed that new thing, and we're going to sacrifice it at the altar of technology," Miller said. "That's just not true."
He argued that spreading lessons across the Army rather than concentrating drone expertise in a permanent unit better fits the goal of making uncrewed systems a routine part of how the larger force fights.
"When we engage with the Ukrainians and we engage with their leadership, it was less a drone corps and was more of one platoon per company, one company per battalion, which looked an awful lot like how we were actually setting up our tactical UAS platoons as a formation anyway," he said.
The Army rejected the idea that ending the battalion's drone-focused mission represents a step backward in its efforts to integrate uncrewed capabilities.
"We are not slowing down on drones or autonomous systems, and we are not walking away from them," Miller said.
Other officials, likewise, said that drone capabilities are continuing to spread across formations regardless.
"We are employing unmanned aircraft systems at all levels," said Brent Ingraham, the assistant secretary of the Army for acquisitions, logistics, and technology, adding that "while there was an experimental drone battalion, we are scaling that capability across the entire Army."
Moving forward, the Army says it has several methods for sharing drone lessons and tips, including a Combined Arms Services platform that acts as a central repository for lessons from different soldiers and units.

The Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI) today launched “Face Auth SDK & Sandbox”, a set of software tools and a testing environment designed to help developers integrate Aadhaar face authentication into digital services. Unveiled on the second day of the Global Fintech Fest (GFF) 2026 in Mumbai, the offering brings together ready-made software components and a controlled testing environment. Developers can use it to build and test face authentication-based services before making them available to users. The UIDAI described the offering as a “plug-and-play” solution aimed at enabling secure and frictionless face authentication. The software development kit (SDK) will allow developers to add Aadhaar face authentication to apps and other digital services without building the underlying technology from scratch. Meanwhile, the sandbox will allow them to test whether the integration works as intended before its wider rollout. The launch is aimed at simplifying the adoption of Aadhaar face authentication across services such as customer verification, telecom enrolment and gig worker onboarding. Face authentication itself is not new. The UIDAI introduced face recognition as an additional option for Aadhaar authentication in 2018, alongside fingerprints and iris scans. The latest offering seeks to make the existing technology easier for developers and businesses to adopt. The development forms part of UIDAI’s wider push to shift Aadhaar services away from paperwork and in-person processes towards digital verification. Speaking at GFF, UIDAI part-time chairperson Neelkanth Mishra said Aadhaar currently handles around 10 Cr authentications a day. The authority is preparing its infrastructure to support 25 Cr to 30 Cr authentications daily as usage grows. More than 600 entities currently use the digital identity infrastructure, according to Mishra. “We are also using AI extensively for fraud detection. The fraudsters keep getting smarter, but we are also getting smarter,” he said during a session. Face Authentication Push The UIDAI has been expanding the use of face authentication while working to address attempts to fool biometric systems using manipulated images, masks and deepfakes. In October last year, the authority launched the SITAA programme to support the development of technology capable of detecting such attacks on Aadhaar face authentication systems. The government has also been expanding the Aadhaar app, which allows users to verify their identities digitally and share selected information instead of handing over physical copies of their Aadhaar cards. Launched in beta in April 2025, the app uses face authentication and QR codes for identity verification. Its features include updating details such as mobile numbers and addresses, locking and unlocking biometrics, and viewing authentication history. “With the Aadhaar app, we have also gone digital. We are trying to shift paper-based and physical journeys to digital, and there are huge advantages that come from that,” Mishra said. The latest launch comes amid growing government and regulatory focus on fraud, cybersecurity and consumer protection as India’s digital financial ecosystem expands. At the inauguration of GFF 2026, Prime Minister Narendra Modi urged fintech companies to strengthen cybersecurity, data protection and consumer safeguards as technologies such as agentic AI, tokenisation and quantum computing reshape financial services. Modi outlined four priorities for the sector — stronger cybersecurity, ethical data protection, better consumer protection, and closer collaboration between companies and regulators. The government has also formed an inter-ministerial group to develop a cybersecurity strategy for India’s financial sector. The seventh edition of GFF is being held from September 8 to 11. Its theme this year is “Potential to Impact: Agentic AI, Tokenisation, Quantum — Trusted, Connected, Global Systems for Inclusive Finance”.

Foodborne illnesses have been a trending headline for most of 2026, leading many readers to write in to Snopes asking for clarification on exactly what they should and shouldn't eat. As of this writing, the CDC listed 36 active investigations into contaminated foods resulting in 11 recall notifications thus far in the year.
For instance, amid an outbreak of thousands of cases of an intestinal disease called cyclosporiasis across the United States, readers asked whether U.S. President Donald Trump's administration cut programs tracking the surveillance of cyclospora, the parasite that causes the illness. Trump's alleged monetary connections to Taylor Farms, the supplier linked to the outbreak, also were a hot topic.
Food contamination claims can run the gamut from alleged heavy metals in Girl Scout cookies to microscopic bugs on Oreos — but as you'll find in Snopes' food investigations, things aren't always as cut and dried as they appear.

LG TVs are facing scrutiny due to a video seemingly showing the devices’ capability to track users when the TVs are off.
YouTube channel Gamers Nexus worked with Level1Techs, a technology-focused YouTube channel, and security researchers to analyze LG TVs’ tracking capabilities. They shared packet captures that pointed to the TVs, including LG’s pricey G5 OLED TV, scanning the LAN for other devices.
“The [G5] crawled our entire network and found dozens of unrelated devices, including smartwatches and phones of our staff who didn’t even know we were working on this,” Steve Burke, Gamers Nexus’ editor-in-chief, said.
LG’s ad business, LG Ad Solutions, has said in recent marketing materials that it can reach 363 million “addressable secondary devices” in the US.
When reached for comment, a company representative shared a statement from LG Electronics via email:
LG TVs can identify compatible devices on the same network to enable features such as device connectivity, content sharing or smart home functionality.
The YouTube channel used Wireshark, a network protocol analyzer tool, and inspected the TV’s firmware and found that LG TVs “are capable of identifying your IP address, geographic location, name of every Wi-Fi network in the vicinity and signal strength, channel numbers of neighboring Wi-Fi networks in range, and other devices on the network, even if not connected to the TV in any way, and the internal IP address of other devices on the network, alongside others.”
It’s unclear if LG TVs use this functionality for any purposes beyond advertising, such as diagnostics, or if this information is all sent to LG. It remains concerning, however, that devices with this technology are sitting in unsuspecting owners’ homes.

The Sapiens Health Foundation has welcomed the Tamil Nadu Government’s announcement of a salt reduction campaign in the Assembly on Tuesday.
Reducing salt intake could help lower the burden of hypertension, stroke, heart attacks and kidney disease. In a press release, the foundation cited the UK’s salt-reduction campaign, initiated in 2005 by Graham MacGregor of the World Action on Salt, Sugar and Health (WASSH), which resulted in a reported 30% reduction in salt in bread.
The Foundation’s salt-reduction campaign began in 2010 with a walkathon at Marina Beach, followed by similar events in Tiruchi and Puducherry and awareness programmes in colleges. In 2014, its founder-chairman Rajan Ravichandran received the Notable Achievement Award from the World Hypertension League for the campaign.
The Foundation has written to more than 300 food manufacturers seeking reductions in salt content and cited reductions in salt in noodles by Nestlé and Hindustan Lever as examples of industry response. It also organised international conferences on salt and health with IIT-Madras and IIT-Bombay in 2017.
The Foundation has conducted salt and health workshops for more than 500 physicians in Chennai, Mumbai, Delhi and Vijayawada. It also welcomed the growing focus on front-of-pack food labelling and said the State’s decision to take forward the campaign will be an important step towards improving population health.

High-end homes are recording steep price falls, while more affordable properties are proving resilient, leaving Australians to experience the market downturn in very different ways, new data shows.
Upper-quartile house values in the country’s two biggest markets, Sydney and Melbourne, are now down more than 10% from their peaks, according to analysis from Cotality.
The gap between upper and lower-value housing is most pronounced in Sydney and Melbourne, while Perth, Adelaide and Brisbane recorded more even – and modest – price declines over winter.
Cotality’s head of research, Gerard Burg, said while the market correction had become more widespread, the largest declines were concentrated among expensive homes.
“Higher-value dwellings in Sydney, Melbourne and Canberra were the first to turn and continue to record the largest cumulative falls,” he said.
In Sydney, upper-quartile houses are valued at $2.1m and above. In Melbourne and Canberra, they are priced at about $1.2m and above.
Australia’s property market is facing a rare price correction, as rising interest rates and less favourable tax settings for investors accelerate a downturn.
National dwelling values fell 3.1% over the past three months, according to Cotality, although price growth remained positive over a 12-month period.
High-end homes tend to record sharper price movements than the rest of the market, given they are widely viewed as more speculative purchases driven by sentiment.
Many of those high-end homes recording steep price reductions rose spectacularly in recent years.
Peter Esho, an economist and chief executive at 13x, said the property market was showing signs of stabilising because the “the budget noise has started to wash out, and buyers who were on the sidelines are seeing this as an opportunity”.
“Investors have moved away from the market, but first-time buyers and other owner-occupiers that were priced out of the market are stepping in,” Esho said.
“There’s a rotation of buyer types.”
While government critics had largely blamed the downturn on Labor’s May budget reforms, which included getting rid of negative gearing for most new investors, the changes were benefiting prospective owner-occupiers.
Buying activity remained robust at lower price ranges, especially when properties were below the caps that allow a first home buyer to access the government’s first home buyer 5% deposit scheme.
The cap in Sydney is $1.5m, while first homeowners can use the low deposit scheme to access homes worth up to $950,000 in Melbourne and $1m in Brisbane.
House values in Sydney’s and Melbourne’s lower quartiles were down less than 6% and 4%, respectively, from their peaks.
While the broader property outlook was complicated by rising oil prices linked to the Iran conflict – which ultimately puts pressure on interest rates – employment levels were still robust in Australia.
“The single biggest risk to the overall housing market is unemployment,” Esho said.
“That’s the one factor that can change it from a market correction into a systemic issue. We don’t yet have unemployment rising to dangerous levels even though it has picked up.”

India Today's 2018 crypto scam exposé leads to arrest of Amit Lakhanpal in UAE
Amit Lakhanpal, accused of masterminding the Money Trade Coin scam, has been arrested in the UAE after Indian agencies traced him. The arrest advances extradition efforts in a case exposed by India Today's 2018 undercover investigation.
Eight years after India Today TV's undercover investigation exposed the multi-crore Money Trade Coin (MTC) cryptocurrency scam, the mastermind, Amit Lakhanpal, has been arrested in the UAE, marking a major breakthrough in a case that defrauded investors of more than Rs 113 crore.
Lakhanpal, who fled India in 2018 after the scam came under scrutiny, was arrested on September 1 following efforts by Indian agencies. A Red Notice had been issued against him at the request of the Thane Police. The Enforcement Directorate (ED), which intensified its probe, shared details of Lakhanpal's whereabouts with authorities, leading to his arrest. The Indian government has since initiated the process for his extradition from the UAE and sought case-related details from investigating agencies.
The arrest comes years after India Today's February 2018 special investigation, "Operation Bitcoin", revealed how investors across the country were being lured into a cryptocurrency scheme promising extraordinary returns.
HOW INDIA TODAY EXPOSED THE MTC SCAM
As part of the undercover operation, India Today reporters posed as wealthy investors and visited the Thane office of the Flintstone Group, the company behind Money Trade Coin.
During the sting, company officials and Digamber Jangle, introduced as a senior MTC functionary, claimed investors could earn returns of 10 to 20 times their investment within four to six months. They also promised benefits such as access to escrow accounts and even citizenship of a Caribbean nation for large investors.
Jangle further claimed that MTC was in discussions with the governments of Antigua and Barbuda and could soon be recognised as legal tender in countries in the region.
The investigation uncovered how such claims were being used to entice investors with promises of quick riches and a lavish lifestyle.
FIR REGISTERED AFTER EXPOSE
Following the India Today investigation, the Thane Police registered an FIR in June 2018 against Flintstone Group owner Amit Lakhanpal and his associates. By then, however, Lakhanpal had already left the country.
Then Thane Crime Branch officer Nitin Thakre had confirmed that cases were registered against Jangle and others linked to the operation. Investigators had also examined allegations that certain police personnel may have had connections to the racket.
At the time, then Thane Police Commissioner Param Bir Singh publicly acknowledged India Today's role in bringing the alleged fraud to light.
ED PROBE REVEALS WIDER FRAUD NETWORK
The ED, in a statement issued on August 20, 2026, said its investigation stemmed from the FIR filed by Thane City Police against Amit Madanlal Lakhanpal, Taha Hafiz Qazi, Sachin Vasant Shelar, Komal Bhimrao Shirsath and others.
According to the agency, investors were induced to invest in the unregulated cryptocurrency between August 2017 and April 2018, resulting in losses of around Rs 113.10 crore.
The ED alleged that Lakhanpal organised seminars in Delhi, Pune and Nashik, falsely portraying himself as a Finance Ministry official and assuring investors that MTC would receive government recognition. He promised substantial returns on investments and projected the scheme as a legitimate financial opportunity.
Investigators also found that several related platforms and exchanges, including Coin Deposit Ratio, MTC Banque, MTCX India and Cryptozaniya, were launched as part of the operation. The agency alleged that MTC coin prices were manipulated and that trading and withdrawal facilities were later suspended, leaving investors unable to access their funds.
ACCUSED ESCAPED USING CARIBBEAN PASSPORTS
The ED claimed that Lakhanpal and his associates fled India after obtaining passports from Antigua and Barbuda and were living in Dubai under assumed identities.
Searches conducted by the agency last month resulted in the seizure of nearly Rs 1 crore in cash, along with digital devices and documents that investigators believe are linked to the alleged money laundering network.
With Lakhanpal now in custody in the UAE, Indian authorities are pushing ahead with extradition proceedings in a case that first came to light through India Today's 2018 undercover investigation.

For as long as ChatGPT has existed, Americans have been asking it, “Could that funny little spot on my toe be cancer?” And as AI has advanced over the past few years, doctors have begun to use specialized models to ask much the same questions in clinics. In the face of these developments, professional medical societies have presented a unified front: Doctors must always have the final say in clinical care.
We disagree. As the medical societies allow, physicians’ enhancing their work with AI tools may be a perfectly good way to deliver medicine. (One of us—Khosla—has in fact invested in a primary-care start-up, co-founded by his son, in which doctors supervise AI assistants.) But for Americans to get the best health care possible, we need to be willing to experiment with models that put AI in control.
This notion has caused a stir in the medical community. When we published a commentary in the Journal of the American Medical Association last month arguing that AI-only care could soon become superior to care provided by human physicians, the CEO of the American Medical Association denounced us as undermining the patient-doctor relationship. The organization’s position was unchanged: AI should be relegated to a supporting role in clinical care. It’s an argument that ignores the available evidence and could hold untold numbers of Americans back from better health.
Much of modern medicine—including managing hypertension, determining the right treatment for many cancers, and addressing chemotherapy side effects—is largely algorithmic. A physician needs to ask a patient targeted questions, determine possible diagnoses, order tests to identify the correct one, offer a treatment plan, and adjust it depending on how the patient responds. That series of actions is steered by detailed guidelines from professional societies.
Yet doctors—despite the best of intentions—make plenty of mistakes when following those steps. Studies indicate that up to 15 percent of American patients are misdiagnosed each year, leading to tens of thousands of preventable deaths. That’s why health-care providers have software that notifies them if they, say, prescribe a deadly dose of a drug. Any software that could practice medicine autonomously would be similarly specialized: not generic ChatGPT, but a model trained in medical knowledge with the appropriate guardrails to minimize risks and mistakes. Such a model could check for drug interactions more consistently and comprehensively than physicians. And it would be able to check in with patients much more frequently than human health-care providers do.
Some AI models have already proved adept at such tasks. In one study published last year, expert physicians judged Google’s Articulate Medical Intelligence Explorer—a highly trained AI model for medical diagnosis and reasoning—as significantly better than human doctors at getting actors playing patients to open up. The “patients” revealed more about their complaints, along with their medical, family, and medication history, all of which can be crucial for an accurate diagnosis. In a 2023 study, patients with type 2 diabetes were randomized to have their insulin dose adjusted by physicians or autonomous AI. The machines got patients to a stable dose faster than human physicians, and their patients took their insulin more reliably and had less distress related to their diabetes.
What about the physician-AI hybrids that medical associations are backing? Research on them is sparse, and more is needed. A 2025 review of 52 studies concluded that, on balance, such hybrids “neither outperformed medical AI alone nor surpassed the best of clinicians.” In at least a few of those studies, human-AI hybrids outperformed AI alone. But in those hybrid teams, the AI controlled the final clinical decision—the opposite of what the AMA and others have in mind.
Medical organizations are not entirely closed-minded to the possibility of change. For example, last week the American College of Physicians published a position paper that allowed that “fully autonomous AI is possible,” but cautioned that its use should be infrequent and “limited to low-risk, low-complexity decisions, and always allow for bringing a clinician into the loop.” John Whyte, the CEO of the AMA, told The Atlantic that he was “disappointed” in the quality of the analysis in our JAMA commentary last month. He questioned the design of the studies we reviewed, many of which involved simulated situations with actors or a retrospective review of existing cases rather than real clinical outcomes, and did not follow patients for years or decades. We agree that longer-term, real-world studies are necessary; hopefully, once advanced AI medical tools have existed for more than a handful of years, results will begin to arrive. Whyte was enthusiastic about further study of physicians controlling AI tools, but only cautiously open to further exploration of autonomous AI in medicine, arguing that the latter would need to be highly regulated.
Reasons exist, of course, to be skeptical of AI-driven medical care. In nine of the 51 studies we reviewed, human physicians outperformed the machines. But some of these tested older AI models or general-use AI models that weren’t trained on medical information and specific guardrails for patient care. Prominent physicians have also argued that real-life doctors are harried by 15-minute appointments and administrative burdens such as prior authorization. That is certainly true, but it is also irrelevant to many of the experiments we reviewed, which examined relatively hassle-free simulations of medical appointments.
One of the most common objections to an AI-doctor future is that robots lack the human connection that patients need to build trust. The American College of Physicians’ recent position paper, for example, cited AI’s inability to make eye contact. But consider that doctors, too, can be robotic. In a Gallup survey conducted late last year, 21 percent of respondents said they had turned to AI because they had previously felt dismissed by a health-care provider. In the 2025 study of Google’s AMIE, patient actors reported that the AI was more emotionally supportive than the physicians were. In a systematic review of 15 studies comparing AI chatbots with physicians, 13 found that AI had significantly higher perceived empathy.
Like human physicians, AI is not and never will be perfect. But isn’t the possibility of reducing fatalities caused by physician error—even by just a little—worth exploring? Instead of writing off a possible source of progress, the medical community should help answer the key questions raised by AI: How should researchers devise ethical, real-world situations to test autonomous AI models? How should governments and professional organizations regulate them? And how should medical education be reformed so that human doctors can continue to do what they uniquely can?
Hundreds of years ago, doctors believed that disease was caused by an imbalance of “humors” in the body. Even after Louis Pasteur proved that bacteria caused infection and Joseph Lister introduced sterile surgical techniques, physicians cut patients to have them bleed out what ailed them, not bothering to clean the knife or their hands. But medicine progresses. Humans have learned from our past mistakes and created new drugs, procedures, and treatments to massively lengthen lifespan and improve quality of life.
Today need not be any different. Doctors have been presented with a powerful tool that has the potential to improve care for millions of people. It’s their duty not to stand in the way.

England demolish Pakistan to take charge of Test
- Published
Third Rothesay Test, Edgbaston (day one of five)
Pakistan 133: Shakeel 43; Tongue 4-42, Robinson 3-15, Archer 3-25
England 156-4: Gay 60, Brook 52*
England are 23 runs ahead
England again demolished the dismal Pakistan batting to move on course for a 3-0 clean sweep on the opening day of the third Test at Edgbaston.
After ripping out the tourists for only 133, England already have a 23-run advantage on 156-4.
Following a week of turmoil in which Pakistan sent seven players home, called up seven more and changed their coach, the outcome was much the same as the first two Tests.
Though the dry pitch seemed good for batting, a moody morning sky convinced England captain Joe Root to field first and his new-look pace attack was outstanding once more.
Pakistan failed to reach 200 for the fifth consecutive innings, while none of the top five made double figures. Saud Shakeel at least managed 43 and the ineptitude of the top order was put into context by last-wicket pair Muhammad Abbas and Mohammad Ali adding 26 in 46 balls - the best partnership of the innings.
Josh Tongue bowled quickly for his 4-42, Ollie Robinson passed 100 Test wickets with his 3-15 and Jofra Archer claimed the remaining three scalps.
In truth, it was a disappointing and dispiriting spectacle, but Pakistan showed some fight with the ball, not least when rapid debutant Razaullah inflicted yet another lbw on Root to leave England 39-3.
Emilio Gay and Harry Brook steadied England, each making half-centuries in a stand of 104 that pushed the hosts into the lead.
Gay dragged on off Razaullah. His gritty 60 was impressive, if perhaps not enough to provide certainty around his place in a congested England batting line-up.
Pakistan changes fail to alter one-sided contest
The pattern of this day was entirely predictable from the moment Root won the toss and there were times in the early going when the action was neither elite sport nor satisfying entertainment.
The conditions for a Test played in September were autumnal and one side of Edgbaston is a building site. Some 15,000 tickets were sold for today, yet the ground was not half-full when play began. The atmosphere was flat.
Pakistan made four changes from the second Test at Lord's, including three debutants. England, as expected, resisted tinkering with their attack and the hosts had the Pakistan innings wrapped up in 33.5 overs.
At least Pakistan landed some blows on the England top-order. Ben Duckett and Jordan Cox played loose shots - potentially costly for Cox as he looks to nail down his place - and Root was lbw for the 10th time in 13 innings in Razaullah's first over in Test cricket.
Gay and Brook restored order in the evening sunshine and it already seems certain England will win before the weekend. It could even be over inside two days.
Quite what Root's developing England team can take from this series is unclear. The disparity between the two sides in these conditions is simply too large.
Gay battles to stake his claim
Gay has had the entire summer to make the opening position his own, though the arrivals of Cox and Dan Lawrence could make him most vulnerable when Jacob Bethell returns from a knee injury.
But Gay has been batting in the hardest position at a time when all batters have struggled for runs. This knock, in an innings when Cox wasted his chance, did his cause no harm without being a compelling case for long-term retention.
The Durham man was patient and watchful and also came through moments of frantic running with Brook. When the opportunity arose, the left-hander scored with handsome strokes through the off side.
Brook arrived when Razaullah was pushing the speed gun, and the England vice-captain also had to battle his recent weakness with the wicketkeeper standing up.
The fourth-wicket pair gradually halted Pakistan's brief spell of momentum, taking England ahead.
For Gay, a third half-century in six Tests came from 95 deliveries. Reaching the close unbeaten would have presented a golden opportunity for a big score on Thursday, only for a limp prod at Razaullah to leave more questions and a sense of what might have been.
Summer of Robinson continues
Robinson began this summer in an exile from the England team that had lasted for more than two years. He ends it as the attack leader, with statistics that stack up alongside some of the all-time greats of the game.
He had already had one lbw decision against Saim Ayub overturned by the time he pinned the same batter again in his second over. It gave Robinson his 100th Test wicket at an average of 19.34 - the first England bowler since Ian Botham to reach 100 wickets at an average below 20.
Indeed, no bowler since World War II with at least 100 Test wickets has a better average than Robinson. His three on Wednesday gave him a total of 27 for the summer at a cost of 7.96 apiece.
Such was their dominance, England could afford Duckett to miss two tough chances at first slip. Root, often captaining from short leg, set fields that crowded the bat, often with seven catchers.
Tongue bowled with high pace and targeted the stumps – all four of his wickets were bowled or lbw. Archer benefitted from two miscues from mid-on, then came back to eventually end the Ali-Abbas last-wicket stand.
The curiosity is Gus Atkinson. He has not bowled badly, yet has somehow missed out on the riches of his fellow seamers. While the rest have cleaned up, Atkinson has just one wicket in the series at an average of 156.

A video showing a woman being brutally assaulted by a man in an open field is being shared on social media (here, here) with the claim that it depicts a real incident involving the assault of a primary school teacher in Maharashtra. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: The video shows a primary school teacher being brutally assaulted in Maharashtra.
Fact: The video does not show an assault on a primary school teacher in Maharashtra. Instead, it shows a scripted fight video posted by a user who regularly shares similar staged fighting videos on his page. Hence, the claim is FALSE.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to an extended version of the video posted on an Instagram account named ‘Vipin Chauhan’ on 11 August 2026. One of the hashtags in the video’s description was #acting. We also found that multiple videos in similar attire were shared, with captions indicating that the man was assaulting the woman after she allegedly cheated on him (here, here, here). The fact that the video was circulated in parts, along with these captions, suggests it was a scripted act rather than a real incident.
The same video was reposted in September 2026, and the description stated that it was a planned video and warned viewers not to try it at home.
Further, the page bio stated that the user was available for WWE-style videos. We also reviewed other content shared on the profile and found multiple videos featuring the same duo seen in the viral video in similar fight scenes (here, here, here). This further indicates that the viral video depicts a staged act rather than a real incident.
To sum up, a scripted fight video is being falsely shared as an assault on a primary school teacher in Maharashtra.
