The Inside Story of What Happened at Stars and Stripes
For generations, the newspaper has served American military families without interference from the government. That work must continue. And it must remain editorially independent.
A “chicken plate,” in military parlance, is a protective shield used in a variety of combat situations. During the Vietnam War, chicken plates were inserted into vests—they are resistant against small-arms fire, but they’re also bulky and hot. So some pilots sat on them instead, which had the added benefit of providing protection against bullets that came from below.
I first encountered another type of chicken plate in Iraq, where I was embedded with a convoy of American service members patrolling outside of Tikrit.
On this particular morning, I sat alongside three soldiers inside an up-armored Humvee while a gunner manned the turret. But that gunner—James Murphy, a sergeant from New Jersey—wasn’t sitting in his sling, which was little more than a seat-belt strap hooked between two sides of the turret. If he sat down, the chicken plate would block his view. This left Murphy with a choice: stand up for hours and expose his head and chest, or remain behind the plate’s limited protection and endanger the convoy by missing a threat.
For the dozen or so gunners I spoke with, the choice was clear. Two of them removed the chicken plate entirely for a better view.
The military had no specific data on gunner casualties or whether the chicken plates were preventing them. Yet an Army general in Iraq was asking his staff why they were losing so many gunners. One officer I spoke with at the time told me that the answer was obvious the moment someone stood in the turret.
I reported a series of stories on gunners for Stars and Stripes, a newspaper with a long history of editorial independence despite being housed within the Department of Defense. A few weeks later, after returning to my home at the time—a room at the bachelor officers’ quarters on a Marine Corps base in Okinawa—I received a message from our Pentagon beat reporter, who told me that military officials had read the series and were fast-tracking improved equipment for deployment. They’d found a way to help protect the gunners without blocking their view from the turret.
I don’t want to overstate my role. At least some military officials were aware of the issue and had been testing prototypes for better shields. But many of the soldiers weren’t willing to discuss with senior leaders the specifics of what they needed, out of concern that they’d be viewed as complaining. I’m grateful that they trusted me enough to tell their stories.
Looking back now, what feels remarkable isn’t the lack of proper equipment. It’s the way the Pentagon was willing to take independent journalism that spotlighted deficiencies and use it to improve conditions for service members.
Uniformed military leaders have not lost the means to analyze and act on useful journalism. But publicly denouncing the reporting or the news outlet makes it far less likely that they will. Attacking people for telling the truth creates a chilling effect for truth tellers—including those who are themselves in the military.
The best journalism unearths information that complex bureaucracies overlook or suppress, intentionally or not. When leaders treat asking tough questions and reporting uncomfortable facts as disloyalty, they devalue a tool that can help them fix crucial problems.
The danger in this devaluation is immense, especially now; it comes as U.S. service members are once again fighting in the Middle East. The Pentagon hasn’t held a press briefing on combat operations in Iran since May 5. The Correspondents’ Corridor, where reporters worked inside the Pentagon for decades, is closed while court appeals continue on press-access restrictions. The New York Times is suing the Pentagon on First Amendment grounds, arguing that the Pentagon’s attempts to prevent independent reporting are clearly unconstitutional. (I should disclose that I, too, am suing the Pentagon. I was fired after I said in an appearance on CBS News that my personal red line would be if the Pentagon ever instructed me not to publish a perfectly accurate story. It is telling that I am being fired for describing the most anodyne of journalistic ethics, a position that any self-respecting reporter in any free society would hold, and that the Pentagon interpreted as insubordination.)
Stars and Stripes has its roots in the Civil War, when Union soldiers took over a printing press in Bloomfield, Missouri. The paper was revived during World War I under General John “Black Jack” Pershing and has published continuously since 1942, when General George C. Marshall recognized the value it provided troops and aimed to follow Pershing’s example. “No official control was ever exercised over the matter which went into” Stars and Stripes, Marshall said of the WWI edition.
It didn’t take long for that editorial freedom to be challenged. General George Patton complained about the “Willie and Joe” cartoonist Bill Mauldin’s depictions of soldiers as they often appeared—tired and dirty. (Mauldin would have known; he was himself a soldier.) But General Dwight Eisenhower rejected Patton’s drive to control the reporting itself. “It is the soldier’s paper,” he said, “and we won’t interfere,” according to the historian Stephen Ambrose’s foreword in a book by Mauldin, whose wartime cartoons earned him the 1945 Pulitzer Prize.
The newspaper continued to operate overseas after World War II, hiring civilian journalists to work alongside service members. But attempts at curtailing Stripes’ independence periodically arose. Congress documented occasional pressures in the 1960s. In the ’80s, a General Accounting Office report to Congress found conclusive evidence of censorship, and pointed out the “inherent cultural conflict” between the First Amendment mission and the military’s own.
Those findings led the House Armed Services Committee to direct the Pentagon to establish an ombudsman, responsible to Congress, who would monitor the free flow of information to service members through Stars and Stripes. And in 1993, a Defense Department directive affirmed that Stars and Stripes is editorially independent of the military chain of command. A subsequent federal regulation added to those protections.
In 2020, the Pentagon proposed cutting all funding to Stars and Stripes, after the department’s comptroller stated that it is “probably not the best way that we communicate any longer.” The idea drew a bipartisan rebuke in Congress. The White House agreed with the lawmakers, and Stripes lived on.
Last November, I moved to Washington, D.C., to accept the editor-in-chief job at the paper, where I’d already been serving as Europe and Middle East chief, based near Ramstein Air Base, in Germany.
Two months later, the Pentagon chief spokesman Sean Parnell fired a broadside at Stars and Stripes. On January 15, he posted on X that the news organization must be rid of “woke distractions that syphon morale.”
The same day, the Pentagon revoked the federal regulation it had established in 1994, calling it unnecessary. The Daily Wire, which reported that half of all Stripes content would come from the military’s public-affairs team, and that civilian reporters would be replaced by military members. When Stars and Stripes reporters called the Pentagon press office for comment and clarification, they received nothing more than a referral to the tweet and the Daily Wire story.
On February 28, the United States and Israel attacked Iran, killing Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. The first Stars and Stripes story came from a wire service, because there aren’t any Stripes reporters inside Iran. But within hours, we had half a dozen stories focused on the U.S. military bases in the region and the people there. In Bahrain, civilians were given the order to evacuate an hour after missiles began falling on the headquarters base of the U.S. Fifth Fleet.
The coverage drew millions of readers, and a video shot by one of our active-duty reporters of a plume rising over the Navy base was viewed all over the world. We worked hard on covering the Iran conflict and thought little of that January tweet—that is, until a Pentagon memo came in mid-March.
The memo simultaneously affirmed our independence and added restrictions. That wire-service story from Iran was now forbidden, along with any other paid wire-service news. So were the comics, of all things. Our publishing decisions would be subject to “good order and discipline”—a line borrowed from the Uniform Code of Military Justice. Our military reporters, who function as interns and receive mentorship from seasoned civilian journalists, now had to wonder whether writing a story might land them in legal jeopardy.
I told military reporters who were worried that a story might hurt their career to let us know, and we’d reassign it. Meanwhile, the staff never compromised on their ethics and values. They reported fairly and accurately and, when called for, held power to account.
The ombudsman wrote a column that assailed the news restrictions, in keeping with the duties set by Congress. Two weeks later, the Defense Department fired her.
By the time I sat down with CBS’s David Martin in late June, I had spoken with no fewer than 16 news outlets and authors about Stars and Stripes. Martin asked me about the “woke distractions” referenced in the January tweet and I answered honestly—that the Pentagon had never explained to us what that meant.
Martin also asked whether I had a personal red line when it came to press restrictions, and I said that I did. If the Pentagon were to say, “Don’t run a perfectly accurate story. Run this instead. Here it is, written by the Pentagon. That would be a red line.”
My response to hypothetical censorship was consistent with what military leaders have said for more than a century, and with the Defense Department’s own directive barring censorship and news management. It is also consistent with basic journalistic ethics: Without editorial independence, journalists cannot uphold their duty to the public.
As part of the CBS interview, the Middle East correspondent Lara Korte stated that she worked for Stars and Stripes, not the Pentagon. She made the distinction to underscore her independence, which is essential to credibility. I learned approximately a week later that the Pentagon press office wasn’t happy about the interview, but that was all I heard.
On August 12, seven weeks after the CBS interview, the Pentagon sent notices of proposed separation for Korte and me to Stripes’ publisher, Max Lederer, and told him to sign them.
Lederer was an Airborne soldier turned Army attorney who was awarded the Bronze Star before he joined Stars and Stripes. He worked his way up through business operations to serve for two decades as publisher.
He reviewed the separation notices and pointed out legal and ethical inconsistencies. Those concerns were dismissed. Rather than sign the notices, he submitted his resignation. (They fired him instead.)
On August 21, the three of us received the separation notices, which listed insubordination as the primary charge. The notices issued to Korte and me cited our CBS comments but didn’t state which order we were purportedly disobeying. Lederer’s firing was for not signing the documents in the first place.
That same day, the Pentagon replaced the directive issued in 1993. Among other things, it bars comics deemed editorial in nature and prevents reporters from using the Freedom of Information Act on behalf of the news organization. I can’t think of another American media outlet with the same restriction.
About an hour after we received our separation notices, the military deputy to the publisher, who’d arrived two weeks earlier, ordered a 10-page document to be published on Stripes.com within 30 minutes. The document stated that Stripes would continue to run independent journalism and that “it is time to take them at their word,” referring to the Pentagon.
I do take them at their word. All of the words they’ve put out since January, along with their actions. The Pentagon has articulated a remarkably narrow view of press freedom. The government may stop short of censoring an individual story. But it will seek to fire newsroom leaders for opposing the replacement of accurate reporting with press releases. It will strip an organization of basic reporting tools it deems unnecessary or distasteful. And it will discredit the source of the reporting if a story is perceived as unflattering to the president or his secretary of defense.
The press isn’t a perfect institution. A global 2026 Reuters Institute survey found that the percentage of people who report trusting the news dropped to the lowest level since Reuters began asking the question in 2015; in the U.S., only 25 percent of Americans said that they trust the news most of the time. Whatever combination of press failures and partisanship produced this decline, public trust has eroded. And it’s that erosion that has made it much easier for officials to delegitimize accurate, balanced journalism.
Reporters, like anyone, make mistakes, but ethical journalism remains fundamentally useful to government and to the citizens who hold it accountable. People in large organizations—the U.S. military included—often avoid delivering bad news for fear of appearing to oppose a leader’s plans. Independent reporting moves information forward, but only if sources know they’ll be able to speak with journalists without fear of reprisal, and if they believe that leaders are open to reacting to criticism like professionals.
That’s what happened in Iraq. The gunners knew what they needed to do their job safely. They didn’t want to be viewed as complainers. Independent journalism sent the message to those who needed to hear it.

Who will reach Super Bowl? - NFL predictions for 2026 season
- Published
The NFL is notoriously difficult to predict and last season was no different.
Seven of the eight division winners were different from 2024, with two of the Super Bowl favourites missing out on the play-offs entirely - the Baltimore Ravens and Kansas City Chiefs.
Two outsiders then made it all the way to the big game, with the Seattle Seahawks beating the New England Patriots for their first NFL championship in 12 years.
So, who will be this season's surprise package? Who will be playing at Super Bowl 61 next February? And who will be the main men?
Here, the BBC's NFL experts make their picks for the 2026 season, which begins this week. Plus you can predict your Super Bowl winner at the bottom of this page.
Who will reach the Super Bowl?
Rob Staton: I think the NFC will be another battle between the Los Angeles Rams and Seattle Seahawks. I'm going to go with the Rams, simply because only two teams have repeated since the turn of the century. I have them facing the Buffalo Bills. Josh Allen finally gets to the big game.
Hugh Ferris: You could argue that, aside from an underwhelming head coach hire, there's little reason the 2026 Bills will be any different to the recent incarnations. I'm picking them to finally get over the line, though, and reach the Super Bowl, but to lose nonetheless. It's incredibly difficult to choose anyone else rather than the Rams, isn't it?
Haydn Parry: Surely the Bills can convert Allen's talent and make it to the season showpiece? Joe Brady's promotion to head coach might prove to be the missing ingredient. From the NFC, I think the Rams look most likely to have a strong tilt this campaign, and I see them winning it.
Joe Bradshaw: The last time the Super Bowl was at SoFi Stadium in 2022, the Rams won on home territory and they look primed to repeat next February. From the AFC, surely Bills quarterback Allen is overdue a trip to the NFL's biggest game, even if it will ultimately end in defeat.
David Brindle: After losing Bo Nix to injury in last season's play-offs, I expect the Denver Broncos to use that as motivation and at least go one further this season. As for the Rams, it's very difficult to look past the consensus predictions for the Super Bowl.
Ben Collins: Full disclosure, I'd seen the above before writing this so here's some leftfield picks... imagine if it's the Los Angeles Chargers that actually get to play in the Super Bowl in their own stadium, and it's former Rams quarterback Jared Goff that leads Detroit to victory.
Who will be the NFL's MVP?
Rob Staton: I'm going with Josh Allen. He now has an offensive-minded head coach running the team. Everything will be geared towards him having a big season.
Hugh Ferris: In an attempt to think outside the box, I'm picking Justin Herbert of the Chargers. You might suggest a quarterback in a Jim Harbaugh team isn't likely to get the chance to have an MVP-level season, but the hiring of Mike McDaniel as offensive coordinator might change that.

This week, Lyft riders in Nashville, Tennessee, who request a ride on the app might get matched with a new driver: a robot.
A new partnership between the ride-hail company and Waymo, the self-driving-vehicle developer, will integrate self-driving rides into Lyft’s platform. (Riders can also request a driverless ride through Waymo’s own app; service there started in April.)
The rollout marks a new milestone for Lyft, which has worked with other, smaller self-driving vehicle companies in the US, but never with a partner as big as Waymo, which operates in 14 US metros. Lyft executives also see the partnership as a continuation of a conversation the ride-hail company has been having for a few years now with its hundreds of thousands of US drivers.
Lyft, like its competitor Uber, insists that its platform will be a “hybrid network” for a long while yet, as human drivers work alongside robot ones. But it’s hard to imagine the transition won’t upend life for some of the millions of professional drivers who work in the US today.
“We've got to make sure we're honest, we're open. We have conversations with drivers and bring them into the journey with proactive communication,” says Jeremy Bird, Lyft’s executive vice president of global growth. “We've done AV [themed] driver forums; we've done driver appreciation events to make sure we're having a conversation. But we're embracing the transformation in the future of AVs.”
A glimpse of what the future might look like can be found in Lyft’s provisional operations depot in Nashville, where employees of its longtime car rental service called Flexdrive now clean, prep, repair, and position Waymos in the right parts of the city so they're ready for passengers. (An 80,000-square-foot, purpose-built depot is set to open in October.) Waymo, which focuses on building autonomous vehicle technology, partners with several companies around the US to help manage and operate its driverless fleets. Of the 72 people who work at this Nashville depot, half of them are former Lyft drivers, the company says.
One of those former drivers, Jonathan Baines, started picking up Lyft riders in 2016 to help support himself as he worked as singer-songwriter. He liked the extra cash but also the people he drove—tourists, locals. “It kind of felt like you were hanging out with your friends more than anything,” he says. Now Baines works as a fleet operations lead, which means he oversees workers cleaning the Waymos, making sure they hit their metrics and standards. It’s the best operations job he’s ever had, he says, “more fun than retail.”
And Baines has to admit: There’s something nice about being alone in a Waymo. “As much as I love to talk to people, to be able to be in the car and relax and not have an obligation to talk with anyone is a nice feature,” he says.
Bird says having Waymos on the Lyft platform will give riders more choice, which is a good thing. Also, more vehicles on the platform means more supply means lower fares. (In a recent earnings call, Lyft executives used data from San Francisco, where it doesn’t offer driverless rides, to suggest that the presence of autonomous vehicles won’t affect the number of rides that human drivers see.) Bird says Lyft intends to continue partnering with different robotaxi companies.
But it may be near-impossible for the new jobs maintaining and directing self-driving cars to neatly replace the driving ones lost. In Washington, DC, where Waymo has fought for months to start service, the company has said that it expects to employ “hundreds” of people if its cars launch there; some 3,200 taxi and ride-hail drivers work in the District (likely many of them part-time). To compensate, Waymo has proposed diverting some of its DC revenue to a fund dedicated to vocational training and workforce development for drivers, to help them transition to other jobs. Waymo did not respond to a request for comment on this story.
Former drivers make up 35 percent of Lyft’s Flexdrive workforce, which is currently in 30 US cities. Hiring former drivers “is an effort we will continue to be very intentional about as AVs become a growing part of the fleet,” Lyft spokesperson Cristian Delgado writes.
Baines is already looking ahead, even beyond that sprawling Waymo depot set to open in October. Part of him misses the “small business” part of being an independent contractor for Lyft. Eventually, he’d like to own his own autonomous vehicle, so it can go out to pick up and drop off passengers without him. “There's the fear of AI taking over,” he says. “I think you can learn how to use AI as a resource.”

Ryan Garcia was a no-show for his first face-off with Conor Benn on Tuesday before their world title fight this weekend in Las Vegas.
The American was scheduled to attend a photo opportunity, but skipped it to leave Benn appearing alone.
Benn, 29, did have the company of his father, boxing legend Nigel Benn, who pretended to face off with his son.
After joking around with his dad, Benn said Garcia "didn't turn up".
"I apologise for Ryan doing what Ryan does and bottling it. We turn up, we're here, ready for the face-off," he said.
"Come Saturday, he's in for a war."
Garcia defends his WBC welterweight title at the T-Mobile Arena in Benn's first world championship bout.
The 28-year-old is the favourite for the contest and after failing to attend the first face-off of fight week, Garcia mocked Benn on Instagram.
"Nice relaxing time as Conor wastes time showing up to a face-off," he said.
"Back to the sauna you go, sausage getting cooked every way."
They are due to meet twice before fight night with the news conference on Thursday and the weigh-in on Friday.
Much has been made of Benn's weight cut for this contest, with the Briton having not fought at 10st 7lb (67kg) since 2022.

Garcia has fought at lightweight and light-welterweight – missing weight for his light-welterweight contest against Devin Haney in 2024 – but is not expected to have issues with the weight, while Benn has said he does not intend to stay long at welterweight.

Colombia's new president loosens gun control rules
- Published
Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has signed a decree which eases restrictions on people carrying legal firearms in public.
De la Espriella, who during his campaign for the presidency promised to take an iron-fist approach to crime, said it was "not right that criminals are armed to the teeth while decent people can't defend themselves".
The decree lifts a suspension that had been in force for a decade, which meant that even those in possession of a permit to carry guns could not do so without additional authorisation.
De la Espriella insisted that the decree would not create a free-for-all and that tight controls over who can own a gun would remain in place.
While signing the decree, the president said he had made good on his campaign promise: "A man's word is his honour, and I have honour, that's why I keep my word."
The restriction on carrying legal guns in public was brought in by the then-President Juan Manuel Santos in December 2015. It was originally meant to be a temporary measure, aimed at improving security during the Christmas and New Year festivities.
But the suspension was extended yearly by Santos and two subsequent presidents from opposing sides of the political spectrum: conservative Iván Duque and left-wing Gustavo Petro.
Under the law, even those with a permit to carry a gun could not take it out of their homes unless they applied for - and were granted - additional authorisation.
De la Espriella has insisted that his decree has removed a restriction which had never been meant to be permanent.
According to Spanish newspaper El País, the decree will affect almost 700,000 people in Colombia who are already in possession of a legal permit to carry a gun.
They will now be able to take their registered gun out of their home, provided their permits remain up to date.
Green Alliance Party Senator Ariel Ávila described the move as a "grave error", arguing that legally held guns would end up in the hands of criminals.
Ávila insisted that it created an ethical dilemma, as it should only be state forces that carry guns and act as guarantors of people's security.
De la Espriella insisted that the measure would not negatively affect security in the country and said forces were targeting those holding illegal guns and had seized more than 15,000 firearms so far this year.
Most of them, according to de la Espriella, belonged to members of breakaway factions of the Farc rebel group and the Gulf Clan criminal gang.

The Karnataka State Travel Operators’ Association (KSTOA) has urged the Transport Department to temporarily keep in abeyance its August 28, 2026, circular directing the installation of fare meters in new and existing taxi and motor-cab vehicles.
The association said the circular does not clearly differentiate between various categories of taxis, including street-hailing cabs, airport and railway-station taxis, app-based aggregator vehicles, and luxury, corporate and tourist vehicles operated by registered travel agencies on advance bookings or contractual arrangements.
The Transport Department has directed all taxis and motor cabs in Karnataka, including app-based cabs in Bengaluru, to install fare meters as per government-notified fares. RTOs have been instructed not to renew fitness certificates of vehicles that fail to comply. The directive applies to both new and existing vehicles under Rule 129 of the Karnataka Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989.
Confusion among operators
Radhakrishna Holla, president of the Karnataka State Travel Operators Association, said: “These categories operate under different permits, business models and fare structures. Applying a uniform fare-meter requirement to all such vehicles has led to confusion among operators.”
He argued that until category-wise guidelines are issued, the absence of a fare meter alone should not be grounds for denying a vehicle a fitness inspection or Fitness Certificate, preventing road-tax-paid vehicles from operating, or initiating penal action against owners or drivers.
KSTOA has requested the Transport Commissioner and the State Transport Authority to consult industry stakeholders and issue clear, category-wise guidelines before implementing the directive.
Meanwhile, officials said that the directive follows a growing number of complaints alleging that some app-based aggregators and taxi drivers are not adhering to the government-prescribed fare structure.
An official said: “Passengers are always complaining about being overcharged by aggregators and other taxi operators. Meanwhile, drivers’ unions have been demanding a uniform fare structure and a standardised revenue-sharing mechanism for app-based aggregators and other taxi operators. The installation of meters will bring uniformity in fare.”
Government-notified fare structure
The mandatory fare-meter rule will cover taxis operating across Karnataka and is expected to affect nearly three lakh taxis and cabs in Bengaluru. Under the government-notified fare structure, taxis priced up to ₹10 lakh will charge a minimum of ₹100 for the first 4 km, followed by ₹24 per km. For vehicles costing ₹10 lakh to ₹15 lakh, the minimum fare is ₹115 for the first 4 km, with an additional ₹28 per km thereafter. Vehicles priced above ₹15 lakh will have a minimum fare of ₹130 for the first 4 km, followed by ₹32 per km.
The fare structure also includes a waiting charge of ₹1 per minute. Trips undertaken between midnight and 6 a.m. will attract an additional 10% charge. Aggregators are also permitted to collect applicable GST, toll fees and other authorised charges from passengers.

Those who remember PC gaming in the days before Steam may have fond memories of the “big box” packaging that made those games stand out as shelf eye candy and sought-after in-home collectibles. Today, PC gaming platform GOG is hoping to reignite some of the nostalgia for those days by adding downloadable 3D models and printable, foldable high-res packaging scans for a handful of PC games on the platform.
Thus far, the “Printable Big Box” collection on GOG is limited to just five games: Armikrog, Descent, Hitman: Codename 47, Myst, and Star Trek: 25th Anniversary. Players browsing those games on the GOG store will now see “3D Boxes” listed among the included “Goodies” before purchase. Owners of those games on GOG can download a ZIP file containing a version of the box art as an animated 3D object file (in an easy-to-open GLB format) and a “flat printable template” in PDF, SVG, and Adobe Illustrator formats. Those downloads allow for what GOG calls “a proper papercraft project for anyone who misses shelves full of PC game boxes.”
“Physical media doesn’t survive the way software can—boxes get lost, crushed, thrown out,” GOG writes in today’s announcement. “Scanning them, and letting you print your own, is preservation in a different shape: the same mission that keeps these games running on modern PCs, applied to the objects they used to come in.”

Apple
 has launched the iPhone Duo, its first foldable phone, at Rs 2,99,900 in India. It comes in two colours, star white and night sky, and it is the first iPhone to drop Face ID for Touch ID, which now sits in the side button.
Shut, the Duo works like a normal phone. The 5.4-inch outer Super Retina XDR screen carries 90 per cent of the screen area of an iPhone 18 Pro. Open it and there is a 7.6-inch inner display, half again as large as the iPhone 18 Pro Max and the biggest Apple has put on an iPhone. Both screens share an aspect ratio, so content scales across them cleanly, and both run ProMotion and Always On at up to 3,000 nits. The inner panel gets a nano-texture finish that cuts glare and, more usefully, makes the crease harder to see.
iPhone Duo price in India and availability: Price starts at Rs 2,99,900 and pre-orders open on October 16
The Rs 2,99,900 starting price covers the 256GB model, with 512GB, 1TB and 2TB options above it. India is in the first group of markets, with pre-orders opening on Friday, October 16 and sales starting Friday, October 23. Apple has two first-party cases for it, the Duo Folio with a kickstand at Rs 14,900 and a two-part case at Rs 8,900. One thing to plan for before buying: the Duo is eSIM-only worldwide, with no tray at all, though Airtel, Jio and Vi all support it.
iPhone Duo specifications: A20 Pro chip, two batteries and a 48MP main camera
Apple has used the chip from the iPhone 18 Pro, built on a 2nm process, with a 6-core CPU that is 20 per cent quicker than the A19 Pro and a 7-core GPU up 40 per cent. A new display engine drives both screens at once, and Apple claims up to 35 per cent better sustained performance than the iPhone 17 Pro thanks to a vapour chamber bonded to the chip package. A battery sits on each side and the two behave as one, giving 31 hours of video on the inner display, 44 hours on the outer, and 24 hours of typical use when both get equal work. Charging reaches 50 per cent in about 20 minutes over cable.
The rear camera is a 48MP Fusion Main with sensor-shift stabilisation and a 2x telephoto crop, paired with the same 48MP Fusion Ultra Wide as the iPhone 18 Pro. Because the phone stands on its own, Apple has built features around that: Smart Take fires the shutter when everyone is posed, Duo Preview puts a live preview on the outer screen for your subject, Kid Cue plays animations to get a child looking at the lens, and Duo FaceTime lets someone beside you join a call on the outer display. Apple Pencil support arrives later this year on either screen.
Durability is the part Apple spent longest on. Under the cover layer sits a custom polymer the company says is up to 40 per cent stiffer than the industry norm, high-strength glass above and below the panel, and adhesives that let the layers slide against each other like pages so the panel does not absorb the bend stress. The hinge alone runs to more than a hundred parts. The frame is grade 5 titanium, the front carries Ceramic Shield 2, and the phone is rated IP68. On the software side, iOS 27 moves the dock and controls to the side and adds Split View, so two apps sit side by side on an iPhone for the first time.

AI researcher quits Anthropic over superintelligence fears: ‘gambling with our lives’
Jacob Coxon says he and others building AI believe it could ‘kill us all by the end of the decade’, as firms race to build advanced models
An artificial intelligence researcher who left OpenAI to join Anthropic has decided to leave the industry, accusing both US companies of “gambling with our lives” in the race to develop AI models capable of self-improvement.
Jacob Coxon, 27, spent the past three years pretraining AI models, first at OpenAI and then, this year, at its rival Anthropic, which he considered more cautious in its approach.
Pretraining is the stage where AI models absorb vast quantities of data.
“Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon said on Tuesday.
“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” he said in a social media post. “This is not a marketing stunt,” he added.
Superintelligence is the theoretical point when AI’s capabilities exceed human intelligence.

Nepal authorities have said they are “confident” that dozens of workers in Nepal’s Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant are still alive, more than a week after deadly flash floods left them trapped in an underground chamber.
Authorities said that at least 639 workers were still missing from hydropower plants built along Nepal’s Bhote Koshi and Triushuli rivers.
Most of the projects were destroyed when a surge of water, debris and mud came coursing down the river valley last week, triggered by the collapse of a melting glacier on the border between Nepal and China-controlled Tibet.
The deadly flash floods reached up to 100mph (160km/h), according to scientists, and travelled more than 60 miles down the river valley, wiping away whole villages, bridges, and hydropower dams.
At least 1,252 people have been confirmed dead from the floods. More than 4,200 remain missing.
According to a preliminary estimate by the UN Development Programme, the disaster created at least 2.2m tonnes of debris, including parts of buildings, rocks and sediment. Large boulders and flood waters deluged the hydropower tunnels, blocking off the entrances, and some were buried deep in mud.
Rescue efforts have increasingly centred on these tunnels, where authorities believe workers may have survived for more than a week due to air pockets. So far, more than 270 people have been rescued from the hydropower projects.
Speaking on Wednesday, officials said they believed 46 people were still alive in an underground room in Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant, and efforts were ongoing to locate them using excavators and other heavy equipment.
“We are very confident that they must be alive after one week because … they have food and water over there in the building,” Amhsu Kiran Shahi, a board member of the Nepal electricity authority, told Reuters.
Durga Gurung, 60, said his brother Jhappad Bhujel was among those trapped in a hydropower tunnel. “Right now, we are just relying on God,” he told the Guardian. “We have not been given any information about whether the people inside are alive or not.
“Neither the army nor the people from the electricity authority are telling us anything. So many days have passed that we have reached a point where it feels like all we can do is hope for a miracle.”
“Our relatives are sitting inside a dark tunnel,” he added. “How long can they possibly survive?”
Major rescue operations were under way or planned at four hydropower projects. Two sites – the Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project and the Upper Trishuli 3A facility – where about 90 people are missing, offered the strongest prospect of finding survivors because of the presence of air inside the tunnels, Shahi said.
The Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project is located in Rasuwa district, about three miles away from the border with Tibet, which was one of the areas of Nepal hardest hit by the floods, and remains almost inaccessible except by helicopter. “This is the only project where it’s possible to walk through the tunnel,” Shahi said. “The army tried doing that three days ago, but they didn’t find the room. We are going in again.”
At the Upper Trishuli 3A facility, another project hit by the floods, it took rescue workers almost six days to find the tunnels because of the thick mud. The authorities believe about 30 to 40 people may still be alive in the tunnel. “We are expecting [survivors] in there because we are told there is a dry space inside. We are trying to break into the tunnel now,” said the Nepali army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet on Wednesday.
The army said the search and rescue operation would go on for as long as there was hope for survivors, but that efforts would also continue to recover the dead bodies. “We are using every technology available in Nepal right now, and we are taking help from the Indians, Chinese, Koreans. We have experts from Australia too,” added Basnet.
Families of those still trapped in the projects have returned to the Nepal electricity office for the past eight days, in the hope for information. Laxmi Adhikari’s brother Jeevanlal Adhikari had gone to the Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project to test the machines, when the floods hit.
She accused the authorities of withholding information from the families, and of not acting fast enough to save their relatives. “We have been running from one ministry to another and from disaster management authority to another government office, trying to find my brother,” she said. “We keep going from place to place, but the rescue operation has not been accelerated.”
She said the lack of answers made the wait even more painful: “When the water came rushing in, where did he go? Did he manage to get to safety? They haven’t even given us definite information about whether our people are alive or not.”
Nepal has invested more than $9bn (£6.7bn) in building hydropower dams across the mountains, huge sums given the country’s small economy. According to preliminary surveys, the floods debilitated or destroyed 11 hydropower plants and knocked out about 10% of Nepal’s total electricity-generation capacity.
According to the authorities, more than 20,000 houses will have to be rebuilt in the aftermath of the flood. Nepal has put the cost of recovery at more than $5bn (£3.7bn).

Data for 2024-25 reveals that 51,249 corneas were donated in India, which met just a quarter of the projected need of around 1,00,000 corneas annually. The reason for this is a utilisation rate of 50% at best, with actual transplants performed ranging only between 25,000 to 30,000.
Why does this happen? The cause for a significant proportion of this gift of vision not reaching an operating table is the donated corneal tissue not being tested or processed in time. Other causes include improper harvesting and storage, as well as the decrease in endothelial cell density, which comes with an increase in age of donors. While some of these factors may not have an immediate or implementable solution, what is fixable, is timing and logistics.
Understanding cornea retrival
Cornea retrieval after death is a race against the clock. First, is the six-hour window after death within which a cornea should ideally be retrieved. This can differ in different weathers. For instance, in winters and monsoon, it can be a time frame of 6-8 hours as well. The second, less-publicly known factor, is the clock that starts once the corneal tissue is in storage. Most Indian eye banks still preserve corneas in McCarey-Kaufman (MK) medium, which keeps tissue usable for about 72 hours. A few use newer intermediate media such as Optisol-GS or Cornisol, extending that window to between 10 and 14 days.
Doctors at the Dr. Rajendra Prasad Centre for Ophthalmic Sciences (RPC), AIIMS Delhi, along with engineers from IIT Delhi, are testing a way to recycle discarded donor corneas using a bioengineered graft. Corneas that fail transplant standards, because of low cell counts or minor damage, can be stripped of living cells and turned into a reusable structural scaffold for patients with surface-level corneal damage. While the trials are still at a very early stage, it does point toward a future where less of what is donated ends up being discarded.
However, until we come up with a way to reuse corneas that miss the deadline, the window closes and the tissue has to be discarded. 72 hours, or even two weeks, is not much time to test a cornea, find a compatible patient, and move tissue from an eye bank to an operating theatre. The challenge is intensified because almost 70% of all corneal collection and use is concentrated in just six states - Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Gujarat, Karnataka, Maharashtra, and Tamil Nadu. A cornea retrieved in a smaller town, with no local surgeon waiting, can become unusable while it is in transit to a city that has one.
What can be done
Extending storage life is the first step. Eye banks must shift from using MK medium to intermediate media, and eventually to organ-culture storage, which some countries use to keep corneas viable for up to a month. This helps to buy precious time to find the right recipient instead of the nearest one. A national, real-time inventory linking every eye bank directly to surgeons in 50 cities, could let a cornea about to expire in Kozhikode be offered to a waiting list in Chennai before it is thrown away.
As fresher corneal tissue survives testing and transplant better, the next focus must be on reducing the time between death and retrieval, and retrieval and preservation. Hospital Cornea Retrieval Programmes, where hospitals proactively notify eye banks of deaths and trained counsellors approach grieving families, help to reduce this time factor and outperform voluntary home collections. Expanding that model into more hospitals, rather than relying on a push only during Eye Donation Fortnight, will help to increase the corneal utilisation rate.
Quality assurance (QA) programmes at eye banks will also help in effectively reducing the discard rate, even with an increase in the volume of donated corneas. A study showed that the discard rate came down from around 40% to 30% with better donor acquisition processes and improvement in tissue recovery due to effective compliance with quality assurance programmes.
While we address the donation aspect with awareness and educating the people on the benefits of organ donation, we must also take care of the delivery with better storage chemistry, faster hospital protocols, and a database that shows, in real time, exactly which cornea is about to run out of time, who needs it and where.
(Dr. Suvira Jain is medical director, ASG Hospital Limited, Worli, Mumbai. Suvira.Jain@asgeyehospital.com)

US Embassy issues health alerts as Cuba’s multiple crises push islanders to breaking point
Daily power outages now surpass 24 hours and clean running water is scarce, leading to an increase in gastrointestinal illnesses
Cubans have painted a grim picture of daily life as multiple crises affecting the island nation worsen, with locals forced to rummage through trash for food and sleep on the street to survive.
For a population of roughly 10 million, the mental burden of sweltering nights, water and power shortages, dwindling fuel and crumbling homes is reaching a critical threshold. And with a U.S. energy embargo and deep economic woes offer, there is no immediate prospect of relief in sight.
"Before there was hope," Dr. Yomeidis Felicó Riverón said. "Right now, what people have lost is exactly that."
A primary care physician, Felicó Riverón has taken on an unexpected secondary role as residents attempt to navigate their challenging environment.
"They come and cry about their troubles, because they have no one else to vent to," she said of her patients. "We end up having to play psychologist."
Parents shield children from Cuba's realities
On a recent sunny afternoon, six girls and one boy gathered around a table while their parents sat in the background, attempting to fan away the suffocating heat. The children were attending a free workshop on crafting gift bags and perfume, designed to offer a temporary respite from Cuba's realities.
"My son doesn’t know if there’s food or if there’s no food," Felicó Riverón said, noting that she conceals financial difficulties from him when she cannot afford things he asks for.
Instead, she shifts his focus: "Let’s go play, let’s go to the park. We’ll come back another day."
Dianne Tamayo was among the mothers present that day. The workshop served as an oasis for her and her daughter, allowing her to converse with others and temporarily forget household concerns.
"My husband is my rock," she said. "When I’m going crazy, my husband tells me, ‘Sit down, breathe … let’s put on some music.’"
He sometimes has to remind Tamayo that their daughter is coming home from school soon, and that they need to keep their troubles, anxieties and frustrations to themselves.
"I do the best I can with the tools I have, but there’s still a moment where I get overwhelmed," she said.
Tears fell as she confided that she doesn’t have anything in her life that relaxes her, and that she has never questioned how to release her feelings about life in Cuba.
"They are exterminating us," she said, "and we remain complacent."
U.S. Embassy issues health alerts
Difficulties on the island intensified after U.S. President Donald Trump announced in late January that he would impose tariffs on any country that sells or provides oil to the Caribbean country. Longtime U.S. sanctions also have taken their toll, Cuba's government said.
From March 2025 to the end of February, "the U.S. policy of economic strangulation" amounted to more than $8 billion, "a record figure," according to Cuban Foreign Affairs Minister Bruno Rodríguez.
Power cuts have grown more frequent this year, and daily outages now surpass 24 hours. Consequently, running water is often scarce, and small protests have erupted, despite the fear of being detained, as anger and frustration boil over.
The worsening situation prompted the U.S. Embassy to issue two public health alerts recently.
On Aug. 28, the embassy noted that "Cuba’s water supply infrastructure is increasingly unstable " and that there are "residential neighborhoods experiencing long periods without water from municipal or public sources."
On Friday, the embassy warned of an increase in gastrointestinal illnesses linked to the "degradation of the water and energy infrastructure. …. Recent cases have included E. coli, norovirus, Shigella, and other gastrointestinal pathogens."
Despite ongoing shortages of water and power, 81-year-old Havana resident Oscar Joaquín López said that he doesn’t dwell on what he lacks.
"Why?" López said. "Because it drives you crazy, and nobody is going to drive me crazy."
On a recent afternoon, he leaned against the doorframe of his home as he watched his 58-year-old roommate fill up nearly a dozen plastic containers with water that flowed from a pipe on the street. Having gone several days without water, they acted quickly.
With temperatures hovering above 90 F (32 C), López said that he sits in his doorframe until midnight to catch a breeze from the nearby ocean, a steel pipe nearby to ward off any intruders. After midnight, he goes to bed, hoping the wooden slat he wedged into his window will catch any wind, however slight.
Nearby, 62-year-old mason José Laó Faviel dug through overflowing garbage on the street, looking for food to feed his pig and her 10 piglets, because he had none to give them.
"What are you going to do?" he said. "We’re living through difficult times."
Minutes later, another man rifled through the same pile of garbage. After opening several bags, he found something to eat.
Cubans find solace in family
Sweat gathered around Armando Lafita’s brow as the 60-year-old pushed a cart through the crumbling buildings in Old Havana. Authorities have evacuated some residents in the area for safety reasons, but those with nowhere else to live now sleep on the street, ducking inside their building when they need something.
Lafita’s cart was filled with red roses and white ginger lilies, Cuba’s national flower. He sells them for 10 to 40 cents a bunch, but sometimes he goes home without a single sale.
"Everybody is fighting to survive here," he said. "It’s getting harder every day."
Like many Cubans, Lafita said the only thing that keeps him going is family: his 19-year-old son.
It’s the same reason that 70-year-old José Manuel Borroto Díaz and his 93-year-old mother, Teresita del Rosario González Ricardo, keep going: they have each other.
"Our situation is like something out of a movie, but we’re going to press on," said Borroto, a retired aviation official who was in Angola during Cuba’s military intervention in the 1970s.
Across the island, Cubans are pressing on even as the crises deepen, including 90-year-old Lázaro Alfonso Oviedo. He recently attended a weekly gathering to help raise the spirits of elderly people.
Oviedo danced and sang in a deep, robust voice "to forget for a little while the suffering the empire puts us through," he said, referring to the United States.
"We are not going to give up," he said as he praised Cubans' unwavering resilience. "We get it precisely from the spirit forged by the revolution itself — a revolution spanning more than 60 years."

UN nuclear watchdog board reports Iran to Security Council for first time in 20 years
The agency says Iran failed to cooperate in a long-running investigation into uranium traces detected by inspectors at undeclared sites
The UN atomic watchdog’s board on Wednesday reported Iran to the UN Security Council for the first time in 20 years, citing it for failure to cooperate in a long-running investigation into uranium traces detected by inspectors at undeclared sites.
Western officials suspect that the traces could provide evidence that Iran had a secret nuclear weapons programme until 2003. Iran says that it is not pursuing nuclear weapons and that its programme is entirely peaceful.
Reporting Iran to the Security Council opens the country to possible sanctions and asset freezes, though such punitive measures are unlikely because Iran’s allies Russia and China hold veto power on the panel.
Twenty-three countries on the International Atomic Energy Agency ’s 35-member board of governors voted for Wednesday’s resolution at IAEA headquarters in Vienna.
China, Russia and Niger opposed it, while eight countries abstained and one did not vote as it was in arrears, according to diplomats who spoke on condition of anonymity to describe the outcome of the closed-door vote.
The resolution was put forward by the US, Britain, France and Germany.

In the middle again - but Mourinho says Alexander-Arnold 'not a midfielder'
- Published
It's the question that just doesn't seem to go away - can Trent Alexander-Arnold really work in midfield?
Gareth Southgate played him there for England during Euro 2024 before ending the experiment after only two group games.
Jurgen Klopp's entire Liverpool gameplan relied on his ability to step into the middle and spray passes around... albeit from a starting position of right-back.
And now Jose Mourinho has become the latest manager to dabble, picking the 27-year-old in midfield for Real Madrid's Champions League win over Inter Milan on Tuesday.
Having struggled to establish himself as Real's first-choice full-back since moving to the Bernabeu last summer, could this be the moment he finally clicks in the middle of the park?
"He has played midfield with England and Liverpool... but he is not a midfielder," insisted Mourinho after his side's edgy 2-1 win.
"He has played very well. He has interpreted what he needed to really well, tactically.
"Both him and Valverde have worked very well at this level."
So while Mourinho was "very grateful" for Alexander-Arnold's efforts in the middle, don't expect to see him play there on a regular basis.
The former Liverpool player's inclusion in midfield was largely circumstantial, with suspensions for Eduardo Camavinga, Arda Guler and Bernardo Silva leaving Mourinho short on options.
Alexander-Arnold lined up alongside Federico Valverde but had a mixed evening, creating two chances and attempting more crosses than any other Real player - but failing to win a tackle. His passing accuracy was also down at 83.3%.
He was substituted shortly after Inter pulled one back on 77 minutes, prompting whistles around the stadium - although this could well have been frustration Madrid supporters felt at their team's performance rather than at Alexander-Arnold individually.
It was the first competitive match in which Alexander-Arnold and fellow right-back Denzel Dumfries had started together. He started both for a pre-season friendly against Fiorentina, with Alexander-Arnold operating at right-back while Dumfries played further forward on the same side.
It is clear Mourinho still doesn't have a definite starting right-back, so in the same way Alexander-Arnold had to fight to start with Dani Carvajal last season, he is doing the same this season with Dumfries.
But BBC Sport understands the Portuguese has been impressed by the England international's performances, values and the versatility he brings to the squad.
Indeed, Mourinho views Alexander-Arnold as different from many traditional full-backs because of his ability to move into central areas and contribute to attacks from midfield positions.
His passing, crossing, through balls and set-piece delivery remain among the strongest parts of his game.
'He left the pitch with nothing left to give'
While Southgate's attempts to convert him into a central player at Euro 2024 ultimately ended in him being dropped from the team, Alexander-Arnold has had some success there in the past.
In June 2023, he was handed the England number 10 shirt for a qualifier in Malta, a game which the Three Lions won 4-0 - and in which Alexander-Arnold himself scored from midfield.
"I haven't played it too much, but it feels comfortable," the 24-year-old told Channel 4 when asked whether this was a position he could see his future in.
"It feels natural, I will say that. It's somewhere I can see myself playing."
Southgate continued to flirt with playing him in that position during the course of the next 12 months, before abandoning the plan after an underwhelming 1-1 draw with Denmark. Alexander-Arnold was brought off before the hour-mark.
After Tuesday's win over Inter, Mourinho admitted the position still caused some difficulties.
"He has lost some balls because it is not the same to play in this position compared to at right-back," he said.
"The intensity of physical work is quite difficult. He has a different engine. He has given 100%. He left the pitch with nothing left to give."

Reporter recounts moment George W Bush was told about 9/11 as aide whispered ‘America is under attack’
Bush had been president less than eight months when his chief of staff interrupted a school reading event to inform him of the unfolding tragedy
President George W. Bush was jogging around a Florida golf course before dawn when I first saw him on September 11, 2001.
As one of two Reuters correspondents traveling with Bush that day, I was covering what was expected to be a routine event with schoolchildren to promote his education policies. He had been president of the United States less than eight months.
Within hours, the untested Bush was confronting the worst attack on American soil since Pearl Harbor in 1941.
The tragedy unfolded as Bush visited the Emma E. Booker Elementary School in Sarasota, Florida. As the president was meeting staff and students, I was in a nearby press center set up for reporters. We watched a live television broadcast showing smoke pouring from one of the World Trade Center twin towers in New York. It had been hit by a plane in what we initially assumed was an accident. Then, as we watched, a second plane struck.
Bush was at the school, reading to children. Cameras captured the shocked look on his face as a White House aide entered the classroom and whispered to him about the second plane, saying "America is under attack."
By the end of the week, Bush would show a range of emotions as he came to grips with events that marked a turning point in his presidency and in American life — horror and anger at the attacks, grief and tears for the victims, and defiant promises to make those responsible pay.
The former president, now 80, plans to attend a ceremony on Friday to mark the 25th anniversary of the attacks at Ground Zero in New York. On Wednesday evening, he will share his reflections on the anniversary at his presidential library in Dallas, while 16 artworks he has painted reflecting the courage and sacrifice of that day will be on display.
"It became evident ... that the world had changed," Bush would later tell CBS's 60 Minutes II.
Bush spent the rest of his presidency working to prevent another such attack. The hijackings exposed security vulnerabilities, spurring increased safety measures at airports and public buildings. His administration drew fire for the harsh interrogation tactics used on some Islamic militant suspects, and his 2003 invasion of Iraq was seen by many as a costly mistake.
The former president declined an interview request from Reuters for this story.
Scrambling to protect the president
A quarter century later, the memories remain vivid.
In the immediate aftermath of the hijacked plane attacks, there was a scramble to protect the president. As Bush was whisked away to Air Force One to leave Florida, the scale of the crisis was becoming clear.
The World Trade Center towers collapsed, leading to the deaths of about 3,000 people. A third plane plowed into the Pentagon, killing 64 people on the plane and 125 in the building. A fourth plane slammed into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers fought back against the hijackers, and all 44 people on board died.
Panic gripped Washington. Plumes of smoke from the Pentagon prompted fears of car bombs. The White House was evacuated, with the Secret Service telling female staffers to take off their heels and run.
Bush spent the day flying across the country on Air Force One, first to Barksdale Air Force Base in Louisiana and then to Offutt Air Force Base in Nebraska. Later, he was to push for improved communications equipment on Air Force One after he had trouble staying in touch with the White House as he flew around the country.
In Nebraska, he entered an underground bunker to hold a teleconference briefing with top national security aides and Vice President Dick Cheney.
Eager to return to Washington, Bush arrived back at the White House late that afternoon. That night he gave an Oval Office address.
"The pictures of airplanes flying into buildings, fires burning, huge structures collapsing, have filled us with disbelief, terrible sadness, and a quiet, unyielding anger," Bush said.
Meanwhile, along with much of the White House press corps, I was still stranded in Florida, unable to fly anywhere as all air travel had been shut down. As president of the White House Correspondents' Association at the time, I helped push for our return home, and we finally took a chartered bus back to the capital.
After a 14-hour drive, our first view of Washington was the smoking gash in the Pentagon.
On September 14, I traveled with Bush to Ground Zero. The towers were still burning, the smell evident miles away. As Bush walked around the ravaged site with then-Mayor Rudy Giuliani, there were worries that some surrounding buildings had weakened to the point of collapse.
A thick layer of ash lay everywhere, on sidewalks, streets and on the shoulders of weary firefighters.
Standing on the remains of a firetruck, Bush told emergency crews that the United States was now at war with Islamic militants.
"I can hear you! I can hear you! The rest of the world hears you! And the people who knocked these buildings down will hear all of us soon!" he said through a bullhorn.
The shoes I wore that day were covered with ash and soot. When I got back home, I put them in a plastic bag and stowed them in a closet.
Twenty-five years later, there they remain. Too ruined to wear, too dear to throw away.

Sudan's healthcare system on brink of collapse after cuts, medical charity warns
- Published
Sudan's fragile health system is on the brink of collapse as global funding cuts have led to the closure of healthcare facilities across the country, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) has warned.
Dozens of organisations were unable to find alternative funding after the US - the largest donor to Sudan - closed USAID, its body for delivering foreign aid, last year, the medical charity said.
MSF urged world leaders gathering at the UN General Assembly in New York to take action.
The war that erupted in April 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, with more than 33 million people needing medical assistance.
MSF said while the US was still the largest donor to Sudan, existing grants to many USAID-funded organisations ran out in June - as European governments were also reducing international assistance.
According to the Paris-based Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), international aid fell globally by 21.3% in 2025 compared to the previous year.
- A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan 
  - Published13 November 2025
- Sudan's invisible children - born in war with no legal identity 
  - Published7 August
"War is driving Sudan's needs; funding cuts are shrinking the response," said Muhammad Ibrahim, the head of charity in Sudan.
"MSF's work in Sudan is privately funded. But when funding disappears from other health services, clinics close, patients have fewer places to go, and pressure shifts to the facilities that remain, including ours."
This has meant that patients often have to make dangerous and long trips to get treatment.
"After a longer and more expensive journey, patients often arrive in a much more serious condition, and the hospital may already be full," explained Sebastián Traficante, MSF's emergency co-ordinator in the western region of Darfur, which has experienced much of the fighting over the last three years.
Between January and April 2026, MSF saw admissions jump by 22.5% in facilities it supports in central Darfur, when compared to the same time last year.
In May alone, 45 healthcare centres in the area had stopped receiving funding, it said.
According to MSF, the closure of frontline services was putting other hospitals under severe strain - as they were losing their capacity to function and medicines were disappearing.
It gave Gedaref state's Tanedba camp, where 18,400 people who have fled their homes live, as an example. Its maternity and surgical wards have closed down after a humanitarian organisation left in June.
As a result, MSF is now running an emergency room there, but pregnant women who need surgery to deliver a baby, have to travel three hours to the nearest city.
In the Um Rakuba camp - also in Gedaref - the number of aid agencies working there has dropped from 35 in 2021, to less than 10.
According to the charity, the camp currently hosts around 17,000 people, most of whom are women and children.
"If support does not increase, more patients will face longer journeys, fewer treatment options and greater risk of arriving too late for care," MSF's UK humanitarian representative Liz Harding said.
At the same time as the health system was struggling with funding, attacks on healthcare workers were continuing, MSF said.
In 2025, Sudan saw 1,620 people killed in attacks on medical facilities - which the charity said accounted for 82% of all global deaths from attacks on healthcare worldwide.
According to the UN, more than 19.5 million people are also experiencing "crisis levels" of food insecurity and more than five million are facing "emergency levels of hunger".
The fighting shows no sign of easing - despite the expected arrival of international diplomats in the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, for consultations aimed at ending the civil war.
Reports from North Kordofan state on Tuesday say at least 11 people have been killed in a drone attack on the army-controlled town of Umm Ruwaba. According to medical sources, the projectile struck a crowded courtyard in a court complex.

Kimi Raikkonen's son Robin, 11, signs for Red Bull
- Published
Robin Raikkonen, the 11-year-old son of former Formula 1 world champion Kimi Raikkonen, has signed for Red Bull.
Nicknamed 'Ace', the youngster has impressed in karting championships and will join Red Bull's driver development programme in 2027.
The programme has produced F1 drivers such as Sebastian Vettel and Max Verstappen - both four-time champions.
Robin's father, nicknamed 'Iceman', was the most recent Ferrari driver to become world champion, claiming his sole title in 2007.
The Finn claimed 21 wins and 103 podiums from 349 F1 starts before retiring in 2021. He also competed in the World Rally Championship and Nascar.
"We are all thrilled and excited that Robin has been chosen to further his racing path as a member of the Red Bull junior team," said 46-year-old Kimi.
"They offer a compelling and comprehensive programme to develop and nurture Robin's progress over the coming years and provide him with all the experience required to develop his natural talent."
Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies said Robin has "already demonstrated exceptional ability in karting".
"His speed, racecraft and natural talent have established him as one of the most promising young drivers in his age group," Mekies added.
"At the same time, he impresses with his maturity, his calm approach and his clear focus on driving.
"Our goal is to develop him step by step, without placing any unnecessary pressure on his shoulders.
"The path through motorsport is a long one and we will give him the time, support and resources he needs to maximise his potential."
Robin follows in the footsteps of Ella Hakkinen, the daughter of Finland's double world champion Mika Hakkinen, who joined McLaren's driver development programme last year.

Exclusive: WWE legend Ric Flair claims ‘influencer talent agency’ duped him into handing over his digital life: lawsuit
‘The Nature Boy is not finished,’ according to court filings obtained by The Independent. ‘The case has just begun.’
Legendary pro wrestler Ric “Nature Boy” Flair is suing a digital talent agency he claims duped him into signing away the rights to his own image and likeness while promising him a six-figure monthly revenue stream that allegedly never materialized.
The 77-year-old Flair, whose real name is Richard Morgan Fliehr, spent four decades “building something… through his body, his blood, his pain, his persona, his craft, and his commitment to excellence at a level that only sixteen world championships can describe,” according to a $10 million lawsuit obtained by The Independent.
But, Flair’s complaint says, FAM Networks, a “cutting-edge talent-first management agency and media company representing some of the most unique and impactful influencers around the world,” pounced on an opportunity to rook the elderly performer out of what was rightfully his.
“What FAM did was simple: it waited until he needed help managing the digital legacy of everything he had built, presented him with a document he was not equipped to understand, told him he had lawyers when he did not, gave him fourteen minutes to read it, and walked away with a perpetual license to his identity,” the complaint contends, adding that the pending legal action is only “the beginning.”
“The Nature Boy is not finished,” the complaint states. “The case has just begun.”
Reached by phone at his home in Hillsborough County, Florida, Fliehr, who last wrestled in 2022, told The Independent that he “wants to bury” the people at FAM Networks, and said he lost out on at least $250,000 in revenues so far.
Messages sent to five different departments at FAM Networks were all returned as undeliverable. A contact form on the company’s website was inoperable on Tuesday; it does not have a publicly listed phone number.
As Ric Flair, Richard Fliehr “electrified arenas across the world,” his complaint explains, calling him “one of the most celebrated, decorated, and recognizable professional athletes in the history of his sport.”
His career transcended the ring and became an indelible part of American pop culture, it goes on.
“A name, a likeness, and an identity that carries commercial value precisely because generations of fans have given it meaning through their devotion,” the complaint states. “That identity – the product of a lifetime of work, sacrifice, and sacrifice again – is what FAM Networks, LLC came for.”
FAM, which maintains offices in New York City and Los Angeles, purportedly defrauded Fliehr by quietly taking control of his social media accounts, recategorizing them to make recovery near-impossible, and milked his persona for profits he never saw.
At 5:57 PM on December 5, 2025, Fliehr opened an email from FAM, which came with a contract attached, according to the complaint, which was filed September 5 in Manhattan Supreme Court.
“At 6:11 PM – fourteen minutes later – he signed it,” the complaint continues. “In those fourteen minutes, without the benefit of legal counsel, without a single attorney reviewing a single word on his behalf, and in direct contradiction of a contractual recital FAM itself drafted declaring that the agreement had been negotiated with counsel, Mr. Fliehr surrendered an irrevocable, perpetual, sublicensable license over his name, image, likeness, voice, accounts, and commercial identity – throughout the universe, without restriction, in all languages, formats, and media now known or later developed.”
FAM “knew he had no lawyer,” the complaint alleges. “FAM wrote the clause saying he did anyway.” (Fliehr has trouble discerning AI-generated content from reality, and often gets confused about things he sees online, according to his daughter Charlotte.)
The company, which promotes online influencers and pairs them up with corporate deals, offered Fliehr a full slate of speaking engagements and appearances with 90 percent of the proceeds going to him, the complaint states. It says FAM pledged 50 percent to Fliehr for “collaborative projects,” and 10 percent for “passive content.” FAM would also restore Fliehr’s “hacked, demonetized” Facebook page, which it claimed would throw off six figures on a monthly basis.
“These were not aspirations,” the complaint argues. “They were contractual obligations.”
However, it alleges, “FAM delivered none of them. It sourced not one speaking engagement. Not one in-person appearance. Not one personal project at the ninety percent royalty tier. It reposted existing content.”
At the same time, FAM enriched itself by as much as $20,000 a month by monetizing Fliehr’s Facebook page, while paying him “next to nothing,” according to the complaint.
It then transferred Fliehr's Facebook page to itself, effectively locking Fliehr’s existing team out and blowing a potential advertising deal they already had in the works, the complaint states. By taking “operational control” of Fliehr’s digital life, FAM was allegedly able to “entrench itself in a position from which it could demand a ransom for his own property's return.”
When Fliehr signed the contract with FAM, the company was already embroiled in an almost identical case involving ufologist Steven Greer, according to the complaint. Yet, FAM “disclosed none of this to Mr. Fliehr before he signed,” because, the complaint argues, “[d]isclosure would have ended the transaction.”
The complaint contends that the contract that FAM convinced Fliehr to sign and later “weaponize[d],” should be declared null and void. It describes the agreement as “not a contract,” but, rather, “a trap,” giving FAM the right to act in Fliehr’s name without his involvement and erecting practically insurmountable barriers preventing him from extracting himself from the deal.
“New York courts of equity do not enforce traps, and they do not enforce perpetual licenses extracted from elderly men in fourteen minutes without counsel on the basis of false recitals and undisclosed litigation,” states the complaint.
Last year, Fliehr sued a cannabis company he was involved in promoting, along with iconic prizefighter Mike Tyson, for $50 million, alleging fraud, self-dealing, and civil RICO conspiracy.
Fliehr is now asking a judge to rescind the agreement with FAM, to order control of his Facebook page returned to him, a declaratory judgment stating that FAM has no right to his name, image, or likeness, and for a “complete accounting of revenues generated in his name.”
He is also demanding compensatory damages, among other things, of at least $5 million for breach of contract; compensatory and punitive damages of at least $5 million for fraudulent inducement; compensatory damages to be determined at trial for violations of New York Civil Rights Law; compensatory and punitive damages for tortious interference with prospective economic advantage, also to be determined at trial; and disgorgement of all amounts by which FAM “has been unjustly enriched at [Fliehr’s] expense,” plus attorneys' fees and court costs.
A trial date has not yet been set.

If you opt for an Android phone over an iPhone, there are certain features you get as standard as part of Android. Then there are other features specific to certain manufacturers, as each Android phone maker puts its own spin on the software.
Pixel phones, for example, get the Now Playing widget on the home screen and lock screen that works like an instant Shazam. It'll tell you the name of the song playing in your environment before you've even searched for it.
With Samsung phones, one of the best perks isn't as widely known about or used as it should be. It's called the Edge Panel, and it works like a customizable shortcut bar that gives you speedy access to the other parts of your phone.
If you own a Galaxy device and have never come across the Edge Panel, or you used it once but have since forgotten about it, here's what it's capable of now—and how you can make the most of it to optimize your mobile experience.
How the Edge Panel Works
You can think of the Edge Panel as being a little bit like the Start menu on Windows, or the dock on macOS. It provides something that Android doesn't have by default, which is a user-configurable launcher for collecting your favorite apps and feature shortcuts.
When it's enabled, the Edge Panel appears as a faint line along the side of the screen, and you can swipe across it to open the pane. If you don't see it, head to Settings and choose Display > Edge Panels to turn it on (via the toggle switch) or customize what the panels show (by tapping the menu entry).
There are actually seven different types of panel to choose from, as you'll see when you start to customize the feature: Apps, People, Tasks, Weather, Tools, Clipboard, and Reminder. You can have just one of them active, or all seven, or something in between (once you've got the Edge Panel up, swipe across it to switch between the different types).
The names of these panels give you some idea of what they can do. You can use the Apps panel to access the apps you use the most, without having to hunt for them in the main app drawer or having them clutter up your home screen. You can also jump to your most important people on the Contacts panel in the same way.
The Clipboard panel gives you quick access to the phone clipboard, while Tasks features shortcuts such as taking screenshots, adding new calendar events, adding alarms, and taking a screenshot. Having these shortcuts on the Edge Panel means you don't have to dig through menus or remember key combinations for the same functions.
Tools is actually just a single tool: a compass that tells you your current location and points you north, south, east, or west. Weather is pretty self-explanatory, while Reminder syncs information from the Reminder app that comes preinstalled on Galaxy devices.
Customize the Edge Panel
The Edge Panel works fine in its default state, but to make the most of it you really need to set it up to suit you and the way you use your phone. From the main Settings menu, choose Display, then tap Edge Panels.
First, select Panels to pick which panes are shown. Put a check next to the panes you want to have available. If you tap the three dots (top right) then Reorder, you're able to choose the order they appear in as well—place the panes you use most often furthest to the left, as they'll be available in fewer swipes.
You can also tap the three dots then Hide on Lock screen if you don't want the Edge Panel to appear before you've unlocked your phone. Bear in mind that you might not want some information—such as the contents of the clipboard or your reminders—being available to anyone who picks up your handset.
With Apps, People, and Tasks, you can customize what's included. Just tap the Edit button underneath the pane. In each case, there are more available options than there are slots on the Edge Panel, so you need to prioritize accordingly.
Back on the Edge Panels screen, there are a couple of other options worth knowing about. If you pick Handle, you can set the properties of the little onscreen strip that Edge Panel is activated through. Pick the size and transparency level of the handle, its color, and which side of the screen it appears on.
Finally, there's the Show in landscape mode toggle switch; disable this if you don't want to see the Edge panel when you're using your phone in its landscape orientation. This mode is mainly used for watching videos and playing games, in which case the Edge Panel and its handle might distract you.
